title: 2027: Tinubu, Atiku, Obi in US lobbying controversies
description:
ADC demands probe of $4.5m contract, Atiku seeks release of President’s unedited interview  • Atiku’s US lobbyist disputes Congress endorsement of Obi, NDC candidate denies seeking foreign backing 

By Beifoh Osewele
A widening row over American lobbying activities has embroiled President Bola Tinub
content:
ADC demands probe of $4.5m contract, Atiku seeks release of President’s unedited interview  • Atiku’s US lobbyist disputes Congress endorsement of Obi, NDC candidate denies seeking foreign backing 

By Beifoh Osewele

A widening row over American lobbying activities has embroiled President Bola Tinubu and opposition presidential candidates, Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, in separate political disputes, raising questions over foreign influence, the use of public funds and claims of international endorsement ahead of the 2027 general elections.

While the African Democratic Congress (ADC) has demanded an investigation into a $4.5 million lobbying arrangement involving the Federal Government, Atiku has challenged Tinubu to release the unedited recording of his interview with American political consultant Diana London and disclose the terms of the contract.

Obi, on his part, has dismissed claims that he sought or secured the endorsement of the United States Congress during his visit to Washington, following a public challenge by an American lobbying firm engaged by Atiku.

The former Anambra State governor and presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has insisted that his meetings with American lawmakers and other influential figures were aimed at strengthening Nigeria’s democratic institutions, addressing security challenges and promoting national development rather than soliciting foreign political backing.

“As I expressly noted in my remarks, my visit to the United States was not intended to secure an endorsement, and I did not characterise my meetings as endorsements of my political aspirations by the US Congress or any of its members,” Obi declared yesterday.

His clarification followed a statement by Karl Von Batten, principal of Washington-based Von Batten-Montague-York, who disputed reports suggesting that Obi’s engagements amounted to an official congressional endorsement.

Von Batten, whose firm is engaged by Atiku, maintained that the event attended by Obi was a private gathering involving individual American political figures and not an official meeting of Congress.

“Congress did not meet with or endorse Mr Obi. The event he attended was private, and no one in the video is a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee or its Subcommittee on Africa,” he said.

The separate disputes have placed the international engagements of Nigeria’s major political actors under scrutiny, particularly the distinction between paid lobbying, private meetings with foreign lawmakers and official institutional endorsements.

At the centre of the controversy involving Tinubu is an agreement signed in December 2025 between Washington-based DCI Group and Aster Legal, a Nigerian law firm engaged in connection with the Federal Government’s efforts to communicate its security policies to American officials.

Documents filed under the United States Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) indicated that the agreement provided for a monthly retainer of $750,000, amounting to $4.5 million for an initial six-month period, with a provision for renewal that could raise the contract’s total value to $9 million.

The arrangement was intended to communicate Nigeria’s efforts to protect Christian communities, address security concerns and sustain American support for counterterrorism operations.

The controversy intensified after London, whose company was linked to the lobbying engagement, recorded an interview with Tinubu at the Presidential Villa, Abuja, and subsequently deleted social media posts praising security cooperation between Nigeria and the United States.

Photographs of the engagement showed Tinubu seated with the American consultant, with Chief of Staff Femi Gbajabiamila also present.

The interview was publicly confirmed by Imran Muhammad, Senior Special Assistant on New Media to APC National Chairman Nentawe Yilwatda, who announced that the recorded conversation would be released soon.

“President Tinubu has held an exclusive interview with Diana London, a prominent American media personality. The interview is anticipated to be released soon,” Muhammad wrote in a social media post.

However, the publicity surrounding the interview has not resolved questions about the lobbying agreement, the source of its funding or whether London’s engagement with the President formed part of the services covered by the contract.

As of last night, no verified statement from the Presidency had been established directly addressing the demands by Atiku and the ADC for disclosure of the contract, relevant payments and the circumstances surrounding the interview.

In a statement issued by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, the ADC Presidential Campaign Council questioned the government’s priorities, arguing that Nigerians deserved an explanation of the expenditure at a time of widespread economic hardship.

“At a time Nigerians are groaning under hunger, insecurity, failing public institutions, unpaid salaries and an unbearable cost of living, the reported expenditure of $4.5 million — running into billions of naira — on foreign image management raises serious questions about the priorities of the Tinubu administration.”

The opposition party demanded disclosure of the source of the funds, the officials who authorised the transaction, the contractual obligations involved and the services rendered.

It also sought clarification of the role played by the Office of the National Security Adviser in facilitating the arrangement.

“This is not merely a public relations issue. It is a matter of accountability, transparency and responsible governance,” the statement declared.

The ADC called on the National Assembly, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) and the Auditor-General of the Federation to investigate the expenditure and make their findings public.

The party argued that foreign lobbying could not replace effective governance or address the economic and security challenges confronting Nigerians.

“You cannot polish failure. You cannot lobby away hunger. And you cannot buy credibility abroad when you have lost the trust of your own people at home,” the council said.

Atiku, in a separate statement issued through his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, also challenged Tinubu to explain the circumstances surrounding the interview and submit himself to similar questioning by Nigerian journalists.

He questioned whether London’s engagement with the President was an independent journalistic exercise or part of a government-sponsored communications arrangement.

The former Vice-President demanded publication of the lobbying agreement, disclosure of relevant invoices and payments, identification of those who authorised the expenditure and release of the complete, unedited recording of the interview.

He argued that Nigerians deserved answers from the President on the rising cost of food, transportation, wages and other economic difficulties rather than what he described as a favourable interview conducted by a foreign consultant.

“Who authorised the $4.5 million payment, and from which public account did it come? At a time when Nigerians are told to endure the pain of fuel subsidy removal, they deserve to know whether the money saved is being spent on foreign publicity,” he said.

Atiku also questioned the presence of a large screen positioned within Tinubu’s line of sight during the recording, suggesting that it might have been used to display prepared prompts.

He challenged the Presidency to release the full recording, including what appeared on the screen, to establish whether the President answered questions spontaneously.

The former VP maintained that Nigerian journalists were capable of conducting rigorous interviews with the President, naming Rufai Oseni, Ojy Okpe, Seun Okinbaloye and Reuben Abati among those who could question him on pressing national issues.

“Tinubu cannot ask families to suffer in silence while millions of dollars are committed to polishing his image. Publish the contract. Show the invoices. Release the unedited interview. Then face Nigerian journalists and answer the people,” Atiku declared.

The lobbying arrangement followed diplomatic tensions arising from allegations of religious persecution in Nigeria and the decision by United States President Donald Trump in November 2025 to designate the country as one of particular concern.

The Tinubu administration rejected suggestions that it was deliberately tolerating attacks on Christians, maintaining that terrorism, banditry and communal violence affected Nigerians across religious and ethnic divides.

The Federal Government subsequently intensified diplomatic engagements aimed at explaining its security policies and strengthening cooperation with Washington.

Against this background, Aster Legal engaged DCI Group under an agreement signed on December 17, 2025, by the Nigerian firm’s Managing Partner, Oyetunji Olalekan Teslim, and DCI Group Managing Member, Justin Peterson.

Further disclosures linked London Global Strategies, a company headed by Diana London, to payments made by DCI Group in connection with the Nigerian engagement.

According to records reported by TheCable, DCI Group disclosed payments of $75,000 and $375,000 to London Global Strategies on December 23, 2025, bringing the total to $450,000.

Although the filings establish a financial relationship between DCI Group and London’s company, they do not establish that the entire $4.5 million retainer was paid to London personally or that her interview with Tinubu was commissioned for that amount.

The distinction is central to the dispute as opposition politicians demand greater transparency over the contract and the nature of the presidential engagement.

In social media posts subsequently deleted, London praised cooperation between Nigeria and the United States, particularly in the area of security.

“The U.S-Nigeria security partnership is delivering results. Peace Through Strength,” she wrote.

She also described Nigeria as an important American ally in Africa and expressed optimism about opportunities for stronger economic and trade relations between the two countries.

The deletion of the posts intensified questions about the engagement, although no verified explanation had been established for their removal.

Meanwhile, the dispute surrounding Obi’s Washington visit also gathered momentum following Von Batten’s challenge to reports suggesting that the NDC candidate had secured the endorsement of the United States Congress.

Von Batten acknowledged that two serving American lawmakers, Marlin Stutzman and Beth Van Duyne, attended the gathering but stressed that neither belonged to the House Foreign Affairs Committee, which oversees aspects of American foreign policy.

“I recognise Congressman Stutzman and Congresswoman Van Duyne, but neither serves on the House Foreign Affairs Committee. They serve on other committees responsible for the budget and small businesses.”

He also maintained that no official of the United States Department of State’s Bureau of African Affairs appeared in the video circulated after Obi’s engagement.

Von Batten said his intervention was not intended to diminish the significance of Obi’s visit but to correct reports suggesting that the American legislature had officially received or endorsed the Nigerian presidential candidate.

“I am not trying to diminish the significance of Mr Obi’s visit, merely to set the record straight since my firm was mentioned,” he said.

The clarification followed Obi’s announcement on Tuesday that he had arrived in Washington on Monday, November 16, for meetings with congressional leaders and other influential American figures.

The former Anambra State governor identified Stutzman, Van Duyne, former Congressman Todd Tiahrt, Suzanne Bock Grisham and retired United States Army Colonel Albert V. Short among those he engaged.

He said the discussions focused on Nigeria’s development, security challenges, citizens’ welfare and the need to strengthen democratic institutions ahead of the 2027 elections.

Obi also disclosed that he granted an interview to American television commentator Glenn Beck, during which they discussed leadership, accountability and the management of Nigeria’s resources.

Responding to the controversy, Obi maintained that the primary purpose of his visit was to engage American political figures on matters affecting Nigeria rather than seek their endorsement of his presidential ambition.

“The primary purpose of the visit was to engage with congressional leaders and other influential American stakeholders, exchange perspectives, and discuss matters related to Nigeria’s development, the welfare of our citizens and, most importantly, the consolidation of our democracy.”

Obi stressed that particular attention was given to the need for credible elections, accountability and the protection of Nigeria’s democratic institutions.

“I am especially concerned with strengthening democratic institutions, advancing accountability, and ensuring that Nigeria’s electoral process produces elections that are free, fair, transparent and credible. These matters should concern every Nigerian who is committed to our country’s future.”

Obi maintained that constructive international engagements were important to strengthening Nigeria’s democracy and urged political leaders to pursue similar discussions with foreign stakeholders.

He cautioned against sensational interpretations of his visit, insisting that his mission was not to obtain foreign political backing.

“Nigeria’s democratic future is far too consequential to be distorted by sensational headlines or inaccurate interpretations. My mission centred on Nigeria, its people and the future of our democracy—not on endorsing any individual,” he said.

His media office also issued a clarification signed by Indris Zekeri Jnr., stressing that the former governor had neither sought nor claimed the endorsement of the United States Congress or the American government.

The office acknowledged that some American political figures made favourable comments about Obi’s leadership record but maintained that such remarks should not be interpreted as an official endorsement.

It also stressed the distinction between meeting individual members of Congress and being formally received or endorsed by Congress as an institution.

The post 2027: Tinubu, Atiku, Obi in US lobbying controversies appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: 202 days after China deal, NNPC under pressure to revive refineries
description:
•Marketers warn Iran-US tensions could trigger fresh fuel supply crisis
202 days after signing a strategic partnership agreement with two Chinese companies, the Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited is under pressure to fast-track the rehabilitation of the Port Harcourt and Warri refine
content:
•Marketers warn Iran-US tensions could trigger fresh fuel supply crisis

202 days after signing a strategic partnership agreement with two Chinese companies, the Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited is under pressure to fast-track the rehabilitation of the Port Harcourt and Warri refineries.

This comes as the Petroleum Products Retail Outlets Owners Association of Nigeria (PETROAN) warned that escalating tensions between Iran and the United States could disrupt global petroleum supplies.

The association argued that any prolonged disruption around the Strait of Hormuz could trigger fresh shocks to crude oil supply, petroleum product availability, shipping costs and international energy prices, leaving Nigeria vulnerable because of its continued dependence on imported refined products.

National Public Relations Officer of PETROAN, Mr. Joseph Obele, who raised the concern in a statement yesterday, said the unfolding geopolitical tensions should serve as a wake-up call for NNPC Limited to move beyond agreements and technical assessments and translate its refinery revival plans into concrete action.

Obele noted that NNPC Limited signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on April 30, 2026, with Sanjiang Chemical Company Limited and Xinganchen (Fuzhou) Industrial Park Operation and Management Co. Ltd. for a proposed technical equity partnership covering the completion, operation, maintenance and expansion of the Port Harcourt and Warri refineries.

However, with exactly 202 days gone since the agreement was signed, he said Nigerians were yet to see the concrete implementation measures needed to bring the facilities back to productive operations.

Although plant assessments had reportedly been conducted on both refineries, the PETROAN spokesman insisted that such exercises must translate into clearly defined implementation timelines, investment commitments and commencement of rehabilitation and upgrade works.

“An MoU must not remain a ceremonial document. It must translate into measurable action, investment, infrastructure development and sustainable petroleum production,” he said.

He called on NNPC to make public the implementation status of the Chinese partnership, including the investment commitments, technical responsibilities, rehabilitation roadmap and expected delivery dates.

Obele also demanded the release of details of the plant assessment reports for both refineries, alongside clear performance targets and accountability mechanisms to ensure that the proposed partnership delivers on its objectives.

The PETROAN spokesman warned that Nigeria’s continued dependence on external refining capacity was a major vulnerability, particularly at a time when geopolitical tensions threaten the stability of international energy supply chains.

He said the consequences of a prolonged disruption in the Middle East would extend beyond the petroleum industry to transportation, food prices, manufacturing, businesses and household incomes.

Beyond the national energy security implications, Obele, an indigene of Ogoni, said the revival of the Port Harcourt Refinery carried significant economic and social implications for its host communities.

He lamented that thousands of Ogoni indigenes and other residents whose livelihoods depend directly or indirectly on the refinery had suffered economic hardship following its prolonged inactivity.

According to him, the shutdown has weakened employment opportunities, commercial activities and other livelihood sources, leaving families and businesses struggling.

He argued that restoring the refinery to productive operations would help revive local businesses, create jobs and rebuild economic confidence among host communities.

Obele urged NNPC to give special consideration to the social and economic importance of restarting the Port Harcourt facility as part of efforts to strengthen confidence between the oil industry and communities that have hosted petroleum operations for decades.

He further called for stronger strategic petroleum product reserves and improved domestic supply preparedness to cushion the country against possible international market disruptions.

“NNPC must recognise that refinery development is not merely a commercial undertaking; it is a critical component of Nigeria’s national energy security,” he said.

He maintained that Nigeria could no longer afford to remain heavily exposed to external refining capacity when its own refineries were yet to operate at their expected potential.

“ Nigeria has the crude oil. Nigeria has the market. What Nigerians urgently need is functional domestic refining capacity. The time for implementation is now. Another international petroleum crisis should not find Nigeria unprepared,” he added.

title: 655 tribunal registrars swear oath of secrecy ahead of 2027 election cases
description:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri



With just 58 days to the general elections, the Court of Appeal on November 16 administered the oath of secrecy to 655 clerks and Deputy Chief Registrars selected to serve on the various election tribunals.



The oath was administered under the supervision of the President
content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri

With just 58 days to the general elections, the Court of Appeal on November 16 administered the oath of secrecy to 655 clerks and Deputy Chief Registrars selected to serve on the various election tribunals.


The oath was administered under the supervision of the President of the Court of Appeal (PCA), Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem.


It specifically invoked the provisions of Section 1(1) of the Official Secrets Act, which concerns the protection of official information. Under the Act, a person commits an offence if they transmit classified matter to a person to whom they are not authorised, on behalf of the Government, to transmit it.


The Act also provides that a person is guilty of an offence if they obtain, reproduce, or retain classified matter which they are not authorised, on behalf of the Government, to obtain, reproduce, or retain, as the case may be. The officials were warned that the oath would remain binding even after their assignments at the tribunal ended, with the PCA vowing to hand over defaulters to security agencies for prosecution.


“Is there anyone among you who did not read the oath form, or who signed it and now wants to withdraw from the assignment?” Justice Dongban-Mensem asked, as the weight of the oath dawned on the officials.


“I am asking because you have just signed evidence against yourselves. Anyone we find doing what we have asked you not to do will be handed over to the Police for prosecution.


“I am taking all the forms you signed to the secret registry of my office, and I will lock them in my safe. In case some of you are not aware, I began my tenure as President of this Court by handing some people over for prosecution, and they were duly prosecuted.
“It is because people are not made to face the consequences of their actions that we have so many problems in this country. But at the Court of Appeal, we give you every opportunity to abide by your oath, and when you don’t, we prosecute.
“Some of you may be approached and asked to give details of the tribunal members’ discussions. You will start eavesdropping to get information to pass on to them. “But when you eavesdrop, you can never get the full details. That is how, before you know it, false judgments start flying around. It often comes from the registry.
“We are watching you, and many other people will be watching you too. Be very careful, be committed to the nation, and let’s get it right,” the PCA warned.
Election Petition Tribunals are established to hear and determine petitions arising from the conduct of elections into political offices.
Section 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, empowers the President of the Court of Appeal to constitute an Election Petition Tribunal in each State of the Federation and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja.
Section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026 further provides that these Tribunals shall be constituted not later than 30 days before the election, and shall open their registries for business seven days before the election.
The registry is a very important organ of an election petition tribunal, and its administrative duties include receiving petitions and other court processes for filing, serving court processes on parties in a timely manner, issuing hearing notices, preparing court proceedings and orders, keeping the tribunal’s documents in safe custody, and compiling records, among various other duties and responsibilities.
The effectiveness, quality, efficiency, transparency and speed of the registry have a direct impact on the performance and justice delivery of the election tribunal.
According to Section 285(5) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, a candidate aggrieved by the outcome of an election must file a petition at the registry of the appropriate tribunal or court within 21 days of the declaration of results by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).
While the tribunal is statutorily mandated to deliver its judgment within 180 days from the date the petition was filed, any appeal arising from the tribunal’s or the Court of Appeal’s judgment must be filed and disposed of within 60 days from the date of the lower court’s decision.
Addressing the 655 tribunal officials at the commencement of a two-day capacity-building workshop that followed their oath-taking session, Justice Dongban-Mensem noted that modern registry practices demand more than manual filing and routine administrative work.
She said they demand a new mindset and the adoption of electronic filing and case management systems that allow for easy tracking and retrieval of cases.
“They demand proper documentation, accurate and systematic archiving. They demand timely service of processes and effective scheduling that respects the strict timelines prescribed by law for election petitions. They demand confidentiality, integrity and professionalism.”
She said the workshop, themed: “Modern Registry Practices for Effective Election Petition Tribunal Administration,” was designed as a platform to equip the participants with hands-on knowledge of the use of technology in case management, best practices in records keeping, and the ethical standards expected of tribunal staff.
Emphasising that the integrity of the judiciary was on the line, the PCA cautioned the court’s registry staff against exploiting their election tribunal assignments for financial gain.
“It is part of your obligation to discharge your duties with utmost good faith and not be carried away by little advances.
“Your integrity and that of the Tribunal and its members are in the public searchlight. You must therefore ensure that you are not used as tools to derail the process.
“Ensure that you live above board so that you do not bring the Judiciary into disrepute. Do not see it as an opportunity to enrich yourselves, but rather go there to build your name and your future, as it is said that a good name is better than silver and gold.
“The Court will not hesitate to deal with anyone found wanting in this regard,” she added.
For his part, the Chief Registrar of the Court of Appeal, Mr. Umar Bangari, said the tribunal officials must be conscious of the fact that “the spotlight of the entire nation will turn on the Judiciary” after the elections.
He maintained that the success, efficiency, and credibility of every Tribunal rests heavily on the shoulders of the registrars and backroom staff.
“You should be aware that you are the custodians of all the processes filed at the Tribunal, the managers of strict statutory timelines, and the primary administrative interface between parties on one hand, and the Bench on the other.
“Accordingly, you are hereby placed on strict notice against engaging in any form of misconduct, including but not limited to collusion, conspiracy, or conniving with any party to manipulate court processes, alter records, or confer an unfair advantage upon one party to the detriment of another.
“You must also avoid file tampering and leaking confidential internal communications, draft rulings, panel deliberations, or privileged case information to unauthorised persons, among so many other acts of misconduct.
“We shall entertain zero tolerance towards any breach of neutrality or ethical standards. Any secretary or staff member found to be conniving with any party or counsel to subvert the course of justice will face severe consequences,” Bangari added.
Noting that election adjudication is sui generis and strictly bound by constitutional and statutory timeframes, the Court of Appeal Registrar implored the participants to adhere strictly to timelines.
“As we all know, a single administrative lapse, delayed endorsement, or misplaced process can occasion a damaging miscarriage of justice. You must treat every filing, service of processes, and transmission of records with utmost urgency and precision.
“Avoid shady practices, such as giving litigants or counsel advance copies of processes. You should also avoid backdating processes in order to bring them within the prescribed time for filing.
“Treat all Panel members of the Tribunal, as well as counsel and litigants, with courtesy, impartiality and professionalism. You are the first point of contact for litigants and counsel.
“You manage the registries, receive and process filings, maintain accurate records, issue hearing notices, and ensure that the strict statutory timelines governing election petitions are never compromised,” he added.
The Deputy Chief Registrar of the Court in charge of the election petition tribunals, Mrs. Maitumbi Altine, disclosed that a total of 223 of the participants have previously served in tribunals, while 432 of them are first-timers.
She said it was the first time in the annals of the court that such training had been organised for staff members who will serve the various election tribunals.
With the earlier inauguration of 375 judges who will serve on various tribunals across the country, the judiciary has clearly sent a loud message that it is ready for the aftermath of the 2027 general elections.

title: Soldiers arrest bandits’ ammunition supplier, recover 300 rounds hidden in beans
description:
From Molly Kilete, Abuja
Troops of the Nigerian Army have arrested a suspected ammunition supplier to bandits and recovered 300 rounds of 7.62 x 39mm ammunition concealed in a sack of beans in Kogi State.
The suspect, identified as 47-year-old Umaru Muhammad of Ashe Village, was intercepted at about
content:
From Molly Kilete, Abuja

Troops of the Nigerian Army have arrested a suspected ammunition supplier to bandits and recovered 300 rounds of 7.62 x 39mm ammunition concealed in a sack of beans in Kogi State.

The suspect, identified as 47-year-old Umaru Muhammad of Ashe Village, was intercepted at about 9:30 p.m. on Tuesday, November 17, by troops of the Atsawa Blocking Force, working in collaboration with local vigilantes, following intelligence on the movement of ammunition allegedly destined for criminal networks.

The Army said preliminary interrogation linked the consignment to two individuals identified as Gimba and Dare, residents of Gori Village along the River Niger corridor in Lokoja, who were described as local vigilantes.

The development, according to the military, has raised concerns over the possible infiltration and exploitation of community security structures by criminal ammunition supply networks.

In a statement, the Army said the suspect allegedly concealed the ammunition in a sack of beans in an attempt to disguise the consignment as legitimate commercial goods and evade security checks.

It said a thorough search of the suspect exposed the concealed ammunition, while other items recovered included a Bajaj motorcycle, a mobile telephone and N30,500 in cash.

The Army said Muhammad remained in military custody as investigations continued to unravel the suspected supply network and identify other persons involved in the transaction.

It described the arrest as part of ongoing operations to dismantle the supply chains providing arms, ammunition and other logistics to bandits, terrorists and kidnapping gangs across the country.

“The successful interception underscores the Nigerian Army’s sustained determination to dismantle criminal supply chains and deny terrorists and bandits access to critical resources required to perpetrate violence against innocent citizens,” the statement said.

The military added that troops would intensify intelligence-driven operations and strengthen collaboration with local security stakeholders to identify and dismantle criminal support networks before they could facilitate attacks on vulnerable communities.

It urged residents to promptly report suspicious movements, particularly the transportation of concealed weapons, ammunition and other prohibited items, to security agencies.

The Army reaffirmed its commitment to disrupting the activities of criminal groups and sustaining security operations aimed at restoring peace in affected communities.

title: FG moves against illegal arms,  destroys 18,000 firearms
description:
•Ribadu raises alarm over possible return of seized guns to criminals
The Federal Government has recovered 22,377 illicit small arms and light weapons across the country, destroying more than 18,000 of them in a renewed effort to curb the proliferation of firearms fuelling terrorism, banditry, kidna
content:
•Ribadu raises alarm over possible return of seized guns to criminals

The Federal Government has recovered 22,377 illicit small arms and light weapons across the country, destroying more than 18,000 of them in a renewed effort to curb the proliferation of firearms fuelling terrorism, banditry, kidnapping and other violent crimes.

Director-General of the National Centre for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons (NCCSALW), Johnson Kokumo, disclosed this in Abuja on Wednesday during the public destruction of another batch of about 1,000 illicitly acquired, decommissioned and unserviceable firearms.

Kokumo said the Nigeria Police Force accounted for the largest share of the recovered weapons, with 11,907 firearms seized during security operations across the country.

He described the destruction exercise as a practical and irreversible contribution to national security, noting that permanently removing illicit weapons from circulation would weaken the operational capacity of terrorists, bandits, kidnappers and other armed groups.

“Every weapon that goes into the furnace today is a weapon that can never again be used to threaten a community, terrorise innocent citizens or facilitate criminal and terrorist activities,” he said.

Kokumo commended the Armed Forces of Nigeria, Department of State Services, Nigeria Customs Service and other security and intelligence agencies for their collaboration in recovering and surrendering illicit firearms for destruction.

He disclosed that the centre was strengthening cooperation with international partners to identify and disrupt external supply channels and trafficking routes through which illegal weapons enter the country.

The NCCSALW boss reaffirmed the centre’s commitment to sustained arms recovery, effective stockpile management and the destruction of illicit firearms as part of efforts to strengthen national security.

Speaking at the event, the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu, warned that the proliferation of illicit firearms remained a major factor sustaining terrorism, insurgency, banditry, kidnapping and communal violence across the country.

Ribadu, represented by the National Coordinator of the National Counter-Terrorism Centre (NCTC), Major General Adamu Laka, said the widespread availability of illegal weapons continued to strengthen criminal networks, prolong violent conflicts and undermine security operations.

He cautioned that firearms recovered from criminal groups could find their way back into circulation if they were not properly documented, secured and eventually destroyed.

“Terrorism, insurgency, banditry, kidnapping and communal conflicts are all sustained by the availability of illegal weapons.

“Every weapon recovered by our security agencies and eventually destroyed represents a threat permanently neutralised,” he said.

The NSA stressed that recovering firearms without ensuring their permanent disposal could undermine the gains recorded by security agencies in the fight against armed criminality.

“However, recovery alone is not enough. Weapons that are seized but poorly treated, stored or accounted for risk re-entering circulation.

“Public destruction, as we witnessed today, closes that loop decisively and ensures that these weapons can never again threaten our citizens,” Ribadu said.

He explained that the Federal Government, under President Bola Tinubu, was implementing a comprehensive security strategy anchored on intelligence-led operations, inter-agency collaboration, disruption of criminal and terrorist financing networks and engagement with international partners.

Ribadu said the destruction of recovered firearms complemented ongoing military and security operations by denying terrorists, insurgents and other criminal elements access to weapons.

He also underscored the importance of international cooperation in tackling illicit arms trafficking, commending the NCCSALW for strengthening collaboration with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to identify external sources of illegal weapons and their financing networks.

The NSA urged Nigerians to support security agencies with timely and credible intelligence on the illegal possession, manufacture and movement of firearms, stressing that tackling insecurity required the collective involvement of communities, traditional and religious institutions and ordinary citizens.

“Security is not the responsibility of government and its agencies alone. It requires a whole-of-society approach involving communities, traditional and religious institutions and ordinary citizens,” he said.

He particularly appealed to traditional and religious leaders to promote peace, tolerance and peaceful coexistence while addressing conditions that expose young people to recruitment by armed groups.

title: AI, fake voter records raise new risks for 2027 elections
description:
…Why media must not rush to publish election claims —Tech players



By Juliet Umeh



As Nigeria prepares for the 2027 general elections, voters may face a new kind of deception.



The society is now rife with images, videos and audios that appear authentic but have been fabricated or altered.
content:
…Why media must not rush to publish election claims —Tech players

By Juliet Umeh

As Nigeria prepares for the 2027 general elections, voters may face a new kind of deception.


The society is now rife with images, videos and audios that appear authentic but have been fabricated or altered.


The concern has grown after the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, said it removed 1,609,553 records from the voters’ register following a technical assessment. The review examined suspected multiple registrations, unusual registration patterns, substituted photographs and irregularities linked to registration transactions.


INEC also found cases in which some registration personnel deliberately bypassed established procedures, including provisions for exceptional circumstances involving persons with disabilities. The commission is investigating some flagged records.


The findings have prompted questions about how the irregularities occurred and whether synthetic images or other AI-generated material could be used to undermine confidence in the electoral process. There is, however, no evidence in the material available that AI-generated images caused the irregularities in the register.


Olaronke Alo of the BBC Disinformation Unit while speaking on Arise Television said its initial verification found that some of the images circulating online were present in the INEC register.


She said: “What we did was to do the initial verification. We went into the INEC portal and began to trace some of the names and pictures being posted on social media. We found that these images were on the INEC register.”


The unit also examined claims about inconsistent records, including one instance in which the same photograph appeared against different names.


Alo said it found examples of apparently incomplete or unusual names and records alleged to belong to deceased people, including former President Muhammadu Buhari.


She said the unit’s task was to verify claims circulating online, rather than assess whether INEC’s response was adequate.

False claims can travel fast


The risks extend beyond the voters’ register. AI tools can generate convincing images, videos and audio of people appearing to say things they never said. A fabricated statement attributed to a political figure could spread rapidly before voters have time to verify it.


INEC has dismissed a social media poster and accompanying text claiming the commission had reaffirmed the leadership of the African Democratic Congress. The poster carried INEC’s logo and an image of National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna. With the matter before the courts, false claims styled as official announcements could mislead the public.


Other risks include political messages tailored to specific groups of voters, fabricated result sheets, screenshots purporting to show updates from INEC’s results portal, or cloned voices announcing false outcomes. Such material could create confusion and deepen doubts about the credibility of the process.


There is no evidence that these tactics have affected election results in Nigeria. But the possibility of manipulated content increases the work required of election officials, journalists and voters as the poll approaches.


Alo urged voters to examine the details of material they encounter online, asking who posted it, why it was posted and whether credible sources have confirmed it.


She cited a video appearing to show Burkina Faso leader Ibrahim Traoré addressing President Bola Tinubu in English. Viewers, she said, should consider whether the language matches what is known about the speaker and whether the video appeared through official channels.

She said: “If a president is addressing another president, it is expected that the national broadcaster of that country is picking up those broadcasts.”


Viewers can also look for inconsistencies in speech, mouth movements, skin tones and framing, she said. Reverse image searches may help establish whether a picture has appeared elsewhere and how it was originally used. People should also check official channels and note when platforms label content as AI-generated.


No single clue proves a post is fake. But checking the source and seeking confirmation before sharing can slow the spread of misleading claims.


Technology needs scrutiny


At a panel discussion on science and technology during election season, speakers said the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS, and INEC’s Result Viewing Portal, IReV, could improve transparency. They cautioned, however, that technology alone could not guarantee credible elections.


Head of Research and Programmes at Kimpact Development Initiative, Oluwafemi John, said BVAS and IReV have different functions.


“BVAS helps with verification and accreditation,” he said, explaining that the device checks voters through fingerprints or facial recognition. After ballots are counted, the presiding officer uses BVAS to transmit an image of the polling-unit result sheet, Form EC8A, to IReV.


He noted: “IReV is not a collation point. We should not mix it up.”


He said questions remained about the legal and evidential status of some election technology records, and urged the public to distinguish between uploading results for viewing and formally collating them at designated centres.


A research analyst at the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development’s Digital Technology, AI and Information Disorder Analysis Centre, Sanusi Sanusi, said online access to polling-unit results had enabled independent scrutiny.


He said: “Technology has really helped make election results transparent. If you know your polling unit, you can trace it on IReV and look at the result.”


But he raised concerns about BVAS devices’ age and performance, citing reports of accreditation difficulties and compatibility problems. He also questioned how differences between electronically generated figures and figures on physical forms were reconciled.


“If there is a disparity between the electronically generated figures and the physical figures, what is the reconciliation process?” he asked. “There is no guideline anywhere to explain that.”


Sanusi said inconsistencies in voter figures and reports of missing ballots needed investigation and clear explanations. He cautioned that discrepancies should not automatically be called evidence of rigging without further verification.
Verify before publishing


For journalists, the challenge is not only interpreting results but also assessing suspicious digital material before it reaches the public.


“Don’t run into publishing,” Sanusi said. “You need to develop your sense of doubt and figure out when something is worth investigating.” Tools that assess potentially AI-generated videos may offer clues, he said, but not definitive proof. “Always use multiple tools to verify.”

The post AI, fake voter records raise new risks for 2027 elections appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Shaibu urges Eagles to keep AFCON hope alive
description:
The Director-General of the National Institute for Sports, Philip Shaibu, has urged the Super Eagles not to give up on qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, insisting that the team’s hopes remain alive despite the goalless draw against Tanzania.
Shaibu spoke after watching Tuesday’s 0-0 dra
content:
The Director-General of the National Institute for Sports, Philip Shaibu, has urged the Super Eagles not to give up on qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, insisting that the team’s hopes remain alive despite the goalless draw against Tanzania.

Shaibu spoke after watching Tuesday’s 0-0 draw in Zanzibar, which left Nigeria with seven points from four Group L games, three behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who beat Madagascar 2-0. Tanzania have already qualified as co-hosts, so only one ticket remains in the group.

In a statement issued by the NIS on Shaibu’s message to supporters and football stakeholders, he said the race was far from over. He pointed to the Matchday Five and Six fixtures in March 2027, when Nigeria travel to Madagascar on March 24 and host Guinea-Bissau four days later.

He asked the Super Eagles to draw inspiration from the Flamingos, who recovered from an opening-day defeat at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco to progress in the competition, and to show the same resilience and determination.

Shaibu also recalled the qualifying campaign for the 2010 World Cup in South Africa. Nigeria appeared to be trailing Tunisia for the group’s only ticket, but Tunisia lost on the final day while the Eagles beat Kenya to qualify. He said such examples should motivate the current squad.

He cautioned the technical crew and players against taking the expectations of millions of Nigerians for granted, and stressed the importance of the team to the nation’s sporting identity and pride. He wished the team an injury-free run ahead of the decisive games.

Nigeria could still revive their campaign with wins over Madagascar and Guinea-Bissau. A strong performance, along with the required goal difference, could see them overtake Guinea-Bissau and take the group’s sole ticket to the 2027 AFCON, which is co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

Head coach Eric Chelle admitted after the draw that Nigeria were in trouble.

“A draw away from home is not a bad result, but in our situation, because we lost to Guinea-Bissau, that is why we are in trouble,” he said.

title: State police: Senate demands safeguards against abuse
description:
• Presses Tinubu to submit operational bill defining powers of federal, state police  • President receives constitutional amendment endorsed by 36 states • AGF to review bill before presidential assent

By Juliana Taiwo-Obalonye and Adesuwa Tsan, Abuja
Amid longstanding concerns over the possible ab
content:
• Presses Tinubu to submit operational bill defining powers of federal, state police  • President receives constitutional amendment endorsed by 36 states • AGF to review bill before presidential assent

By Juliana Taiwo-Obalonye and Adesuwa Tsan, Abuja

Amid longstanding concerns over the possible abuse of state police by governors and the danger of conflicting authority between federal and state security agencies, the Senate has called for urgent legislation to clearly define the powers, responsibilities and operational boundaries of the proposed decentralised policing system.

The upper chamber warned that the constitutional amendment establishing state police must be complemented by a comprehensive operational law to prevent jurisdictional disputes and ensure that the new security arrangement does not create conflicts between the Nigeria Police Force and police services to be established by the 36 states.

The demand came as President Bola Tinubu received the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, following its approval by all 36 state Houses of Assembly, clearing a major constitutional hurdle in the proposed restructuring of Nigeria’s policing architecture.

Although the amendment has secured the required legislative endorsements, concerns have persisted over the possibility of state governors deploying police formations against political opponents, intimidating dissenting voices or interfering in electoral processes, particularly in states where political competition is intense.

The fears have featured prominently in the national debate over state police, with opponents of decentralised policing warning that placing armed security personnel under the control of state authorities without adequate safeguards could expose citizens to political intimidation and abuse of power.

Supporters, however, have maintained that state police would improve intelligence gathering, strengthen community policing and enable faster responses to security threats, particularly in rural communities where federal police presence is inadequate.

Against this background, the Senate insisted that the proposed National Policing Bill must establish clear lines of authority, operational responsibilities and mechanisms for cooperation between the two policing structures before the new arrangement becomes operational.

Leading debate on a motion of urgent public importance, Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele urged Tinubu to forward the operational legislation to the National Assembly for scrutiny and passage, stressing that constitutional recognition of state police alone would not resolve the practical challenges of implementing the system.

Bamidele said the legislation was necessary to define the powers and responsibilities of state police services, establish their relationship with the Nigeria Police Force and provide safeguards against jurisdictional conflicts.

He urged the chamber to mandate the Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, to transmit the constitutional amendment to the President in accordance with the Acts Authentication Act, 2004, while formally requesting the submission of the National Policing Bill for expeditious consideration.

“Thank Mr. President for taking ownership and boldly supporting the Bill throughout the process; and also urge him to forward the National Policing Bill that will enable the operationalisation of subnational policing, for legislative scrutiny and expeditious passage by the National Assembly,” Bamidele said.

Senate President Godswill Akpabio reinforced the demand, warning that the next critical stage of the reform must address the relationship between federal and state police authorities to avoid overlapping powers and operational disagreements.

“The next step is to address the operationalisation of the system and ensure that there is no conflict between the State Police and the Federal Police.” Akpabio described the constitutional amendment as a major achievement of the 10th National Assembly, expressing confidence that state police could contribute significantly to tackling insecurity across the country.

“This is a legislation that will not be forgotten. It is a major achievement of the 10th National Assembly.”

Akpabio also expressed optimism that the establishment of state police could address about 70 per cent of Nigeria’s security challenges, although he acknowledged that the success of the initiative would depend on an effective operational framework.

Deputy Senate President, Barau Jibrin, said the proposed state police system was intended to complement, rather than replace, the Nigeria Police Force, arguing that cooperation between both institutions would strengthen the country’s response to security threats.

“This is a collective achievement that deserves to be celebrated. The proposed State Police system is designed to complement the operations of the Nigeria Police Force, strengthening our overall policing structure and enhancing our capacity to address security challenges across the country,” Jibrin said.

Meanwhile, the Presidency has confirmed that Tinubu had formally received the constitutional amendment after its endorsement by all 36 state legislatures, surpassing the minimum approval of 24 states required under Section 9(2) of the Constitution.

Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, disclosed in a statement on Wednesday that the bill was transmitted to the President by his Special Advisers on Senate and House of Representatives Matters, Basheer Lado and Wasiu Olanrewaju-Smart.

Gbajabiamila said the President would review the amendment in consultation with the Attorney-General of the Federation before giving his assent at a formal signing ceremony.

He explained that the proposed National Policing Bill, which would establish the legal and administrative framework for the new security structure, was still undergoing executive consideration.

As Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on State Police, Gbajabiamila disclosed that the group had completed extensive stakeholder engagements and nationwide consultations towards developing the operational legislation.

He said the draft had been submitted to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting validation, after which it would be reviewed by the working group and presented to the President.

“Upon receipt of the validated version, the Working Group will review it and present it, alongside its report, to Mr President for consideration,” he said.

Gbajabiamila commended the leadership and members of the National Assembly, the 36 state governors, state legislatures and other stakeholders for their contributions to the constitutional amendment process.

The renewed push for an operational law comes against the background of decades of controversy over decentralised policing in Nigeria, with successive administrations confronting demands for state-controlled security formations as insecurity spreads across the country.

While advocates have consistently argued that policing should be brought closer to communities to improve intelligence gathering and response times, critics have pointed to the country’s political history and the potential for governors to use state-controlled security agencies to suppress opposition activities, influence elections and settle political disputes.

The controversy has also raised questions about the independence of state police leadership, recruitment standards, funding, disciplinary procedures, accountability and mechanisms for resolving disputes between federal and state authorities.

These concerns have made the proposed National Policing Bill a critical component of the reform, as lawmakers seek to establish a framework that would strengthen local security without creating competing centres of coercive authority.

With the constitutional amendment now before Tinubu, attention is shifting to the proposed operational legislation and the safeguards it will provide against political interference, abuse of authority and jurisdictional conflicts between the two policing structures.

The post State police: Senate demands safeguards against abuse appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Army seeks land for armoured corps training in Bauchi
description:
…Commends Bala Mohammed for supporting military operations, infrastructure development



By Christopher Ameh



The Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has appealed to the Bauchi State Government to allocate land for the establishment of a dedicated training facility for the Niger
content:
…Commends Bala Mohammed for supporting military operations, infrastructure development

By Christopher Ameh

The Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has appealed to the Bauchi State Government to allocate land for the establishment of a dedicated training facility for the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps in the state.

Shaibu made the appeal during a courtesy visit to Governor Bala Mohammed at the Government House, Bauchi, where he commended the governor for supporting the Nigerian Army and promoting infrastructural development in the state.

The Army Chief said the request had become necessary following the expansion of the Nigerian Army from eight to 12 divisions, a development that had increased the number of officers and soldiers requiring specialised training.

He explained that Bauchi had remained a major training centre for armoured officers, noting that military personnel usually begin their professional careers in the state through the Young Officers’ Course and other specialised programmes.

According to him, armoured officers spend more than 15 years of their military careers attending various courses in Bauchi before moving to other locations as they advance in rank.

He said the proposed facility would provide a dedicated centre for the continuous training of officers and soldiers throughout the year.

Shaibu disclosed that the Corps Commander of the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps would formally present the request to the governor, urging him to give it favourable consideration.

“With this expansion, a lot of officers and soldiers have been coming into the Corps, and they will require this training consecutively throughout the year. Once that proposal comes, I crave your indulgence to please consider it,” he said.

The Army Chief appreciated Mohammed for his administration’s support for the Armoured Corps, particularly the establishment of some military units in Alkaleri as part of efforts to expand the Army’s operational capacity.

He also commended the governor’s infrastructural development efforts, describing the transformation of the Government House as remarkable.

“Being an armoured officer myself and having started my career from here in Bauchi, I must acknowledge the massive infrastructural development taking place here. In fact, I did not recognise the Government House when I was coming,” he said.

Shaibu further disclosed that he was in Bauchi to attend the grand finale of Exercise Mugunbugu, conducted in the Alkaleri general area.

He described the exercise as the Nigerian Army’s major end-of-year training activity, designed to consolidate the various military exercises conducted throughout the year.

The Army Chief also attended the maiden edition of the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps reunion and pulling-out ceremony, which attracted more than 100 retired senior officers.

He said the reunion would provide an opportunity for retired officers to reflect on their contributions to the development of the Corps and share experiences that could strengthen the institution.

Shaibu reiterated the appreciation of officers and soldiers of the Nigerian Army to the Bauchi State Government for its continued cooperation and support, expressing optimism that the partnership would further enhance military training and operational effectiveness.

title: Wike, APC group rally traders, northern  voters for Tinubu, dismiss opposition threat
description:
From Juliana Taiwo-Obalonye, Abuja and Noah Ebije, Kaduna
Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has directed market associations across Abuja to nominate representatives for President Bola Tinubu’s 2027 re-election campaign, as a Kaduna-based All Progressives Congress (APC) s
content:
From Juliana Taiwo-Obalonye, Abuja and Noah Ebije, Kaduna

Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has directed market associations across Abuja to nominate representatives for President Bola Tinubu’s 2027 re-election campaign, as a Kaduna-based All Progressives Congress (APC) support group declared that the opposition lacked the political strength to unseat the President.

Wike, who gave the directive at a town hall meeting with traders and market leaders in Abuja yesterday, warned that verbal endorsements of Tinubu would amount to little unless translated into votes, while the Tinubu Uba Sani Consolidation Front (TUSCOF) dismissed the opposition’s chances of defeating the President and Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani despite the country’s economic and security challenges.

The minister urged each market association to nominate two representatives to participate in the FCT presidential campaign structure, promising support for grassroots mobilisation and regular engagement with traders.

His directive followed endorsements of Tinubu, Vice-President Kashim Shettima and other candidates backed by the administration, including former FCT senator Philip Tanimu Aduda, by market leaders who pledged to mobilise voters through trade unions, cooperatives, religious groups and community associations.

“So for me, if you agree with me, you know what I want. What you want, you have to demonstrate it. You know me, I’ve been in this game for years. When you come and tell me, ‘We are for you, we are for you,’ no problem. You must show it. And I will know,” Wike told the traders.

In Kaduna, TUSCOF Chairman Mohammed Sada Jalal, speaking ahead of the inauguration of the group’s state campaign committee, argued that internal disputes and political uncertainty had weakened opposition parties, leaving them poorly positioned to challenge the APC in 2027.

Although he acknowledged that insecurity and economic hardship could cost the ruling party some votes, Jalal maintained that the challenges would not prevent Tinubu and Uba Sani from winning their respective elections.

Wike, meanwhile, used the Abuja engagement to defend Tinubu’s removal of petrol subsidy, arguing that the policy had prevented an economic collapse and improved the Federal Government’s capacity to fund infrastructure, pay outstanding obligations and increase allocations to other tiers of government.

He said successive administrations had acknowledged that the subsidy regime was unsustainable but lacked the political courage to end it, leaving the country with mounting financial obligations.

“I want to appeal to all of us to keep this at the back of our minds: we have grown too used to living a fake life. Yes, it is true. We like to live a fake life. This country was nearly gone. Nearly gone,” he said.

According to him, Tinubu took the difficult decision because the country could no longer sustain paying trillions of naira in fuel subsidies while struggling to meet salary and pension obligations and fund critical services.

“For the President to change what had been happening, he had to lay a solid foundation first, and a foundation needs time to grow.”

Wike urged Nigerians to reject promises by opposition politicians to reverse the policy, insisting that the benefits of the reforms would become more evident if they were allowed to mature.

“If we allow these policies that the government has put in place to mature, what is going to happen in the next four years will be good. Forget about people coming to tell you stories,” he said.

The minister cited increased revenue allocations to states and local governments, the settlement of pension arrears and what he described as the absence of strikes by the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) for more than three and a half years as evidence that the reforms were producing results.

He also cited the payment of more than N80 billion in outstanding gratuities owed to former Nigeria Airways workers as one of the benefits of improved government revenue.

Wike credited Tinubu with providing funds for major infrastructure projects in the FCT, including the Apo-Karshi road, the reconstructed Saburi road corridor and the Bwari-Kubwa road, which he said was expected to be completed before the end of the year.

“All these roads you are talking about, all these things you are talking about in the FCT. Without the President, how will it be? Who is releasing the money?” he asked.

He said road construction and rehabilitation across the city centre and satellite towns were intended to improve commercial activities, ease transportation difficulties and reduce costs for traders.

The minister also highlighted institutional changes introduced in the FCT under Tinubu, including the appointment of an indigene of the territory to the Federal Executive Council, the establishment of the FCT Civil Service Commission and the creation of Mandate Secretariats for Women and Youth.

Wike challenged traders to judge political leaders by their performance rather than ethnic or regional affiliations.

“Governance has nothing to do with where I come from. It is not about Hausa, Yoruba, or Igbo; it is about ‘If I do my business here, am I happy?’”

He also criticised prominent opposition figures, particularly former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi, accusing them of presenting misleading accounts of their records in public office.

Wike questioned Atiku’s role in past privatisation exercises and alleged that Amaechi’s administration wasted N14 billion on a mosquito fumigation project, paid $39 million for a specialist hospital that was never built and spent N68 billion on an uncompleted monorail project in Rivers State.

He urged Nigerians to assess presidential aspirants by their records rather than campaign appearances or public displays of humility.

Earlier, a representative of Arewa market traders in the FCT, Adams Hassan, pledged support for Tinubu, Shettima and APC candidates, arguing that traders constituted an important voting bloc because of their numerical strength and contributions to employment, revenue generation and local security.

He, however, urged the FCT Administration to give market associations greater involvement in policies and programmes affecting commercial activities.

“We are ready to make every necessary contribution to ensure the success of His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, Vice President Senator Kashim Shettima, and all APC candidates in the FCT in the 2027 general election,” he said.

A representative of Wuse Market traders, Okerie Okechukwu, announced plans for cluster-by-cluster mobilisation under what he described as a “rainbow coalition.”

He said the campaign would extend to trade unions, cooperatives, community groups and church unions, with traders supporting Tinubu, Aduda and candidates seeking election into the House of Representatives.

“Today, Your Excellency, we want to confirm to you that we are going into cluster mobilisation and campaign under the rainbow coalition,” he said.

Okechukwu attributed the traders’ support to infrastructure and market development initiatives by the FCT Administration and appealed for the construction of additional shops and malls in emerging districts, including Katampe and Kaura.

Chairperson of the National Assembly Quarters Market, Abiola Adekanbi, also pledged the support of market women for Tinubu’s re-election, citing road construction and rehabilitation projects as evidence of the administration’s performance.

She said traders would not only vote for the President but would remain at polling units to protect their votes.

“It is very simple: we are going to follow who knows the road. We are going to follow the ‘talk-and-do,’” she said.

Group Managing Director of Abuja Investment Company Limited (AICL), Maureen Tamuno, commended the minister for approving a dedicated fire truck and fire station for Wuse Market, reconstructing the Saburi road corridor and allocating additional district markets.

Acting Managing Director of Abuja Markets Management Limited (AMML), Onya Ojiji, also highlighted road and drainage projects around Dei-Dei and Kubwa markets, as well as the commissioning of Karu Modern District Market, Utako Farmers Market and Gwagwalada International Market.

He listed the distribution of free shops and the relocation of mechanics and traders to Wassa among the administration’s interventions.

Responding to requests from the traders, Wike approved a proposal for AICL to develop additional markets across the FCT and promised to institutionalise consultations with market associations at least twice yearly.

Meanwhile, in Kaduna, Jalal said TUSCOF’s confidence in Tinubu and Uba Sani was based on what he described as the administration’s achievements and the opposition’s internal weaknesses.

He cited interventions in education, healthcare, infrastructure and other public services as achievements that would strengthen the Kaduna governor’s re-election prospects.

According to him, Uba Sani’s efforts to promote unity across the state had helped address longstanding political divisions between Kaduna North and Southern Kaduna.

Jalal dismissed complaints about the distribution of projects and political appointments, citing road construction in Zone One and appointments involving individuals from Zaria as evidence that the administration had spread development opportunities.

He also blamed the country’s electricity crisis for some of the difficulties confronting businesses, criticising the outcome of power-sector privatisation undertaken during the administration in which Atiku served as Vice-President.

Defending Tinubu’s second-term ambition, Jalal argued that the South should be allowed to complete an eight-year presidential tenure under the country’s informal power-rotation arrangement.

He recalled Tinubu’s political support for northern leaders, including former President Muhammadu Buhari, and urged the region to reciprocate the gesture in 2027.

The TUSCOF chairman also cited federal infrastructure projects in Kaduna, including the Abuja-Kaduna road and railway projects, as reasons residents should support the President’s re-election.

On the political influence of former Kaduna State Governor Nasir El-Rufai and his son, Bello El-Rufai, Jalal dismissed suggestions that they posed a serious electoral threat to the APC.

He expressed optimism that political differences involving Uba Sani and his predecessor could eventually be resolved, maintaining that there was no crisis between the two politicians.

Speaking on preparations for the elections, Jalal said TUSCOF had established grassroots mobilisation structures, including a constitution, bank account and formal registration.

He disclosed that the organisation had appointed more than 50 patrons and about 60 advisers, with an organisational structure modelled after a campaign council.

Jalal, who said he participated in previous campaign organisations, including the 2023 presidential campaign, expressed confidence that the group’s experience and political network would strengthen mobilisation for Tinubu and Uba Sani ahead of the elections.

The post Wike, APC group rally traders, northern voters for Tinubu, dismiss opposition threat appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Courts dismiss suits against ADC, NDC candidates in Kano
description:
From Desmond Mgboh, Kano
The Federal High Court in Kano has dismissed separate suits challenging the nominations of Ibrahim Ali Amin as the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate and Tijjani Husseini Gandu as the National Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate for Kano Municipal State
content:
From Desmond Mgboh, Kano

The Federal High Court in Kano has dismissed separate suits challenging the nominations of Ibrahim Ali Amin as the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate and Tijjani Husseini Gandu as the National Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate for Kano Municipal State Constituency in the 2027 elections.

The judgments, delivered by Justices M.M. Shuaibu and Simon Amobeda, respectively, cleared the two candidates of the legal challenges to their nominations, with the court in the ADC case ruling that the action was filed outside the constitutionally prescribed period for pre-election disputes.

In the first suit, marked FHC/KN/CS/375/2026, Sheikh Ibrahim Khalil Idris had approached the court through his counsel, A.Y. Gumel, seeking a declaration that he was the duly elected governorship candidate of the ADC.

He joined the party, Amin and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) as first, second and third defendants, respectively.

The dispute arose from the party’s governorship nomination process, during which both aspirants reportedly signed an agreement on May 27, 2026, accepting a consensus arrangement and authorising the party leadership to select its candidate.

Following consultations, the ADC leadership nominated Amin, a decision Khalil challenged in court, insisting that he was entitled to the ticket.

However, Amin’s legal team, led by N.A. Ayagi, raised a preliminary objection challenging the court’s jurisdiction to entertain the suit.

Delivering judgment, Justice Shuaibu upheld the objection, ruling that the action was statute-barred because it was instituted outside the 14-day period prescribed by the Constitution for filing pre-election matters.

The judge held that the cause of action arose during the nomination process and submission of Amin’s name to INEC between July 4 and August 5, 2026, rather than in September when Khalil commenced the action.

The court also found deficiencies in the plaintiff’s claim, particularly his reliance on an alleged party primary held on May 22, 2026.

Justice Shuaibu observed that INEC had confirmed that it neither participated in nor monitored the alleged primary, while the plaintiff failed to produce an official commission report authenticating the exercise.

The court further faulted a letter tendered by Khalil, noting that it was signed by the party’s state chairman, whereas the authority to transmit candidates’ names to INEC rested with the party’s National Working Committee or National Executive Committee.

It also held that Khalil failed to exhaust the party’s internal dispute resolution procedures as required under Section 10.9 of its guidelines.

Consequently, the court dismissed the suit, leaving Amin’s nomination as the ADC governorship candidate undisturbed.

In a separate judgment, Justice Simon Amobeda dismissed a suit challenging the nomination of Tijjani Husseini Gandu, a Kwankwasiyya political singer, as the NDC candidate for Kano Municipal State Constituency in the 2027 House of Assembly election.

The action was instituted by Aminu Isyaku Yusuf, who alleged that he purchased the party’s nomination forms to contest the election but that Gandu’s name was subsequently forwarded to INEC and published as the party’s candidate.

Yusuf contended that the process leading to Gandu’s nomination was marred by irregularities and sought judicial intervention to challenge the party’s decision.

However, counsel to Gandu, Badamasi Suleiman Gandu, opposed the suit and urged the court to uphold his client’s nomination.

In his judgment, Justice Amobeda accepted the defence submissions and dismissed the action, leaving Gandu’s candidature intact.

The two judgments resolve the challenges at the Federal High Court, subject to any appeals that may be filed by the dissatisfied parties.
