title: Malawi hire ex-Falcons coach Waldrum ahead of W’Cup
description:
Former Super Falcons coach Randy Waldrum was appointed head coach of Malawi’s women’s national team on Wednesday ahead of the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
Waldrum signed a two-year contract with Malawi following the team’s run to the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of N
content:
Former Super Falcons coach Randy Waldrum was appointed head coach of Malawi’s women’s national team on Wednesday ahead of the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.

Waldrum signed a two-year contract with Malawi following the team’s run to the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations final.

The former Houston Dash and Nigeria women’s coach was unveiled as the replacement for Lovemore Fazili, who will serve as his assistant while reportedly furthering his coaching qualifications.

NWSL star Temwa Chawinga and OL Lyonnes’ Tabitha Chawinga were the standout players in a WAFCON campaign in which Malawi defeated Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria en route to the final, where they lost 3-0 to Cameroon. Despite the defeat, Malawi secured qualification for next year’s FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

“I watched the games during WAFCON and followed the team very closely,” Waldrum said during his unveiling, according to a statement by the Malawi FA (FAM).

“Over the next few days, before we head to China, I will spend some time with the team in camp.

“If you know anything about my background, I am a very attack-minded coach. I love to control games through possession.

“The modern game involves a lot of attacking transitions, and you need that quality in your team. I know that quality is already there with the talent you have.”

FAM president Fleetwood Haiya described Waldrum’s appointment, following his stint as Nigeria coach at the 2023 Women’s World Cup, as a step up ahead of next year’s tournament.

“This is another important day as we continue to fulfil the commitments of our strategic plan,” Haiya said.

“When we took office, we promised Malawians that we would invest in building a sustainable women’s national team and developing women’s football.

“The appointment of Coach Randy is part of that commitment. We want to strengthen the technical team and ensure there is a clear pathway for our players, from grassroots to elite football.

“I want to recognise Coach Fazili and his technical team for the wonderful job they did at WAFCON and for leading us to the World Cup.

“They did a very good job. However, the World Cup is another bigger stage, and we felt it was important to bring in someone with the qualifications and experience of coaching at that level.

“Coach Randy brings that experience, qualification and competence.”

Waldrum resigned as Super Falcons coach in September 2024, citing family reasons. Before his departure, he had been at loggerheads with the Nigeria Football Federation, accusing the federation of maladministration in the management of the team during preparations for the 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup.

The post Malawi hire ex-Falcons coach Waldrum ahead of W’Cup appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Osayi makes Uganda breakthrough after Nigeria switch
description:
Nigerian-born goalkeeper Kingdom Osayi has made an impressive start to his international career with Uganda, stepping in for veteran Denis Onyango and subsequently earning his first start for the Cranes during the November international break, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
The 22-year-old made his sen
content:
Nigerian-born goalkeeper Kingdom Osayi has made an impressive start to his international career with Uganda, stepping in for veteran Denis Onyango and subsequently earning his first start for the Cranes during the November international break, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.

The 22-year-old made his senior international debut on October 5, 2026, in a 1-1 friendly draw against DR Congo before making his competitive debut in Saturday’s 1-1 draw against Botswana in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

Osayi replaced Onyango in the 41st minute after the experienced goalkeeper sustained an injury and produced several important saves after the break to help Uganda secure a point.

He was handed his first start on Tuesday in another 1-1 draw against Botswana in Gaborone, completing an encouraging international break with two appearances.

“Not the result we wanted. We keep getting better. Glad to have made my first start. Thank God for a successful international break and also maintaining the top spot in the 2027 AFCON qualifiers,” Osayi wrote on X.

Although born and raised in Nigeria, the goalkeeper qualifies to represent Uganda through his maternal grandmother, who was born in Kaberamaido, according to the Ugandan football authorities. He accepted an invitation from the Federation of Uganda Football Associations in September 2026.

Despite already securing qualification for next year’s tournament as co-hosts, Uganda remain top of Group H in the qualifiers, which also features Libya and Tunisia.

Before switching international allegiance, Osayi developed his career in Nigeria, featuring prominently for MFM FC, where he spent three years between 2019 and 2022.

He rose to prominence at Doma United during the 2023/2024 Nigeria Premier Football League season, keeping 15 clean sheets in 29 appearances. He also went 540 minutes without conceding a goal, earned Player of the Month recognition and attracted calls for a Super Eagles invitation.

Osayi joined Rangers International in 2024 before moving to Swedish club Assyriska FF in 2025.

title: Abuja’s creation took over 90% of Nasarawa land – Sule
description:
Nasarawa State Governor, Abdullahi Sule, has highlighted the state’s historical and geographical ties with the Federal Capital Territory, saying it contributed more than 90 per cent of the territory used to create Abuja.
Sule said the present-day Abuja was carved out of areas that previously belonge
content:
Nasarawa State Governor, Abdullahi Sule, has highlighted the state’s historical and geographical ties with the Federal Capital Territory, saying it contributed more than 90 per cent of the territory used to create Abuja.

Sule said the present-day Abuja was carved out of areas that previously belonged to Nasarawa, Plateau and Niger states, making Nasarawa one of the closest neighbours to the nation’s capital.

The governor stated this while speaking at the Global Alliance World Public Relations Forum in Abuja, where he sought greater recognition of Nasarawa’s historical contribution to the establishment of the FCT.

He said the state’s proximity to Abuja made it strategically important, noting that residents could drive into Nasarawa within minutes from the capital.

He said, “Even where you are sitting right now was part of Nasarawa State because it was part of Plateau. The present day Abuja was taken out of Nasarawa State, Plateau and Niger State.

“But we constituted over 90 per cent of what was taken to create the capital Abuja. So Nasarawa State is just next-door neighbour to you.”

Sule added that the state’s proximity to Abuja offered opportunities for stronger economic and social relations between the two territories.

title: Eyesan seeks 25% women representation in oil sector leadership
description: The Chief Executive of the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission, Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, has urged women in the oil and gas industry to remain resilient in the face of career setbacks, recounting how she spent eight years in the same position without promotion before rising to become one o
content:
The Chief Executive of the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission, Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, has urged women in the oil and gas industry to remain resilient in the face of career setbacks, recounting how she spent eight years in the same position without promotion before rising to become one of the industry’s most senior executives.

Eyesan also called for more deliberate efforts to increase women’s representation in the petroleum industry, advocating that at least 25 per cent of leadership and decision-making positions should be occupied by women.

She made the call on Wednesday while speaking on the topic, ‘Breaking Barriers’, at the 2026 Women in NNPC Limited event held at the NNPC Towers, Abuja, under the theme, ‘Powered by Her’.

According to a statement issued by the Head of Media and Corporate Communications of the NUPRC, Eniola Akinkuotu, Eyesan said professional advancement required competence, resilience, patience and continuous learning, particularly in an industry where women continued to face barriers to leadership positions.

The statement read, “The Commission Chief Executive, Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission, Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, has called for greater opportunities for women in the petroleum sector even as she asked women to also prioritise competence, resilience and continuous learning as critical tools for breaking barriers.

“The NUPRC boss urged women not to be discouraged by delayed promotions, stressing that professional growth requires patience, perseverance and commitment to excellence.”

Drawing from her career experience, the regulator’s chief executive said delayed promotions should not discourage women from pursuing their professional ambitions, stressing that consistency and commitment to excellence were essential to long-term career growth.

She disclosed that she spent eight years in the same position without promotion but remained focused on developing her professional capacity.

Eyesan also challenged the notion that women’s advancement should be treated as an exclusively female responsibility, calling for greater involvement of men in conversations and efforts to promote gender inclusion.

She said some of the most significant breakthroughs in her career came through men who recognised her competence and gave her opportunities to occupy leadership positions.

“I spent eight years in the same position without promotion but remained committed to my career.

“I was appointed the first female Head of Strategy, not by a woman, but by a man who believed in my competence. I was also appointed as the first female EVP Upstream, NNPCL, by a man who believed in my competence, and today I stand as the first female CCE of NUPRC by Mr President, who is a man who believes that I will deliver,” she said.

The NUPRC boss said her experience demonstrated the importance of creating an environment where professional competence, rather than gender, determined access to opportunities.

She acknowledged that the petroleum industry had made progress in opening up opportunities for women but insisted that the pace of change remained insufficient to achieve meaningful representation.

title: Reforms unlock household credit but borrowing costs high – Experts
description:
Banking and finance experts have said that the Central Bank of Nigeria’s reforms, particularly the banking sector recapitalisation exercise, have begun strengthening banks’ lending capacity, with households and businesses reporting greater access to credit.
They said the improvement reflected strong
content:
Banking and finance experts have said that the Central Bank of Nigeria’s reforms, particularly the banking sector recapitalisation exercise, have begun strengthening banks’ lending capacity, with households and businesses reporting greater access to credit.

They said the improvement reflected stronger bank balance sheets, rising liquidity and increased financial inclusion, although the high cost of borrowing remained a major obstacle to the full benefits of expanding credit.

The experts spoke against the backdrop of the CBN’s Q3 2026 Credit Conditions Survey, which showed increased demand for secured, unsecured and corporate loans, alongside higher approval rates and lower default rates across major lending categories.

The survey showed that the demand index for secured lending stood at 25.6, driven largely by consumer loans to households, which recorded 42.9, and credit for house purchases at 28.0. Mortgage and remortgage lending recorded 12.0, while lending to small businesses by households declined to -19.7.

Speaking with The PUNCH, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Optimus Bank, Dr Ademola Odeyemi, said banks had increased lending following the recapitalisation exercise, noting that stronger capital positions would enable lenders to expand credit and improve profitability.

“Lending has actually picked up truly because banks raised capital, and capital can only be utilised profitably by lending. If you don’t lend, you don’t make money. So, lending is actually, truly picking up,” Odeyemi said.

He, however, stressed the need for a supportive economic environment that would enable borrowers to deploy credit productively and repay their loans.

“The important thing is to have a very good environment through which customers will effectively use that money. If the economy is not conducive, the loan will go bad. So, we need a very workable economy, we need a growing economy, we need a conducive economy where customers can borrow effectively, use the money effectively, and be able to pay back,” he said.

Odeyemi warned that a weak business environment could trigger another wave of bad loans, undermining the gains recorded in the banking sector.

He also commended the CBN Governor, Yemi Cardoso, for restoring confidence in the financial system through reforms and stronger regulatory supervision.

“The recapitalisation exercise was also very successful because almost every bank succeeded in getting it. So, which was also a major challenge that people have overcome. So, right now banks are well capitalised, and again, the level of supervision is quite high,” he said.

He added that sustaining the reforms would strengthen the banking industry and provide the financial foundation needed to support economic growth.

Similarly, the Chief Executive Officer of Economic Associates, Dr Ayo Teriba, said Nigeria was experiencing a liquidity expansion that was beginning to spread beyond the foreign exchange and capital markets into bank lending to households and businesses.

In a phone interview, Teriba attributed the development to the impact of economic reforms and the appreciation of the naira, arguing that the resulting improvement in liquidity was beginning to translate into increased access to credit.

He said, “There are four liquidity buckets: there’s foreign reserves, there’s market cap, there’s the bond market, and there’s the banking system. And the point is that in past tides, you’ve seen the rising tide in 2006 to 2007. A rising tide of reserves, a rising tide of market cap, there’s a rising tide of banking loans.”

The economist noted that the current expansion in liquidity is increasingly reaching households and businesses through higher bank lending, unlike previous periods when stock market gains largely benefited listed companies and investors.

Teriba maintained that the growing availability of credit would support business expansion, employment and household incomes, while predicting that borrowing costs would eventually decline to single-digit levels.

He added that the current recovery differed from the liquidity expansion recorded in 2006 and 2007 because the latest improvements stemmed from domestic policy reforms rather than favourable international oil prices.

Teriba added that the reforms had helped strengthen the naira, moderate inflation and improve liquidity across the economy, creating conditions for a more sustained expansion in lending.

Also, the Founder of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, Dr Muda Yusuf, attributed the improvement in household credit partly to the expansion of financial inclusion, particularly through financial technology companies and digital lending platforms.

He said fintech companies and commercial banks had widened access to consumer credit through small loans and overdraft facilities, helping households meet spending needs and supporting demand for goods and services.

“The level of financial inclusion in the last few years, driven largely by the fintechs, has led to an increase in consumer credit, and that has made a lot of difference in terms of consumer credit,” Yusuf said.

The post Reforms unlock household credit but borrowing costs high – Experts appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Stakeholders call for credit plans for women, young entrepreneurs
description:
Stakeholders at the Africa Credit Expo 2026 have urged players in the finance industry to build practical credit infrastructure that would be accessible to women, young entrepreneurs, and small businesses across Africa.
In a statement on Wednesday by the organisers, CreditRegistry, the charge was le
content:
Stakeholders at the Africa Credit Expo 2026 have urged players in the finance industry to build practical credit infrastructure that would be accessible to women, young entrepreneurs, and small businesses across Africa.

In a statement on Wednesday by the organisers, CreditRegistry, the charge was led by Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, who was represented at the event by his head of the Research, Strategy, and Training Department, Mr Bolarinwa Mustapha, on November 13 at the University of Lagos.

The governor insisted that to achieve the $1 trillion economic agenda of the federal government, opportunities should be made available to its people.

Speaking on the theme,  “Reimagining Africa Credit Economy: unlocking capital, trust, and opportunity,” Sanwo-Olu stressed the need for building practical partnerships that will strengthen credit infrastructure and expand financial inclusion.

He said, “I encourage stakeholders across the continent to move beyond discussion and build practical partnerships that will strengthen our credit infrastructure, expand financial inclusion, and make financing more accessible to women, young entrepreneurs, and small businesses.”

The governor further noted that an “economy cannot grow beyond opportunities available to its people. And those opportunities cannot flourish without access to capital, confidence in the financial system, and the trust that makes investment possible.

“The theme of the expo, ‘Reimagining Africa Credit Economy: unlocking capital, trust, and opportunity,’ speaks to a challenge we cannot afford to ignore across Africa. We have talented entrepreneurs, ambitious young people, innovative businesses, and communities with enormous business potential.

“Yet many of these people struggle to access the financial resources they need to grow. The question, therefore, is whether the opportunities exist and whether our financial system is structured to make those opportunities accessible. Credit must be seen as more than borrowing money. It is an important tool for economic growth. When businesses can access affordable finance, they expand operations, employ more people, improve productivity, and contribute to the economy. When individuals have access to responsive credit, they can invest in their future and improve their quality of life.

“However, access to credit must be built on trust; financial institutions need reliable information to make informed lending decisions, while individuals and businesses must understand the importance of financial discipline and responsible borrowing. This is where stronger credit reporting systems, digital innovation, and financial literacy become essential.

“We must also understand the role of technology, especially artificial intelligence and digital financial services in transforming credit assessment and reaching people who have traditionally been excluded from the formal financial system. Innovation must, however, go hand in hand with data protection, transparency, and consumer protection. Our responsibility is to continue creating an environment where enterprise can thrive, investment is encouraged, and opportunity is accessible.

“I encourage stakeholders across the continent to move beyond discussion and build practical partnerships that will strengthen our credit infrastructure, expand financial inclusion, and make financing pioneering initiatives, like our campus Work-Study programme, that will empower students to earn income and build strong credit habits while in school because they are our legacy.”

Dr Jameelah Sharrieff-Ayedun, who is the Managing Director/CEO of CreditRegistry, ACE 2026, said the  Expo examined the issues shaping Africa’s credit ecosystem, from access to finance and reliable credit information to financial literacy, consumer protection, digital innovation and responsible lending.

“No single institution can reimagine Africa’s credit economy alone. Lenders, regulators, policymakers and innovators each hold part of the solution, and ACE exists to bring them into the same room,” Sharrieff-Ayedun noted

ACE 2026 also featured keynote presentations, executive and student panels, fireside chats, exhibitions and networking. Speakers include Foyinsolami Akinjayeju, Managing Director/CEO, EFInA; Dr. (Mrs.) Markie Idowu, President and Chairman of Council, National Institute of Credit Administration (NICA); Tinuola Aigwedo, Executive Director, Strategy and Operations, National Credit Guarantee Company (NCG)

title: Residents lament as flooding, bad roads cripple Ogun community
description:
Residents of the Oke-Afa community in Magboro, Obafemi Owode Local Government Area of Ogun State, have appealed to the state government to rehabilitate their roads and address persistent flooding, saying the situation has caused hardship for several years.
The residents who spoke with PUNCH Metro co
content:
Residents of the Oke-Afa community in Magboro, Obafemi Owode Local Government Area of Ogun State, have appealed to the state government to rehabilitate their roads and address persistent flooding, saying the situation has caused hardship for several years.

The residents who spoke with PUNCH Metro correspondent last Wednesday said the poor condition of the roads had made movement difficult, particularly during the rainy season, forcing landlords and community members to contribute money towards repairs.

Our correspondent, who visited the area, observed that a section of the road was flooded after a brief rainfall.

It was also observed that commercial motorcyclists resorted to using water from the flood to wash their motorcycles after the rainfall.

The residents lamented that despite repeated appeals to the government, the community had yet to receive any intervention to address the worsening road conditions.

A resident, Omoniyi Familola, said, “For about 25 years, our community has not enjoyed good road infrastructure.”

He attributed the flooding partly to the flow of water into the community during rainfall, saying it had worsened the condition of the roads.

Familola added that the situation was usually worse between June and August, when residents struggled to move around, and parents faced difficulties taking their children to school.

He also said floodwater sometimes carried snakes and other dangerous reptiles into the community, posing additional risks to residents.

According to him, the Community Development Association and the Community Development Committee had made several efforts to draw the government’s attention to the situation, adding that the community had also featured on Channels Television.

Another resident, Odunsi, who said he had lived in the community for almost 20 years, attributed part of the road deterioration to the movement of heavy-duty vehicles, including trucks and tippers transporting sand and granite.

Odunsi said, “This place leads to my house. Whenever I see that the road is in bad condition, I call two people so that we can contribute money to fill it and make it motorable.”

Similarly, Adebijo Omowunmi described the situation as distressing, saying heavy rainfall often left the roads submerged, making it difficult for residents to identify drainage channels.

She appealed to the government to visit the community and provide a lasting solution to the problem.

Also speaking, a CDA chairman who identified himself simply as Mr Ahmed said residents had repeatedly appealed to the government since he moved into the area in 2005.

“Since I moved into this community in 2005, we have been appealing to the government to rehabilitate, repair or reconstruct the road,” Ahmed said.

Ahmed said schoolchildren and adults had fallen into damaged sections of the roads, while vehicles sometimes struggled to pass through certain areas.

He added that residents spent millions of naira annually on grading and maintaining the roads, but their condition continued to deteriorate.

When contacted for a reaction, the Special Adviser to Governor Dapo Abiodun on Media and Strategy, Kayode Akinmade, attributed the community’s vulnerability to flooding partly to its geographical location, describing Oke-Afa as a naturally low-lying floodplain.

The government said the area’s topography presented challenges for road construction, drainage infrastructure and physical development, particularly during heavy rainfall.

He said, “The Ogun State Government is aware of the concerns of residents of Oke-Afa and the surrounding communities in Magboro. However, it is important to appreciate the peculiar geographical and environmental characteristics of the area.

“Oke-Afa is situated within a naturally low-lying floodplain, making it particularly vulnerable to flooding, especially during periods of heavy rainfall. This geographical reality presents significant challenges for road construction, drainage infrastructure and physical development.

“In areas with such environmental characteristics, sustainable development requires proper land-use planning, adequate drainage infrastructure and compliance with established building regulations. The government has undertaken flood-mitigation interventions in the wider Magboro axis, including the dredging of Oke-Afa Stream, to improve water flow and mitigate flooding.”

On the proposed road rehabilitation, the government said the scheduling of specific projects depended on technical assessments, prioritisation, funding and administrative considerations.

It added that any lasting intervention would require adequate drainage and water-management solutions, noting that road repairs without addressing the drainage challenges could provide only temporary relief.

On allegations that drainage water was being diverted into the community, Akinmade said the claims required technical investigation to determine whether there had been unauthorised alterations to natural waterways or drainage channels.

He continued, “Allegations of drainage water being diverted into the community require proper technical investigation to establish the facts.

“The relevant authorities will need to examine the natural waterways, existing drainage channels and adjoining developments to determine whether there have been unauthorised alterations to the natural flow of water.”

He also urged property owners in the flood-prone area to comply with building regulations, including raising building foundations and floor levels to minimise flooding risks.

He concluded that the OGSG would continue to work through relevant ministries and agencies to identify appropriate interventions to improve drainage infrastructure and address road rehabilitation needs.

The post Residents lament as flooding, bad roads cripple Ogun community appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Official denies  MTN customers’ data theft
description:
Telecommunications Company, MTN Nigeria has insisted that stealing customers’ data is against its values, saying data usage depends on what individual users do with their subscription.
The company also disclosed that peoples’ lifestyle including appetite for various applications and how they are use
content:
Telecommunications Company, MTN Nigeria has insisted that stealing customers’ data is against its values, saying data usage depends on what individual users do with their subscription.

The company also disclosed that peoples’ lifestyle including appetite for various applications and how they are used may determine how fast their data runs, clarifying that the company does not compromise what it gives to subscribers.

Chief Customer Relations and Experience Officer, MTN Nigeria, Ugonwa Nwoye made the clarification while fielding questions from newsmen during an event to address complaints from the network subscribers tagged ‘Data On Trial’ held in Port Harcourt.

Nwoye also said with the advent of sophisticated phones, people are communicating with various equipment across the world to entertain themselves, to become more productive in their work, among others sometimes unaware that data is running out.

She stated: “Data on Trial” is something that we have put together so that we have a one-on-one, face-to-face interaction with our customers to discuss a burning topic. So a topic that our customers have been talking about to us in different formats is about how their data is used.

“They want to understand what uses data? Where did my data go? Why am I charged the way I’m being charged?

“They say that sometimes they sleep and they wake up and they don’t have data. This is what we’re here to discuss today. So, we’re doing it in a courtroom format.

“We have asked our customers to choose who is going to prosecute for them. Who is going to be the judge and we (MTN) are going to be on the defense. I am going to be on the defense, working with my colleagues to answer the questions that our customers have so that we have a fruitful dialogue.”

Nwoye said that through forum customers would learn more about how their data is used and how they can track the use of their data on their phone or on platforms the network has built them.

“So, we have tools that we have built for our customers so that they can check both on their phones and on the tools that we have to solve this burning problem of what is my data being used for? Those tools will help them know how to manage their data.

“One of the things we find is that all of us have a very high appetite for various kinds of applications. And we’re going to show you how those applications work and the tools that are within your hands already to reduce if you want the use of your data on those applications.

“We don’t steal data. MTN does not steal. We’re aside from the fact that we’re a public company it is not within any of our values to steal. So, when we say something is monthly, what we mean is that it is valid for one month,” she assured.

“Not that you can use it anyhow and it will last for one month. So, what is important to us is a common understanding.

“What we know is that ever since networks got faster and people started using the kinds of phones that you’re showing here, at the very beginning of GSM, you were using what we now call Balasa phones.

“Those phones did not even have the ability to take photographs,” Nwoye added: “Now, your phones not only have the ability to take photographs, the photographs are very high definition.

“Some people are already complaining that you guys are using your phones to steal the jobs of cameramen because the phones are now really sophisticated.

“The kinds of things that you like to do first thing in the morning when you join your prayer sessions or when you join school are things that actually use data.

“So your phone is actually communicating with various equipment all across the world to either entertain you, to bring you closer to the world, to make you more productive, to entertain you.

“Those things use data and some people are not always fully aware how much data they’re using. We’re here to dispel any issues today.”

Nwoye further said in the last two years MTN with the industry regulator has been exploring questions and carrying out campaigns on the internet educating customers how to control their WhatsApp and YouTube applications, adding, “We already know the kinds of applications that use a lot of data.

“What MTN decided to do was to take it to another notch, to decide we were going to have one-on-one conversations. One-on-one conversations sometimes are better than just talking, talking to you without you having the chance to actually interact. This is why you’re here today.”

The post Official denies MTN customers’ data theft appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: COP31: Between climate promises and the unfinished business of development
description: There is something almost predictable about the atmosphere surrounding international climate conferences. World leaders arrive with carefully crafted speeches, negotiators retreat into rooms filled with technical documents, civil society organisations stage colorful demonstrations, and the world wai
content:
There is something almost predictable about the atmosphere surrounding international climate conferences. World leaders arrive with carefully crafted speeches, negotiators retreat into rooms filled with technical documents, civil society organisations stage colorful demonstrations, and the world waits for a declaration that promises to save the planet.

Yet, beyond the diplomatic choreography, ordinary people whose livelihoods are threatened by climate change keep asking a simpler question: when will these promises translate into something that changes our lives?

This question has become particularly important as the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, enters its decisive phase here in Antalya, Turkiye. With the conference scheduled to close on November 20, the negotiations have moved into their second week, and the familiar disagreements between developed and developing countries are once again coming to the surface.

The COP31 is being hosted by Türkiye under a unique arrangement in which Australia leads the negotiations. Its central challenge is to move international climate cooperation from declarations towards implementation. So far, there has been progress, but the road to consensus remains difficult.

The negotiations leadership reported that countries had agreed on 48 items, while about 30 negotiating mandates remained outstanding as the second week began. These figures indicate movement in the negotiating process, but they should not be mistaken for 48 new, fully implemented climate commitments.

On November 16, the Presidency circulated the first draft of an overarching political decision, popularly known as the cover decision. This is an important development because it attempts to bring the conference’s various priorities together in one political framework. However, the document remains a negotiating draft, not a final agreement.

The real test of Antalya, therefore, is whether governments can overcome their differences and produce an outcome that recognises countries’ unequal capacities, vulnerabilities and development circumstances.

For developing countries, climate finance remains the most consequential issue at COP31. It is difficult to discuss adaptation, mitigation, technology transfer, or a just energy transition without confronting the question of who will pay for them.

At COP29 in Baku, countries agreed to a new climate-finance goal of at least $300bn annually for developing countries by 2035, alongside efforts to scale up finance from all sources to $1.3tn annually by the same year.

However, the developing world continues to question the adequacy, accessibility and delivery of these commitments. Many vulnerable countries argue that climate finance is either insufficient, arrives too slowly or comes in forms that deepen their debt burdens.

This is why African countries are insisting that climate finance must be predictable, accessible and substantially grant-based, particularly for adaptation.

In my mind, Nigeria must pay close attention to this debate. The country faces increasing climate-related expenditure arising from flooding, desertification, coastal erosion, agricultural disruption and extreme heat. These are not simply environmental inconveniences; they are threats to economic productivity, food security, public health and national development.

The challenge is to ensure that Nigeria’s climate-finance priorities are translated into well-designed, investment-ready projects capable of attracting international support.

Another difficult conversation concerns the future of fossil fuels. The draft political outcome includes competing formulations, including reaffirming the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and stronger language proposing a phase-out. Countries remain divided over how far the final agreement should go.

For Africa, this discussion must be situated within the realities of energy poverty and industrial development. Nigeria, for instance, cannot discuss energy transition without considering electricity access, domestic energy security, employment, industrialisation and the economic implications of dependence on petroleum revenues.

This does not mean that Africa should abandon the global transition towards cleaner energy. Rather, it means the transition must be supported by adequate finance, technology transfer, infrastructure investment and credible arrangements to protect affected workers and communities.

A transition that leaves millions of people without affordable energy or alternative livelihoods cannot reasonably be described as just.

Perhaps the most consequential discussions for the African continent concern adaptation. While much of the global conversation has traditionally focused on reducing greenhouse-gas emissions, countries such as Nigeria are already confronting the consequences of a changing climate.

Communities are losing farms to floods, farmers are struggling with changing rainfall patterns, coastal settlements are threatened by erosion, and rising temperatures are creating additional pressures on public health and livelihoods.

The negotiations on the Global Goal on Adaptation have therefore attracted considerable attention. Developing countries are pressing for stronger adaptation finance, clearer indicators and a workable framework for measuring progress.

There is also a strong demand to triple adaptation finance by 2035, with countries debating the baseline, methodology and accountability arrangements needed to achieve this ambition.

For Nigeria, adaptation must become a practical development programme rather than another policy expression.

Our hydrological institutions, particularly the Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency, must be empowered to translate scientific information into early warning, community preparedness and bankable water-resilience projects.

The value of hydrological data is not merely in knowing how much rain has fallen or how high a river has risen. Its greatest value is in helping governments and communities anticipate danger, protect lives, safeguard infrastructure and plan their economic activities.

This is the connection between climate science and development that Nigeria must strengthen.

Another important development at COP31 is the continuing negotiation around a Just Transition Mechanism. The proposal is intended to strengthen international cooperation, technical assistance, capacity-building and knowledge-sharing to help countries navigate the social and economic implications of climate transition.

This discussion’s significance extends beyond the energy sector. For Nigeria, a just transition must include workers in the oil and gas industry, rural women, young people, informal-sector workers, farmers and communities whose economic activities depend on carbon-intensive industries.

It must also create new opportunities in renewable energy, clean cooking, sustainable agriculture, waste management, environmental restoration and green entrepreneurship.

Another issue that deserves greater prominence in Nigeria’s climate diplomacy is the relationship between climate change and public health. Extreme heat, changing disease patterns, flooding, water contamination and air pollution are already creating additional public-health challenges across the developing world.

Nigeria should, therefore, approach climate action as an integrated development agenda involving the environment, health, agriculture, water resources, energy and education.

Climate-resilient healthcare facilities, heat-action plans, disease surveillance, clean cooking, and reliable water infrastructure should become important components of the country’s adaptation priorities.

Similarly, food security must feature prominently in the Nigerian position. Climate-smart agriculture, indigenous farming knowledge, irrigation, improved agricultural forecasting and resilient food systems are essential to protecting livelihoods.

Beyond formal negotiations, another dimension of climate action deserves greater attention: culture. Having followed the Entertainment and Culture for Climate Action conversations at COP31, I am increasingly convinced that the global climate movement must do more to recognise the power of storytelling, indigenous knowledge, and cultural participation.

Climate change is not merely a scientific phenomenon. It is a human experience, shaped by how people relate to their environment, understand their traditions and organise their communities. Across Africa, indigenous communities have developed knowledge systems for protecting forests, conserving water, managing agricultural landscapes and living within ecological limits.

As COP31 approaches its final days, Nigeria must look beyond the excitement of international participation and ask what concrete national priorities should emerge from the conference. First, the country must strengthen its capacity to access international adaptation finance and develop credible climate-resilient infrastructure projects.

Second, it must integrate hydrological intelligence, early-warning systems and community preparedness into national and subnational development planning. Third, it must pursue a just energy transition that recognises the realities of energy poverty, employment and industrial development.

Fourth, it must connect climate action with public health, food security, biodiversity conservation and the protection of vulnerable communities. And thirdly, Nigeria must recognise culture, indigenous knowledge and public communication as essential instruments of climate implementation.

These priorities also provide an opportunity for stronger collaboration among universities, government institutions, civil society, development partners and the private sector. The emerging challenge is to build institutions and partnerships that can turn international commitments into measurable results. Antalya’s real success will be determined by what happens when delegates go home.

The post COP31: Between climate promises and the unfinished business of development appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Building a working waste management system for Lagos
description:
For Lagos residents, an effective waste system means timely collection, clean streets and drains, and safe handling. Delivering it across Lagos is a complex challenge.
Lagos generates thousands of tonnes of waste daily. Managing it takes collection vehicles, roads and facilities, adequate funding, c
content:
For Lagos residents, an effective waste system means timely collection, clean streets and drains, and safe handling. Delivering it across Lagos is a complex challenge.

Lagos generates thousands of tonnes of waste daily. Managing it takes collection vehicles, roads and facilities, adequate funding, capable operators, oversight and public responsibility.

To picture the scale, at the upper estimate of 17,000 tonnes a day, Lagos’s waste weighs as much as 340,000 bags of 50kg rice. If each bag were laid end to end, they would stretch roughly 306 kilometres, about 26 times the 11.8-kilometre Third Mainland Bridge.

Waste management can also create businesses, jobs and environmental benefits. Since 1977, the Lagos Waste Management Authority has evolved with the city. Its efforts to improve collection, involve private waste companies, upgrade infrastructure and increase recycling provide a foundation to build on. The task now is to make the system more coordinated, financially sustainable and accountable, and this can be done on five pillars:

Plan around the waste Lagos actually produces: Household, market, industrial, construction and healthcare waste need different collection and treatment. Decisions should reflect how much of each type there is, what it contains and where it comes from.

A World Bank study found significant amounts of plastic in waste at Olusosun. But dumpsite waste may not represent all waste generated: informal collectors recover some materials, and some waste bypasses the formal system.

Regular waste studies across communities, markets and industrial areas should guide investment in collection, transport, recycling, food-waste processing, waste-to-energy and safe disposal. Each type needs a workable solution. Better information can show where useful materials are lost and services are missing.

Waste becomes a useful resource only when its quality, quantity, collection and buyers are understood. Without this evidence, facilities may be costly and underused.

Strengthen local accountability and central coordination: Waste services are local. Residents see missed collection in their streets and markets. Lagos State Waste Management Authority should set standards for the whole state and clarify local responsibility.

Each service area should have a named manager, clear standards and an easy way to report problems. Boundaries should reflect population, roads, waste volumes, company capacity and access to treatment or disposal sites.

Residents should know collection days, which company serves them and where to report missed service.

Private waste collection companies, often called PSP operators, remain essential. Their contracts need clear duties, fair incentives and transparent checks, with payment terms that support reliable service. LAWMA should coordinate infrastructure and enforce standards across Lagos. Reviews should assess both company performance and whether routes, equipment and payment terms allow reliable service.

Turn waste into useful products and jobs: Reliable collection can turn plastics, food waste, metals and paper into useful products, businesses and jobs. Organic waste is especially relevant in Lagos, with its food markets, hospitality businesses and manufacturers.

My work in organic waste recovery has shown how rubbish can become a useful resource. But a facility needs a steady supply of suitable material, reliable transport, skilled staff, operating capital and buyers. Poorly sorted or irregular supplies lower quality and raise costs, so collection must meet the needs of processors and customers.

The government can support this through clear rules, facilities and incentives; businesses can bring investment, expertise and customers. Bringing informal collectors and sorters into safer formal work can improve conditions, recycling and livelihoods.

Waste can also produce energy where the material, safeguards and costs make sense. No technology solves every waste problem. A circular economy keeps useful materials in use instead of dumping them.

Even with more recycling, some waste will still need safe disposal.

Fund the whole waste system: Building facilities is not enough. Collection vehicles need fuel and maintenance. Transfer stations, where waste is gathered before being moved, need reliable transport. Processing plants need money to operate and buyers for their products. Disposal sites need environmental controls and long-term management.

Lagos needs a plan to pay for collection, transport, treatment and disposal. Funding could combine public budgets, clear waste service charges, manufacturers helping pay to collect and recycle their packaging, private investment, sales of recovered materials and development finance. A credible plan should show who pays for each stage and how the money is tracked.

Charges should be clear and tied to reliable service, with support to protect lower-income communities. Investors need predictable rules, credible contracts, reliable information and confidence they will be paid as agreed.

Judge investments by whether facilities operate reliably and affordably over time, not simply by whether they are built.

Make performance visible and involve residents: Lagos should publish measures showing whether waste is collected on time, how much is collected and safely treated, how much is recycled, operating costs, illegal dumping and complaint resolution. Reports should distinguish proposed projects from facilities that are operating. Reliable, independently checked data would help residents judge progress and guide spending.

Residents, businesses and markets also have responsibilities. Sorting fails if waste is mixed together again during collection, and enforcement needs convenient disposal options. Schools, markets and community groups can promote good habits. Clear schedules, simple sorting instructions and incentives can help; enforcement should support reliable service, not replace it.

 Shared accountability means residents dispose of waste properly and government delivers reliable services.

 Lagos has delivered major infrastructure programmes; waste management deserves the same long-term commitment.

 The next phase should connect government, waste companies, investors, communities and businesses through clear policy, sound financing and measurable results.

 Lagos can move from simply moving rubbish to reliable collection, recycling, useful products and safe disposal, supporting health, jobs, business and a more resilient city.

 Success means waste is collected when promised, useful materials are recovered where possible, and the rest is handled safely. That is the foundation of a waste system fit for Lagos’s future.

 Olumide Thompson, an entrepreneur with a speciality in waste recovery and resource utilisation, writes via olumide.thompson@gmail.com

The post Building a working waste management system for Lagos appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Fani-Kayode’s ego trip to South Africa
description: The choleric man Nigeria appointed as its ambassador to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, had not even spent a full day at his duty post when he started breaking things apart. On Saturday, after the occasion when Fani-Kayode and 14 other ambassador-designates presented their letters of credence to Pre
content:
The choleric man Nigeria appointed as its ambassador to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, had not even spent a full day at his duty post when he started breaking things apart. On Saturday, after the occasion when Fani-Kayode and 14 other ambassador-designates presented their letters of credence to President Cyril Ramaphosa, our man jumped on Twitter to rant about how the South African Presidency deliberately cut off the Nigerian delegation (him, actually) from the broadcast during the ceremony (it turns out that he got that detail wrong; it was the SABC that supposedly did). Before long, he had dragged the Nigerian High Commission in South Africa, the South African presidency, and the South African Broadcasting Corporation into an impolite exchange online and elsewhere. In his Twitter post, Fani-Kayode moaned that ‘some elements in South Africa do not want to hear what we have to say or see our faces, but we are here as long as we are welcome and have the confidence of President Ramaphosa, which I am sure we do.’ In that sentence alone, Fani-Kayode proved himself unfit for the exalted position to which Bola Tinubu, the renowned headhunter, promoted him.

First, you must be the most unthinking man in the world to imagine your actions endeared you to President Ramaphosa to the point that you would pit him against his people. Second, if they truly do not want to see or hear you, have you not justified their prejudice? If you want to act like an agbero, you could have done yourself a favour and waited until you returned to Lagos. Nigeria is not small among countries where our national representative will have a full-blown public meltdown simply because a South African media channel refused to platform him. Nigeria has many challenges, but what we do not lack by any measure are electronic media platforms to platform ourselves. If the situation were reversed, would a South African envoy to Nigeria have gone crazy because a Nigerian television station did not cover his speech? What is so earth-shaking about what you have to say that the world must stop to acknowledge you? By Fani-Kayode’s own admission, two Nigerian television stations were present at the event and recorded the ceremony. You could simply have shared their recording of the event instead of disgracing yourself. Also, if you truly suspect you were deliberately slighted, you could have raised the issue through official channels or back channels. Why yell like a college fresher who just discovered aluta? He has barely started at the job, and they have already censured him. That is not to Nigeria’s credit.

All this drama was Tinubu’s fault because, if he were the sort of person who recruits people based on merit and not because of how much they can worship his majestic ego, he should never have made a temperamental fiend like Fani-Kayode an ambassador. Yorubas popularly analogise character with smoke. They say you can try hard to bottle character, but it will seep out somehow and express its nature. That is why Fani-Kayode could not even wait to learn if his suspicions about SABC were valid or not before he started smoking out and polluting the air. He is irascible, the type of person who does not care for decorum and takes a fight public easily. Meanwhile, he does not go public to engage in a battle of ideas or take a principled stance, but merely to yell and insult. His domestic affairs are public entertainment because he is constantly getting into spats and shouting matches. Not too long ago, he and one of his wives took their domestic issues public, and they did not stop talking until they had shredded their mutual dignity. His wife blames his problems on his erectile dysfunction, and he calls her “crazy.”

The same Fani-Kayode once got into a Twitter spat with Jimoh Ibrahim, and running out of insults, began to spew homophobic insults. That alone should ordinarily disqualify him from public office if Tinubu took standards and accountability seriously. Who can forget how Fani-Kayode tore into a Daily Trust journalist, Eyo Charles, during a press briefing in Calabar, Cross River State? The journalist had simply done his job of asking him a pertinent question, only for Fani-Kayode to explode in rage. His mercurial nature extends to his political habits. He has a history of spouting tribalistic nonsense depending on which part of the political divide he finds himself. The same Fani-Kayode who labelled the APC with ethnic and religious slurs (he called them the party of the “janjaweed” and “the Taliban”) defected to join them once they won the 2015 election. Unstable as water, he will swing in any and every direction.

For someone emotionally dysregulated, lacking self-mastery, and too uncouth for civilised company like Fani-Kayode, a diplomatic assignment was tantamount to casting pearls before a swine. Even if he had to be compensated with an ambassadorial position, he should not have been assigned to South Africa, whose xenophobic citizens frequently threaten the welfare of Nigerians. The ambassador you send to a country like South Africa must be a person of great wisdom, who understands the art of diplomacy, is assertive, and level-headed without being a pushover. S/he must understand that it is not cowardice to approach an issue with diplomatic tact. Even if you are a registered aluta warrior, in that role you must set your insurgent tendencies aside; you do not alienate the people with whom you are supposed to work.

The Nigerian High Commission said Fani-Kayode was treated with ‘contempt and disdain, and by extension so was Nigeria.’ I disagree. Nigeria was disdained by its own thin-skinned representative. Nobody in Nigeria would have lost anything if Fani-Kayode had not dragged us into his ego fights. The shame is on him for using the Nigerian High Commission in South Africa to spill out his unedited guts online. Some characters, like Former Kaduna Central Senator Shehu Sani, applauded Fani-Kayode for reacting hormonally when he should have let reason prevail. They seem to have confused the nature of international diplomacy with the gbas gbos language of the internet in which they are well-versed. You break the walls of hostilities by building good relations, not by acting before thinking. Even if you must break protocols and take an issue public, it should be on substantial issues, not petty matters like whether they put you on their television or not. No ambassador who goes around howling for “respect” will be taken seriously; if he does not learn to discipline himself, he will simply be ignored.

Now that the news report of Fani-Kayode’s past confession of having been previously treated for mental illness is circulating around South Africa, I am reminded of Nwibe, a character from Chinua Achebe’s short story, The Madman. A prosperous man, Nwibe was about to take the prestigious Ozo title when he let his emotions get the better of him. He chases a madman into the marketplace, gets mistaken for a madman, and subsequently loses his social prestige. The story concludes that anytime Nwibe asks the elders about his pending Ozo title, they change the subject. Just like no one would take Nwibe seriously again, South Africans are reading the report, looking at an ambassador who typed furious things on Twitter, and thinking, “no wonder.” Sincerely, I am not so bothered that Fani-Kayode will be looked on by South Africans as an aláwòkù—a sick person who has been treated for their madness, but whose actions still contain the residues of lunacy. My rage is that their thoughts about his state of mental health will affect the thousands of Nigerians who live, study, and work in that country, and on whose behalf he is supposed to advocate.

The post Fani-Kayode’s ego trip to South Africa appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Return of violent campaigns
description: IT is déjà vu, and a particularly ugly one. As Nigeria inches towards the January and February 2027 general elections, political violence is once again rearing its ugly head, with thugs and armed gangs turning campaign grounds into theatres of bloodshed. This barbaric culture is not only destructive
content:
IT is déjà vu, and a particularly ugly one. As Nigeria inches towards the January and February 2027 general elections, political violence is once again rearing its ugly head, with thugs and armed gangs turning campaign grounds into theatres of bloodshed. This barbaric culture is not only destructive but also an indictment of a political class that has repeatedly shown little regard for human lives or democratic values.

Violence is a major reason Nigerians are increasingly losing faith in elections and staying away from polling booths. When campaigning becomes potentially fatal, democracy is the ultimate casualty.

In recent days, rival political thugs have disrupted campaigns and political gatherings in Delta, Benue, Gombe, Enugu, Lagos, Ekiti and Kano states.

In Bichi, Kano State, thugs attacked Rabiu Kwankwaso, the National Democratic Congress presidential running mate.

In Lagos, hoodlums invaded an NDC town hall meeting in Ikeja on November 12. The Ekiti State chapter of the Peoples Democratic Party alleged that political thugs attacked its deputy governorship candidate.

Similar incidents have been reported in Gombe and Enugu, further heightening tensions, although police claim they made some arrests.

The National Peace Committee’s monitoring report, covering August 19 to October 27, documented 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord across 26 states and the Federal Capital Territory in just 10 weeks.

That translates to an average of about 11 violations weekly, an alarming indication of how rapidly the political environment is deteriorating.

Political violence and thuggery topped the list with 33 incidents, representing 30.3 per cent of the total. Misinformation and disinformation accounted for another 29 cases, or 26.6 per cent.

Attacks on political activities and campaign assets recorded 19 incidents (17.4 per cent), while intimidation and threats accounted for 15 (13.8 per cent). The report documented seven restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly, four inflammatory statements, one intra-party conflict and one case of voter inducement.

The committee identified Kaduna, Edo and Enugu as election flashpoints, citing recurring violence, armed disruptions and other security concerns. The FCT recorded seven incidents, while Kaduna had the highest number, with nine.

The findings should alarm every Nigerian who values democracy. The committee called for investigations into reported violations and urged security agencies to provide equal protection for lawful campaign activities.

It challenged political parties and candidates to condemn violence, disown armed groups and ensure accountability for threats and intimidation.

President Bola Tinubu has rightly called for peace, stressing that political differences should not turn opponents into enemies.

The House of Representatives has also expressed concern and urged peaceful electioneering.

But condemnations and appeals will remain empty rhetoric unless backed by decisive action against perpetrators and their sponsors.

INEC has fixed January 16, 2027, for the presidential and National Assembly elections, while governorship and state House of Assembly elections will hold on February 6. Campaigns for the first set of elections began on August 19, while those for the latter commenced on September 9.

Before the campaigns began, 19 political parties signed the National Peace Accord in Abuja on August 18, committing themselves to 12 standards designed to promote peaceful, issue-based electioneering.

They pledged to reject violence, threats and intimidation, disseminate truthful political information, use digital media responsibly, encourage inclusive participation, respect electoral and security institutions, reject the partisan misuse of public authority and maintain civil communication.

The gulf between these lofty commitments and the reality on the ground is disturbing.

Political parties cannot sign peace agreements with one hand and unleash thugs with the other. Their candidates cannot preach democracy while their supporters intimidate, maim and terrorise opponents.

Worse, the violence is already becoming a familiar feature of Nigeria’s electoral landscape.

Ahead of the August 15 governorship election in Osun State, at least 30 people were reportedly killed in election-related violence.

On October 30, a viral video captured suspected thugs attacking the African Action Congress presidential candidate, Omoyele Sowore, and his supporters with machetes in Ado-Ekiti, Ekiti State.

The police subsequently described the incident as an altercation, a characterisation that raises more questions than it answers. Such casual dismissal of a violent attack undermines public confidence in the police and their willingness to investigate political crimes impartially.

The historical toll is even more chilling. At least 870 people have reportedly died in election-related violence since 2015: 106 in 2015, 626 in 2019 and 109 in 2023, according to figures attributed to the NPC, led by former Head of State, Abdulsalami Abubakar. This is in addition to the estimated 800 Nigerians killed in the post-election violence of 2011.

It is unacceptable that lives are being cut short, families shattered and communities scarred by the primitive pursuit of political power. That Nigeria continues to tolerate such bloodletting decades after independence is a damning indictment of its democratic development.

The frightening expression, “Rig & Die,” now circulating in the tense political atmosphere ahead of 2027, is another ominous sign. It reflects a growing fear.

No election, however fiercely contested, should become a licence for bloodshed. Neither rigging nor the threat of violence in response to it can be justified in a democracy.

Political violence is barbaric, undemocratic and indefensible. If politics is fundamentally about competing interests and the contest for public office, what possible justification can there be for taking another person’s life over an ephemeral political advantage? No office is worth a human life.

The security agencies have been conspicuously inadequate in confronting this menace. Their responsibility is not merely to provide security for political rallies but also to identify, arrest and prosecute those who sponsor, finance and execute attacks.

Selective enforcement or the tendency to dismiss politically sensitive incidents as ordinary disagreements will only embolden the perpetrators.

INEC and the security agencies must therefore move beyond routine assurances. They must guarantee equal protection for all candidates and parties, regardless of political affiliation, investigate reported attacks promptly and ensure that those responsible face the full weight of the law.

Nigeria has no shortage of historical warnings. The infamous ‘Operation Wetie’ killings in the old Western Region, characterised by arson and political bloodletting, contributed to the instability that culminated in the collapse of the First Republic.

Yet, decades later, politicians are still exploiting poverty, unemployment and youth frustration to recruit impressionable young people as instruments of political violence.

They arm them, pay them to intimidate opponents and abandon them when the political battles are over. This cynical weaponisation of poverty is a vicious cycle that must be broken.

The Ambassador and Head of Delegation of the European Union to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Gautier Mignot, has warned that political violence undermines democratic gains and prevents citizens from participating fully in the electoral process. He is right.

A democracy in which citizens cannot freely attend rallies, express political preferences or vote without fear is democracy in name only.

The Electoral Act 2026 provides a legal framework for confronting electoral offences. Section 96 outlines relevant offences and penalties, while Sections 148, 150 and 151 place responsibilities on INEC concerning the investigation and prosecution of electoral offences. The provisions must not remain decorative clauses in a statute book.

It is against this background that the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project has given INEC seven days to obtain from the Nigeria Police Force case files and relevant investigation materials concerning persons arrested over reported incidents of electoral and political violence since the commencement of the 2027 campaigns. It demanded the prompt prosecution.

This is a welcome intervention. INEC cannot continue to express concern about electoral violence while those responsible enjoy impunity.

The police cannot make arrests and allow investigations to disappear into bureaucratic limbo. The sponsors of political thuggery must also be pursued, not just the foot soldiers who wield machetes and other weapons.

Public institutions must be held accountable for their constitutional and statutory responsibilities. Democracy cannot thrive where political violence is rewarded with impunity and public office becomes a prize worth killing for.

The 2027 elections must not become another grim chapter in Nigeria’s history of electoral bloodshed. The time to act is now, before the campaign trail becomes a killing field and the country’s democratic future is once again held hostage by political desperados.

title: Lessons from US midterms
description: IN keeping with pre-election projections, the Democratic Party secured a landslide in America’s November 3 midterm elections. It is proof of how genuine democracy works and sustains itself. Voters reward performance and punish failure. They vote according to their daily realities, rather than politi
content:
IN keeping with pre-election projections, the Democratic Party secured a landslide in America’s November 3 midterm elections. It is proof of how genuine democracy works and sustains itself. Voters reward performance and punish failure. They vote according to their daily realities, rather than political slogans or burdensome promises. What unfolded across America was a referendum on the Donald Trump administration.

Nigeria’s political leadership should draw valuable lessons from the blue wave.

The Republicans lost control of Congress – the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The Democrats captured (flipped) Senate seats in traditional Republican strongholds such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas. Kansas had not elected a Democratic senator in almost a century. This reflected deep public dissatisfaction with the direction of President Trump. He now faces a difficult two years left in his White House tenure, which Americans dub “a lame-duck presidency.”

His approval rating crashed to an average of just 39 per cent, while 59 per cent of Americans disapproved of his performance. The rejection came even from voters in states he had comfortably won only two years earlier.

The message from the electorate was clear: lived experience matters far more than campaign promises or the size of an incumbent’s ego.

The American voters’ primary concerns were inflation, expensive food items and other daily needs, and rising energy costs. They griped about high tariffs and the war in Iran.

Trump’s immigration policy was also a factor, as many voters believed that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents had crossed the line in Trump’s crackdown on immigrants. Some citizens who contributed significantly to sectors such as agriculture, construction, hospitality and childcare were rounded up and pushed out. There were fatalities too.

Perceptions of corruption further damaged the administration. Trump’s cryptocurrency ventures and financial dealings with foreign interests reportedly came under intense scrutiny. The president reportedly earned about $2.2 billion in 2025, with more than half attributed to cryptocurrency businesses.

American voters took note.

For Nigerians, the more than three and a half years of the Bola Tinubu administration have brought extraordinary economic hardship. To be fair, some of the administration’s reforms have produced measurable gains.

The removal of the petrol subsidies has largely eliminated persistent fuel shortages. The foreign exchange reforms have also significantly reduced uncertainty in the currency market.

Yet these gains have come at enormous cost. Petrol sells for between N1,300 and N1,400 per litre. This has dramatically increased transportation costs, food prices and the cost of virtually every essential service.

In a country that pays a minimum wage of N70,000, this matters. Inflation at around 14.05 per cent eats up incomes and pushes millions deeper into hardship.

Insecurity is pervasive. Nigeria ranks among the most terrorised countries globally, and over two million citizens remain displaced in internally displaced persons’ camps.

More than 140 million Nigerians live in multidimensional poverty. Healthcare, education, electricity, manufacturing and agriculture continue to struggle despite repeated government assurances.

Many citizens question government priorities. Projects such as the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway have generated considerable debate at a time when many believe scarce public resources should be directed toward hospitals, schools, security, rural roads, food production and social protection.

History documents such electoral earthquakes when the electorate used their votes to express dissatisfaction with incumbent governments.

In Venezuela’s 2015 parliamentary elections, the opposition Democratic Unity Roundtable secured a stunning two-thirds majority in the National Assembly. That upset ended 16 years of legislative dominance by President Nicolás Maduro’s ruling party. Soaring inflation, dwindling oil revenues, food shortages and widespread economic misery drove voters to the opposition.

The Taiwanese delivered a similar verdict in the 2022 local elections, with the opposition Kuomintang capturing 13 of the 22 mayoral and magistrate seats. It was the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s worst electoral defeat. Voters were concerned about economic conditions, infrastructure and governance.

Argentina followed the same pattern in its 2021 legislative midterm elections. President Alberto Fernández’s governing coalition suffered heavy losses as inflation exceeded 50 per cent and poverty worsened.

The scandal of a birthday party at the presidential residence was probably the last straw. Citizens concluded that leaders who asked for sacrifice should themselves demonstrate discipline and accountability.

Across the democratic world, economic hardship, insecurity, corruption and poor governance carry political consequences.

For Nigeria’s political class, the challenge is especially urgent. With less than two months before the polls, there is hardly any room for dramatic policy corrections.

But beyond this election cycle, one lesson must not be lost. Leaders must never become insulated from the citizens. Lived experiences matter more than government statistics.

America’s blue wave is a reminder that democracy ultimately belongs to the people.

title: Jigawa herder-farmer clash leaves three killed, two injured
description:
No fewer than three persons have been killed following a violent clash between suspected herders and local farmers at the Wauta Fulani settlement in Rafin Marke Ward, Kanya District, Garki Local Government Area of Jigawa State.
PUNCH Metro learnt on Wednesday that the violence, which reportedly star
content:
No fewer than three persons have been killed following a violent clash between suspected herders and local farmers at the Wauta Fulani settlement in Rafin Marke Ward, Kanya District, Garki Local Government Area of Jigawa State.

PUNCH Metro learnt on Wednesday that the violence, which reportedly started at about 3am, left at least two other residents with varying degrees of injuries.

Details of the violent clash were contained in a statement by the spokesperson for the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, Badruddeen Mahmud.

According to the NSCDC, the violence, which occurred on Wednesday, started when a herd of cattle from the Babura Local Government Area axis, belonging to suspected herders, encroached on a guinea corn farm reportedly owned by a resident identified only as Amadu Saleh.

Following attempts by the farmers to save their crops from being grazed by the cattle, the statement said they were allegedly attacked with dangerous weapons, including cutlasses, bows and arrows.

The violence reportedly resulted in the death of 35-year-old Amiru Saleh, while two other farmers, Amadu Saleh (50) and Haruna Saleh (37), sustained injuries.

“The ensuing reprisal led to the death of two unidentified members of the herding group, while the remaining herders fled with their cattle towards Gabasawa Local Government Area of neighbouring Kano State.

“All three deceased individuals were evacuated to Garki General Hospital, where medical personnel confirmed their deaths.

“While Amiru Saleh’s remains were released to his family around 11:30 am on Wednesday for burial according to religious rites, the bodies of the two unidentified herders remain at the hospital morgue pending official identification and further procedures.”

The statement added that the NSCDC had deployed operatives alongside sister security agencies to monitor the area, maintain law and order, and prevent a breakdown of peace in the affected communities.

Reacting to the incident, the State Commandant of the NSCDC, Muhammad Ingawa, warned residents against taking the law into their own hands or staging further reprisal attacks.

“The State Commandant strongly cautions residents against taking the law into their own hands or engaging in reprisal attacks. He urges members of the public to remain calm, exercise restraint, and promptly report any suspicious movements or security threats to the appropriate authorities,” the statement added.

The incident comes less than a week after a similar clash led to the death of one person, while two others sustained varying degrees of injuries following a confrontation between herders and a convoy of unidentified political campaign vehicles in the Guri Local Government Area of Jigawa State.

According to a report by PUNCH Metro on Monday, the fatal incident occurred along the Abunabo–Jangon Fulani Road, Kadira District, Guri LGA, on Saturday at about 6:40pm.

The post Jigawa herder-farmer clash leaves three killed, two injured appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Four C’River youths nabbed for alleged motorcycle theft
description:
Four youths have been arrested by the Cross River State Police Command over their alleged involvement in two separate motorcycle-snatching incidents in the Akamkpa Local Government Area of the state.
The suspects, identified as Oyo Effiong Nakanda, 40; Udeme Bright Felix, 23; Saviour Victor Felicia,
content:
Four youths have been arrested by the Cross River State Police Command over their alleged involvement in two separate motorcycle-snatching incidents in the Akamkpa Local Government Area of the state.

The suspects, identified as Oyo Effiong Nakanda, 40; Udeme Bright Felix, 23; Saviour Victor Felicia, 18; and Moses Ernest Felicia, 17, were arrested at about 5.47am on Wednesday following a tip-off from a member of the public.

The command disclosed this in a statement issued by its Police Public Relations Officer, ASP Sunday Akata, on Wednesday.

Akata said operatives of the Violent Crime Response Unit, Section 2, Akamkpa, carried out an intelligence-led operation at a suspected hideout along the Calabar–Ikom Highway before Ekomita Junction, leading to the arrest of the suspects.

He added that a machete and suspected criminal charms were recovered during the operation.

The police spokesperson said the suspects were being investigated in connection with two separate motorcycle-snatching incidents reported at Hitech Junction and Usang Road, both in Akamkpa.

According to him, investigations are ongoing to establish their possible involvement in the incidents, recover other weapons, identify and arrest other accomplices, and determine whether they are linked to other criminal activities.

The Commissioner of Police, Cross River State Command, CP Ajo Geoffrey Ordue, commended the operatives for their prompt response and acknowledged the contribution of the informant.

He reaffirmed the command’s commitment to intelligence-led policing and urged residents to continue providing credible and timely information to security agencies.

“The investigation will be pursued professionally,” the commissioner assured, while encouraging residents to report suspicious activities or emergencies through the command’s control room numbers: 0704 177 7060 and 0705 335 5415.

The post Four C’River youths nabbed for alleged motorcycle theft appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
