title: Senate urges INEC to disqualify candidates over violence
description:
By Henry Umoru



ABUJA — The Senate has urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to disqualify political candidates found, through established court convictions, to have instigated or participated in electoral violence, irrespective of their party affiliations.







The upper ch
content:
By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — The Senate has urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to disqualify political candidates found, through established court convictions, to have instigated or participated in electoral violence, irrespective of their party affiliations.

The upper chamber also called on state governors to stop denying opposition parties access to public facilities, including hotels and stadia under their control, for political activities.

The resolutions followed the adoption of a motion sponsored by Senator Abdul Ningi (Bauchi Central) on Tuesday, expressing concern over the growing incidence of political violence, intolerance and attacks on political leaders and their supporters ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The Senate condemned what it described as the increasing frequency and spread of political violence across the country, warning that attacks on political leaders, supporters and political gatherings posed threats to national security, democratic participation and the peaceful conduct of the 2027 elections.

It also urged security agencies to conduct impartial and transparent investigations into reported incidents of political violence in Abuja, Edo, Delta and Sokoto states, identify the perpetrators and their sponsors, and ensure their prosecution in accordance with the law.

The lawmakers further called on the Federal Government to direct the Inspector-General of Police and other security agencies to strengthen security arrangements for political leaders, candidates, supporters and political gatherings nationwide.

They urged the establishment of effective early-warning and rapid-response mechanisms to prevent attacks and other forms of violence ahead of the elections.

The Senate also mandated its Committees on National Security and Intelligence, Police Affairs, and INEC to engage relevant institutions and report back within one week on measures to prevent political violence and safeguard the 2027 general elections.

The motion followed reported attacks on political figures and gatherings, including the incident involving President Bola Tinubu’s motorcade after he observed Friday prayers at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque, Garki, Abuja.

Presenting the motion, Ningi recalled reported attacks on former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi and other political stakeholders in Benue, the disruption of a political procession involving supporters of the Nigeria Democratic Congress and the Obidient Movement in Asaba, Delta State, on November 7, which reportedly left one person dead and five others injured, as well as an attack on the convoy of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar in Sokoto State.

He warned that failure to investigate and prosecute those responsible for political violence could encourage further attacks, deepen political divisions and undermine public confidence in the electoral process.

Contributing, Senate President Godswill Akpabio urged INEC to enforce the provisions of the Electoral Act 2026 against electoral violence, stressing that offenders should face the consequences prescribed by law.

Akpabio said Sections 121 to 128 of the Act provided for offences relating to electoral violence, intimidation and the snatching of Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) machines, ballot boxes and other electoral materials.

He said the lawmakers had recommended penalties ranging from 12 months to five years’ imprisonment, without an option of fine for aggravated offences involving attacks with dangerous objects.

According to him, Section 92 also empowers INEC to suspend elections in areas where violence is reported and reschedule them within 24 hours.

He added that the Electoral Offences Commission Bill 2025, passed alongside the Electoral Act, provided for a dedicated mechanism to address electoral offences, including vote-buying, violence and attacks on electoral officials.

Akpabio said the enactment of the laws placed responsibility on the executive to ensure their effective implementation.

In another resolution, following an additional prayer by Senator Sampson Ekong (Akwa Ibom South), the Senate urged the Federal Ministry of Information and the National Orientation Agency to intensify public enlightenment campaigns against political violence.

Ekong said legal provisions alone would not adequately address the problem without sustained public awareness, particularly among young people who could be recruited into violent political activities.

Also contributing, Senator Binos Yaroe (Adamawa South) urged state governors to ensure that opposition parties and candidates were not denied access to public facilities, including arenas and hotels controlled by state governments.

He said restrictions on such facilities could undermine the principle of a level playing field for political parties and create avoidable political tensions.

Senator Ali Ndume (Borno South) supported the motion and proposed that security agencies prohibit the carrying of dangerous weapons during political campaigns.

He called for the arrest of anyone found carrying knives, sticks or other harmful objects at campaign venues, irrespective of political affiliation.

Ndume also proposed the establishment of mobile courts to ensure the prompt prosecution of offenders during campaign activities.

He said political campaigns should be conducted with legitimate campaign materials rather than weapons, adding that the measures should apply equally to all political parties, including the ruling All Progressives Congress.

Ndume further cautioned against campaign slogans that could heighten political tensions, citing slogans such as “Tinubu Must Go”, “Atiku Must Go” and “Obi Must Go”.

He said political disagreements should be resolved through peaceful engagement rather than violence.

Senator Sumaila Kawu (Kano South) also expressed concern over the presence of supporters carrying dangerous weapons at political gatherings.

Kawu described it as a shame for candidates contesting elections into the Senate, House of Representatives or governorship positions to be surrounded by supporters carrying weapons.

He questioned the conduct of politicians who, despite making laws against electoral violence, allowed their supporters to engage in activities capable of undermining the electoral process.

“It is a shame to see candidates contesting for the Senate, House of Representatives or governorship surrounded by supporters carrying dangerous weapons. Where are we going as lawmakers when we appear to encourage conduct that violates the laws we enacted?” he said.

The Senate urged political parties, candidates and their supporters to embrace peaceful political engagement and respect the rule of law ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Speaking on the significance of the recognit
content:
Media expert, public analyst, and the Publisher, 4th Estate Reporters, Njoku Macdonald Obinna, has joined other prominent Nigerians to congratulate High Chief Anthony Obele on his recognition by The Sun Publishing Limited as the Investor of the Year 2026.

Speaking on the significance of the recognition and the broader implications of the 24th edition of the award, Obinna, who attended the ceremony, described the recognition of Dr. Obele as a significant moment for indigenous entrepreneurship and investment in Nigeria.

He noted that the true value of investment should not be measured exclusively by financial returns but, also, by its impact on infrastructure, employment generation, economic empowerment, and community development.

He stated: “The recognition of High Chief Dr. Anthony Ikenna Obele as Investor of the Year particularly draws attention to the importance of indigenous investment in our national development.

“I strongly believe that Nigeria’s economic transformation cannot be left to the government alone. We need visionary entrepreneurs and investors who are willing to commit resources, build businesses, create employment opportunities, and participate in addressing the infrastructure challenges confronting our communities.

“One thing that stands out about this recognition is the opportunity it provides us to look beyond the award itself and examine the responsibilities that come with investment. Building a successful business is commendable, but building an enterprise that contributes to the economy and creates opportunities for other people is even more significant.

“High Chief Obele’s recognition should encourage more Nigerian entrepreneurs, particularly young people, to appreciate the importance of productive investment, innovation, local capacity development, and long-term economic planning.

“An award is an honour, but the greatest achievement is the legacy an individual leaves behind through the lives touched, opportunities created, and communities positively impacted,” he said.

title: COP31: African workers declare ‘no more empty promises’ as unions demand climate justice, decent jobs
description:
By Victor Ahiuma-Young



Representing 18 million organised workers across 52 African countries, the International Trade Union Confederation–Africa, ITUC-Africa, has challenged world leaders at COP31 to move beyond climate change rhetoric and deliver concrete action, demanding climate finance, decen
content:
By Victor Ahiuma-Young

Representing 18 million organised workers across 52 African countries, the International Trade Union Confederation–Africa, ITUC-Africa, has challenged world leaders at COP31 to move beyond climate change rhetoric and deliver concrete action, demanding climate finance, decent green jobs, workers’ protection and a just transition that puts African workers at the centre of decision-making.

The African workers, under the banner of ITUC-Africa, issued the message at the COP31 Political March in Antalya, Turkey, declaring that the continent’s workforce would no longer tolerate empty promises and delayed commitments on climate action.
In a statement by its General Secretary, Akhator Joel Odigie, the regional labour organisation warned that African workers were bearing the devastating consequences of climate change despite contributing comparatively little to the crisis.

Speaking under the theme, “Deliver, Don’t Delay – Move from Dialogue to Action,” Odigie said the climate emergency was no longer an abstract environmental concern but an immediate threat to workers’ lives, livelihoods and fundamental labour rights.
“We are the 18 million organised workers of Africa, represented here by ITUC-Africa across 52 countries. We are the ones who build, transport, farm, mine, and power this continent. And we are the ones who will pay the highest price if COP31 ends in more talk and no delivery,” he declared.


He stressed that workers were already experiencing the devastating effects of extreme weather conditions, including unbearable workplace heat, destructive flooding and prolonged droughts that threaten agricultural production and community livelihoods.
“The climate crisis is not abstract for us. It is the unbearable heat on a construction site, the flood that destroys a community, the drought that kills a harvest,” Odigie stated.


Citing International Trade Union Confederation data, he disclosed that extreme workplace heat already claims nearly 19,000 lives annually, while heat stress could wipe out working hours equivalent to 136 million full-time jobs by 2030.

“This is a labour rights crisis. And it demands a labour response,” he insisted.

Workers reject slow progress on climate commitments

ITUC-Africa expressed concern that despite COP31 being presented as the “COP of implementation,” progress on translating climate commitments into tangible benefits for workers and vulnerable communities remained inadequate.

The organisation particularly criticised the slow progress on the Just Transition Work Programme, arguing that workers’ rights and participation must not be relegated to the margins of climate negotiations.

According to Odigie, although procedural progress had been recorded, the mechanism’s design remained unresolved, with no substantive agreement reached on how it would operate.

“The Just Transition Work Program—the one space where workers’ rights should be front and centre—has made procedural progress, but its mechanism design is still open, with no substantive agreement yet,” he said.

He maintained that the ongoing negotiations in Antalya represented a critical opportunity to move from discussions to concrete commitments that would guarantee workers a meaningful role in shaping the continent’s economic and environmental future.

Demands climate finance, not debt

A major concern raised by the African labour movement is the persistent inequality in global climate financing, particularly the limited resources reaching African countries despite the continent’s vulnerability to climate change.

ITUC-Africa noted that while the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap seeks to mobilise $1.3 trillion annually by 2035, sub-Saharan Africa receives less than three per cent of global climate finance, with much of the funding provided through loans rather than grants.

The organisation also highlighted the funding gap surrounding the Loss and Damage Fund, stating that although $826 million had been pledged, only $456 million had actually been received.

Odigie further expressed disappointment that the African Group of Negotiators’ push to triple adaptation finance had not received a standalone agenda slot.

He argued that African countries should not be forced to accumulate more debt to address a climate crisis they contributed relatively little to creating.

“So when we say ‘deliver,’ we mean: stop congratulating yourselves on roadmaps and start signing the cheques, with grants, not debt,” he declared.

The labour movement called on developed countries to provide new, additional, predictable and adequate climate financing, primarily through grants and highly concessional public financing.

It also demanded debt relief, progressive taxation and windfall taxes on extractive industry profits as alternative ways of mobilising resources for climate action and essential public services.

“Africa should not be forced to borrow its way out of a crisis it did not cause. We reject loans as climate contributions,” the statement stressed.

New form of economic colonialism

ITUC-Africa also warned that the global transition to clean energy must not become another avenue for exploiting Africa’s natural resources while denying its people the economic benefits of industrialisation.

The organisation argued that Africa must move beyond exporting unprocessed critical minerals, including lithium and cobalt, and develop the capacity to process these resources locally.

It insisted that the continent’s mineral wealth should support industrial development, create decent employment opportunities and improve the living standards of African workers.

“The global energy transition must not become a new colonialism. Africa must use this shift to industrialise, not remain a supplier of unprocessed raw materials,” Odigie declared.

He called for local processing of critical minerals to ensure that the jobs and economic opportunities generated by the global green transition remain within African economies.

The organisation also warned against the potential impact of the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism on African producers and workers, arguing that the costs of the global transition should not be unfairly transferred to developing economies.
Another major demand is the establishment of an effective Just Transition Mechanism that guarantees workers formal representation and meaningful influence over decisions concerning employment, investment and industrial transformation.

ITUC-Africa maintained that workers must be involved in designing and implementing national transition pathways rather than being subjected to decisions reached without their participation.

It called for the operationalisation of a mechanism capable of providing technical assistance, capacity-building and financial support to countries pursuing climate-friendly economic transformations.
“A mechanism without worker participation is a shell. Trade unions must have formal representation and meaningful influence—not token consultations—in decisions affecting employment, investment, and industrial transformation,” he said.

He added that the proposed Belém–Antalya Mechanism must be developed in partnership with workers and their representative organisations.

“The proposed Belém–Antalya Mechanism must be built with us, not for us,” he emphasised.

Protect jobs, workers’ safety

The African trade union body further demanded comprehensive employment and social protection measures to ensure that the transition to a green economy does not leave millions of workers unemployed or economically vulnerable.

It called for employment-impact assessments, skills development, retraining, redeployment opportunities, job or income guarantees, occupational safety and health protections, and universal social protection to be incorporated into every transition plan.

The organisation stressed that women, young people, migrant workers and those employed in the informal economy required specific protection because of their vulnerability to economic and environmental disruptions.

Particular attention was drawn to extreme workplace heat, which ITUC-Africa said must be formally recognised as an occupational hazard, with enforceable safety measures introduced to protect workers.

The organisation argued that climate policies would remain incomplete if they addressed environmental sustainability without guaranteeing decent working conditions, employment security and social protection.
In a message, ITUC-Africa warned that COP31 must not become another international climate conference where vulnerable populations are asked to wait while governments and global institutions continue making promises without delivering results.

Odigie argued that the consequences of global warming were already being felt, making urgent action essential to prevent African workers from bearing an even greater share of the crisis.

“The question is not whether we will transition—the question is whether that transition will be just, or whether it will leave millions of African workers behind while a few extract the profits of a green economy built on our backs,” he warned.

He insisted that African workers were not attending the climate negotiations merely to appeal for sympathy but to demand their rightful place in decisions that would determine their economic future.

“We are not here to beg. We are here to negotiate. We are here to demand. And we are here to stay,” he declared.

Reaffirming the organisation’s position, he outlined four central demands: climate finance through grants rather than debt; an operational Just Transition Mechanism with workers fully represented; African industrialisation rather than continued extraction of raw materials; and decent, green and unionised jobs for the continent’s workforce.
He said: “Deliver the finance—grants, not debt. Deliver the Just Transition Mechanism—with workers inside, not outside. Deliver industrialisation—not extraction. Deliver decent, green, unionised jobs for Africa’s workers.”

Odigie concluded with a call for world leaders to translate their climate commitments into measurable outcomes, stressing that African workers would continue to press for accountability and justice.
“Move from dialogue to action, now,” he declared, ending his address with the rallying cry, “Amandla!”

The post COP31: African workers declare ‘no more empty promises’ as unions demand climate justice, decent jobs appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Kolmani oilfield set for December exploration resumption – Gombe
description:
The Gombe State Government says oil exploration activities in the Kolmani oil field are expected to resume in the first week of December 2026, as it intensifies efforts to prepare residents for emerging opportunities in the oil and gas sector.
The Commissioner for Energy and Mineral Resources, Sanus
content:
The Gombe State Government says oil exploration activities in the Kolmani oil field are expected to resume in the first week of December 2026, as it intensifies efforts to prepare residents for emerging opportunities in the oil and gas sector.

The Commissioner for Energy and Mineral Resources, Sanusi Pindiga, disclosed this on Monday while briefing journalists on the outcome of the 57th State Executive Council meeting.

Pindiga said the government’s consultant, Rift Oil Nigeria Limited, had completed 12 of 14 deliverables under its engagement to facilitate Gombe’s institutional recognition and registration as an oil and gas-producing state.

He said the progress was aimed at positioning the state to benefit from the anticipated resumption of exploration activities while equipping its citizens with relevant skills.

According to the commissioner, 100 graduates have been trained in artisan skills, including plumbing, carpentry, information and communication technology, and welding.

He said the beneficiaries were also provided with starter kits and financial assistance to enable them to establish businesses and become economically self-reliant.

“The idea is not just to position Gombe State institutionally for opportunities in the oil and gas sector, but also to ensure that our young people are prepared to take advantage of the opportunities when they emerge,” Pindiga said.

The commissioner explained that the consultant had also provided documentation and institutional support to strengthen the state’s engagement ahead of the anticipated resumption of exploration in the Kolmani area.

He described the expected December development as a significant opportunity for Gombe to expand its economic base and create new avenues for employment and enterprise.

With two of the 14 deliverables outstanding, Pindiga said “The state was making progress in building the institutional and human capacity needed to participate in the oil and gas industry.”

“The resumption of drilling activities presents an important opportunity for our state, and we are working to ensure that Gombe and its people are not left behind,” he added.

title: MRS, QuickFuel begin self-service PMS, other retail sales
description:
Motorists in Nigeria may soon have greater control over how they purchase Premium Motor Spirit, as MRS Holdings in partnership with QuickFuel Nigeria Limited has introduced a self-service fuel dispensing technology aimed at transforming the traditional petrol retail experience.
The initiative, unvei
content:
Motorists in Nigeria may soon have greater control over how they purchase Premium Motor Spirit, as MRS Holdings in partnership with QuickFuel Nigeria Limited has introduced a self-service fuel dispensing technology aimed at transforming the traditional petrol retail experience.

The initiative, unveiled in Lagos on Tuesday, has begun at one of the MRs filling with promises to get it spread to about 40 of its filling stations in Lagos state to allow customers to dispense fuel themselves, make payments through approved channels and complete transactions without depending on attendants.

Speaking at the unveiling, the Executive Director, Technological Services, QuickFuel, Oludare Owolabi, said the initiative was designed to challenge the existing model of fuel dispensing and address longstanding concerns surrounding delays, customer experience and accountability.

He said the innovation is expected to introduce greater convenience, transparency and accountability into fuel retailing, while providing motorists with the flexibility to purchase petrol beyond the conventional operating hours of filling stations.

He stated, “Today, we are not here simply to unveil another fuel pump. We are here to challenge an old way of buying fuel and introduce a better one.”

Owolabi observed that the traditional process, which requires motorists to queue, wait for attendants and depend on them to complete transactions, had continued to create inconveniences for customers.

He emphasised that the new technology would enable motorists to drive into participating stations, select their desired quantity, make payments and dispense fuel themselves, with transactions digitally recorded.

“Nigerians deserve their time back. Customers deserve confidence. Dealers deserve stronger controls, and the industry deserves a new standard,” he added.

According to him, the innovation is also expected to support round-the-clock fuel retailing at enabled stations, allowing customers to purchase petrol at any time, including late at night and during early morning hours.

He said the flexibility would particularly benefit commercial drivers, commuters, healthcare workers returning from night shifts and other motorists whose schedules might not align with conventional filling station operations.

Aside convenience, Owolabi said the technology would strengthen accountability by providing digital records of fuel deliveries, dispensing activities, payments and inventory movements.

“Every litre should be accounted for. Every payment should be traceable. Every discrepancy should be visible,” he said.

He explained that the system would help dealers monitor stock levels, reconcile daily sales and identify possible discrepancies between fuel received, fuel dispensed and revenue collected.

The added that the technology would provide clearer transaction records and greater confidence in their purchases, while operators would benefit from improved oversight and reduced operational losses.

Owolabi, however, stressed that the introduction of self-service would not undermine existing safety standards, meter calibration, equipment maintenance or regulatory compliance.

He added that trained personnel would remain necessary to guide customers, maintain equipment and provide technical support.

The QuickFuel executive also disclosed that the initiative would incorporate customer reward opportunities for eligible patronage, with applicable conditions communicated at participating stations.

Also speaking at the event, Chairman of MRS Group, Sayyu Dantata, said the introduction of technology-driven self-service fuel dispensing was informed by his 34 years of experience in the petroleum industry and the need to address longstanding distribution and retail challenges.

Dantata recalled that some filling stations operated round the clock in the late 1980s, although dispensing was entirely manual and customers sometimes had to wake up sleeping attendants before receiving service.

He explained that while 24-hour fuel retailing was not entirely new in Nigeria, the latest innovation offered a technology-based approach that would address security concerns, improve convenience and eliminate some of the limitations associated with the traditional system.

He said, “I have been in the industry for 34 years and I have seen through the process. I look at things and I said, why can’t I do something to help the industry?.

The post MRS, QuickFuel begin self-service PMS, other retail sales appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Businesses struggling despite five-month inflation decline, OPS warns
description:
Despite five consecutive months of declining inflation, businesses are still shutting down in Nigeria, while the prices of essential goods and services remain high, the Organised Private Sector has said.
Private sector leaders welcomed the further decline in headline inflation to 14.06 per cent in O
content:
Despite five consecutive months of declining inflation, businesses are still shutting down in Nigeria, while the prices of essential goods and services remain high, the Organised Private Sector has said.

Private sector leaders welcomed the further decline in headline inflation to 14.06 per cent in October, 2026, but warned that improved macroeconomic indicators had yet to translate into meaningful relief for businesses and households.

They called on the Federal Government to intensify interventions to reduce the cost of living, support struggling enterprises and ensure that inflation management aligns more closely with poverty reduction objectives.

The National Bureau of Statistics disclosed on Monday in its October 2026 Consumer Price Index report that headline inflation declined to 14.06 per cent from 14.63 per cent in September, representing a 0.57 percentage point reduction.

Speaking in separate telephone interviews with The PUNCH, OPS leaders, including the President of the Association of Small Business Owners of Nigeria, Dr Femi Egbesola, described the inflation slowdown as encouraging but said the development had yet to reflect in the prices of goods and the survival of businesses.

Egbesola said, “The situation is consistently coming down, and that’s our prayer. It shows that we are having macroeconomic change, which is good for the country, and will also engender investments.

It also means that the reforms of government are yielding positive fruits.

“But beyond that, if you go to the markets, you see that the prices of goods and commodities are still very high. A true test of the success of inflation is actually the reduction in prices. Rather than coming down, you also see that many of these commodity prices are still where they are, and some of them are even going up.”

He stressed that the continued difficulties facing businesses showed that the gains from economic reforms had yet to reach the productive sector, citing a recent report which indicated that 60 per cent of bankers were struggling.

Egbesola said, “You also look at it that businesses are still challenged. If you look at the report of last week from the Bankers Association, which said 60 per cent of bankers are still struggling, you know it means that businesses are still dying.

“And that’s how to really measure whether the reform is working fine, or translated to be effective or not. So when it is not reflected in households and in businesses, it means that there is a gap. And that’s why we are saying to the government that it needs to begin to intervene.”

He called for more sustainable support programmes for households and businesses, arguing that existing interventions remained inadequate to address the scale of economic hardship.

Also speaking, the National Vice-President of the National Association of Small-Scale Industrialists, Segun Kuti-George, described the declining inflation rate as a positive development, saying it indicated greater stability in the economy.

Kuti-George attributed the improvement to exchange rate and interest rate stability, as well as relative stability in the prices of petroleum products.

He said, “If that is happening, you know, it’s a positive development. It shows stability generally in the economy. And that can be accounted for by stable exchange rates, and stable interest rates. So, those are the things that could account for it. It means our monetary and fiscal policies are working positively.”

Meanwhile, the Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, Dr Muda Yusuf, called for a shift in inflation management towards affordability and household welfare, warning that declining inflation did not necessarily mean falling prices.

In a policy brief on the October inflation report, Yusuf said the moderation in headline and core inflation represented progress in economic stabilisation but warned that persistent pressures on essential household expenditure continued to undermine living standards.

He said, “Declining inflation does not necessarily imply declining prices. It primarily indicates that prices are rising at a slower rate. This distinction is particularly important for households already struggling with elevated living costs.”

Yusuf noted that food and non-alcoholic beverages contributed 5.63 percentage points to headline inflation, transportation 1.50 percentage points, housing and utilities 1.18 percentage points, while education and healthcare jointly contributed 1.72 percentage points.

He said these essential expenditure categories accounted for approximately 71 per cent of headline inflation, making their affordability particularly important to low-income households.

“The CPPE therefore stresses that inflation management must be more closely aligned with poverty reduction objectives. Government interventions should prioritise the affordability of food, transportation, housing, education and healthcare, given their disproportionate impact on the poor,” he said.

The post Businesses struggling despite five-month inflation decline, OPS warns appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: West Africa’s power deficit offers Nigeria $8.5bn solar opportunity
description:
Nigeria could position itself as a major solar manufacturing and distribution hub for West Africa, with experts identifying the region’s electricity access deficit, abundant mineral resources and growing demand for alternative power as investment opportunities worth billions of dollars.
They said th
content:
Nigeria could position itself as a major solar manufacturing and distribution hub for West Africa, with experts identifying the region’s electricity access deficit, abundant mineral resources and growing demand for alternative power as investment opportunities worth billions of dollars.

They said the country must move beyond importing solar panels and other renewable energy technologies to developing local manufacturing, mineral processing, battery production and assembly facilities capable of serving the domestic and regional markets.

The experts also identified solar-powered agriculture, irrigation, cold storage and agro-processing as emerging investment opportunities, while calling for affordable financing, stronger product standards and technical skills development to make the energy transition inclusive.

They spoke at an event organised at the Nigerian Pavilion on the sidelines of the ongoing 31st session of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye. The discussion, themed ‘Just Transition: Unlocking Nigeria’s Solar Opportunities’, was part of activities marking the conference’s Ocean, Seas, Nature and Land Use thematic day on Tuesday.

Speaking during a presentation at the event, the Executive Director of the Global Initiative for Food Security and Ecosystem Preservation, Michael David, said Nigeria possessed the mineral resources and market potential to build a competitive solar industry but was missing out on the economic benefits by depending heavily on imported technologies.

He identified 12 minerals, including silica, lithium, copper, aluminium, iron ore, graphite, manganese, nickel, cobalt, tin, zinc and silver, which could support different stages of solar panel and battery production.

According to him, the resources are available in several states, including Nasarawa, Kogi, Kwara, Niger, Zamfara, Plateau, Bauchi, Ondo and Osun.

He said, “Solar energy is not just an opportunity. It is industrialisation. It is investment. It is an economic transformation opportunity for Nigeria. The opportunity goes beyond just deploying solar panels.

“It includes local manufacturing, minerals processing, battery storage, job creation, agricultural productivity and even regional exports. And so Nigeria must move from just importing solar panels to producing, manufacturing, assembling and exporting clean energy technologies.”

David disclosed that Nigeria imported about 2.9 million solar panels last year, spending more than N450bn, despite having some of the raw materials required for domestic production.

He argued that developing local manufacturing capacity would reduce import dependence, create employment and enable Nigeria to capture a larger share of the regional renewable energy market.

Making a case for the West African market, he cited figures showing that the region accounted for about 33 per cent of the 565 million people without electricity access in sub-Saharan Africa in 2023, representing approximately 185 million people.

He said the scale of the electricity deficit presented an opportunity for Nigerian manufacturers to serve neighbouring countries rather than concentrate only on the domestic market.

David added that the International Finance Corporation had identified about $8.5bn in commercially viable solar investment opportunities in Nigeria by 2030, while broader distributed renewable energy opportunities could exceed $18bn over the next decade.

He stated, “Let’s look at the entire West Africa as the big market size for the solar market. The entire sub-Saharan Africa has a population of about 565 million people. And out of this number, within West Africa, we are looking at nearly 33 per cent of that. That is a huge market.

On the government’s position, the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Technologies, Olamide Fagbuji, said Nigeria was working to create an enabling policy environment to attract private investment into renewable energy.

He identified the Electricity Act, which allows states to participate in electricity generation and distribution, as an important development for expanding decentralised power supply.

Fagbuji said Nigeria’s Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0 had set ambitious renewable energy targets, including increasing the share of renewables in the energy mix by nine per cent annually towards 50 per cent by 2030.

He, however, stressed that achieving the targets would require substantial financing and stronger collaboration between government and private investors.

However, the Executive Director of Bridge That Gap Initiative, Gloria Bulus, said affordability remained the biggest obstacle preventing low-income households and underserved communities from adopting solar energy.

She explained that unlike conventional electricity payments, which consumers could make gradually, solar installations often required substantial upfront payments for panels, batteries and other components.

“For communities, it is not about the accessibility of solar panels. It is not about the solar itself. It is about the affordability of those panels and even the battery,” she said.

The post West Africa’s power deficit offers Nigeria $8.5bn solar opportunity appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Atiku’s candidacy: ADC files 17-ground appeal
description: The African Democratic Congress has asked the Court of Appeal to restrain the Independent National Electoral Commission from altering its leadership records and the nomination particulars of its presidential and governorship candidates pending the determination of its appeal against the judgment of
content:
The African Democratic Congress has asked the Court of Appeal to restrain the Independent National Electoral Commission from altering its leadership records and the nomination particulars of its presidential and governorship candidates pending the determination of its appeal against the judgment of Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja.

The party said it had filed a 17-ground appeal challenging the November 5, 2026 judgment, which it described as fundamentally flawed, arguing that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the leadership dispute.

In a statement issued on Tuesday by the Director of Strategic Communication, ADC Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, the party said it was also challenging an earlier ruling that granted Bala Gombe leave to amend his originating summons despite an unresolved objection to the court’s jurisdiction.

The ADC maintained that allowing INEC to implement the November 5 judgment before the Court of Appeal determines the issues raised could undermine its appeal and expose its candidates to uncertainty.

It therefore urged the appellate court to preserve the party’s existing leadership and candidate records until the legal dispute was resolved.

Shaibu said the 17 grounds of appeal questioned the jurisdiction of the Federal High Court, Gombe’s standing to institute the action, the assessment of disputed evidence and the orders made against the party.

“The 17 grounds challenge the foundation, findings and orders of Justice Lifu’s judgment. The ADC has asked the Court of Appeal to examine whether the trial court had jurisdiction, whether the claimant had standing, whether disputed evidence was properly assessed, and whether the sweeping orders made against the party can stand in law,” he said.

The party is also challenging the July 24, 2026 ruling in a separate appeal, arguing that the trial court granted Gombe permission to amend his originating summons while deferring its decision on the ADC’s preliminary objection to jurisdiction.

According to the statement, the party contends that the proposed amendment altered the description of parties and the capacity in which a defendant was sued without prior leave of court.

The appellant’s brief challenging that ruling was settled by Chief J.S. Okutepa (SAN), who leads the ADC’s legal team in the appeal.

The party is asking the Court of Appeal to set aside the amendment order and determine the outstanding objection to the trial court’s jurisdiction.

The ADC further argued that Justice Lifu proceeded to deliver judgment on a court process whose validity was already being challenged before the appellate court.

It expressed concern that INEC could act on the judgment before the appeal is determined, potentially creating a situation that would be difficult to reverse even if the appellate court eventually rules in its favour.

“INEC must not make changes that could preempt the court’s decision or put the party’s candidates in jeopardy while our applications are pending. We are asking the court to protect the subject of the appeal so that its eventual decision has practical effect,” Shaibu added.

The party said its decision to make the legal challenge public was intended to clarify the issues before the appellate court and assure its members and supporters that it would pursue the matter through lawful judicial processes.

The dispute centres on the leadership of the ADC and the legal validity of the processes through which its leadership records and related party affairs are being contested.

Justice Lifu’s November 5 judgment in the suit instituted by Gombe has thrown the party’s leadership structure and its preparations for the 2027 general elections into fresh legal uncertainty.

The latest appeal comes amid continuing litigation over the ADC’s leadership, with the party insisting that earlier court decisions recognising its leadership transition remain valid and have not been set aside.

The ADC said it would defend the rights of its members, its leadership and the decisions taken by the party, urging that no administrative action be taken on the basis of a contested judgment before the Court of Appeal has considered the issues raised.

The party’s applications and appeals are now before the appellate court for determination.

The post Atiku’s candidacy: ADC files 17-ground appeal appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Heritage Energy advances OML 30 drilling campaign, targets 100,000bpd
description: Heritage Energy Operational Services Limited, Operator of OML 30 on behalf of its Joint Venture Partners, NNPC Exploration and Production Limited and Shoreline Natural Resources Limited, is advancing its drilling campaign to unlock the asset’s significant hydrocarbon potential, accelerate reserves g
content:
Heritage Energy Operational Services Limited, Operator of OML 30 on behalf of its Joint Venture Partners, NNPC Exploration and Production Limited and Shoreline Natural Resources Limited, is advancing its drilling campaign to unlock the asset’s significant hydrocarbon potential, accelerate reserves growth and support increased production.

The Company’s Assistant General Manager, Technology Portfolio Development, Adejare Oni, who represented the Chief Executive Officer, Ado Oseragbaje, at the recently concluded 44th Nigerian Association of Petroleum Explorationists Annual International Conference and Exhibition, highlighted the strategic importance of the campaign in advancing the company’s asset development and production growth ambitions.

He noted that the drilling campaign underscores Heritage Energy’s commitment to maximising the value of OML 30 through sustained investment, subsurface resource optimisation and disciplined operational execution.

“Unlocking the full potential of our assets requires sustained investment, a deeper understanding of subsurface resources and disciplined execution,” Oni stated.

Heritage Energy is targeting production of 100,000 barrels of oil per day by 2030, underpinned by a focused strategy encompassing sustained capital investment, disciplined reservoir management, technological advancement and operational excellence.

“Achieving this ambition requires an integrated approach to asset development, combining strategic investment, effective reservoir management, operational excellence and a deeper understanding of our subsurface potential. Our focus remains on maximising asset value, replenishing reserves and delivering sustainable, long-term value for Nigeria’s energy industry,” he added.

Oni further highlighted the importance of integrating drilling activities with effective reservoir management, technological innovation and operational discipline to sustain production growth and strengthen the asset’s long-term performance.

He also emphasised the company’s commitment to strengthening its technological capabilities through an accelerated digital transformation agenda and the implementation of its flagship Operating Management System.

These initiatives are designed to standardise processes, enhance operational efficiency, strengthen performance management and improve the quality of business and operational decision-making.

“The future competitiveness of Nigeria’s upstream industry will depend on our ability to translate resource potential into tangible value through technical innovation, strategic investment and operational discipline,” he said.

The post Heritage Energy advances OML 30 drilling campaign, targets 100,000bpd appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Transporter rewards driver with vehicle under ownership scheme
description:
Cross Country Limited has rewarded one of its drivers, Lucky Umuakpero, with a vehicle through its Drive-to-Own Scheme, underscoring its commitment to staff empowerment, financial stability and recognition of employee dedication.
The vehicle was handed over at the weekend in Lagos during the company
content:
Cross Country Limited has rewarded one of its drivers, Lucky Umuakpero, with a vehicle through its Drive-to-Own Scheme, underscoring its commitment to staff empowerment, financial stability and recognition of employee dedication.

The vehicle was handed over at the weekend in Lagos during the company’s second Drive-to-Own ceremony of the year, held to honour drivers who had attained the organisation’s prescribed performance benchmarks.

Addressing the gathering, Cross Country Limited’s Managing Director, Mrs Omodunni Ogunkua, said the programme demonstrated the company’s commitment to providing employees with opportunities to achieve greater milestones beyond the traditional career path.

“Our vision goes beyond having drivers work for the organisation. We want to create opportunities for them to become owners of their own vehicles through commitment, dedication and hard work.

“We believe that when people are given the right encouragement and opportunities, they can achieve remarkable things,” Ogunkua said.

She explained that the Drive-to-Own Scheme, which dates back to the inception of City Bus, was designed to reward commitment and provide drivers with a pathway to vehicle ownership after meeting established targets.

Also at the event, LASTMA Zonal Commander, Yaba, Williams Dele, described the initiative as an unusual and commendable approach to employee empowerment.

“While I have heard of companies giving vehicles to their drivers through hire-purchase arrangements, what Cross Country Limited is doing is quite remarkable. The company is creating an opportunity for its drivers to own vehicles by successfully meeting stipulated targets. This is a commendable way of recognising hard work and empowering employees,” Dele said.

He urged the company to sustain the initiative, noting that such programmes could motivate workers and encourage greater commitment to their responsibilities.

Dele also delivered a road safety lecture, emphasising responsible driving, compliance with traffic regulations and the need for drivers to make safety a priority.

An earlier recipient of the scheme, Mr Olalekan, expressed appreciation for the opportunity, describing the experience as fulfilling despite the difficulties encountered along the way.

He urged fellow drivers to remain committed and focused, noting that their dedication would eventually bring rewarding results.

The latest beneficiary, Umuakpero, also thanked the company’s management, particularly its chairman, for the encouragement and support that sustained his motivation throughout the programme.

He admitted that the process came with challenges but said his determination and perseverance ultimately helped him accomplish his goal.

The post Transporter rewards driver with vehicle under ownership scheme appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Union disputes airline service classification, backs 5% ticket levy
description:
The designation of airline operations as essential services has attracted renewed criticism from the Association of Nigeria Aviation Professionals, which maintains that, within the aviation industry, the classification should be restricted to air traffic control services.
The union’s Deputy General
content:
The designation of airline operations as essential services has attracted renewed criticism from the Association of Nigeria Aviation Professionals, which maintains that, within the aviation industry, the classification should be restricted to air traffic control services.

The union’s Deputy General Secretary, Ocheme Aba, maintained that airline operations should not be classified alongside services whose disruption could endanger public safety.

He further cautioned against efforts to scrap the five per cent Ticket Sales Charge, stressing that the levy provides vital funding for institutions tasked with supporting and sustaining the aviation industry.

Speaking with journalists in Lagos, Aba argued that halting airline operations would not pose the same level of public danger as withdrawing air traffic control services.

He noted that the International Labour Organisation defines essential services as those whose interruption could expose a significant proportion of the population to serious risks.

Drawing a comparison with road transportation, he said suspending commercial airline services was similar to shutting down road transport operations and should not, by itself, warrant classification as an essential service.

“The only essential service that is rendered in aviation is that provided by air traffic control in relation to aircraft in the air,” he said.

He further explained that interrupting services to an aircraft already in flight could put passengers’ lives at risk, while preventing an aircraft from taking off would, in practical terms, minimise potential dangers.

Aba also cited a 2023 ruling by the National Industrial Court in a suit instituted by Aero Contractors against aviation unions, which he said affirmed that airline operations did not qualify as essential services.

He emphasised that airline operations should be treated separately from air traffic control functions, except where airline workers are directly involved in providing such critical services.

Moving beyond the essential services controversy, the labour leader challenged the regulatory provisions empowering the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority to oversee trade union activities.

He argued that the responsibility for regulating trade unions already rests with the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment under its statutory mandate.

Addressing the controversy surrounding the five per cent Ticket Sales Charge, Aba rejected calls for its outright abolition, insisting that airlines should contribute to financing the agencies and infrastructure that support their operations.

He noted that similar funding arrangements existed in the maritime and road transport sectors, where operators also contribute towards maintaining the systems that enable their businesses to function.

According to him, the TSC was introduced to provide funding for critical aviation institutions and should not be viewed merely as an additional cost imposed on airline operators.

The five per cent levy, which is currently collected by the NCAA before being distributed, is shared among five aviation agencies according to an established allocation formula.

Under the arrangement, the NCAA receives 56 per cent of the proceeds, while the Nigerian Airspace Management Agency gets 22 per cent. The Nigerian Meteorological Agency is allocated nine per cent, the Nigerian College of Aviation Technology receives seven per cent, and the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau gets six per cent.

However, Aba admitted that the collection and remittance process required improvement. Instead of scrapping the levy, he proposed that the Federal Government introduce a centralised electronic collection system to facilitate deductions at source and automatically transfer the proceeds to the respective beneficiary agencies.

He maintained that the proposed arrangement would remove the dependence of government agencies on airlines for the remittance of funds collected on their behalf.

“Instead of leaving the money in the purse of the airlines and running after it, let us have a system, a portal, where this money can be deducted at source and split and sent to the various agencies that own it. And I think that is doable,” he said.

The ANAP official also warned against transferring the responsibility for collecting the levy to the International Air Transport Association, arguing that the organisation would probably charge the government for the service, resulting in additional expenses.

Aba also disclosed that aviation unions had raised the TSC dispute with the Director-General of Civil Aviation, Chris Najomo, at a recent meeting.

The post Union disputes airline service classification, backs 5% ticket levy appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Financial institutions urged to deepen consumer protection against fraud
description:
Financial institutions have been urged to strengthen consumer protection through improved fraud-prevention measures and sustained public education as digital financial services expand in Nigeria.
The call comes as financial fraud tactics continue to evolve, raising concerns about the need for custom
content:
Financial institutions have been urged to strengthen consumer protection through improved fraud-prevention measures and sustained public education as digital financial services expand in Nigeria.

The call comes as financial fraud tactics continue to evolve, raising concerns about the need for customers to understand emerging threats and take steps to protect their accounts and personal information.

PalmPay, a digital financial services company, made the call as it marked its annual Fraud Awareness Week with activities aimed at promoting digital safety, fraud prevention and consumer education across Nigerian communities.

The company said the initiative, which it has sustained for three consecutive years, forms part of its PalmPay Dey for You campaign, aimed at equipping customers and the public with the knowledge to recognise potential threats, protect their accounts and make informed financial decisions.

According to the company, protecting consumers requires more than deploying technology, as public awareness and the ability to recognise fraudulent activities are equally important in reducing exposure to financial scams.

Speaking on the initiative, PalmPay Nigeria’s Managing Director, Chika Nwosu, said the company was combining security tools with public education to strengthen consumer protection.

“At PalmPay, our first commitment to our customers is providing secure financial services. This means that we are providing the relevant tools to fight fraud. Beyond that, PalmPay will continue to drive awareness and education to enable users to identify potential threats and make informed decisions,” Nwosu said.

He said the annual Fraud Awareness Week provided an opportunity to take fraud prevention discussions beyond digital platforms and engage communities directly.

Through its annual Fraud Awareness Walk, the company engages residents, business owners, commuters and other members of the public, sharing practical information on how to recognise and prevent fraud.

The activities are also designed to encourage individuals and communities to take an active role in creating a safer digital financial environment, reflecting the company’s position that consumer protection requires shared responsibility among financial institutions, customers, industry stakeholders and the wider public.

This year’s campaign focuses on helping consumers identify suspicious communications, safeguard account information, recognise impersonation attempts and verify information before taking action.

The initiative complements PalmPay’s broader consumer protection campaign, which combines customer education with security features, including its Security Centre and other tools designed to strengthen account protection.

The company said it had continued to use its Fraud Awareness Week to collaborate with industry stakeholders and extend consumer education through public engagement and community outreach.

As digital financial adoption grows, the emphasis on consumer awareness highlights the importance of equipping users with the knowledge to identify potential threats and protect themselves when carrying out financial transactions.

title: Reps probe 22 states over unpaid pensions
description:
The House of Representatives has called on the Federal Government to prevail on state governments owing pensioners to clear their outstanding retirement benefits and comply with the provisions of the Pension Reform Act, 2014.
The House also resolved to investigate the failure of 22 states to pay ret
content:
The House of Representatives has called on the Federal Government to prevail on state governments owing pensioners to clear their outstanding retirement benefits and comply with the provisions of the Pension Reform Act, 2014.

The House also resolved to investigate the failure of 22 states to pay retirement benefits regularly, following concerns that thousands of elderly retirees are being subjected to hunger, poverty and preventable deaths as a result of unpaid pensions.

The resolutions followed the adoption of a motion of urgent public importance sponsored by the member representing Apapa Federal Constituency of Lagos State, Adesola Adebayo, at plenary on Tuesday.

Moving the motion, the All Progressives Congress lawmaker cited a newspaper report indicating that only 14 of Nigeria’s 36 states pay pensions regularly, while the remaining 22 owe retirees several months or, in some cases, years of entitlements.

He described pensions as an earned right rather than a privilege or charity, insisting that retirees who had devoted between 30 and 35 years to public service deserved to enjoy their benefits without unnecessary hardship.

The lawmaker expressed concern that many pensioners aged between 70 and 90 were dying in poverty because they could not afford food, medication, rent and other basic necessities.

He also raised concerns over the practice of subjecting elderly retirees to prolonged verification exercises, forcing some to queue for days under harsh weather conditions, with reports of pensioners collapsing and dying in the process.

Adebayo argued that the non-payment of pensions violated constitutional provisions and undermined human dignity, while creating anxiety among serving public workers who could begin to regard retirement as a death sentence.

He said, “The House notes, with grave concern, a scandalous report published by a public newspaper revealing that only 14 out of the 36 states of the federation, excluding the Federal Capital Territory, pay pensions regularly to their retired workers, while the remaining 22 states owe pensions several months and, in some cases, several years.

“The House also notes that the pension is not a privilege, favour, or charity, but a defined wage, a constitutional right, and a moral debt owed to citizens who spent their productive lives, 30 to 35 years, serving their fatherland as teachers, nurses, civil servants, police officers, soldiers, and other public servants.

“The House further notes that the 1999 Constitution (as amended) explicitly provides that a person who has held office in the public service of the federation or a state shall be entitled to pensions and gratuity as prescribed by the National Assembly or the House of Assembly of the state, and that such pensions shall not be delayed or altered to the disadvantage of the pensioner.”

The lawmaker lamented that “many states have failed to remit both employer and employee contributions, failed to fund accrued rights, failed to domesticate the Act, and have left thousands of retirees without access to their retirement savings accounts.”

He added that “many elderly pensioners, some aged 70, 80, and 90, are now dying in penury, unable to afford food, medication, rent, and medical care, while others are forced to queue for days under the sun and rain at pension verification centres with some collapsing and dying in the process.”

He further argued that the non-payment of pensions constituted a breach of the Constitution, “a violation of human dignity, a threat to national security, and a discouragement to serving workers, who now see retirement as a death sentence, and all other than blood of rest.”

Lawmakers divided

The motion, however, generated disagreements among lawmakers over the constitutional powers of the National Assembly to intervene in pension matters involving state governments.

Contributing to the debate, APC lawmaker representing a constituency in Akwa Ibom State, Mark Esset, opposed the motion, arguing that pension obligations at the state level fell within the jurisdiction of state governments and their respective Houses of Assembly.

He cautioned against any suggestion that the Federal Government could deduct money from states’ allocations to settle outstanding pension liabilities, describing such an approach as unconstitutional.

Esset urged the House to concentrate on pension challenges facing military personnel, who, he said, had repeatedly protested over their entitlements.

“I understand the patriotism of the mover of the motion but these are purely state matters. Emotions are not enough for this motion to be heard by the House. The issue of pensions at the state level are purely for the State Houses of Assembly to handle,” he said.

Similarly, Dominic Okafor (APGA, Anambra) cautioned against generalising the allegations against all states, noting that some governors had fulfilled their pension obligations.

He cited Anambra State, which he said had cleared its pension liabilities, arguing that the motion should distinguish between states that had failed to pay and those meeting their responsibilities.

On his part, Billy Osawaru (APC, Edo) urged the House not to abandon the motion, proposing amendments to remove provisions that fell outside its constitutional jurisdiction.

“We know what our fathers are going through. We know what it means for a man to work for 35 years only to be called to stand in the sun, under the sun, to review, to keep reviewing until he can’t stand it no more.

“So, Mr Speaker, instead of killing this beautiful motion, I would like to go in for amendments. I would like to take out areas our mandates don’t cover and go with those areas that our mandates cover.”

The Deputy Speaker, Benjamin Kalu, who presided over the plenary, subsequently directed lawmakers to examine the House Standing Orders to establish the jurisdiction of the Committee on Pensions.

Reading the committee’s mandate, Kalu noted that it was empowered to examine pension-related issues across the public service, recommend measures to ensure the timely payment of retirement benefits and investigate employers’ failure to meet their pension obligations.

Its responsibilities, he said, included oversight of the National Pension Commission (PenCom), the Military Pension Board and other relevant institutions.

Also speaking, Terseer Ugbor (APC, Benue) urged the House to allow the motion to proceed, arguing that the suffering of pensioners across the country warranted urgent legislative attention.

Another lawmaker, Zainab Gimba, also supported the motion, citing Section 210 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, which protects the pension rights of persons in the public service of a state.

She particularly drew attention to Section 210(2), which provides that pension benefits due to a person under the law shall not be withheld or altered to the person’s disadvantage, except as permitted by law.

Gimba argued that although state pension liabilities must be distinguished from federal obligations, the National Assembly had the constitutional authority to debate the issue, make recommendations and encourage state legislators to exercise the necessary oversight.

She warned that continued failure to pay pensions could trigger humanitarian challenges, undermine the dignity of retirees and negatively affect their families and society.

“The law says that pensioners should be paid both at the national and state level. It is an entitlement protected by the Constitution. We must not forget that the condition of pensioners today can cause a humanitarian crisis,” she said.

The House Leader, Prof Julius Ihonvbere, also defended the motion, insisting that lawmakers should not shy away from addressing the plight of Nigerians simply because some of the affected matters fell within the jurisdiction of state governments.

Ihonvbere argued that members of the National Assembly represented Nigerians across the country and had a responsibility to speak out when citizens were subjected to hardship.

He maintained that the House could intervene through motions, investigations and recommendations without necessarily usurping the constitutional powers of state governments.

Recalling previous interventions by the Ninth Assembly in matters involving state governments, he said the parliament had a responsibility to engage relevant authorities where circumstances demanded it.

“We need to be very careful not to diminish our powers and responsibilities by hiding behind some of the local sections, under the Standing Order of the Constitution, not to perform our duties.

“Technically, there is nothing in which this House or the National Assembly cannot engage in, whether they are in the local government, the state, or anywhere, because we represent the entire country,” he maintained.

He further called on governors who had yet to clear outstanding pension liabilities to fulfil their obligations, insisting that the availability of public funds should not be an excuse for abandoning retired workers.

He also commended governors who had maintained regular pension payments, urging others to follow their example.

Following the deliberations, the House unanimously adopted the motion and resolved to call on the Federal Government, through the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, to prevail on state governments to prioritise the payment of pensions.

It also mandated its Committee on Pensions to interface with PenCom and engage state governments to ascertain the challenges responsible for irregular pension payments, identify possible solutions and report its findings to the House.

The investigation is expected to provide the House with a clearer picture of pension arrears across the affected states and the institutional and financial challenges responsible for the delays.

Nigeria operates a contributory pension system under the Pension Reform Act, with PenCom regulating and supervising the pension industry. However, pension arrangements and obligations at the state level involve state-specific legal and administrative frameworks, making the question of federal legislative intervention a subject of debate.

Section 210 of the 1999 Constitution guarantees pension and gratuity entitlements for persons who have served in the public service of a state, while Section 173 provides similar protection for federal public servants. Both provisions underscore the constitutional recognition of retirement benefits as an entitlement rather than a discretionary payment.

title: Summit targets growth of events industry

The convener, Coach Bisi Sotunde, said the platf
content:
The BusyBee Event Business Summit is targeting the growth of Nigeria’s events industry through business education, technology adoption and stronger professional networks, as it prepares to mark its 10th anniversary with a three-day programme in Lagos.

The convener, Coach Bisi Sotunde, said the platform had evolved from a small masterclass attended by 33 delegates in Ikeja in 2017 into an industry network that had reached more than 3,000 event professionals across Nigeria and the diaspora.

She said the summit was established to strengthen the business side of the events industry by equipping practitioners with the knowledge, relationships and structures needed to build sustainable enterprises.

Addressing a pre-event press conference in Lagos, Sotunde said the platform gauged its success not merely by the number of attendees but also by the businesses it had strengthened, partnerships it had facilitated and professionals whose capacity to thrive in the industry had improved.

“We did not measure success only by the number of people who sit in our conference rooms. We measure it by the conversations that continue long after the summit, the businesses that are strengthened, the collaborations that are formed, and the professionals who become better equipped to lead,” she said.

The 10th edition, themed ‘SHIFT: Think Different | Build Better | Lead Forward’, is scheduled to hold from 24 to 26 November at the Hyde Park Event Centre,

title: New initiative targets youth skills, enterprise devt in Oyo
description:
A new initiative to drive youth enterprise and skills development in Oke-Ogun, the Sir Advocate Movement, has been launched in Iseyin, Oyo State.
Speaking at the launch held at Iseyin City Hall, the Movement’s Convener, Amb. Abdur-Rahman Olalekan, Esq., said the initiative was established to amplify
content:
A new initiative to drive youth enterprise and skills development in Oke-Ogun, the Sir Advocate Movement, has been launched in Iseyin, Oyo State.

Speaking at the launch held at Iseyin City Hall, the Movement’s Convener, Amb. Abdur-Rahman Olalekan, Esq., said the initiative was established to amplify young people’s voices and promote positive attitudes towards values and work.

Abdur-Rahman said the idea behind the initiative was driven by the question: “Why does a generation filled with talent, energy and promise often feel unheard?”

He lamented that despite the considerable potential among young people in the zone, many lacked proper guidance, noting that, “The future of Oke-Ogun is not far away but already present in the young people of the zone.”

He explained that the Movement would pursue three key objectives: encouraging young people to take charge of their future, ensuring their ideas reach policymakers and bringing together students, artisans, traders and graduates across Oke-Ogun.

He stressed the need to address a decline in values, saying, “A society that teaches children to cheat, lie, bribe and celebrate dishonest wealth should not be surprised when those children grow up and practise the same behaviour in positions of authority.” “Leaders are products of the society that raised them,” he added.

Abdur-Rahman said the presentation of books and writing materials to students at the launch marked the first practical step towards achieving the Movement’s goals, assuring that its activities would be conducted transparently and accountably. He also called on leaders to “invest not only in roads and buildings but also in the development of people,” stressing that leadership is about character and responsibility, not just holding office.

Speaking on the theme, ‘From Competence to Mastery: Why Focus Is the Bridge Between Being Good and Being Unforgettable,’ Dr Olaniyan Solomon of the University of Ibadan urged participants to move beyond basic skills to mastery through concentration and consistency.

He stated,“Nigeria of Our Dream: From Slogan to Reality.”

President of the Council of Iseyin Youth Organisation, Aare Babajide Oniyo, said citizens must move from making demands to taking practical steps towards national development.

Another speaker at the event, Mr Ismail Tijani, who spoke on “Efficacy of Education and Its Societal Impact,” linked education to employability and community growth.

Earlier in his welcome address, the Chairman of the occasion, Alhaji Azeez Mubasiru, expressed support for the vision behind the establishment of the Movement and the need for partnership.

The unveiling ceremony attracted several dignitaries, including the Aseyin of Iseyin, Oba Sefiu  Oyebola, Adeyeri III; the Executive Chairman of Iseyin Local Government and Special Guest of Honour, Hon. Bisi Fadiran; Chief Adeniyi Falade, Esq.; and the Chairman of the Iseyin branch of CAN, Apostle Sunday Ogundairo, among others.

title: NDIC urges corps members to save in insured banks
description:
By Vincent Ujumadu

The advice was given during a f
content:
By Vincent Ujumadu

AWKA — The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) has urged members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) in Anambra State to cultivate sound financial habits and ensure they save their money in banks insured by the corporation.

The advice was given during a financial literacy and sensitisation seminar organised by NDIC officials at the NYSC orientation camp in Awka South Local Government Area of the state.

The corporation urged the corps members to embrace what it described as a smart financial lifestyle built around earning, saving, investing and spending wisely.

The Communications Manager of NDIC, Chinenye Chimezie-Amadi, advised the corps members to exercise caution when choosing where to save their money, stressing the importance of using deposit-taking institutions insured by the corporation.

She urged them to develop the habit of budgeting, distinguishing between their needs and wants, and setting aside part of their earnings for emergencies and future investments.

According to her, many people earn money without keeping track of how they spend it, making it difficult for them to build savings.

“Our presence at the orientation camp is to help you learn a kind of life you need to live in future as you begin to make decisions for yourselves.

“Some people won’t have savings, but you see them carrying expensive hairs and mobile phones. That is living a false life. We are looking at a situation where you save for emergency and for your future,” she said.

Amadi urged the corps members not to dismiss the possibility of saving because of their present earnings, saying even small amounts could accumulate into substantial savings when set aside consistently.

She also advised them to prioritise essential expenses before discretionary spending and develop the habit of paying themselves first by setting aside a portion of their income.

On the choice of financial institutions, she warned against depositing money in unregulated schemes offering unusually high returns, urging them to verify that their banks were insured by NDIC.

“Even when you have a house, you still need to set aside your house rent as a way of saving. If you do it consistently, you will be surprised at the amount you save,” she said.

The NDIC Controller, Enugu Zonal Office, Mr Chidi Nwankwo, urged the corps members to acquire financial literacy skills ahead of their transition from national service into the labour market.

Speaking on the topic, ‘Know Your Deposit Protection: A Practical Guide for NYSC Corps Members’, Nwankwo explained the corporation’s role in protecting depositors and outlined the applicable deposit insurance limits.

He advised the corps members to confirm that any deposit-taking bank with which they intended to transact was insured by NDIC, explaining that eligible deposits were protected within the limits prescribed for different categories of financial institutions.

According to him, deposits in deposit money banks are insured up to N5 million per depositor, while those in microfinance banks, primary mortgage banks and payment service banks are covered up to N2 million.

Using an example, Nwankwo explained that a depositor with N6 million in a deposit money bank that subsequently fails would receive insurance compensation of up to N5 million, while recovery of the remaining N1 million would depend on the realisation of the failed bank’s assets.

He encouraged the corps members to understand the scope of deposit insurance and make informed financial decisions to protect their savings.
