title: Women push greater inclusion in energy industry leadership
description:
Women in Nigeria’s energy industry are demanding greater access to executive positions and business opportunities, as industry leaders face renewed calls to translate gender inclusion commitments into measurable changes in recruitment, promotion and corporate decision-making.
The Women in Energy Net
content:
Women in Nigeria’s energy industry are demanding greater access to executive positions and business opportunities, as industry leaders face renewed calls to translate gender inclusion commitments into measurable changes in recruitment, promotion and corporate decision-making.

The Women in Energy Network made the call at its just-concluded 2026 Gala and Awards in Lagos, where it launched a Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Benchmark Report in collaboration with KPMG to assess workplace inclusion and track companies’ progress through an annual scorecard.

The initiative is intended to move the industry beyond policy statements and public commitments by providing a framework for measuring how organisations create opportunities for women, particularly in senior leadership and across the energy value chain.

WIEN President, Eyono Fatayi-Williams, said the industry could no longer afford to repeat conversations about gender inclusion without demonstrating what had changed, arguing that qualified women needed fair opportunities to compete for leadership positions.

“As we celebrate six years, we also have to ask ourselves an important question: What does the next six years look like? Because we cannot spend the next six years having the same conversations we have had in the last six years,” Fatayi-Williams noted. “We cannot continue to talk about inclusion without asking what has changed.”

She said the network was not seeking preferential appointments but wanted companies to identify, develop and give qualified women opportunities to demonstrate their capabilities and compete for executive roles.

“For us at WIEN, diversity, equity and inclusion must mean something beyond a statement in a company policy or a paragraph in an annual sustainability report. It must be visible in the workplace. It must be reflected in the opportunities available to women. And it must be seen in the decisions organisations make every day,” she noted.

The push comes amid persistent gaps in women’s participation in the energy industry, particularly in technical positions, corporate leadership and access to contracts.

Figures cited by WIEN from the International Energy Agency indicate that women account for about 20 per cent of the global energy workforce, with their representation in senior executive positions remaining limited. In Nigeria, audits by the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative put women’s share of the extractive sector workforce at 18 per cent.

Industry surveys cited by the network also indicate that 64 per cent of women working in Nigeria’s renewable energy sector occupy non-STEM and administrative roles, while women-owned businesses account for fewer than two per cent of companies registered on the national Joint Qualification System for oil and gas contracting.

The figures highlight the gap between the industry’s growing emphasis on diversity and the participation of women in the technical, commercial and leadership roles that influence investment and business decisions.

Chairperson of WIEN’s Board of Trustees, Cecilia Umoren, said the network had expanded opportunities for women since its establishment six years ago, contributing to more appointments and a broader pipeline of women entering science, technology, engineering and mathematics fields.

However, she said the progress had not translated into parity, noting that men continued to occupy most leadership positions in the industry.

“In the six years that WIEN has been in existence, we have created more opportunities for women, resulting in numerous appointments and an expanded STEM pipeline,” Umoren noted.

“However, progress is not parity; we are ultimately aiming for true parity. We must acknowledge that most leadership positions today are occupied by men, meaning we cannot achieve our objectives without partnering with them to create access,” she added.

Umoren also urged women to create opportunities where existing structures did not provide them, saying, “If the room is not created for you, create your own room, set your own table, and be at your own table.”

The network’s Executive Secretary, Asanimo Omezi, said WIEN had grown from an initial group of 30 women to more than 1,000 members, with 30 corporate partners supporting its activities.

She said the DEI benchmark would provide a basis for assessing corporate commitments and making inclusion more visible and accountable.

“The newly unveiled DEI benchmark will move us from mere conversation to visible accountability,” Omezi noted.

She added that the growing membership demonstrated the presence of women with the knowledge and professional experience to take on more influential positions in the industry.

Delivering the keynote address, Chairman of the Sage Centre for Leadership Excellence, Mutiu Sunmonu, urged the network to sustain its advocacy for fair and equitable standards across the energy industry.

He said companies should maintain standards that allow qualified women to compete on a level playing field, without compromising the requirements for professional and executive positions.

The benchmark was unveiled following remarks by KPMG Partner, Bimpe Afolabi, as part of the network’s efforts to establish a framework for assessing workplace practices and measuring corporate inclusion progress.

WIEN said the initiative would help determine whether companies’ commitments were translating into tangible opportunities for women, including greater participation in executive roles and women-owned businesses’ access to opportunities across the energy value chain.

The event also featured an executive leadership fireside chat moderated by Rosario Osobase, which examined the role of corporate leadership and male allyship in addressing gender disparities.

The panel included Executive Director of Human Resources at ExxonMobil Affiliates in Nigeria, Emem Abraham; Managing Director of Oando Energy Resources, Alex Irune; Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Seplat Energy, Effiong Okon; and Managing Director of Nigeria LNG Limited, Adeleye Falade.

Falade disclosed that women accounted for more than half of the applicants in NLNG’s recent recruitment exercise, while 50 per cent of the candidates selected for the positions were women.

The disclosure highlighted women’s willingness to participate in recruitment processes when opportunities arise, but the network is seeking broader inclusion beyond employment to cover promotions, technical positions and representation at senior decision-making levels.

The event also featured remarks from the Minister of Women Affairs, delivered by the Director-General and Chief Executive Officer of the Maryam Babangida National Centre for Women Development, Adedayo Benjamins-Laniyi.

The gala marked WIEN’s sixth anniversary and brought together policymakers, energy executives and professionals at the Metropolitan Club in Lagos.

Omezi said the organisation’s expansion from 30 founding members to more than 1,000 members and 30 corporate partners reflected the growing network of women working across the energy industry.

The ceremony also recognised individuals and organisations for their contributions to the sector through the Winning With Women in Energy Awards.

Folake Soetan received the WIEN Woman of the Year and Outstanding Woman in Power awards, while Moroti Adedoyin was recognised with the Lifetime Achievement Award.

Bassey Adie received the Female Energy Entrepreneur of the Year award and was also named Outstanding Woman in Midstream, Gas and Energy Logistics. Caroline Eboumbou was recognised for her contribution to renewable energy, while Funmi Ogbue was honoured for her advocacy for girls in science, technology, engineering and mathematics and the energy sector.

Maryamu Idris received recognition for leadership in the downstream sector, while Judith Ikwuwunna was named Emerging Woman in Energy, also called as the Rising Star award.

On the corporate side, ExxonMobil and Seplat Energy jointly received the Corporate Champion for Women-Owned Energy Businesses award. Seplat Energy also won the Excellence in Diverse Leadership award, while the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board was named Public Sector Champion for Women in Energy.

Telmek Global Resources received the Employer of Choice award.

Five other industry professionals received recognition as Outstanding Women and Special WIEN Honourees. They included Audrey Joe-Ezigbo, Ibilola Amao, Elohor Aiboni, Olu Verheijen and Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan.

The post Women push greater inclusion in energy industry leadership appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Experts seek greater govt investment in visual arts
description:
Nigeria’s visual arts industry needs stronger government backing, corporate investment and international support to sustain local galleries in the country, improve the visibility of artists and build a viable market, art professionals have said.
They said limited institutional funding was making it
content:
Nigeria’s visual arts industry needs stronger government backing, corporate investment and international support to sustain local galleries in the country, improve the visibility of artists and build a viable market, art professionals have said.

They said limited institutional funding was making it difficult for galleries to sustain their operations and provide the support required by artists at different stages of their careers, despite the growing number of galleries and increasing activity in the country’s art scene.

The experts spoke at a recent press conference for the Art Masters Affairs Exhibition, organised by Fobally Art World Africa in Lagos, where they also called for greater recognition of established artists and clearer standards for distinguishing masters from other practitioners.

An art master and retired art lecturer at Yaba College of Technology, Dr Kunle Adeyemi, said government support for visual arts remained limited compared with the attention given to the performing arts.

He urged the government to extend at least half of the attention it gives to the performing arts to visual arts, arguing that galleries needed institutional support to remain sustainable.

“If they can give the same attention, 50 per cent attention they are giving to the performing arts, they can give it to visual arts. It won’t be where we are today,” Adeyemi said.

He said government assistance to visual arts was not sufficiently widespread, with only a few galleries receiving support from state authorities.

“There is a need for both governments, corporates, and international bodies’ support for Nigerian galleries to be able to continue the good work,” he said.

Adeyemi said artistic passion alone could not guarantee the survival of galleries and the wider industry, stressing that practitioners needed business structures and support systems to sustain their activities.

He noted that artists could spend decades developing their practice before gaining the recognition and commercial opportunities needed to earn a stable income.

“Passion drives you, but the business too, because as much as we are doing passion, the business is very important because it will be sustained,” he said.

He added that galleries could improve their chances of survival by developing programmes for different categories of artists and collectors, rather than concentrating on a single segment of the market.

The exhibition’s Managing Director and Founder of Fobally Art World Africa, Folasade Abiola, said the gallery was established to promote African art and artists by improving their visibility locally and internationally.

She said its programmes were designed to serve different classes of artists within the art ecosystem, including secondary school students, undergraduates, emerging artists, mid-level professionals, senior artists, masters and grandmasters.

Abiola said the gallery organised a grandmasters exhibition in the previous year and was staging the masters exhibition as part of a programme it intended to sustain in subsequent years.

She said the gallery’s approach was informed partly by the different interests of art collectors, noting that while some collectors actively sought works by established masters, others were more interested in emerging artists or mid-level professionals.

According to her, galleries needed to support different classes of artists to ensure that all levels of artists received attention and opportunities across the board.

Abiola also explained that the selection of a younger artist for the masters exhibition was not based solely on age or years of practice, but on other technical impact in the art space over the years.

She further stated that the organisers considered the impact of an artist’s work, including whether it had attracted recognition and purchases locally and internationally.

She noted that young practitioners must show that their work has made a significant impact beyond Nigeria to be considered eligible, adding that the selection process also considered professionalism, technical quality, artistic contributions and the acceptance of an artist’s work.

He said the exhibition featured approximately 27 to 28 artists whose studio work, professional achievements and contributions to the development of other practitioners had distinguished them.

He explained that the selection process aimed to celebrate artistic excellence and honour practitioners whose contributions had significantly advanced the profession: “We look at the contributions, we look at their artistic practice, we look at the excellence that they have come to play. We consider those individuals whose lives they have positively impacted.”

He said the organisers had aimed to ensure that the exhibition reflected the country’s geographical diversity, but high transportation costs prevented some artists from the far north and southernmost parts of Nigeria from taking part.

Rasheed Amodu, an artist, historian, critic and consultant, said the proliferation of galleries had made it harder for collectors and the public to distinguish established masters from less accomplished practitioners.

He said the exhibition was conceived partly to address concerns about artistic evaluation and the standards used to recognise accomplished artists.

Amodu maintained that such recognition should be based on the quality and craftsmanship of an artist’s work, years of consistent practice, depth of ideas and contributions to the profession.

He said some practitioners had spent 50 to 60 years developing their careers, adding that years of practice and the quality of work should carry weight in determining who qualified as a master.

“The class, the finesse of the work, defines who is a great artist,” Amodu noted.

He warned that the absence of clear distinctions could allow artists with limited experience or less accomplished work to claim the status of masters, creating confusion among collectors and the public.

Amodu cited a 1984 observation made by Professor David J. Gidley concerning “junk artists” and collectors buying “junk artworks” because they could not distinguish between different levels of artistic quality.

He said the exhibition was intended to establish a clearer marker of artistic accomplishment and draw attention to practitioners who had earned recognition through sustained work.

“The exhibition, per se, is just trying to show that there are masters and there are masters,” he said.

Amodu further revealed that an 81-year-old artist had been invited to the exhibition but could not attend due to personal circumstances.

The exhibition will feature works addressing Nigerian culture, social issues, philosophical themes and landscapes, with artists working across different media, including printmaking, painting, sculpture, carving, metalwork, fibreglass and tapestry.

Adeyemi said the works were intended to encourage viewers to look beyond their immediate appearance and consider the ideas and interpretations embedded in them.

He said the organisers hoped the exhibition would help strengthen public understanding of visual arts and the contributions of practitioners to the country’s cultural sector.

Abiola said Fobally Art World Africa would continue developing programmes for different categories of artists, with the aim of improving the visibility of African art in local and international markets.

title: Nigeria steps up scrutiny of retail pricing practice
description:
Retail businesses in Nigeria are facing increased regulatory scrutiny over pricing practices, product information and competition as the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission steps up efforts to protect consumers and promote fair trading in the country’s marketplace.
Speaking at the
content:
Retail businesses in Nigeria are facing increased regulatory scrutiny over pricing practices, product information and competition as the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission steps up efforts to protect consumers and promote fair trading in the country’s marketplace.

Speaking at the Africa Retail Congress held at Lagos Business School on Saturday, the FCCPC’s Zonal Coordinator, Olubunmi Otti, who represented the Executive Vice-Chairman of the commission, said consumers were entitled to fair prices, quality products, accurate information and effective channels for resolving complaints.

The commission warned that businesses engaging in price fixing, price gouging and other anti-competitive practices risk sanctions under the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018, which empowers it to prosecute offenders, impose fines, seal businesses and withdraw products from the market.

The warning comes as Nigeria’s retail industry expands across fast-moving consumer goods, pharmaceuticals, food and other merchandise, raising concerns about the need to balance business growth with consumer protection and fair competition.

She said the commission’s responsibility extended across formal retail outlets, informal markets and digital platforms, stressing that the growth of the sector must not undermine consumer rights.

“For us, scale must never come at the expense of fairness,” Otti said.

She identified transparent pricing, the absence of hidden charges, quality goods and services, and ethical business practices as essential elements of consumer trust.

Otti disclosed that the commission had sealed about three businesses in Lagos this year as part of its enforcement activities, although she said the regulator preferred voluntary compliance through consumer and business education.

“We want voluntary compliance by the business. So, consumer and business education is critical to our mandate,” she said.

She explained that the commission was working to increase awareness of consumer rights and responsibilities while educating businesses about the implications of violating the law.

The FCCPC also highlighted its role in reviewing mergers and acquisitions to prevent transactions that could create market dominance and restrict competition.

According to Otti, the commission assesses proposed mergers based on whether they promote innovation, expand the variety of goods and services available to consumers or are designed to stifle competition and prevent smaller businesses from thriving.

She said the regulator would not approve transactions intended to undermine competition, adding that it had mechanisms to distinguish business combinations that benefit consumers from those that concentrate market power.

The commission also said it was collaborating with sector-specific regulators to address consumer complaints and improve accountability across industries.

Otti cited recent engagements with electricity distribution companies following complaints from consumers, saying the commission had brought relevant operators and regulators together to resolve disputes.

She urged consumers to report grievances through its complaint resolution channels, adding that consumer protection required cooperation among regulators, businesses, the media and civil society organisations.

Meanwhile, industry discussions at the congress highlighted the importance of business strategy and technology in strengthening the retail sector.

The Alternative Academic Director of the Africa Retail Academy at Lagos Business School, Chidi Okoro, said retail businesses needed viable business models and the capacity to execute their strategies before pursuing expansion.

He cited the collapse of several retail companies in Kenya as an example of how businesses could struggle when their models were not grounded in market realities or supported by adequate execution capabilities.

Okoro, who presented a book titled Strategy to Execution, said Nigeria’s retail industry was expanding across several categories, making strategic planning and operational capacity increasingly important to sustainable growth.

He said having a strategy was not sufficient without the ability to implement it, urging businesses to consider their capabilities before seeking financing or expanding their operations.

The congress also examined the role of digital infrastructure in retail operations, with MTN Nigeria presenting broadband solutions designed to support business connectivity.

The company’s Manager of Broadband Regional Sales, Fixed Broadband, Anastasia Ehidiamhen, said reliable internet access could help businesses monitor transactions, maintain records and support multiple users.

She said MTN’s fixed broadband plans ranged from 50 megabits per second to one gigabit per second, with the entry-level 50Mbps package priced at N30,000 for 30 days and the 100Mbps plan costing N45,000.

The Chief Executive Officer of SLOT Systems Limited, Nnamdi Ezeigbo, also highlighted the growing importance of after-sales services in the smartphone retail market.

He said the company had introduced its Slot Elite Card, an annual N300,000 membership programme for eligible customers with smartphones valued at N1.5m and above.

The programme offers services including screen replacement, repairs, priority attention, trade-in opportunities and free home delivery, reflecting efforts by retailers to improve customer experience beyond the initial sale of devices.

The Africa Retail Congress was themed ‘Leading Africa’s Retail Strategy: People, Process, Planning and Resources’.

The post Nigeria steps up scrutiny of retail pricing practice appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Nigeria’s childcare gap threatens $22.9bn GDP opportunity – W’Bank
description:
Nigeria could generate an additional $22.9bn in annual economic output by narrowing gender gaps in economic participation, as women continue to bear a disproportionate share of childcare responsibilities, according to the World Bank Group.
The estimate was presented by Senior Economist at the World
content:
Nigeria could generate an additional $22.9bn in annual economic output by narrowing gender gaps in economic participation, as women continue to bear a disproportionate share of childcare responsibilities, according to the World Bank Group.

The estimate was presented by Senior Economist at the World Bank Group’s Gender Innovation Lab, Ayodele Fashogbon, at the National Care Forum in Lagos on Tuesday. The forum was themed ‘Advancing Nigeria’s Care Economy: Jobs, Growth and Opportunity.’

Fashogbon said Nigerian women spend an average of 76 minutes daily caring for children, compared with 13 minutes for men, meaning women devote almost six times as much time to childcare.

The gap is wider in rural communities, where women spend about eight times as much time on childcare as men.

The economist said the unequal distribution of unpaid care responsibilities limits women’s ability to participate fully in the labour market, develop businesses and pursue better-paying employment opportunities.

The economic cost is particularly significant for women aged between 25 and 39, who spend an average of 139 minutes daily on childcare. These are also the years when many people build careers, establish businesses and acquire professional skills.

Fashogbon said household responsibilities become more demanding when a child under six joins a family. Women’s working time falls by about 36 per cent, from 244 minutes daily to 156 minutes, while men’s working time increases by approximately 30 per cent.

Nigeria also faces a significant shortage of formal childcare services, with fewer than five per cent of children below three years enrolled in centre-based care.

According to Fashogbon, about 75 per cent of childcare providers reported difficulties accessing financing, while only five per cent of private sector employers invest in childcare.

Head of Office, International Finance Corporation, Nigeria, Christian Mulamula, said 92 per cent of childcare facilities were small and independently owned, while 76 per cent of childcare entrepreneurs lacked access to formal finance.

He said childcare businesses needed funding to expand their operations, employ trained workers and improve service quality.

Mulamula also said 67 per cent of working parents believed they would become more productive with better access to childcare.

The World Bank economist said investment in childcare could improve women’s employment, increase household earnings and strengthen children’s development.

Research in Jamaica also that children who benefited from childcare during their early years earned about 25 per cent more in later life than those without access to such services.

Speaking at the forum, the Minister of Women Affairs and Social Development, Hajiya Imaan Sulaiman-Ibrahim, called for increased investment in childcare and other essential care services.

Represented by Director of the Child Development Department, Andrew Madugu, the minister said childcare should be treated as economic infrastructure rather than only a family responsibility.

She said government alone could not finance or provide the services needed to expand the care economy, urging private investors, employers and development partners to support the sector.

The minister identified financing, institutional coordination, community-based infrastructure and the development of a skilled care workforce as priorities for implementing Nigeria’s National Care Policy.

Earlier, Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, represented by the Commissioner for Finance, Abayomi Oluyomi, called for stronger partnerships between the government and private-sector investors to develop sustainable care solutions.

In his address of welcome, Oluyomi said economic productivity depended not only on jobs, infrastructure and investment capital but also on support systems that allowed people to participate fully in economic activities.

He noted that many workers, especially women, struggled to balance their jobs and businesses with childcare and other family responsibilities.

“These responsibilities determine whether they can take up employment opportunities, expand their businesses or pursue opportunities that will improve their livelihoods,” he said.

The post Nigeria’s childcare gap threatens $22.9bn GDP opportunity – W’Bank appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Police bust arms rings, seize grenade launcher, machine gun
description:
The Nigeria Police Force has arrested eight suspected kidnappers and arms dealers and killed two armed men during separate operations targeting criminal networks across several states.
The police said it also recovered 16 firearms, including a general-purpose machine gun and a grenade launcher.
The
content:
The Nigeria Police Force has arrested eight suspected kidnappers and arms dealers and killed two armed men during separate operations targeting criminal networks across several states.

The police said it also recovered 16 firearms, including a general-purpose machine gun and a grenade launcher.

The Force Public Relations Officer, Ani Iniedu, disclosed in a statement on Tuesday, adding that the operations, conducted between October 10 and November 8, 2026, also led to the recovery of 1,000 rounds of live ammunition.

Iniedu stated that five suspects were arrested during the first operation for their alleged involvement in a kidnapping and armed robbery syndicate operating across Kaduna, Jigawa, Katsina and Kano states.

He identified them as Auwalu Yakubu Kura, 35; Hamisu Yasu, 35; Sabo Gambo, 34; Sulaiman Musa, 27; and Haruna Adamu, 19.

The FPO noted that investigations indicated that the syndicate, allegedly led by Kura, had operated for more than six years and recruited younger members to sustain its network.

He added that forensic and investigative findings had allegedly linked the suspects to several incidents involving kidnapping, armed robbery and culpable homicide.

He stated, “Those in custody are Auwalu Yakubu Kura, male, 35, of Dogarawa, Zaria LGA, Kaduna State; Hamisu Yasu, male, 35, of Giwa LGA, Kaduna State; Sabo Gambo, male, 34, of Sabon Titi, Pan-Shekara, Kumbotso LGA, Kano State; as well as Sulaiman Musa, male, 27, and Haruna Adamu, male, 19.

“Police investigations indicate that the syndicate, allegedly led by Auwalu Yakubu Kura, has operated for over six years, actively recruiting younger operatives to sustain its cell structure.

“Forensic and investigative findings have linked the network to several violent incidents involving kidnapping, armed robbery, and culpable homicide.”

In a separate operation targeting cross-border arms trafficking, Iniedu noted that police operatives arrested three suspects accused of smuggling firearms from the Niger Republic into Nigeria.

He identified the suspects as Aminu Ibrahim, 33; Masa’ud Bala, 35; and Idris Ahmed, 43.

According to him, Ibrahim was arrested on November 7 in Gode Forest along the Mai’Adua-Koza axis of Katsina State, while Bala was apprehended during a follow-up operation in Daura.

Iniedu stated that investigations indicated that Bala coordinated the movement of weapons from foreign suppliers, while Ibrahim allegedly served as a local courier, delivering firearms to armed bandit groups in Nigeria.

He added that Ahmed was arrested on November 8 at Magama, Toro LGA of Bauchi State, over his alleged involvement in distributing arms across the North-East, North-West and North-Central regions.

The FPRO noted that the arrest was followed by a gun battle after armed members of Ahmed’s gang opened fire on the approaching operatives.

“In the ensuing gun battle, two armed assailants sustained gunshot injuries and were evacuated to a hospital for medical treatment, where they were confirmed dead by doctors and deposited at the morgue,” he added.

Iniedu listed the recovered weapons as one General Purpose Machine Gun, four AK-47 rifles, seven AK-100 rifles, three M16 CQ rifles and one Milkor grenade launcher.

Other exhibits recovered included 1,000 rounds of 7.62 x 54mm GPMG ammunition, seven empty rifle magazines, a Kia Sorento SUV, a Volkswagen Golf, a Galaxy van and a Daylong motorcycle.

He added that the recovered firearms and ammunition were undergoing forensic and ballistic analysis, while efforts were ongoing to arrest other members of the syndicates.

The FPRO noted that the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, commended the operatives for their professionalism and urged them to sustain efforts to dismantle criminal networks and disrupt the supply of illegal firearms.

Iniedu urged members of the public to provide credible information to the police and warned against confronting armed suspects or taking the law into their own hands.

The post Police bust arms rings, seize grenade launcher, machine gun appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Elektron Energy acquires Daystar Power Group from Shell
description:
Elektron Renewables Limited, a subsidiary of Elektron Energy Development Strategies Limited, has signed an agreement to acquire Shell Overseas Investments B.V.’s 100 per cent ownership interest in Daystar Power Group.
Daystar operates an approximately 150 megawatts solar and hybrid energy platform a
content:
Elektron Renewables Limited, a subsidiary of Elektron Energy Development Strategies Limited, has signed an agreement to acquire Shell Overseas Investments B.V.’s 100 per cent ownership interest in Daystar Power Group.

Daystar operates an approximately 150 megawatts solar and hybrid energy platform across five West African markets: Nigeria, Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal and Togo, serving commercial and industrial customers.

Its capabilities complement Elektron’s existing energy infrastructure and renewable-energy platform, bringing together Elektron’s experience in developing complex energy infrastructure with Daystar’s regional footprint, renewable-energy expertise and established customer base.

“In our recent history, Elektron has been committed to developing, commercially viable energy infrastructure designed around the needs of mission-critical businesses. Daystar’s strong and complementary solar and hybrid capabilities accelerate our strategy to build a diversified cleaner energy platform, strengthening our ability to deliver reliable and scalable energy solutions across West Africa.”  said Co-CEO and CFO of Elektron Energy, Deen Solebo.

The transaction is subject to regulatory conditions and approvals. Until completion, there are no changes to Daystar Power’s day-to-day operations.

title: Ex gov candidate debunks interest in Awka traditional stool
description:
A governorship candidate of the Action Alliance in the November 8, 2025 Anambra State governorship election, Jeff Nweke, has debunked claims that he is interested in becoming the next traditional ruler of Awka amidst Igweship tussle in the accient kingdom.
Nweke dismissed the rumour while addressing
content:
A governorship candidate of the Action Alliance in the November 8, 2025 Anambra State governorship election, Jeff Nweke, has debunked claims that he is interested in becoming the next traditional ruler of Awka amidst Igweship tussle in the accient kingdom.

Nweke dismissed the rumour while addressing journalists at his office in Awka, calling on the residents to disregard the rumour and insisting that he had no interest in becoming the traditional ruler of the town.

Speaking further, Nweke blamed Awka kingmakers for adopting what he called “eyeservice” in selecting and installing monarchs.

He said, “What is currently happening in Awka Kingdom is majorly fuelled by the kingmakers. The procedure the Awka Kingmakers use in selecting, electing and installing the current monarch was the same procedure they applied for another monarch.

“As it stands now, Awka has two traditional rulers. It’s a seriously disturbing situation in our peaceful and united town with a total of 32 villages.

“Anything you heard me say on social media is a call for peace, orderliness and togetherness in Awka and not for canvassing to become the next traditional ruler of the town.

“My coming into this World is to empower people that I am more than and not to suppress, and which is why I venture into politics to actualise the mission.

“You media should please and please help me to tell the public that Ozo Jeff Nweke, the immediate past governorship candidate of the Action Alliance, in the November 8, 2025 gubernatorial election in Anambra State, is not interested in becoming the next traditional ruler of Awka Kingdom.

“I don’t even want to be a cabinet member. I choose to be an ordinary Awka indigene from Amikwo village precisely.

“I am a core philanthropist with five wives and 18 well-to-do children. I am interested in becoming the next governor of Anambra State to build and develop Awka, and the state as a whole and not Eze-Uzu as being speculated across the town.”

He commended the media for projecting his candidacy before, during and after the governorship election.

He promised to continue to work with the media for a better Anambra State and Nigeria at large.

The post Ex gov candidate debunks interest in Awka traditional stool appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: 2027: Jonathan fears post-election violence
description:
Former President Goodluck Jonathan has expressed concern over growing political intolerance ahead of the 2027 general elections, noting that incendiary rhetoric could trigger a post-election crisis.
Jonathan, the founder and chairman of the Goodluck Jonathan Foundation, gave the warning on Tuesday a
content:
Former President Goodluck Jonathan has expressed concern over growing political intolerance ahead of the 2027 general elections, noting that incendiary rhetoric could trigger a post-election crisis.

Jonathan, the founder and chairman of the Goodluck Jonathan Foundation, gave the warning on Tuesday at the 2027 Peace and Security Conference in Abuja, themed ‘Safeguarding Peace and Strengthening Social Cohesion in a Competitive Political Environment.’

Political attacks on candidates and supporters of major parties have intensified as Nigeria prepares for the 2027 general elections.

The convoy of President Bola Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress presidential candidate, came under attack on November 13, 2026, shortly after he observed Jumu’ah prayers in Garki, Abuja, with some individuals reportedly throwing stones and other objects at it.

On November 15, 2026, suspected thugs attacked the campaign convoy of Nigeria Democratic Congress vice-presidential candidate, Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso, and its Kano governorship candidate, Aminu Gwarzo, in Bichi Local Government Area, leaving several vehicles damaged and supporters injured.

Earlier in November, the convoy of Nigeria Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Peter Obi, was attacked in Calabar, Cross River State, while some of his supporters were reportedly assaulted at a Lagos town hall meeting last week.

Supporters of the African Democratic Congress presidential hopeful, Atiku Abubakar, have also reportedly faced attacks in Edo, Kaduna, and Cross River states.

Similarly, the African Action Congress presidential candidate, Omoyele Sowore, and his entourage were attacked on October 30, 2026, at a restaurant in Ado-Ekiti, Ekiti State. The Allied Peoples Movement and other parties have also reported attacks on their supporters.

The ex-President also raised concerns about conflicting judicial pronouncements, particularly decisions by courts of coordinate jurisdiction, warning they could undermine public confidence in the judiciary and push citizens toward self-help.

He stated, “As we gradually approach the 2027 general elections, certain developments in our political environment are becoming increasingly worrisome. As a former President, I receive calls from Nigerians and friends of our country across the world who express concern about the direction Nigeria is heading. Rather than the confidence and optimism we should be inspiring, there is growing apprehension about the likelihood of crises that may follow the elections. We must not ignore these concerns.

“Among the issues demanding urgent attention is the growing culture of political intolerance. There appears to be an increasing unwillingness among political actors to accommodate opposing views or recognise the legitimate right of others to compete for political power.’’

“This is compounded by political thuggery, the exploitation of our young people as instruments of violence, and acts of political brigandage. Equally disturbing are controversies surrounding some judicial pronouncements, particularly those involving courts of coordinate jurisdiction.

“While the judiciary has the constitutional responsibility to interpret the law and adjudicate disputes, conflicting decisions on similar matters can undermine public confidence in the institution and create unnecessary tension. We must protect the integrity and independence of our judiciary,” he further said.

Jonathan warned that declining public confidence in the judiciary could lead to citizens taking the law into their own hands, with potentially disastrous consequences for the country’s stability.

He also cautioned against the use of ethnic sentiments in the 2027 elections, warning that political rivalry could deepen divisions and threaten national unity.

The former President added, “These are precisely the concerns that inform this conference. We seek to hold a mirror before our political leaders and citizens, encourage reflection and promote a change in conduct that respects our laws, democratic values and shared responsibilities.

“As I observed a few days ago in Lagos, if Nigeria must make meaningful progress, we must review our political recruitment process. Our present system remains vulnerable to ethnic, religious and other primordial considerations, which often prevent competent and credible individuals from emerging as leaders.

“As we approach the 2027 elections, Nigerians will be choosing leaders at both national and sub-national levels. We must therefore be deliberate about the quality of people we recruit into public office at both the state and federal levels. The future of our country depends on the choices we make. Leadership is very critical in the growth of any nation.

“Let us choose competence over prejudice, service over personal ambition, and national interest over narrow considerations. Our democracy must produce leaders capable of uniting our people and advancing our collective development.”

Earlier in his remarks, former Vice-President Namadi Sambo, who is the Chairman of the occasion,  urged the political leaders to view political differences as opportunities for constructive engagement rather than sources of division.

Sambo called for inclusive governance, responsible leadership and respect for the rule of law, stressing the need to build bridges across ethnic, religious and political differences to strengthen national cohesion.

“As a nation, we must continually remind ourselves that political differences should be viewed as opportunities for constructive engagement rather than sources of division. Our collective responsibility is to promote tolerance, inclusive governance, responsible political leadership and respect for the rule of law.

“Having had the privilege of serving our country at the highest level of government, I strongly believe that national cohesion must transcend political affiliation and personal interest. We must deliberately build bridges across our ethnic, religious and political differences and create an environment where every Nigerian feels valued, protected and represented.”

The former leader expressed optimism that the discussions and recommendations at the conference would strengthen public trust, democratic institutions and national unity, stressing that “Our democracy must be competitive, but our nation must remain united.”

In his goodwill message, the Minister of Defence, Gen Christopher Musa (retd.), cautioned political leaders against allowing political competition to fuel national disunity, violence and insecurity, urging them to prioritise peace and national unity.

The minister, represented by his Special Adviser on Strategic Communications, Mercy Bala, stated that, “Political competition is a fundamental feature of democracy. It provides citizens with the opportunity to make choices, express their opinions and hold those entrusted with public responsibilities accountable. However, political competition must never be allowed to become a source of national disunity or insecurity.

“We must understand that political parties and their candidates may have different ambitions, ideologies and programmes, but the peace and unity of Nigeria must remain a common priority for all. The language of political engagement matters. The conduct of political leaders matters. The responsibility of the media matters.

“Above all, the choices we make as citizens matter. We must discourage the use of inflammatory language, hate speech, misinformation and divisive narratives that exploit our ethnic, religious and political differences. Our political leaders must demonstrate restraint, maturity and statesmanship, particularly in moments of heightened political tension.

“Democracy should provide a platform for healthy competition and constructive disagreement, not an avenue for violence, intimidation or the breakdown of mutual respect. Ultimately, no political ambition is worth the loss of innocent lives, the destruction of property or the destabilisation of our country.”

The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Prof. Joash Amupitan, cautioned political actors, sponsors and supporters against violence, intimidation and attacks on campaign convoys ahead of the 2027 elections, warning that those responsible would face prosecution.

Amupitan, represented by INEC National Commissioner, May Agbamuche-Mbu, said, “The Commission condemns in the strongest and most unequivocal terms the widespread incidents of political violence, intimidation, and attacks on campaign convoys and party supporters recorded across parts of the country in recent weeks. Democracy cannot flourish in an atmosphere of fear and bloodshed.

“Let me issue a clear and unambiguous warning to all political actors, sponsors, and their foot soldiers: the law will take its full course, and security agencies working alongside the commission will go after the promoters and perpetrators of violent campaigns without fear or favour.

“Equally, I must sound a stern warning against any form of harassment, intimidation, or physical attack directed at the leadership, staff, or ad hoc workers of INEC by supporters of any political party — whether within Nigeria or abroad. Election officials are public servants discharging a sacred constitutional duty; assaulting or threatening them is an assault on the Nigerian state and will be met with decisive legal consequences.

“Let me remind all political parties, candidates, and their supporters that the Electoral Act 2026 speaks with unmistakable clarity on campaign conduct. Sections 96 and 97 of the Act prohibit the use of abusive, intemperate, or slanderous language designed to provoke violent reactions, ban the deployment of private guards, thugs, or masquerades at political rallies, and criminalise any threat or use of force to intimidate voters or opponents.”

The INEC chairman noted that the Electoral Act 2026 increased penalties for electoral offences fivefold, prescribing fines of up to N5m or 12 months’ imprisonment for individuals and up to N10m for political parties.

He added that the law also empowers the commission to prosecute electoral offenders upon receiving investigation reports from the police.

The INEC chairman declared, “Peaceful campaigns are not a favour granted to the commission; they are a constitutional obligation owed to the Nigerian people. I urge party leaders present here today to hold their candidates and supporters, particularly the youth wings, to the highest standards of discipline, and to utilise the Inter-Party Advisory Council as a genuine platform for dialogue rather than a theatre of brinkmanship.”

In a related development, a former President of the ECOWAS Commission, Omar Touray, has identified public trust in democratic institutions and electoral processes as essential to sustaining stable democracies.

Touray added that public confidence in electoral and judicial institutions would help societies manage political disagreements and accept election outcomes, warning that a lack of trust could trigger political tension and instability even after credible elections.

Ahead of the Nigeria 2027 polls, he recommended that, “Political parties and candidates must exercise restraint and responsibility. Electoral complaints must be supported by evidence and pursued through established constitutional and legal mechanisms rather than through intimidation, incitement or extra-constitutional actions.

“The judiciary must be independent, accessible and capable of delivering timely and credible justice. Its decisions must command respect because they are grounded in law, impartiality and due process.

“Security institutions must remain professional and politically neutral, protecting citizens and democratic processes without fear, favour or discrimination.

“The media, in turn, must uphold the highest standards of accuracy, impartiality and professional responsibility, recognising that the irresponsible dissemination of unverified information can deepen political divisions and undermine public confidence.”

The Executive Director, Goodluck Jonathan Foundation, Ann Iyonu, warned that insecurity, economic pressures and declining public trust could heighten political tensions ahead of the 2027 elections.

She cited an Afrobarometer survey showing that fewer than four in 10 Nigerians believe the 2027 polls will be free and fair, warning that electoral violence could threaten regional stability.

Iyonu noted, “As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general elections, our nation faces a complex and evolving political landscape. Political realignments, persistent insecurity, economic pressures, and declining public trust in institutions are converging to create a fragile environment in which political contestation, if not responsibly managed, could deepen divisions and heighten social tensions.

“The central issue before us today is not political competition itself. Indeed, healthy political competition is a defining feature of every vibrant democracy. The challenge lies in ensuring that competition is conducted responsibly, inclusively, and within the framework of democratic norms, and that political differences are managed in ways that strengthen rather than undermine national cohesion.

“At a time when West Africa is grappling with democratic pressures, violent extremism, unconstitutional changes of government, and growing public distrust in institutions, this conference could not be timelier.

“Across the region, governments, political actors, and citizens are confronted with the shared responsibility of ensuring that contests for political power contribute to national stability and democratic consolidation rather than fuel division, polarisation, and insecurity. Political competition must therefore be conducted in ways that strengthen, rather than weaken, social cohesion, peace, and regional security.”

She added that the survey found that many Nigerians fear vote buying, electoral violence, violation of electoral laws and manipulation of results during the 2027 elections.

Iyonu observed that most respondents still intend to vote, stressing that public confidence in the electoral process is vital to national unity, peace and democratic stability.

“Your Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, the implications extend far beyond Nigeria’s borders. As West Africa’s biggest democracy and economy, and a critical anchor of regional security, Nigeria’s ability to conduct peaceful, credible, and transparent elections is central to the stability of the sub-region.

“During its October 2026 pre-election fact-finding mission to Abuja, ECOWAS underscored that Nigeria’s management of the 2027 elections will serve as a barometer for the sub-region’s democratic and security trajectory. At a time when parts of West Africa continue to grapple with democratic backsliding, unconstitutional changes of government, a disputed or violence-marred election in Nigeria could have far-reaching consequences.

“It could further erode confidence in democratic governance across the sub-region, strain ongoing counterterrorism and border security efforts, trigger humanitarian pressures through population displacement, and disrupt trade and economic stability. For these reasons, safeguarding the integrity of our electoral process is not only a national priority but also a regional peace and security imperative.”

The post 2027: Jonathan fears post-election violence appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: HFM brings EPL trophy to Lagos, thrills fans
description:
Global financial brokerage firm HFM has brought the English Premier League trophy to Lagos as part of the Arsenal FC Africa Trophy Tour, giving Nigerian supporters an opportunity to see the iconic silverware up close.
Speaking at the event, HFM Managing Director Oladapo said the initiative was desig
content:
Global financial brokerage firm HFM has brought the English Premier League trophy to Lagos as part of the Arsenal FC Africa Trophy Tour, giving Nigerian supporters an opportunity to see the iconic silverware up close.

Speaking at the event, HFM Managing Director Oladapo said the initiative was designed to go beyond corporate sponsorship by strengthening the bond between the club and its supporters. He described the tour as recognition of the loyalty Arsenal fans have shown over the years.

Lagos hosted the first leg of the three-city African tour, which will also visit Nairobi, Kenya, and Cape Town, South Africa. More than 2,000 registered fans attended the public viewing, which featured football celebrations, music and other entertainment activities.

“This celebration is for the people, and it is for Nigerians,” Oladapo said. “It is an opportunity to celebrate years of resilience, ambition, and commitment, especially for Arsenal fans, and to send a message that if you keep pushing and believing, you can succeed in whatever you try to do.”

Addressing questions about the absence of former Arsenal striker Nwankwo Kanu, Oladapo apologised on behalf of the club, explaining that unforeseen scheduling conflicts prevented the Nigerian football legend from attending.

He, however, assured supporters that future editions of the tour would seek to feature former and current players in person.

The event also featured live music, entertainment and interactive activities, while fans had the opportunity to take photographs with the Premier League trophy.

The post HFM brings EPL trophy to Lagos, thrills fans appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: OPay names top finalists of N18m National Innovation Challenge
description: OPay, a leading digital bank in Nigeria, in partnership with Google and the Federal Government’s 3 Million Technical Talent Programme, has unveiled five finalist teams for the 2026 National Innovation Challenge, following an intensive selection, training, and mentorship process that attracted over 1
content:
OPay, a leading digital bank in Nigeria, in partnership with Google and the Federal Government’s 3 Million Technical Talent Programme, has unveiled five finalist teams for the 2026 National Innovation Challenge, following an intensive selection, training, and mentorship process that attracted over 11,000 students across Nigeria.

The National Innovation Challenge is part of the broader OPay Scholars Programme 2026, which also includes the N1.2bn, 10-year scholarship initiative and OPay Futures. The programme reflects OPay’s commitment to supporting young Nigerians with the education, digital skills and opportunities they need to build successful careers and create solutions that address real-life challenges.

The challenge attracted over 2,200 student teams from across the country. Following a rigorous selection process, 48 teams were shortlisted for a six-week employability webinar designed to strengthen their knowledge, develop workplace-relevant skills and prepare them for the next stages of the competition.

At the end of the webinar, 10 outstanding teams emerged and advanced to an intensive Boot Camp. During the Boot Camp, the teams worked closely with experienced mentors and industry professionals to develop, test, and improve their innovative solutions.

While only four teams were initially expected to advance to the final stage, the exceptional performance demonstrated during the Boot Camp led to the selection of an additional wildcard finalist, bringing the total number of finalists to five.

The five finalist teams were selected from participating universities across Nigeria. They are Lyrclip from Miva Open University, Team Paye from Adeleke University, CoursePass from Lagos State University of Science and Technology, CampusCheck from the Federal University, Oye-Ekiti, and ResearchFlow from Olabisi Onabanjo University.

The finalists, listed in no particular order, represent their respective institutions and will compete in the next stage of the programme.

The five finalist teams will now have the opportunity to present their refined solutions to leading technology industry experts and angel investors at the grand finale. Beyond the opportunity to win cash prizes, the finalists will gain valuable exposure, industry connections and feedback that can help them take their ideas further.

The top three teams at the finale will share the N18m prize pool, with N10m going to the first-place winner, N5m to the second-place winner and N3m to the third-place winner.

Corporate Social Responsibility Manager, OPay, Itoro Udo, said: “We believe young Nigerians should have the opportunity to turn their potential into progress. Through this programme, we are investing in their skills, ideas and future, while supporting solutions that can make a real difference in Nigerian communities.”

Head, SSA Android Partnerships & Ecosystem, Google, Ngozi Madueke Dozie, said:

“Africa’s next wave of innovation will be built by young people whose tools match their ambition. These finalists are a wonderful example, using Gemini to move from idea to working product and to create solutions that serve Nigerians every day. We’re thrilled to support them alongside OPay and the 3MTT Programme, and excited for what they build next.”

Head, Learning Systems and Talent Development, 3MTT, Theophilus Osifo, said:

“3MTT exists to move young Nigerians from training into real economic opportunity, and this partnership with OPay and Google shows what that takes: a real problem to solve, industry mentors, and selection on demonstrated capability rather than credentials alone. We congratulate all five finalists and look forward to the Grand Finale.”

The National Innovation Challenge further strengthens OPay’s commitment to education, youth empowerment and financial inclusion. Through the wider OPay Scholars Programme, the company continues to support young Nigerians through access to education, practical skills development and opportunities to build a better future.

For more information, visit www.opayweb.com/innovation-challenge/ and follow OPay on LinkedIn, @OPay_NG on X, and @opay.ng on Instagram for updates.

title: Nigeria’s mutual fund assets fall to N10.06tn
description:
Nigeria’s mutual fund assets fell by N36.48bn in the week ended 30 October, 2026, as losses in dollar funds outweighed gains in money market funds and other investment categories.
Data from the Securities and Exchange Commission showed that the net asset value of collective investment schemes declin
content:
Nigeria’s mutual fund assets fell by N36.48bn in the week ended 30 October, 2026, as losses in dollar funds outweighed gains in money market funds and other investment categories.

Data from the Securities and Exchange Commission showed that the net asset value of collective investment schemes declined by 0.36 per cent to N10.06tn from N10.10tn recorded on 23 October.

The decline was mainly driven by dollar funds, which lost N77.59bn, representing a 4.26 per cent drop from N1.82tn to N1.74tn.

The loss in dollar funds was greater than the combined gains recorded by several other investment categories, pushing down the industry’s overall assets.

Dollar funds accounted for 17.34 per cent of total mutual fund assets during the period, making them the second-largest category after money market funds.

Money market funds, which continued to dominate the industry, gained N31.95bn, or 0.47 per cent, to N6.90tn from N6.86tn.

The category accounted for 68.55 per cent of total industry assets, showing that a large share of investors’ money remained concentrated in money market investments.

Together, money market and dollar funds controlled 85.89 per cent of Nigeria’s mutual fund industry.

The figures show that the performance of these two categories has a major influence on the overall direction of the market, as the decline in dollar funds outweighed the growth in money market funds.

Several other investment categories recorded increases during the week, although their gains were not enough to prevent an overall decline.

Shariah-compliant funds recorded the highest percentage growth among the major categories, rising by 1.57 per cent to N154.24bn.

Balanced funds gained 1.44 per cent to N196.57bn, while equity-based funds increased by 1.25 per cent to N239.76bn.

Bonds and fixed-income funds also recorded growth, rising by 0.44 per cent to N234.16bn.

Real estate investment trusts increased marginally by 0.03 per cent to N520.98bn, while specialised funds remained almost unchanged at N54.40bn after declining by 0.01 per cent.

Ethical funds fell by 0.78 per cent to N19.74bn, making them one of the few categories to record a decline.

Exchange-traded funds rose by 2.51 per cent to N34.26bn from N33.42bn.

Despite the weekly decline, Nigeria’s mutual fund industry recorded growth over the eight weeks to 30 October.

SEC data showed that total fund assets increased from N9.59tn on 4 September to N10.06tn on 30 October, representing an increase of N466.20bn, or 4.86 per cent.

Money market funds recorded strong growth over the period, while balanced funds also contributed to the increase in industry assets.

Dollar funds also remained above their September level despite the sharp decline recorded in the latest week.

However, the latest SEC figures do not show whether the fall in dollar funds resulted from investor withdrawals or changes in the value of their underlying investments.

This distinction is important because a mutual fund’s net asset value changes with new investments, withdrawals, investment income and movements in the prices of the assets it holds.

Dollar funds are also reported in naira, meaning exchange rate movements can affect their reported value even when the dollar value of their investments remains unchanged.

The weekly decline therefore does not necessarily mean investors withdrew N77.59bn from dollar funds.

The post Nigeria’s mutual fund assets fall to N10.06tn appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Centre calls for probe into alleged diversion of firearms by Anambra security outfit
description: The Rule of Law and Accountability Advocacy Centre has called on the Anambra State governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo and the Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, to investigate claims that some operatives of Operation Udo-Ga-Chi divert issued firearms to individuals involved in kidnapping and arme
content:
The Rule of Law and Accountability Advocacy Centre has called on the Anambra State governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo and the Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, to investigate claims that some operatives of Operation Udo-Ga-Chi divert issued firearms to individuals involved in kidnapping and armed robbery.

RULAAC, also called for witness protection, an immediate firearms audit and a review of the outfit’s leadership in light of pending allegations and recurring reports of misconduct.

The group stated this in a press statement signed by its Executive Director, Okechukwu Nwanguma, and made available to our correspondent in Awka, on Tuesday.

Nwanguma said a social critic and public commentator, Dr Uche Nworah, drew public attention to the allegations, which he attributed to a commercial transport operator from Eziowelle, Idemili North Local Government Area of the state.

He said the gravity of the claims called for immediate preservation of evidence, protection for the person who came forward, and an investigation independent of the police and its chain of command.

Recall that the Anambra State Government established Agunechemba under the Anambra State Homeland Security Law, 2025, and launched Operation Udo Ga-Achi as a security intervention to complement regular policing.

RULAAC, however, said the government has a responsibility to account for the weapons entrusted to its operatives and to ensure that residents can report suspected misconduct safely.

The group, therefore, calls for the following action, “The Inspector-General of Police should appoint an independent investigative team.

Investigators should obtain the transport operator’s account confidentially, seek corroborating evidence and determine whether any officially issued firearms can be linked to reported kidnappings or armed robberies.

“The police should provide a secure reporting channel and assess the witness’s protection needs promptly. The Governor should order an immediate firearms and ammunition audit and preserve relevant records.

“The state should secure armoury registers, weapons issue and return records, and relevant duty rosters, while auditors should reconcile the records with a physical inventory, document discrepancies and make their findings available to investigators.

“The Governor should review the outfit’s leadership and appointment process. Leadership appointments should follow rigorous checks of integrity, competence and disciplinary history. The review should examine pending allegations, recurring reports of misconduct and how commanders handled earlier complaints.

“Where credible evidence warrants interim action, the state should consider temporarily removing implicated personnel from armed duties or supervisory roles, with due process.

“The state should strengthen recruitment, periodic vetting and oversight. Every operative entrusted with a firearm should be identifiable in the records, and supervisors should routinely verify weapons custody and review misconduct complaints. Residents should have a clear channel for lodging complaints outside the outfit’s chain of command.

“The authorities should inform the public of the outcome.* The Governor and the Inspector-General should announce who will conduct the investigation and provide updates consistent with witness safety and the integrity of the inquiry.

“Where evidence supports criminal charges, the police should refer the case for prosecution. Any proven supervisory or disciplinary failures should also be addressed.

“People who report suspected abuses by security operatives should be able to come forward without fear of retaliation. The immediate test for the authorities is whether they can protect the witness, account for the weapons and establish what happened through an independent investigation.”

However, efforts to get the reactions of the Operation Udo-Ga-Chi through their Spokesman, Nweke Nweke, proved abortive as he did not take several calls to his phone and failed to reply to messages as at the time of filing this report.

The post Centre calls for probe into alleged diversion of firearms by Anambra security outfit appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Easing inflation raises  prospects of interest rate cut
description:
Nigeria’s continued decline in inflation has strengthened expectations of a possible interest rate cut by the Central Bank of Nigeria, as easing price pressures could give monetary policymakers room to reconsider the country’s tight monetary stance.
The National Bureau of Statistics reported on Mond
content:
Nigeria’s continued decline in inflation has strengthened expectations of a possible interest rate cut by the Central Bank of Nigeria, as easing price pressures could give monetary policymakers room to reconsider the country’s tight monetary stance.

The National Bureau of Statistics reported on Monday that headline inflation moderated to 14.06 per cent in October 2026 from 14.63 per cent in September, extending the disinflationary trend.

The latest decline represents a 0.57 percentage-point reduction in the inflation rate, suggesting that price pressures are gradually easing.

The moderation could influence the Monetary Policy Committee’s decision at its next meeting, particularly as policymakers weigh the need to sustain disinflation against the cost of maintaining high borrowing rates.

The CBN had reduced the Monetary Policy Rate by 350 basis points to 23 per cent in September 2026 from 26.5 per cent, signalling a shift towards monetary easing after an extended period of aggressive tightening.

However, the committee faces the challenge of ensuring that lower inflation is sustained before making further reductions in borrowing costs.

A reduction in the MPR could lower the cost of credit for businesses and households, although the extent of its impact would depend on how quickly commercial banks adjust their lending rates.

Manufacturers and other businesses have continued to face expensive financing, with high interest rates adding to production costs and limiting access to working capital.

Nigerian manufacturers paid an average interest rate of 32.2 per cent to access credit in 2025, underscoring the heavy financing burden confronting businesses in the sector, according to exclusive documents seen by The Punch.

Data from the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria showed that the average interest rate paid by manufacturers stood at 32.5 per cent in the first half of 2025 before easing marginally to 31.8 per cent in the second half.

The two half-year averages put the cost of borrowing for manufacturers at 32.2 per cent for the full year.

Analysts say a lower policy rate could also affect yields on government securities, as investors reassess the returns available on Treasury bills, Federal Government bonds and other fixed-income instruments.

For the government, declining yields could eventually reduce the cost of raising funds from the domestic debt market, although this would depend on investor demand and broader liquidity conditions.

Nevertheless, inflation remains an important consideration for the CBN, particularly as exchange rate movements, energy costs and food prices could disrupt the downward trend.

An Abuja-based economist and consultant, Chukwunonso Iheoma, said the falling inflation is a positive development, noting, however, that the CBN should not rush into cutting interest rates simply because headline inflation has declined.

“What matters is whether the decline is broad-based and sustainable. Food prices are still high year-on-year, so this decision should not be rushed.

“However, monetary policy cannot remain excessively tight indefinitely without consequences for economic growth. High interest rates increase the cost of borrowing, discourage private investment and make it difficult for manufacturers and small businesses to expand. If inflation continues to moderate, the CBN should consider a gradual easing of rates, while closely monitoring exchange rate movements and liquidity conditions,” he added.

Food inflation stood at 19.13 per cent year-on-year in October, compared with 16.30 per cent in October 2025, representing an increase of 2.83 percentage points.

However, on a month-on-month basis, food inflation stood at -0.75 per cent, compared with -1.55 per cent in September, indicating that average food prices declined for the second consecutive month, although at a slower pace.

Energy prices have gradually declined as US President Donald Trump has adopted a less confrontational stance towards Iran following Republicans’ losses in the US midterm elections. Oil prices were less than $100 per barrel on Tuesday.

The post Easing inflation raises prospects of interest rate cut appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
