title: My mental struggles inspired me to help others – Life coach
description:
Life coach and founder of Reworded, Ayomide Adedayo-Adeleke, speaks with BIODUN BUSARI about her life, passion, career and efforts to build a community that challenges mediocrity

What best captures who you are beyond your professional roles?
I like to describe myself without titles. I’m an author a
content:
Life coach and founder of Reworded, Ayomide Adedayo-Adeleke, speaks with BIODUN BUSARI about her life, passion, career and efforts to build a community that challenges mediocrity

What best captures who you are beyond your professional roles?

I like to describe myself without titles. I’m an author and public speaker. I work with the belief that we are motivated by what we believe. My conviction is that you cannot build beyond what you can see or think. Many times, we do things based on our experiences, but I’m someone who likes to challenge people’s beliefs. If I see what you’re building and know that you can achieve more, I’ll challenge you to do more. So, I’m a transformational woman.

What influenced your decision to study Business Administration?

I went to Covenant University. My mum’s fashion business inspired me because I wanted to understand the business aspect of what she did. Initially, I wanted to study Mass Communication because, from childhood, I had envisioned speaking to people in different settings. I also enjoyed exploring the business side of my mum’s enterprise, using it as a case study. I think that influenced my choice of course.

Did the course influence what you do currently?

Definitely. Business has to do with customers, and I’m someone who wants to understand my customers. I can be very inquisitive. I want to know why you are buying and why you aren’t buying. This influences everything I do because I work with people who are building their lives, brands, relationships and finances, among other things. My background in business has helped me understand that space, and it has been very useful.

You mentioned your childhood desire to study Mass Communication. What happened to that ambition?

People often talk about not abandoning their childhood passions, and I eventually found my way back to mine. After obtaining my certification in brand strategy, I wanted to improve my communication skills. I subsequently graduated from the National Broadcast Academy and was expected to undertake an internship. I went to TVC, where I worked on the breakfast show. I had to get to work very early, read the newspapers, write scripts and look for punchy headlines.

You also mentioned being certified as a brand strategist.

I would say curiosity inspired me to go into brand strategy. As I mentioned, my mum owned a fashion business, and I wanted to learn how to sew. However, despite several attempts, I couldn’t. I became the only one among my mum’s children who couldn’t learn the skill. So, I decided to focus on other areas.

I realised that I often felt bad about myself because of that, so I started concentrating on how to use my mind and intellectual abilities. My brother told me about a particular academy, and I enrolled in a brand strategy programme. There, I learnt to think, work and relate differently so I could become better.

I initially thought I would be given software that would transform the way I think, but I realised that achieving what I wanted still depended on how I used my brain and mind. That experience has contributed significantly to my personal growth.

How have these experiences shaped your personality?

It has been a tremendous journey. I can say that I’m a woman who can do well at anything I decide to pursue. However, that can also be a weakness because it means having many things to do.

I have worked in the fashion industry and sold food, among other things. I’ve done quite a lot, but I’m currently building Reworded, which demands a significant part of my time and energy.

What is Reworded all about?

First, I would say that Reworded was born out of a personal experience. There was a period in my life when I was struggling mentally and needed people around me to encourage me, but I wasn’t getting that support. I had believed many things about myself that were not true.

At a point, I left a place, and someone spread rumours about me. I started explaining to people that the allegations were false. Whenever anyone approached me to ask what had happened, I would spend time explaining my side of the story. I did that for a long time until the Holy Spirit warned me that by constantly meeting people to correct the falsehoods, I was helping to spread the very lies someone had told about me. The person involved was influential.

The Holy Spirit directed me to return to my Bible, write down everything God had said about me and begin to affirm those things. I realised that the answer was not to keep proving that I was not the person someone had portrayed me to be, but to affirm who God says I am.

That was the idea behind Reworded. I returned to the Word of God to remake, remould and reinvent myself. I began putting the idea into practice when I met several young girls in a particular community who were involved in teenage pregnancies. I reoriented them and gave them reasons to believe they could build better lives. Some embraced the message and became testimonies to others.

Are you organising a gathering to advance this vision?

Yes. The first Reworded Conference will be held on November 21, 2026. However, it is not just a conference; it is an ecosystem. We also have a programme called Inner Architect, which we plan to launch early next year. It focuses on the inner mind.

I often describe the mind as a step-down transformer when it comes to building something. No matter what happens, it will always bring you to the level at which you can see. The conference theme is See Differently, Build Differently. It is intended to help people understand that their experiences do not have to define the limits of what they can achieve.

Two people can go through the same situation but emerge with different perspectives. I know the story of a man who died as an alcoholic. He had two sons. One stayed away from alcohol, while the other became an alcoholic. Their different responses were influenced by how they perceived their father’s lifestyle. Those perceptions eventually shaped how they built their lives.

Similarly, when I experienced someone spreading falsehoods about me, I eventually realised that the experience was something I could use to build my life rather than allow it to define me negatively.

Who are the guest speakers?

The speakers and panellists are experts in their respective fields. They are people I have seen making meaningful contributions to the ecosystem.

The theme of the panel session is Who Told You That? It is the second chapter of my book and seeks to address false beliefs that society has conditioned people to accept, which often become limitations.

We have five panellists who will discuss different subtopics. Essentially, the questions are designed to challenge conventional thinking about why we are where we are.

For instance, we will ask: Who told you that becoming a mother means putting your life on hold? Many women have paused their personal ambitions because they became mothers.

Another question is: Who told you that leaving means you have to lose the relationship? Some people believe that walking away from someone necessarily means ending the relationship, but it does not always have to be so.

We will also ask: Who told you that starting again means you have failed? Some people can pursue different interests and thrive in all of them, but society has made us believe that pursuing multiple interests is impracticable.

We need to challenge such beliefs. We are multi-hyphenated individuals, and the conference is not exclusively for women or any particular audience. It is for anyone building something. If God created you to build, then it is for you. Whether you are going through a season of transition in your relationship, business, career, ministry or academics, you are welcome.

You mentioned that Who Told You That? is the second chapter of your book. What is the book about?

The title is Before You Become Someone Else. I cannot recall exactly how I arrived at the title, but I know the inspiration was spiritual.

The book explores who God designed us to be. I believe we all have a design. When you buy a product, for instance, it comes with a manual. However, what most people do is ignore the manual until something goes wrong. That is when they return to it.

The same applies to our lives. God created us and gave us a manual, but we are often quick to say that we live in a modern world where everybody has their own truth. People are in a hurry to do whatever they want without necessarily considering whether they are doing the right thing. However, I care about the original design and what God has said.

Another part of the book discusses the idea of being Too Early, Too Late. Sometimes, people tell you that you are too early, while at other times, they say you are too late. But who has the authority to determine where you should be at a particular point in your life?

I agree that some opportunities have time limitations. For instance, you cannot become a professional footballer at 70, but there are other ways to pursue aspects of that dream.

Many successful business owners did not start early. I once came across an eight-year-old who wrote a book. She did not write it based on experience but as an expression of herself. So, what is wrong with me expressing myself as an author? Nobody owes you permission to pursue your dreams because you are supposedly too early or too late. That is the mindset I’m trying to build through this community.

What does the community stand to gain?

Reworded is an ecosystem with different components. We have the conference and the Reworded Room, which is our community.

The idea behind the Reworded Room is to bring women together in a private development space where we challenge existing beliefs, grow together and take action. It is a place where something must change within you.

Remember I mentioned being a brand strategist and how people approach me for different things? In the Reworded Room, I can respond to people’s questions based on their individual needs. If someone needs a therapist, we refer them to one. If the issue concerns branding, we can provide the necessary guidance.

Members will also have their thinking challenged every month. The Bible talks about renewing our minds; it does not say we should renew them just once.

I once saw a post that asked whether, when a fish is sick, you give the fish medication or put the medication in the water. The point is that your environment matters.

Membership of the Reworded Room runs for one year, with payment options available annually, quarterly or monthly to accommodate different financial capacities. Members can ask questions and participate in the community.

We also have Inner Architect, a six-week programme designed to challenge people’s beliefs and reshape their thinking.

What advice would you give people at different stages of their personal or professional journeys about overcoming challenges?

There are different stages in the process of building something. There are people at the foundational stage, those in the middle and those who have reached the accomplished stage.

Some people support your vision from the beginning. Those at the middle stage begin to support you when they see evidence of what you are building, while others only show up after you have achieved success.

Some people may see you at the beginning of a project but refuse to contribute or support you. They may even pretend not to notice your efforts. However, don’t write them off because they may eventually become the people who say, ‘We knew her when she started.’ They can testify to how your efforts paid off.

Above all, you must believe in your dreams. People must believe in their dreams. Otherwise, you risk becoming like the third servant in the biblical Parable of the Talents, whom his master called wicked for failing to use the talent entrusted to him.

The post My mental struggles inspired me to help others – Life coach appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Healthy, productive workforce, critical to sustainable national development – NSITF
description: The Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund has called on employers to protect workers, ensure a healthy, secure, and productive workforce, describing it as a critical investment in building successful businesses, productivity, business continuity, industrial harmony and sustainable national development
content:
The Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund has called on employers to protect workers, ensure a healthy, secure, and productive workforce, describing it as a critical investment in building successful businesses, productivity, business continuity, industrial harmony and sustainable national development.

NSITF also urged employers to prioritise workers’ welfare by enrolling their employees in the Employees’ Compensation Scheme to promote workplace safety and sustainable economic growth.

The call was made by the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of NSITF, Oluwaseun Faleye, during the NSITF special day at the 40th Lagos International Trade Fair, according to a press statement issued on Tuesday.

Speaking on the theme, “The employee at the centre of growth, secured by the employees’ compensation scheme”, Faleye said employees are not simply participants in the production process, but are the human force behind enterprise and economic progress.

He said, “This year’s theme, “40 years of trade, growth and global connection”, celebrates the enduring importance of commerce in building prosperous economies and connecting nations. I congratulate the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry on sustaining this important platform for 40 years.

“But as we celebrate the achievements of enterprise, we must also recognise a fundamental truth: behind every successful business is a workforce whose contributions make that success possible.

“Every product manufactured, every service delivered, every transaction concluded and every innovation brought to life depends on the knowledge, commitment and effort of people.

“Employees are not simply participants in the production process; they are the human force behind enterprise and economic progress.

“This is why, at the NSITF, our message is clear: the employee must remain at the centre of economic growth, and the employee must be protected.

“Our theme, ‘The employee at the centre of growth, secured by the employees’ compensation scheme’, captures a conviction that guides our work at the NSITF: that economic growth is only truly meaningful and sustainable when the people who create that growth are protected, valued and supported.

“A business may have capital, technology, infrastructure and an ambitious vision, but without a healthy, secure and productive workforce, its capacity to grow is limited. Protecting workers is therefore not separate from building successful businesses. It is an investment in productivity, business continuity, industrial harmony and sustainable national development.”

According to him, this conviction underpins the Employees’ Compensation Scheme, administered by the NSITF under the Employees’ Compensation Act, 2010, adding that the Scheme provides compensation and support to employees who suffer work-related injuries, occupational diseases, disabilities or death, with benefits extended to eligible dependants where the law so provides.

He said the scheme provides a safety net for workers and their families when an unfortunate workplace incident threatens their health, livelihood and financial security.

“The Employees’ Compensation Scheme is a social protection arrangement designed to ensure that when a worker suffers an injury, disease, disability or death arising from work, the worker or eligible dependants are not left to bear the consequences alone.

“The process is straightforward. Employers can register through the NSITF Employer Self-Service Portal at ecsonline.nsitf.gov.ng, by creating an account and following the registration process. They can also walk into any NSITF office for guidance and assistance with registration.

“To our employers, particularly those operating small businesses and enterprises, I encourage you to take advantage of these channels. Do not allow a lack of information or uncertainty about the process to keep your workers outside the protection available under the law. Visit our stand, speak with our officers and take the first step towards securing your workforce.

“At the NSITF, we recognise that expanding social protection in Nigeria requires us to go beyond the traditional formal workplace. This is why, over the past few years, we have progressively intensified efforts to reach micro, small and medium-sized enterprises as a pathway towards broader engagement with the informal economy,” he added.

He said in July 2011, the Fund registered 214,519 employers and covered 8,005,027 employees across the public and private sectors, integrating 73 Ministries, Departments and Agencies into the Scheme.

“In 2025, we registered 21,937 employers and covered 160,971 employees. Between January and October 2026, a further 17,435 employers were registered, and 250,144 employees were brought under coverage. Significantly, the number of employees covered within the first 10 months of 2026 has already exceeded the total recorded for the whole of 2025.”

In his goodwill message, the President and Chairman of the Council, Leye Kupoluyi, said workers’ protection was essential to economic progress.

He noted that behind every successful business was a workforce responsible for driving production, innovation and service delivery.

Some beneficiaries of the scheme also expressed appreciation to the Fund for the financial support received following work-related incidents, urging employers to enrol their workers to guarantee access to compensation when necessary.

The post Healthy, productive workforce, critical to sustainable national development – NSITF appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: African countries deserve easier access  to climate finance – Environment minister
description:
The Minister of Environment, Balarabe Lawal, Iin this interview with DAMILOLA AINA, discusses Nigeria’s expectations at COP31, climate finance inequalities, adaptation priorities and efforts to secure fairer funding and support for African countries in global negotiations

How would you assess Niger
content:
The Minister of Environment, Balarabe Lawal, Iin this interview with DAMILOLA AINA, discusses Nigeria’s expectations at COP31, climate finance inequalities, adaptation priorities and efforts to secure fairer funding and support for African countries in global negotiations

How would you assess Nigeria’s experience at the ongoing 31st edition of COP, particularly in terms of your engagements with global leaders on climate change?

As we all know, this is the United Nations Climate Change Conference of the Parties 31, and it is a conference focused on implementation. We have had many Conferences of the Parties, particularly COP28, where several promises were made and substantial funds were mobilised. This COP is special because it is expected to begin to show actual results.

From the moment we started, things have been going very well. Apart from the conference itself, we have signed a number of agreements. For example, we signed an agreement with China. About five agreements have been signed, and I believe that by the end of the conference, we will have a comprehensive list of all the agreements. I do not have the details at hand now, but I believe we will have them before the end of the week.

There is a lot of hope for this COP because several sectors are being considered. We are looking at the environment, which is very important, climate change, water resources, agriculture, health, trade and investment. We expect all these sectors to be represented, and we already have some of the ministers here.

The Minister of Agriculture is here, and we have signed an agreement under the National Agricultural Land Development Authority. The Minister of Water Resources is also expected to sign an agreement with the German Agency for International Cooperation later in the day. The Minister of Livestock also held a session, which I am sure you attended, and I believe there will be an outcome from that engagement.

This COP is going to be different because, for a long time, we have been talking about loss and damage. To me, it was like a mirage, but now I am beginning to see the light at the end of the tunnel. At least, the fund is now in place, and some money has been committed to it.

We are talking about $2bn. It is still far below what we expected because, in Dubai, $100bn was promised. However, up to this moment, we are talking about slightly above $1bn in the fund. Nigeria is also among the countries expected to benefit from it.

We have submitted our request, and it is receiving very good consideration from the fund. So, we are doing well this time, and I believe this is not like some of the previous COPs, which were more like talk shows. This is an important conference where I think we are beginning to make progress.

Nigeria’s relationship with China has continued to strengthen. You signed an agreement with China two years ago. Could you explain what the agreement concluded at this COP provides and what benefits it offers Nigeria?

The agreement we signed two years ago is not different from the current agreement. This one is intended to provide the material support needed to implement the agreement we signed previously.

The earlier agreement was the starting point. What we have signed now concerns the materials and equipment that China will bring in to support its implementation. We have to agree on the conditions under which these materials will be brought into the country, including taxes, customs duties and other related issues. That is what we have agreed with them.

We are receiving substantial equipment, instruments, machinery and other materials to support the earlier agreement. So, it is not entirely a new agreement. It is a continuation of the agreement we signed previously.

Nigeria now has a National Adaptation Plan in place. What does this signify for the country, particularly given that its development has been ongoing for the past four to five years?

The National Adaptation Plan was started in 2021, and this year, we have been able to complete it with the support of several partners, particularly the Food and Agriculture Organisation, the United Nations Environment Programme and other development partners.

The plan is designed to examine Nigeria as a whole and identify areas affected by climate change so that we can develop appropriate measures to adapt to those challenges. Most importantly, the plan is expected to help us mobilise resources to address them.

The report is ready, and our partners are willing to support us in mobilising the resources required for its implementation.

We are looking at the entire country. In the North, we are examining the challenges of Sahelian encroachment and desertification. Moving towards the Middle Belt, we are looking at the effects of land degradation and changing environmental conditions. Further south, we have forests that are increasingly being threatened by deforestation and other activities. We also have swamp and mangrove ecosystems, which are disappearing because of oil production and other human activities.

The plan examines Nigeria’s overall environmental challenges, identifies the affected areas and proposes measures through which we can adapt to or mitigate the effects of climate change.

It is important because many people are being forced to move away from their communities and traditional territories because of land degradation. That is why we must look at the issue from a national perspective.

One of the major takeaways from this COP is the support we have received. You cannot begin implementation without a proper plan. The plan has been in the pipeline for a long time, but we have now completed it, and it is available for people to examine and support its implementation.

You also participated in a meeting with the United Nations Secretary-General on the Grid Acceleration Initiative. What were the key outcomes and commitments arising from the discussions?

Yes, I had two meetings with the Secretary-General. The first concerned electricity, particularly the deployment of solar power, solar grids and other renewable energy solutions. They are already supporting Nigeria in that area.

About $500m has already been committed to supporting us in expanding mini-grids and integrating more grids into our electricity system. That was the first meeting, and we are grateful for the support.

The second meeting was convened by the outgoing United Nations Secretary-General, who invited four ministers and three presidents to participate in the discussion. The meeting was intended to review the progress made so far, identify outstanding challenges and examine what still needed to be done as he prepares to hand over to his successor.

We are very grateful for what he has done for Africa, particularly because he has been a champion of climate change action since he became Secretary-General 10 years ago.

It was a very open meeting. We were given the opportunity to raise the issues we believed needed attention, and he took notes. I was actually surprised because he was taking notes like a student.

The Vice-President of Gabon spoke first, and I spoke second. Other participants also made their contributions, and it was a very productive meeting.

I believe this is the way we can begin to implement and monitor what has been discussed over the years. No Secretary-General has worked so hard to address climate change as the outgoing one. He has done so much, particularly with Africa in focus.

He is more African than many people we know. He thinks about Africa, works for Africa and has consistently supported the continent. That is why we need to celebrate him and thank him for his contributions. We did that during the meeting.

With negotiations still ongoing, what are the key priorities and expected outcomes for Nigeria and Africa at this COP?

That is why we have brought representatives of all the relevant sectors here to present issues that are important to Nigeria.

We are looking at agriculture because we need to improve our food security, increase agricultural production and address land degradation.

When it comes to the environment generally, we are experiencing flooding in several parts of the country. Areas that ordinarily should not experience such levels of flooding are now being affected. Places such as Sokoto, Maiduguri, Katsina and other areas have experienced flooding.

So, we are looking at adaptation, mitigation and, at the same time, mobilising resources for climate finance.

Yesterday, we also strongly raised the issue of carbon credits, an area where we believe developing countries are not receiving fair treatment. We have noticed that applicants from some countries appear to receive more favourable consideration than those from countries like Nigeria. We raised this concern strongly, and other African representatives shared similar views.

Following our meeting, discussions were held with representatives of developed countries to examine how applicants from developing countries could benefit more fairly from carbon credit arrangements.

Nigeria has already developed its own plans and framework, which was launched by the President in Abu Dhabi. I believe we are making progress and will achieve as much as possible in this area.

I expect more from this COP than from some of the previous conferences because there are more concrete issues on the ground.

At least, we can now see that funds are available.

What we have strongly advocated is making it easier for countries to access these funds. In most cases, the processes involved in obtaining climate finance are very difficult and complicated.

This time, however, the Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and other relevant officials have assured us that efforts will be made to simplify the processes, particularly for African countries and small island developing states.

We are working towards ensuring that the process of accessing climate funds becomes easier for countries that need the resources most.

There are concerns about disparities in the interest rates charged to countries borrowing funds for climate-related projects. While some countries reportedly enjoy lower rates, others, including Nigeria, face significantly higher borrowing costs. For instance, Germany is said to borrow at three per cent, compared with Nigeria’s seven per cent. What is your reaction to this disparity, and what should be done to ensure fairer access to climate finance for developing countries?

This is exactly the kind of inequality we have been discussing. Just as we have raised concerns about carbon credits, we have also observed that some countries enjoy more favourable financing conditions than others.

When you examine the situation, you find that lenders consider a country’s credit rating. That is why it may be easier for Germany to obtain financing at three per cent, while Nigeria is charged seven per cent.

However, this is one of the issues we discussed during our meeting, and we are pushing for a more equitable arrangement that will bring the rates to a reasonable level.

What borrowing interest rate do you believe would be fair and sustainable for Nigeria?

One per cent is fine. Thank you very much. We also have to examine the data to determine the interest rate that will help us achieve net zero in the future.

The post African countries deserve easier access to climate finance – Environment minister appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Lagos job fair targets 250 placements for applicants
description:
The Lagos State Government has set a target of securing at least 250 verified job opportunities for more than 2,500 job seekers participating in its 2026 employment fair, as it seeks to address the disconnect between the skills of young people and the demands of employers.
The fair, organised by the
content:
The Lagos State Government has set a target of securing at least 250 verified job opportunities for more than 2,500 job seekers participating in its 2026 employment fair, as it seeks to address the disconnect between the skills of young people and the demands of employers.

The fair, organised by the Ministry of Wealth Creation and Employment, brought together job seekers, employers and recruitment professionals at the University of Lagos on Tuesday, with activities including direct recruitment, CV clinics and career counselling.

The initiative formed part of the activities marking the fourth Lagos Employment Summit, which focused on bridging the gap between young people and employment opportunities.

Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, represented by the Chairman of the Lagos State Civil Service Commission, Dapo Thomas, said the ability of an economy to provide sustainable livelihoods should be a major measure of its performance.

He described youth empowerment as a priority of his administration, arguing that economic growth would remain incomplete if young people were unable to access opportunities to put their skills and talents to productive use.

“A society cannot reach its potential when its young people have the energy, talent, and willingness to work but lack access to opportunities that will allow them to succeed,” the governor said.

He explained that the job fair was designed to move beyond discussions about unemployment by providing a platform for direct engagement between prospective employees and organisations seeking qualified workers.

“This initiative goes beyond discussions about unemployment; it provides practical opportunities for recruitment, career counselling, CV clinics, and direct engagement with prospective employers,” he said.

The governor also highlighted the changing nature of employment, particularly the growing influence of artificial intelligence and emerging industries, saying his administration was committed to preparing young Lagosians for evolving labour market demands.

In his keynote address, the Commissioner for Wealth Creation and Employment, Akinyemi Ajigbotafe, said the state government had continued to develop interventions aimed at improving employability, promoting entrepreneurship and connecting residents with decent employment opportunities.

He described the job fair as an important component of the employment summit, providing a direct link between job seekers, employers and recruitment professionals.

“This gathering represents another significant step in our collective commitment to expanding employment opportunities, strengthening workforce capacity and creating sustainable pathways to economic prosperity for the people of Lagos State,” Ajigbotafe said.

The commissioner, however, acknowledged that unemployment was not simply a question of the availability of jobs, pointing to the mismatch between the competencies possessed by job seekers and the skills required by employers.

His remarks highlighted the challenge facing employment initiatives that seek to connect graduates and other job seekers with available vacancies without adequately addressing the skills gap.

The Executive Secretary of the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund, Feyisara Alayande, commended Sanwo-Olu for his commitment to employment generation, human capital development, entrepreneurship and inclusive economic growth.

She called on employers, educational institutions, private sector organisations and development partners to strengthen collaboration in developing industry-driven training programmes.

Alayande said educational and skills development systems must respond to changing labour market requirements to improve the prospects of young people seeking employment.

title: Delta Secondary School dominates GCU Relays
description:
Delta Secondary School, Warri, stamped its authority on the 8th Government College Ughelli Relays, winning the overall male and female titles at the inter-collegiate athletics competition in Ughelli, Delta State.
Beyond their dominance on the track, the Warri-based school had another reason to celeb
content:
Delta Secondary School, Warri, stamped its authority on the 8th Government College Ughelli Relays, winning the overall male and female titles at the inter-collegiate athletics competition in Ughelli, Delta State.

Beyond their dominance on the track, the Warri-based school had another reason to celebrate as one of its athletes, Theophilus Beauty, secured a scholarship through university education, alongside financial and training support to advance her athletics career.

Beauty was named Victrix Ludorum, while her schoolmate, Abruthe Ogenevwegba, claimed the Victor Ludorum award, giving Delta Secondary School a clean sweep of the competition’s two major individual honours.

The scholarship was announced by Chief Andrew Oru,  who pledged to sponsor Beauty’s education through university level in Nigeria.

His intervention goes beyond academic sponsorship, with a commitment to provide the coaching and training resources needed to nurture her sporting ability.

He also promised financial assistance to Delta Secondary School and the coaches who have played a role in developing her talent.

The school contingent equally benefited from immediate cash rewards following its impressive outing.

In the relay events, Idia College, Benin City, demonstrated its strength in the women’s category, winning gold in both the 4x100m and 4x400m races. Novena University Staff School took the men’s 4x400m title.

Traditional rulers HRM Uche Irenuwa, the Obi of Abavo, and HRM Albert Akpomudje, SAN, the Owhorode of Olomu Kingdom, joined Chief Oru in presenting awards to the outstanding participants.

However, while the performances provided plenty of reasons for celebration, the state of the competition venue emerged as a major concern, with the athletics tracks now requiring urgent attention.

Akpomudje, in his closing remarks, acknowledged the difficulties faced by the organisers and praised committee chairman Ejiro Omonode for ensuring the successful staging of the competition despite the deteriorating condition of the facility.

He subsequently announced plans to establish a body that would drive the comprehensive reconstruction of the 10-year-old tartan tracks.

Shell Petroleum Development Company originally constructed and donated the facility to Government College Ughelli, providing the platform for the inaugural GCU Relays in 2018.

“We acknowledge Shell’s contribution to the development of the facility which heralded the first edition in 2018, but for now and moving forward the track now requires rehabilitation or replacement after years of consistent use,” Akpomudje said.

The proposed reconstruction is expected to give the competition a much-needed facelift and restore the facility to a standard capable of supporting the development of young athletics talents.

Organised by the Government College Ughelli Old Boys Association the annual GCU Relays was established to bring secondary school athletics back into focus, discover future stars and create a platform for young athletes to compete and develop.

The event continues to enjoy backing from the GAMSU Foundation and the school’s old boys, whose support has helped sustain the competition as an important fixture on the secondary school athletics calendar.

The post Delta Secondary School dominates GCU Relays appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: U-23 AFCON: Olympic Eagles crush DR Congo 4-0, face Zambia
description:
Nigeria’s U-23 side, the Olympic Eagles, overturned their first-leg deficit with a commanding 4-0 victory over the Democratic Republic of Congo to reach the final qualifying round of next year’s U-23 Africa Cup of Nations, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
Having lost the first leg in Lubumbashi four days
content:
Nigeria’s U-23 side, the Olympic Eagles, overturned their first-leg deficit with a commanding 4-0 victory over the Democratic Republic of Congo to reach the final qualifying round of next year’s U-23 Africa Cup of Nations, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.

Having lost the first leg in Lubumbashi four days earlier, the Olympic Eagles responded emphatically at the Remo Stars Stadium in Ikenne-Remo, taking the lead in the eighth minute through Alex Oweilayefa.

The forward tapped into an empty net after the Congolese goalkeeper spilled a fierce close-range effort from Umar Abubakar, with Nigeria having already missed a couple of chances before breaking the deadlock.

The hosts maintained their attacking pressure, pinning the visitors back as Oweilayefa, Abubakar, Peter Osayande, Saleh Sadiq, Aderemi Adeoye and Wilfred George continued to threaten.

Sadiq came close to doubling Nigeria’s lead in the 38th minute, but his effort was cleared off the line, while Abubakar missed from close range four minutes later as the Olympic Eagles continued to dominate.

Nigeria resumed the second half with greater intensity, and their pressure paid off two minutes after the restart when Osayande finished from close range following good work down the left by Oweilayefa and Adeoye.

The goal drew the tie level on aggregate, leaving the Olympic Eagles needing another to complete the turnaround.

Osayande subsequently moved to the left flank, where his pace and direct running caused further problems for the Congolese defence.

One of his attacking runs created the opportunity for substitute Victor Samuel to score Nigeria’s third, finishing from close range after the visitors failed to deal with the move.

The Olympic Eagles sealed their passage in the third minute of added time when substitute Abdulmuiz Adeleke converted a penalty to complete the 4-0 victory and a 4-2 aggregate win.

Nigeria will now face Zambia in the final qualifying round after the southern Africans edged Burkina Faso 3-2 on penalties following a 1-1 aggregate draw.

Zambia and Burkina Faso had finished level over two legs before the former prevailed in the shootout to book their place in the final round.

title: Eagles face AFCON qualifiers hurdle as Chelle admits trouble
description:
Super Eagles coach Eric Chelle has admitted that Nigeria have a mountain to climb in order to qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations after Tuesday’s goalless draw against co-hosts Tanzania left them three points behind Group L leaders Guinea-Bissau, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
Nigeria were held
content:
Super Eagles coach Eric Chelle has admitted that Nigeria have a mountain to climb in order to qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations after Tuesday’s goalless draw against co-hosts Tanzania left them three points behind Group L leaders Guinea-Bissau, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.

Nigeria were held to a 0-0 draw by Tanzania in Zanzibar, leaving the Super Eagles with seven points from four matches, while Guinea-Bissau moved to 10 points after beating Madagascar 2-0 in Bissau.

Éric Chelle’s side had beaten Tanzania 3-1 in Uyo on Friday, with substitute Tolu Arokodare scoring twice after the visitors cancelled out Alhassan Yusuf’s early opener.

However, there was nothing to separate the teams in Zanzibar as the hosts threatened to hurt Nigeria, who also squandered several scoring opportunities.

Tanzania were forced into two first-half substitutions, with Novatus Chilambo and Charles M’Mombwa coming off injured, while Nigeria introduced Akor Adams and Alex Iwobi shortly after the hour before bringing on Alhassan Yusuf.

The Super Eagles also lost Bruno Onyemaechi to injury late in the game, with Ola Aina replacing the defender.

With Tanzania already assured of a place at the finals as co-hosts alongside Kenya and Uganda, only one additional qualifying spot is available in Group L, leaving Nigeria and Guinea-Bissau in a battle for the ticket.

“A draw away from home is not a bad result, but in our situation, because we lost to Guinea-Bissau, that is why we are in trouble,” Chelle said after Tuesday’s match.

“We are in trouble because if they win, we have to score many goals. Now we have to win in Madagascar and the last game.

“We had to win both games to be in the same situation, but in football, if you cannot score goals, you cannot win. We had a lot of chances but didn’t score. Every time something was missing, maybe the last kick, the last pass or the pass before the last pass.

“This is not about some players missing and others not missing, but in my opinion, we have to be more aggressive,” he added.

Nigeria’s 3-0 defeat to Guinea-Bissau in September has left their qualification hopes outside their complete control, with the Super Eagles needing maximum points from their remaining fixtures and hoping the group leaders drop points.

Chelle’s men will travel to face Madagascar on March 24 before hosting Guinea-Bissau four days later in what could be a decisive encounter for the group’s remaining ticket.

title: What America’s midterm elections teach Nigeria
description:
From Texas to Kansas, the 2026 US midterm elections remind us that political power is borrowed from the people, never permanently owned by those who hold it.
There is something profoundly instructive about watching a political stronghold change hands—not because one political party is inherently bet
content:
From Texas to Kansas, the 2026 US midterm elections remind us that political power is borrowed from the people, never permanently owned by those who hold it.

There is something profoundly instructive about watching a political stronghold change hands—not because one political party is inherently better than another. At the same time, an electoral defeat does not necessarily mean every policy of the losing party was wrong. Still, it reminds us of a fundamental democratic truth: the people who give political power retain the right to take it away.

On November 3, 2026, Americans went to the polls for the midterm elections. By the following morning, the political landscape had shifted considerably. Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress. At the same time, Republicans suffered defeats in states where their electoral dominance had endured for decades: Kansas, Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Ohio, and Georgia.

Places whose political histories had long defined what was assumed electorally possible suddenly produced different results.

For Nigerians watching from thousands of miles away, these elections raise a vital question: What happens when citizens refuse to treat political power as the permanent property of those who occupy it?

Consider Kansas. For 94 years, the state had not elected a Democrat to the United States Senate—not since 1932. Yet on November 3, Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall. Nearly a century of electoral history did not prevent voters from choosing differently.

Then there is Texas. For decades, the state has been central to Republican strength, having elected neither a Democratic US senator since 1988 nor a governor since 1990. In this election, however, Democrat James Talarico won the Senate race, while Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott. Texas did not erase its political history; its voters exercised their right to write a new chapter.

South Carolina offered another example, electing Democrat Annie Andrews to the Senate and ending a drought stretching back to 1998. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek won a Senate seat in a state that had not elected a Democrat to the chamber since 2008. Democrats also captured governorships in Georgia and Ohio, breaking years of uninterrupted Republican control.

North Carolina tells a similar story. For 18 years, Republicans held the Senate seat previously occupied by Thom Tillis. Yet on November 3, former Democratic Governor and a fundamental character became the first Democrat elected to the US Senate since 2008. While North Carolina is competitive in statewide contests, this result shows that even an established pattern of party control remains subject to the voters’ final verdict.

These outcomes do not mean every voter in those states changed their political allegiance, nor that each state’s fundamental character transformed overnight. But collectively, the results challenge one of politics’ most persistent assumptions: yesterday’s electoral dominance does not guarantee tomorrow’s victory.

Political parties often speak about strongholds as though they were the electorate’s consent; the state belongs to us. That region will always vote for us. Those voters have nowhere else to go.

Such language is painfully familiar in Nigeria. We speak of states as the personal territories of governors, political godfathers, and dominant parties. We describe entire regions as though their political preferences were permanently fixed, sometimes treating a politician’s popularity as a substitute for the electorate’s consent.

But citizens are not political property. Their loyalty is not an inheritance, and their votes should never be regarded as an entitlement. A person who supported a party in one election has every right to reconsider that support in the next. Changing one’s political preference is not betrayal; it is the essence of democratic freedom.

According to Associated Press reporting, affordability, high living costs, concerns about corruption, and dissatisfaction with federal government policy heavily influenced American voters. While these concerns affected individuals differently, they ensured voters could reassess political leadership against their current realities. A political mandate is permission to govern, based on citizens’ priorities and future judgement.

Nigeria’s own political history makes this lesson acutely relevant. In 2015, Nigerians voted out an incumbent president for the first time, proving that federal incumbency does not guarantee victory.

However, democratic progress cannot be measured solely by whether an incumbent loses. A functioning democracy must protect citizens’ right to retain a government they support just as much as it protects their right to replace one they no longer want. Both outcomes must emerge from a credible process.

Consequently, Nigeria’s political discourse must move beyond merely predicting which party will win the next election. The more fundamental questions concern the conditions under which citizens vote: Do they feel safe? Are they confident that their ballots will be counted? Do electoral institutions act impartially? Are disputes resolved through credible legal processes? And do political actors respect outcomes? Are disputes resolved through lawful procedures? Without satisfactory answers, the language of popular sovereignty is difficult to reconcile with political reality. The power of the people is meaningful only when the electoral system respects what the people decide.

American elections offer another vital lesson: political competition requires alternatives that voters regard as credible. In Nigeria, conversations about opposition politics too often revolve around personalities, defections, tactical alliances, and the race for the next presidential ticket.

While these matters attract attention, an opposition party’s democratic responsibility extends far beyond identifying government failures. It must articulate what it proposes to do differently. What is its economic programme? How would it tackle insecurity? What structural reforms would it pursue in education, healthcare, employment, and public finance?

Cooperation between opposition parties is a legitimate choice where shared policy priorities and democratic principles exist. However, collaboration does not automatically produce public confidence, just as fragmentation does not automatically signal a lack of seriousness. What matters is whether parties build accountable structures, communicate coherent policies, select candidates transparently, and demonstrate absolute respect for democratic rules. The same standards apply equally to governing parties.

The American experience also warrants careful interpretation. Its electoral system faces significant controversies, including disputes over redistricting, campaign finance, voter access, and administration. The 2026 results do not imply that American democracy is flawless; indeed, ballots were still being counted days after the polls closed. But the elections underscore the importance of robust institutions through which political competition takes place and outcomes remain publicly verifiable.

For Nigeria, strengthening those institutions requires sustained, active attention between electoral cycles. The Independent National Electoral Commission must possess the operational capacity and independence to administer credible elections. Security agencies must protect voters and officials without partisan bias. Political parties must democratise their internal processes, and courts must adjudicate electoral disputes fairly and promptly. Civil society organisations and journalists must continue scrutinising public resource management, while citizens demand unhindered access to reliable information. Credible elections do not emerge automatically from neglected institutions.

As citizens, we must also examine our own criteria: How do we evaluate those seeking to govern us? By ethnicity? Religion? Party loyalty? Personal relationships? Or by evidence of performance, integrity, policy commitments, and the capacity to deliver public goods?

Nigeria’s political choices occur within complex socio-economic realities. Many citizens face severe barriers to participation, including insecurity, financial hardship, and institutional distrust. It would be unfair to place the burden of democratic shortcomings entirely on voters. Government and electoral authorities carry profound obligations.

Still, where citizens have meaningful freedom to participate, their choices matter. We must be willing to question politicians we support, demand accountability from those in office, scrutinise challengers, and reject the notion that political loyalty demands permanent agreement. Democracy does not demand that citizens always change their leaders; it demands that they remain free to do so.

The 2026 American midterm elections will generate extensive debate about the direction of US politics and the legacy of the presidential term. But the core lesson extends far beyond American shores.

Political power remains subject to public judgement. Kansas went 94 years without electing a Democratic senator; Texas went decades without a Democratic statewide victor. Yet those patterns changed. For Nigeria, the lesson is not that a particular party must win or another must lose, but that no political office should escape electoral accountability.

No governor owns a state. No president owns a country. No party owns a people’s loyalty, and no citizen owes permanent allegiance to a politician. The ballot must remain powerful enough to change a government without pushing the nation into violence.

That is the democratic principle worth defending. And as another election cycle approaches, the most critical question for Nigeria remains: When Nigerians speak through their votes, will our institutions faithfully deliver their verdict?

Ukoh, a PhD student and coauthor of Built By The Ancestors, writes from New York, the United States

The post What America’s midterm elections teach Nigeria appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Bassey has what Barca lack – Ex-Fulham player
description:
Nigeria defender Calvin Bassey could be an ideal fit for Barcelona, with former Fulham player Javi Pereira insisting the full back possesses qualities missing from Hansi Flick’s defensive options, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
Speaking to Marca (h/t Mundo Deportivo), Pereira made a strong case for the
content:
Nigeria defender Calvin Bassey could be an ideal fit for Barcelona, with former Fulham player Javi Pereira insisting the full back possesses qualities missing from Hansi Flick’s defensive options, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.

Speaking to Marca (h/t Mundo Deportivo), Pereira made a strong case for the 26-year-old, highlighting his physical strength, recovery speed and ability to drive the ball forward.

Although Bassey has not emerged as a concrete Barcelona transfer target, Pereira believes his profile addresses some of the club’s needs as they seek to strengthen their defence.

“I honestly believe that Barcelona don’t have a centre-back like Bassey. He has a distinct physical and athletic profile, something Flick is lacking in important matches.

“He can play in a high defensive line, knows how to push forward, is aggressive in the opposition’s half and has great top speed. He could play,” Pereira said.

The former Fulham player believes Bassey’s athleticism would offer Barcelona a different defensive dimension, particularly when operating with a high defensive line.

His versatility is another quality Pereira believes could appeal to the Spanish giants. Having started his career as a left-back, Bassey can operate in different defensive positions and provide cover across the left side.

“What’s more, he plays every game and hardly ever gets injured. Bassey started out as a left-back, so he’d also be adaptable to playing in a back three or, as Barcelona do, starting with three at the back.

“In that case, he could cover the entire left flank. What’s more, he’d bring versatility: he could fill in at full-back, like Gerard Martin at times,” Pereira noted.

Pereira also highlighted Bassey’s ability to progress the ball, describing it as another asset that could fit into Barcelona’s possession-based approach.

The Nigerian is comfortable receiving possession under pressure and driving into midfield, offering an alternative to building attacks through short passes.

“Fulham are a team who build up play from the back and Bassey is very reliable with his passing.

“He has something else that Barcelona, with the exception of Pau Cubarsi, don’t have: the ability to break through defences with his dribbling. He’s one of the best in the Premier League in this regard.

“If they shut down Pedri or Rodri… he’d be capable of picking up the ball and driving into the opposition’s half. He has no qualms about it. That would give him another string to his bow.”

Barcelona are assessing centre-back options ahead of the January transfer window as Flick looks to strengthen his defensive resources. However, Bassey has not been identified as a concrete target in reports surrounding the club’s search.

The Nigerian is in his fourth season at Craven Cottage and has established himself as an important member of Fulham’s defence and leader under Alvaro Arbeloa.

He was named the club’s Player of The Season for the 2024/25 campaign.

description: Following Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde’s admission that his administration has spent the N30bn intervention fund released by the Federal Government for the January 16, 2024, Bodija explosion in Ibadan, affected residents have urged the Federal Government to release the outstanding N20bn to enable
content:
Following Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde’s admission that his administration has spent the N30bn intervention fund released by the Federal Government for the January 16, 2024, Bodija explosion in Ibadan, affected residents have urged the Federal Government to release the outstanding N20bn to enable them to receive adequate compensation.

The residents, under the aegis of the Bodija Residents Association, also called for a review of the compensation process, alleging that the amount paid by the state government was inadequate and that several victims were excluded from the exercise.

The Chairman of BERA, Muyiwa Bamgbose, made the appeal in an interview with The PUNCH on Tuesday, saying the N4.085bn disbursed to victims represented only about 40 per cent of the association’s assessment of their losses.

He said the association’s assessment, conducted with the assistance of professionals, put the total cost of restoring affected properties and replacing destroyed vehicles at more than N10bn.

Bamgbose explained that the government reduced the assessment after citing financial constraints, adding that some claims were excluded because the affected properties were considered to be outside the designated impact area.

He said, “Our total recommended sum was over N10bn, but when they came with the N4bn argument, it amounted to about N4bn. N4bn is 40 per cent of our estimate.”

He said the association was appealing to the Federal Government to release the outstanding N20bn from the N50bn intervention fund reportedly promised to Oyo State, following Makinde’s disclosure that the state had spent the N30bn already received.

“The governor has said that N30bn has been expended. We are appealing to the Federal Government to release the remaining N20bn and look at the records we drew up,” Bamgbose said.

He, however, stressed that BERA did not want the money paid into its account, proposing that the Federal Government could verify the association’s records and pay the affected residents directly.

“We don’t want the money to come to BERA. We can provide the Federal Government of the records of victims, and the money can be paid directly to the affected victims,” he said.

Bamgbose said the association was particularly concerned about residents whose properties were damaged but whose claims were either reduced or excluded during the compensation exercise.

He explained that the association had engaged professionals to assess the cost of restoring the affected buildings to their pre-explosion condition, including the replacement of vehicles destroyed in the incident.

According to him, the government subsequently applied a formula that reduced the assessed claims to about 40 per cent, while some categories of victims were removed from the final list.

He said, “What was estimated was 40 per cent of people’s requests. The government said it did not have money, that it was not compensation but support.”

The BERA chairman said the association wanted the government to revisit the initial assessment and apply the same formula in reverse to restore the amounts deducted from the claims of affected residents.

He added that some victims had already rebuilt their homes with personal resources and were hoping to receive additional financial support to offset their expenditure.

“Some who can afford to rebuild their houses have returned; they are hoping to get more money to offset some of the money that they spent,” he said.

Bamgbose also said the association had reported cases of residents who claimed not to have received the financial support to the state government for further consideration.

He maintained that although the state government’s road rehabilitation projects were commendable, the immediate priority should be the welfare and accommodation of those whose homes were affected by the explosion.

“Doing the road is good, but the priority should be for people to have habitable abodes,” he said.

The appeal comes after Makinde’s latest disclosure that his administration had spent the N30bn released to the state.

The governor made the disclosure during an interview on Arise Television on Friday, explaining that the state engaged the Nigerian Society of Engineers and professional valuers to assess properties affected by the explosion before making payments to their owners.

He said the money had initially remained in a bank account while his administration anticipated what he described as attempts to use the Federal Government’s intervention to blackmail him politically.

Makinde said, “We’ve spent the money. We got the Nigerian Society of Engineers, we got valuers, you know, they went out there, had the valuation of the properties, and then we gave money back to those people.”

He added that he subsequently directed the Commissioner for Finance to deploy the funds to projects after presenting his administration’s account of the transaction.

“I instructed the Commissioner for Finance, please put this money now on project because they’ve done what we thought they were going to do,” he said.

The fund generated controversy after former Ekiti State Governor Ayodele Fayose accused Makinde of failing to account for the Federal Government’s intervention money, alleging that the state received N50bn but disbursed only about N4.5bn to victims.

The Oyo State Government had previously maintained that the Federal Government’s intervention money remained untouched in a dedicated bank account.

However, it had disclosed that it spent N24.6bn from its own resources on infrastructure and other interventions following the explosion, in addition to the N4.085bn disbursed to affected residents.

Speaking with The PUNCH on Tuesday on Makinde’s latest disclosure, some of the Bodija victims expressed dissatisfaction with the amount received, describing the payments as inadequate in relation to the losses they suffered.

One of the victims, Mohammed Danesi, who said his residence was close to the epicentre of the explosion, described the state government’s payment scheme as inadequate.

He said he received about N1.4m despite losing virtually everything in the explosion, adding that he and his two children were admitted to a private hospital after the incident.

Danesi added that the family incurred medical expenses following the incident and was subsequently instructed to forward the bills to the state Ministry of Health for possible reimbursement.

“We complied, and nothing has been received to date,” he said.

Another victim, Dr Akinyele Coker, said the amount he received was about 40 per cent of the loss assessed by BERA.

Coker, 88, who lives on Aderinola Street, described himself as one of the fortunate victims because he had personal savings with which he could rebuild his property.

He said only two residents on his street had so far been able to rebuild their homes, adding that both had relied on personal resources to supplement the financial support received from the government.

Another victim, Toyin Olujumi, said she had received payment about two to three weeks earlier, although she stated that it was N15m less than the amount quoted by BERA as her losses.

She also claimed that the distribution was faulty, as some people whose houses were not affected received substantial amounts, while some tenants who suffered significant losses received relatively little.

Olujumi, however, said she appreciated the state government for providing some support to victims, adding that residents needed to move on with their lives after the tragedy.

The January 16, 2024, explosion in the Bodija area of Ibadan caused extensive damage to residential buildings and other properties, leaving several people dead and many others injured.

The post Bodija explosion: Victims urge FG to release N20bn appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Rotary club extends intervention to Ogun school
description:
A Rotary club based in Lagos has renovated an administrative block and provided eight toilets at Ajuwon Senior High School, Ogun State, in an intervention aimed at improving the school’s facilities and sanitation.
The Rotary Club of Omole-Golden, District 9111, commissioned the facilities on Thursda
content:
A Rotary club based in Lagos has renovated an administrative block and provided eight toilets at Ajuwon Senior High School, Ogun State, in an intervention aimed at improving the school’s facilities and sanitation.

The Rotary Club of Omole-Golden, District 9111, commissioned the facilities on Thursday, with the District Governor, Bukola Bakare, formally opening them for use, according to a statement made available to The PUNCH on Tuesday.

The project brings the club’s community development intervention to Ajuwon, a community in Ogun State bordering Lagos, with the renovation addressing the condition of the school’s administrative building and inadequate sanitation facilities.

Speaking at the commissioning, the club’s Impact President, Omowunmi Bakare, said the intervention reflected Rotary’s commitment to improving education, public health, human dignity and environmental sustainability.

She said the club recognised that inadequate infrastructure could undermine the quality of education, regardless of the efforts of teachers and school administrators.

“Education remains one of the most powerful instruments for individual advancement, community development and national transformation. However, quality education cannot thrive in an environment where essential infrastructure is inadequate,” she said.

Bakare said a functional learning environment required adequate administrative facilities and hygienic sanitation infrastructure to protect students’ health and promote their general well-being.

She added that the intervention aligned with Rotary’s areas of focus, particularly basic education and literacy, water, sanitation and hygiene, and environmental protection.

The District Governor, Bukola Bakare, commended the club for undertaking the renovation and providing additional toilet facilities for the students.

The school’s Principal, Okusaga Adejoke, said the administrative block had previously been in a deplorable condition, describing the intervention as a significant improvement to the school’s working and learning environment.

She said the project went beyond physical renovation to address issues affecting the dignity, health and morale of the school community.

“Rotary Club of Omole-Golden, you have done more than renovate buildings. You have restored dignity, improved health, boosted morale and created an environment where teaching and learning can truly thrive,” she said.

Adejoke added that the collaboration between the club and the school demonstrated the importance of partnerships in improving educational infrastructure.

A representative of the Ogun State Ministry of Education, Emmanuel Asegbe, said the state government appreciated individuals and organisations contributing to development within their communities.

The post Rotary club extends intervention to Ogun school appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: NSF: Unfinished facilities force Enugu to seek postponement
description:
Enugu State has asked the National Sports Commission to postpone the 23rd National Sports Festival from November 26–December 11, 2026, to the first week of May 2027, citing concerns over the readiness of key sporting facilities, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
The request, made by the Enugu State Minist
content:
Enugu State has asked the National Sports Commission to postpone the 23rd National Sports Festival from November 26–December 11, 2026, to the first week of May 2027, citing concerns over the readiness of key sporting facilities, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.

The request, made by the Enugu State Ministry of Youth and Sports and the Local Organising Committee, followed an assessment of facilities at the Nnamdi Azikiwe Stadium and Awgu Games Village, which organisers said might not be ready to meet the required standards before the scheduled commencement of the Games.

The National Sports Commission is yet to confirm whether it will approve the proposed change of dates.

In a statement signed by the LOC Media Officer, Brian Okechukwu, on behalf of the committee, the organisers said the decision followed an internal inspection of the facilities to determine their level of readiness for the national sporting event.

“Although the contractors handling the projects expressed confidence that the facilities would be completed within the expected timeframe, the Enugu State Ministry of Youth and Sports and the LOC, after a careful assessment, observed that the level of work remaining raised concerns about the readiness of the stadium and Awgu Games Village to meet the required standards before the commencement of the Games,” the statement read.

The organisers, however, clarified that other essential arrangements, including accommodation and logistics, were ready for the festival, insisting that the completion of the stadium and Games Village remained critical to hosting a successful event.

Commissioner for Youth and Sports and LOC Chairman, Lloyd Ikechukwu Ekweremadu, said the proposed postponement would provide sufficient time to complete outstanding work and ensure the facilities meet the required standards.

The statement added that the zonal eliminations had been completed, while the state was preparing to move into the closed-camping phase ahead of the festival.

Enugu State reiterated its commitment to hosting a successful competition, saying the additional time would allow it to provide adequate facilities, safety standards and effective coordination for athletes, officials and spectators.

“The postponement is aimed at ensuring that Enugu State delivers a world-class National Sports Festival characterised by adequate sporting facilities, the highest standards of safety, effective coordination and a memorable experience for athletes, officials, spectators and other stakeholders from across the country,” the statement added.

The post NSF: Unfinished facilities force Enugu to seek postponement appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Eno calls for unity among Akwa Ibom indigenes
description:
Akwa Ibom State Governor, Umo Eno, has urged indigenes of the state living in Lagos and other parts of the country to unite behind his administration’s development agenda, saying their collective support is important to the state’s progress.
According to a statement seen by The PUNCH, the governor m
content:
Akwa Ibom State Governor, Umo Eno, has urged indigenes of the state living in Lagos and other parts of the country to unite behind his administration’s development agenda, saying their collective support is important to the state’s progress.

According to a statement seen by The PUNCH, the governor made the appeal at the Akwa Ibom Interdenominational Prayer Rally in Lagos, where he was represented by the state’s Liaison Officer in Lagos, Anthony Isonguyo.

Eno said the liaison office was intended to strengthen the relationship between the state government and Akwa Ibom indigenes living outside the state, particularly by bringing them together to contribute to its development.

Speaking on behalf of the governor, Isonguyo said uniting Akwa Ibom residents in Lagos had been his principal assignment since assuming office.

“When I came in here, I kept saying one thing: Akwa Ibom people in Lagos have to be united. And that is the mandate I was given when I was appointed the liaison officer of Akwa Ibom in Lagos. Go to Lagos and unite all Akwa Ibom people. So my project in Lagos is Akwa Ibom United,” he said.

He said he was encouraged that speakers at the rally repeatedly emphasised unity, arguing that cooperation among indigenes outside the state would strengthen their capacity to support its development.

The governor also described prayer as a central pillar of his administration, saying spiritual guidance remained important to its activities.

“The backbone of the government in Akwa Ibom is prayers. Aside from the fact that the governor is an ordained man of God, whatever we do, our background is prayers,” he said.

Eno described the gathering as timely and urged Akwa Ibom indigenes in Lagos and the diaspora to support projects being undertaken by his administration, including the state airport and Arise Palm Resort.

The rally, organised under the theme ‘Arise & Shine’, was convened by the Apostolic Overseer of Sure Word Assembly Global, Dennis Inyang.

Inyang said the initiative was inspired by a spiritual prompting to bring Akwa Ibom people together to pray for the state and strengthen their bonds, particularly among those living outside its borders.

He urged the governor to remain focused on delivering development, expressing the hope that a second term would provide an opportunity for greater achievements if Eno secured re-election.

“I believe that we are at a very critical point in the history of our state. We will either move forward or go backwards. And when we are at that point, we need God to help us navigate through whatever challenges there may be,” Inyang said.

The chairman of the planning committee, Sunny Obot, called on Akwa Ibom indigenes to pray for peaceful elections in 2027, warning political stakeholders against actions that could trigger violence.

Obot, who described the governor’s performance as encouraging, said expectations had risen about what his administration could accomplish in the coming years.

The gathering attracted Akwa Ibom indigenes from the state’s 31 local government areas and other participants.

The post Eno calls for unity among Akwa Ibom indigenes appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: RCCG foundation to open new dialysis centre in Edo
description:
The Redeemed Christian Church of God is set to expand access to kidney treatment in Edo State with the commissioning of a new dialysis centre at the University of Benin Teaching Hospital, Benin City.
The facility, named the Enoch and Folu Adeboye Dialysis Centre, is an initiative of His Love Foundat
content:
The Redeemed Christian Church of God is set to expand access to kidney treatment in Edo State with the commissioning of a new dialysis centre at the University of Benin Teaching Hospital, Benin City.

The facility, named the Enoch and Folu Adeboye Dialysis Centre, is an initiative of His Love Foundation, the church’s Christian Social Responsibility arm, and is expected to strengthen the hospital’s capacity to provide treatment for patients requiring regular dialysis.

The centre is scheduled to be commissioned on November 24, 2026, by the Edo State Governor, Monday Okpebholo, according to a statement obtained by The PUNCH on Tuesday.

The project adds to the foundation’s network of dialysis facilities across the country, bringing to 15 the number of centres listed by the organisation in different states and the Federal Capital Territory.

The existing facilities are located in Lagos, Abuja, Bauchi, Ogun, Ondo, Oyo, Anambra, Borno, Enugu, Osun, Akwa Ibom, Ekiti and Delta states.

The foundation said the intervention was part of its broader commitment to improving access to specialised healthcare and addressing humanitarian needs through practical social interventions.

Beyond healthcare, His Love Foundation operates programmes covering education, feeding, social enterprise, environmental architecture, prison impact and rehabilitation.

The organisation said its interventions had reached communities in 650 local government areas across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

The foundation, established as the social responsibility arm of the RCCG, said its activities were driven by the objective of demonstrating Christian values through interventions in healthcare, education and social welfare.

The post RCCG foundation to open new dialysis centre in Edo appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Lagos-bound BA plane skids off London runway
description:
A British Airways flight bound for Lagos was forced to abort its journey on Tuesday after the aircraft veered off a taxiway at London Heathrow Airport, leaving its nose landing gear stuck in a grass verge.
The incident, which involved flight BA75, occurred as the Boeing 787-10 Dreamliner prepared to
content:
A British Airways flight bound for Lagos was forced to abort its journey on Tuesday after the aircraft veered off a taxiway at London Heathrow Airport, leaving its nose landing gear stuck in a grass verge.

The incident, which involved flight BA75, occurred as the Boeing 787-10 Dreamliner prepared to depart Heathrow for the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, with 215 passengers on board.

Although the incident disrupted the passengers’ travel plans, no injuries were reported among those on board or the crew.

The PUNCH gathered that the aircraft, with registration number G-ZBLF, had pushed back from Terminal 5, Gate C56, at about 10:40 a.m. local time.

It was taxiing towards the runway when it suddenly veered off the designated path, sending its nose wheel into a grass verge.

Photographs from the scene showed the aircraft’s nose landing gear partially embedded in the grass, with emergency services subsequently deployed to assist.

The incident forced the cancellation of the Lagos-bound flight, leaving passengers to contend with unexpected travel disruptions.

Heathrow Airport confirmed the development, saying it was providing assistance following the aircraft’s departure from the taxiway.

British Airways, in a statement published on its website, apologised to affected passengers and said it was working to minimise the disruption by arranging alternative travel.

The airline said: “We are very sorry to our customers for the disruption to their flight. Our teams are working to get them on their way as quickly as possible and are in touch with them to put things right.”

The post Lagos-bound BA plane skids off London runway appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
