title: MAPOLY Lecturers Begin Indefinite Strike Over Unpaid Allowances, Welfare Demands
description: Academic activities have been disrupted at the Ogun State-owned Moshood Abiola Polytechnic (MAPOLY), Abeokuta, following an indefinite strike by lecturers over unpaid allowances and other welfare-related demands.Members of the Academic Staff Union of Polytechnics (ASUP) and other unions at the insti
content:
Academic activities have been disrupted at the Ogun State-owned Moshood Abiola Polytechnic (MAPOLY), Abeokuta, following an indefinite strike by lecturers over unpaid allowances and other welfare-related demands.

Members of the Academic Staff Union of Polytechnics (ASUP) and other unions at the institution embarked on the industrial action after the expiration of a 15-day ultimatum issued to the Ogun State Government to address their grievances.

The demands include the payment of Earned Academic Allowances, a review of the monthly subvention to tertiary institutions and the implementation of the Consolidated Academic Staff Salary Structure (CONTISS), among other welfare-related issues.

Chairman of the MAPOLY chapter of ASUP, Adeleke Amos-Adebayo, said the union had made several attempts to get the state government to address the issues before resorting to the strike.

He said a letter outlining the union’s demands was first sent to the governor on August 5, 2026, followed by another reminder on September 21.

Amos-Adebayo explained that the decision to embark on the strike followed a resolution reached at the union’s National Executive Council (NEC) meeting in Abuja on October 22, where state governors were given an ultimatum to implement the outstanding demands.

According to him, a directive from the national body was subsequently issued on October 26, with the 15-day ultimatum taking effect on October 27 and expiring on November 11.

He said the Ogun State chapters of the union, with the approval of the zonal and national leadership, commenced the strike on November 11.

The ASUP chairman appealed to Governor Dapo Abiodun to intervene, expressing confidence that the governor would be willing to address the concerns of the lecturers.

He said, “I want to believe maybe Mr Governor has not been carried along, because we know him to be a listening leader who has listening ears for the people of the state.

“I don’t mind using this medium to call his attention to what is happening in those tertiary institutions, so that he can intervene and find a way to resolve this matter.”

Amos-Adebayo added that the union did not want the strike to continue for long, noting that its members were equally concerned about the disruption to academic activities.

“We don’t, as union leaders, expect this industrial action to last long because we have our children here, we have relatives here, and this is our own Jerusalem that we will not want anything to happen to it,” he said.

He urged the governor to intervene and ensure that the outstanding demands were addressed to facilitate the resumption of academic activities.

A visit to the institution showed that academic activities had been grounded, with classrooms deserted as lecturers stayed away from their duties.

The strike has also left many students uncertain about the continuation of the academic session, with some expressing concerns over delays to their studies.

One of the students, Tope Adeleke, said the industrial action would disrupt academic activities and affect students’ motivation, particularly those who had only recently resumed classes.

“There will be a small delay in a lot of activities. We have a lot of activities, classes. There will be a lot of delays.

“My appeal is that whatever they know they can do for us, they should do it to help ensure that this strike is called off. We want to get back on track to continue our studies and do what we know is best for us in the institution,” he said.

Adeleke described the strike as unexpected, saying students had become accustomed to relatively uninterrupted academic activities since the appointment of the institution’s new rector.

He said the development had raised concerns among students about how long the disruption could last and whether they would be able to complete their academic activities as scheduled.

Other students also appealed to the lecturers and the state government to return to the negotiating table and resolve the disagreement.

“We are making a passionate appeal to all concerned to consider the plight of the students, come to the negotiating table, resolve the impasse and allow us to have a smooth academic session,” one student said.

The lecturers, however, said they were willing to return to the classrooms once their demands were addressed by the institution’s management and the state government.

Efforts to obtain the reaction of the institution’s management were unsuccessful, as the Rector, Babatunde Jolaoso, was said to be unavailable for an interview.

The post MAPOLY Lecturers Begin Indefinite Strike Over Unpaid Allowances, Welfare Demands appeared first on Channels Television.

title: Fountain of Life trustees release founder’s video, insist on Jimmy’s removal
description:
The Board of Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church has released a video in which its late founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, named Pastor Kunle Areogun as his preferred successor, while insisting that his son, Pastor Jimmy Odukoya, is no longer recognised as the church’s Senior Pastor.
In a statement
content:
The Board of Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church has released a video in which its late founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, named Pastor Kunle Areogun as his preferred successor, while insisting that his son, Pastor Jimmy Odukoya, is no longer recognised as the church’s Senior Pastor.

In a statement dated November 17, 2026, the trustees reaffirmed their November 16 decision to withdraw recognition of Jimmy as Senior Pastor and announced the appointment of Pastor Rotimi Okpaise to oversee the church’s spiritual and administrative affairs in an interim capacity.

The development has deepened the leadership crisis at the church, with Jimmy’s camp rejecting his purported removal as constitutionally invalid and insisting that he remains the duly appointed Senior Pastor and Chairman of the Board of Trustees.

The video, reportedly recorded in December 2021, captures the late founder outlining his preferred succession arrangement in the event of his death or incapacity. He named Areogun as the next Senior Pastor and assigned Jimmy administrative and youth ministry responsibilities.

“But the reason I’m doing this is to let you know that incase of my demise, which I don’t expect to happen soon, or a situation where I cannot write or talk, please, the next pastor of the church should be Kunle Areogun and to be his immediate assistant, that is in terms of administration, is Jimmy Odukoya, who will be the head of the youth church,” Taiwo said in the recording.

He explained that the instructions were intended to address a provision in the church’s constitution that was undergoing review.

“Every other thing remains the same as laid out in the constitution. The reason I am doing this again is this, because that is an aspect of the constitution that we are trying to rework which we haven’t concluded. We will continue to do that but if for any reason I am not able to see that through this is what I intend they should folllow,” he said.

According to the trustees, they did not see the recording until late December 2025, more than two years after the founder’s death in August 2023.

They alleged that the video was not disclosed during deliberations that led to Jimmy’s appointment as Senior Pastor in September 2023, despite his assurance that his father had handed over the leadership mantle to him.

“Upon enquiry by the Board, Pastor Jimmy Odukoya informed the Board, and subsequently the Church, that our late Senior Pastor had handed the mantle of leadership over to him. The Board placed considerable reliance upon this assurance in its deliberations on the succession,” the statement said.

The trustees said they appointed Jimmy in good faith based on the information available to them and their understanding of the church’s constitutional provisions.

However, they argued that the emergence of the recording raised questions about whether the succession process was conducted with full disclosure of relevant information.

“Significantly, the individual nominated in that recording was not Pastor Jimmy Odukoya,” the Board stated.

It added that the recording was not presented during the original deliberations, depriving members of the Board of information that could have influenced their decision.

The trustees said they had reviewed the recording, the circumstances surrounding Jimmy’s appointment and the implications for the legitimacy of the succession process, taking into account the church’s constitution and other governing instruments.

They also accused Jimmy of failing to cooperate sufficiently with efforts to resolve disagreements over the church’s administration and governance.

According to the Board, months of consultations and reconciliation efforts, including interventions by respected Christian leaders described as “Fathers of the Faith”, failed to resolve the disagreements.

“Regrettably, notwithstanding these interventions, repeated representations and efforts at reconciliation, the substantive concerns raised by the Board remain unresolved.

“Pastor Jimmy Odukoya has not provided the level of engagement and cooperation necessary to achieve a satisfactory resolution,” the statement alleged.

The trustees said the dispute extended beyond the succession recording to concerns about church administration, governance arrangements and the preservation of the ministry’s founding vision. They also referred to what they described as moral and doctrinal controversies but did not provide specific details.

Reaffirming its decision, the Board said Jimmy was no longer recognised as Senior Pastor and was required to relinquish the office and its functions with immediate effect.

“Accordingly, having previously called upon Pastor Jimmy Odukoya to step down, the Board, at its meeting held on 16 November 2026, resolved that Pastor Jimmy Odukoya is no longer recognised as Senior Pastor of The Fountain of Life Church, with immediate effect. He is required to step down forthwith from the office and all functions of Senior Pastor,” it said.

The trustees subsequently announced Okpaise’s appointment to oversee the church pending consultations and other processes to establish a substantive leadership structure in line with its governing instruments.

The appointment has raised questions about the status of Areogun, whom the late founder named in the recording as his preferred successor. The trustees did not explain whether he had been approached or how his designation would feature in the process of selecting a substantive leader.

The leadership dispute has also extended to control of the church’s official communication channels. The trustees alleged that Jimmy or individuals acting on his behalf had taken control of the church’s social media platforms without their authorisation.

They accused those managing the accounts of publishing an inaccurate and misleading account of the controversy and warned members, journalists and the public against treating posts on the platforms as the Board’s official position.

The trustees said they were taking steps to restore what they described as authorised control of the church’s communication channels.

However, Jimmy’s camp has rejected the Board’s position, insisting that his appointment remains valid.

In a counterstatement issued on behalf of the church, his camp described the purported removal as constitutionally invalid and accused the trustees behind the announcement of acting outside the church’s governing framework.

It alleged that the trustees concerned had been asked to resign in March 2026 over repeated violations of the church’s constitution and founding principles.

The statement maintained that Jimmy’s appointment was unanimously approved by the Board in September 2023 and that no constitutionally valid decision had removed him from office.

The competing statements have therefore raised questions over the late founder’s succession instructions, the validity of Jimmy’s appointment and which faction has the authority to make binding decisions on behalf of the church.

The trustees, however, said their decision was not motivated by personal hostility but was necessary to protect the church’s integrity and reputation.

“The Board emphasises that this decision is not intended as an act of vindictiveness, humiliation or personal condemnation,” the statement said.

“Rather, it is a necessary and proportionate response to circumstances which, if left unaddressed, could inflict lasting damage on the Church and the legacy entrusted to its care.”

The Fountain of Life Church was founded in 1992 by Taiwo and his late wife, Pastor Bimbo Odukoya, and is headquartered in Ilupeju, Lagos. Following Taiwo’s death in August 2023, Jimmy was appointed Senior Pastor.

The trustees appealed to members to remain peaceful and prayerful as efforts to resolve the leadership and governance issues continue.

title: Yahoo boy poses as woman to blackmail, extort Canadian teenager
description:
A Nigerian man identified simply as Ayomide pretended to be a woman named Ava on TikTok to trick a Canadian teenager into sending nude photos, then threatened to leak them unless he was paid, according to an investigation by the Associated Press and PBS FRONTLINE.
The joint investigation, published
content:
A Nigerian man identified simply as Ayomide pretended to be a woman named Ava on TikTok to trick a Canadian teenager into sending nude photos, then threatened to leak them unless he was paid, according to an investigation by the Associated Press and PBS FRONTLINE.

The joint investigation, published on Tuesday, detailed how the young Nigerian used fake profiles and messaging apps to sexually extort teenage boys overseas.

The Canadian victim, now 18, said he was 15 when ‘Ava’ first followed him on TikTok.

Thinking he was talking to a girl, he chatted with the account before being convinced to continue the conversation on Zangi, an encrypted messaging app.

Ayomide, said to be in his early 20s, allegedly sent the boy a nude image lifted from the internet, passing it off as his own, and then talked his victim into sending an intimate photo back.

Once he had the image, he threatened to send it to the teenager’s family, friends and employer if he did not pay up.

The boy first paid $500 in the hope that it would stop the threats, but the demands kept coming.

“Not just yet. This isn’t that simple,” Ayomide reportedly told the teenager after he asked that they part ways.

Investigators said they examined more than 200 WhatsApp messages Ayomide sent to the victim, many of them threatening to reveal his identity and post his intimate photo.

In one message, Ayomide threatened to disappoint the victim’s mother by sharing the photos online, apparently to force him to comply with the demands.

He also sent the victim personal identification details and screenshot of his Tiktok followers to reinforce the message.

In all, the victim said he lost lost close to $2,000, although Ayomide said he only got a few hundred dollars from him.

Ayomide went on to send more than 100 WhatsApp messages over 11 days, but the teenager eventually stopped responding.

Ayomide told the AP he never released the boy’s photograph.

Reporters met Ayomide in Lagos, where he showed them chat histories from some of his scams, including the exchange with the Canadian victim.

The teenager was only contacted after he turned 18. He spoke on condition of anonymity because of the trauma of an experience he had not even told his family about.

“Scamming is not good,” Ayomide, who is barely older than his victim, told the AP.

The self-professed computer science student said he turned to internet scam to meet financial needs, including payment of school fees and rent.

But the investigation found he did not quit. About a year after promising to stop, he had teamed up with a group of other Yahoo Boys at his university, the investigation found.

How he operated

Ayomide’s approach was straightforward: pose as an attractive woman, follow hundreds of foreign men and boys on TikTok, and strike up conversations with those who followed him back — “What’s your name? Are you alone today? Do you want to have fun?” — before shifting the chat to a private messaging app.

He said that for every 50 people he follows on TikTok, about 10 follow him back, and five of those are willing to chat.

He collected payments through gift cards, including Apple and Steam cards, the investigation further found.

The AP described Ayomide as part of a wider network of Nigerian online fraudsters, widely known as Yahoo Boys, who target young people in Western countries through social media.

Financial sextortion is when criminals pressure victims into sharing nude images or videos and then threaten to publish the material unless they are paid.

The FBI has warned of a sharp rise in financially motivated sextortion targeting minors.

By August, the National Centre for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) said it had received over 40,000 reports of financial sextortion, compared with about 50,000 for the whole of last year.

According to AP, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) in Nigeria had worked with US law enforcement on efforts to tackle transnational cybercrime.

EFCC Chairman, Olanipekun Olukoyede assure the news agency that Nigeria would sustain its fight against internet fraud.

“Rest assured, Nigeria is no longer going to be a safe haven for fraudsters or criminal activities,” he said.

title: Fountain Of Life Trustees Name Interim Leader, Insist On Jimmy Odukoya’s Removal
description: The Board of Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church has named Rotimi Okpaise as its interim spiritual and administrative leader, reaffirming its decision to remove Pastor Jimmy Odukoya as Senior Pastor.The trustees announced the appointment in a fresh statement dated Tuesday, November 17, 2026, ins
content:
The Board of Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church has named Rotimi Okpaise as its interim spiritual and administrative leader, reaffirming its decision to remove Pastor Jimmy Odukoya as Senior Pastor.

The trustees announced the appointment in a fresh statement dated Tuesday, November 17, 2026, insisting that their resolution of November 16 withdrawing recognition of Odukoya remained in force.

The development comes amid a leadership crisis at the Lagos-based church, with Odukoya rejecting his removal and insisting that he remains the church’s duly recognised Senior Pastor.

In the latest statement, the board provided further details about the circumstances surrounding Odukoya’s appointment, particularly a video recording allegedly made by the church’s late founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, in December 2021.

According to the trustees, the late founder had asked Jimmy to make a video recording in which he expressly identified his preferred successor. The recording was reportedly witnessed by his elder brother, Pastor John Odukoya.

The board said the person identified in the recording was not Jimmy Odukoya and alleged that the video was not presented to it until late December 2025, more than two years after the founder’s death.

It said it had relied on Jimmy’s account that his late father had handed over the mantle of leadership to him when considering his appointment as Senior Pastor.

The trustees described the non-disclosure of the recording as a significant development, arguing that it could have influenced their deliberations.

“The Board considers this omission particularly grave, as the disclosure of such information could reasonably have influenced its deliberations and the ultimate decision reached,” the statement said.

The board added that it had completed its review of the recording, the circumstances surrounding Jimmy’s appointment and the implications for the church’s succession process.

It said the issue was not merely about the identity of the person appointed but whether the decision was reached with full and transparent disclosure of relevant information.

“The fundamental issue, therefore, is not simply the identity of the person appointed, but whether the Board’s decision was reached on the basis of full, accurate and transparent disclosure of all material information relevant to the succession process,” it stated.

Board Cites Governance, Doctrinal Concerns

The trustees said the present controversy was not an isolated incident, disclosing that they had spent several months trying to resolve concerns about leadership succession, church administration and adherence to established governance arrangements.

According to the board, it had preferred dialogue, reconciliation and peaceful resolution over public confrontation.

It also said it sought the intervention of respected Christian leaders whom the church’s founding pastors held in high esteem.

However, the trustees alleged that their efforts had not produced the desired outcome, accusing Jimmy of failing to provide the cooperation required to resolve the disagreements.

“Pastor Jimmy Odukoya has not provided the level of engagement and cooperation necessary to achieve a satisfactory resolution,” the statement said.

The board further cited what it described as unresolved governance concerns, alongside moral and doctrinal controversies, as reasons for its intervention.

It said it could not remain indifferent while the church’s spiritual heritage, institutional integrity and public reputation faced what it described as continuing erosion.

“The responsibility of the Board is therefore not merely administrative or custodial. It is also a solemn obligation to preserve the integrity of the Church, safeguard its doctrine and protect the spiritual welfare of its congregation,” it stated.

Okpaise Named Interim Leader

Following its meeting on November 16, the board resolved that Jimmy was no longer recognised as Senior Pastor of the church, with immediate effect.

It also directed him to relinquish the office and all its functions.

The statement said, “Accordingly, having previously called upon Pastor Jimmy Odukoya to step down, the Board, at its meeting held on 16 November 2026, resolved that Pastor Jimmy Odukoya is no longer recognised as Senior Pastor of The Fountain of Life Church, with immediate effect.”

The trustees subsequently announced Okpaise’s appointment to oversee the church’s spiritual and administrative affairs pending the conclusion of consultations and processes for establishing a substantive leadership structure.

“The Board has further resolved that the interim spiritual and administrative leadership of the Church be entrusted to the Pastor Rotimi Okpaise,” it added.

The board said the arrangement would remain in place until the necessary processes were completed in accordance with the church’s governing instruments and established procedures.

It described the decision as necessary to create an atmosphere for restoring peace, rebuilding trust and resolving the leadership crisis.

Board Raises Alarm Over Church’s Social Media Accounts

The trustees also accused individuals acting on behalf of Jimmy Odukoya of taking control of the church’s official social media accounts without their authorisation.

According to the statement, the platforms had been used to publish accounts of the leadership dispute which the board considered inaccurate and misleading.

It warned members of the church, the media and the general public that statements appearing on the platforms did not represent its position.

“Only statements issued and signed for and on behalf of the Board of Trustees should be regarded as the official position of the Church on these matters,” it said.

The board added that it was taking steps to restore the church’s official communication channels to what it described as proper and authorised control.

Jimmy Odukoya Rejects Removal

However, Odukoya had earlier rejected the trustees’ announcement, insisting that he remains the duly appointed Senior Pastor and Chairman of the Board of Trustees.

In a counter-statement published on the church’s website, his camp described the purported removal as constitutionally invalid.

It argued that the individuals behind the announcement were operating outside the church’s constitutional framework and maintained that some trustees had been asked to resign in March 2026 over alleged violations of the church’s constitution and founding principles.

The statement maintained that Odukoya’s appointment was approved by the board in September 2023 and that no constitutionally valid decision had been taken to remove him.

The competing statements have deepened uncertainty over the church’s leadership, with both sides claiming authority to speak on its behalf.

The Fountain of Life Church was founded in 1992 by Pastors Taiwo and Bimbo Odukoya. Jimmy succeeded his father following his death in August 2023.

He was announced as Senior Pastor in September 2023, while his sister, Pastor Tolu Odukoya-Ijogun, was appointed Associate Senior Pastor.

The latest dispute also follows controversy surrounding Jimmy’s remarriage. He introduced his new wife, Pastor Mo Odukoya, to the congregation on November 1.

title: Tinubu’s Reforms: Nigerians yet to feel impact of gains – Oshoniyi
description:
By Boluwatife Adeyefa



President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms have recorded measurable gains in macroeconomic stability, infrastructure development and revenue mobilisation, but millions of Nigerians are yet to feel their impact, a United States-based Nigerian businessman, Dr Atilade Oshoniyi, h
content:
By Boluwatife Adeyefa

President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms have recorded measurable gains in macroeconomic stability, infrastructure development and revenue mobilisation, but millions of Nigerians are yet to feel their impact, a United States-based Nigerian businessman, Dr Atilade Oshoniyi, has said. Oshoniyi, founder and Chief Executive Officer of Green Light Drivers Ed & DUI School LLC, in this interview, examines the administration’s performance since assuming office in 2023, particularly its controversial removal of petrol subsidy and foreign exchange reforms. While acknowledging that Tinubu inherited an economy burdened by debt, weak revenue and structural challenges, he argues that the administration cannot use inherited problems to excuse policy failures or the worsening hardship confronting citizens.

Could we say President Tinubu inherited the economic crisis his administration is dealing with, or did his reforms and policies create hardships?

Mr President inherited an economy burdened by substantial public debt, rising debt-service obligations, an expensive petrol subsidy regime, multiple exchange-rate windows, weak revenue mobilisation, infrastructure deficits and declining investor confidence.

However, acknowledging inherited problems should not become an excuse for every subsequent failure. Every administration must be judged by the condition of the country it inherited and the decisions it subsequently made.

Tinubu’s decisions to remove petrol subsidy and liberalise the foreign exchange market addressed longstanding structural weaknesses but also produced immediate economic shocks. The question is whether the transition has been managed effectively and whether Nigerians are beginning to enjoy the benefits of the sacrifices demanded of them.

Could there have been an alternative to petrol subsidy removal and foreign exchange reforms, which worsened the economic situation?

There is a distinction between the necessity of reform and the manner of implementation. Successive governments recognised that petrol subsidy was unsustainable, while multiple exchange rates encouraged arbitrage and discouraged productive investment.

The IMF’s June 2026 assessment acknowledged that the reforms improved macroeconomic stability and strengthened external buffers. However, it estimated that poverty had reached 63 per cent of the population under Nigeria’s national poverty line, while about 27 million Nigerians experienced food insecurity in autumn 2025.

The government could have prioritised timely cash transfers, public transportation, targeted food support, affordable healthcare and protection for small businesses. Reform must demonstrate that its eventual benefits outweigh the sacrifices and that vulnerable Nigerians are not abandoned.

What would you say are the achievements of the incumbent administration against the opposition’s argument that he has done nothing?

The claim that the administration has done absolutely nothing does not reflect its documented record. The government has undertaken economic restructuring through subsidy removal, foreign exchange reforms, revenue changes and a new tax framework. The Nigerian Education Loan Fund has expanded financing opportunities for students in public tertiary institutions.

In infrastructure, major projects include the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Super Highway and Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano road. The Presidency reported that more than 2,700 kilometres of highways and major roads were under construction, reconstruction or rehabilitation as of May 2026.

The Electricity Act 2023 has opened opportunities for states to participate in electricity generation, transmission and distribution. Other interventions include agricultural mechanisation, fertiliser support, healthcare, CNG transportation and the ₦70,000 national minimum wage.

These are identifiable actions, but their scale, completion and impact must be independently assessed. Announcements are not completed projects.

As a businessman in the Diaspora, what do institutions such as the IMF and World Bank say about the administration’s performance?

Their assessments provide an external perspective on the reforms. The IMF’s June 2026 Article IV assessment acknowledged improvements in macroeconomic stability, external buffers and foreign exchange market functioning. It estimated economic growth at four per cent in 2025 and projected 4.1 per cent for 2026.

The World Bank’s October 2026 Nigeria Development Update reported that the economy grew by 4.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, compared with 3.9 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025.

Nigeria’s removal from the Financial Action Task Force grey list in October 2025 was another significant development in its financial integrity framework.

However, neither institution has declared that Nigeria’s economic problems have been solved. The IMF continues to highlight poverty, food insecurity and insecurity. The World Bank has also emphasised the need to translate growth into employment, better household incomes and improved public services.

The fair conclusion is that macroeconomic stabilisation is progressing, but widespread prosperity remains a challenge.

Can you identify the major sectors in which the Tinubu administration has recorded measurable progress, and how should Nigerians assess these achievements?

Education, infrastructure, power, agriculture and public finance offer measurable examples.

NELFUND reported cumulative disbursements of ₦372.62 billion to 1,659,853 students across 319 tertiary institutions as of October 30, 2026. This represents an important financing opportunity, although the scheme must also be assessed by its accessibility and sustainability.

In infrastructure, more than 2,700 kilometres of roads were reported to be at different stages of construction and rehabilitation. The Electricity Act provides a framework for state electricity markets and private investment.

Agriculture has received mechanisation, fertiliser and agro-industrial interventions, while the minimum wage increased from ₦30,000 to ₦70,000.

In public finance, improved revenue mobilisation has increased resources available to states and local governments.

The proper test is not the number of programmes announced but beneficiaries reached, projects completed, jobs created and improvements in citizens’ lives.

If President Tinubu’s achievements are real, why are so many Nigerians still experiencing acute economic hardship?

There is a genuine disconnect. Macroeconomic stability and household prosperity are related, but they are not the same.

An economy can record GDP growth, stronger reserves and increased revenue while households struggle with food prices, rent, transportation, school fees and healthcare.

The IMF estimated that 63 per cent of Nigerians were living below the national poverty line. It also reported that 9.2 million households had been enrolled in the cash transfer system against a target of 15 million. Those enrolled had received at most three transfers of ₦25,000 since 2023.

These figures demonstrate the gap between policy intentions and delivery. The government must move beyond aggregate economic indicators and demonstrate improvements in employment, purchasing power, food security and access to essential services.

Has Tinubu done enough to address insecurity, particularly banditry, kidnapping, terrorism and attacks on farming communities?

Security remains one of the most difficult areas in which the administration must demonstrate stronger results.

There have been military operations, intelligence interventions and equipment acquisitions, but persistent attacks, kidnappings, displacement and disruption of farming indicate that the challenge remains unresolved.

The government must improve protection while addressing illegal arms proliferation, unemployment, weak local intelligence, poor border management and ineffective governance in vulnerable communities.

Economic reforms cannot deliver their full benefits if farmers cannot safely cultivate their land and businesses cannot operate without fear.

With the renewed move to establish state police, does this represent the kind of security restructuring Nigeria needs, and what safeguards should accompany it?

State police could provide an important opportunity to decentralise security management and make policing more responsive to the peculiar challenges of individual communities.

As of November 4, 2026, 30 State Houses of Assembly had approved the proposed constitutional amendment, exceeding the required two-thirds threshold of 24 states. The measure was being processed for transmission to the President for assent.

However, establishing state police alone will not solve insecurity. There must be clear constitutional safeguards against political interference, victimisation of opposition figures and abuse of authority by governors.

There must also be independent oversight, adequate funding, professional recruitment, proper training and respect for human rights.

The Federal Government should retain responsibility for national security coordination, while state police services address local crimes and community-level intelligence. The objective should be complementary policing, not competing security structures.

Three years into Tinubu’s presidency, has the government sufficiently addressed corruption, wasteful expenditure, accountability and transparency?

This remains an important area for scrutiny. Improved revenue collection does not automatically guarantee accountability in expenditure.

Nigerians deserve to know how savings from subsidy removal are being deployed, how capital projects are funded, how contracts are awarded and whether procurement procedures are followed.

The government should publish accessible reports showing actual savings, social intervention expenditure and project outcomes. Allegations of corruption must be investigated irrespective of the political identity of those involved.

One of the administration’s major arguments is that the economy is recovering. How sustainable is this recovery?

The World Bank’s reported 4.2 per cent growth in the first half of 2026, stronger external balances and improved public revenues provide evidence of recovery.

However, sustainability depends on whether Nigeria can expand domestic production, improve electricity supply, support manufacturing and create productive employment.

The economy remains vulnerable to international oil price fluctuations, insecurity and high production costs. The government must therefore consolidate the gains through diversification rather than excessive dependence on oil revenue, borrowing and short-term capital inflows.

As Nigerians approach the 2027 presidential election, what exactly will be at stake? Is the election simply about choosing another president, or will it amount to a referendum on Tinubu’s reforms and leadership?

The election will provide an opportunity to assess the country’s direction since 2023. It will involve questions about economic management, security, accountability, federalism and governance.

The ruling party will seek another mandate to consolidate its policies, while the opposition will attempt to persuade Nigerians that another approach would produce better outcomes.

For the electorate, the central consideration should be which candidate and programme can address immediate difficulties while building a sustainable economic and political future.

If Tinubu wins a second term in 2027, what could Nigerians gain? What are the possible advantages of continuity?

A second term would provide an opportunity to continue policies and programmes already initiated.

Economic reforms in taxation, foreign exchange management, energy and infrastructure may require more time to produce their intended results. Continuity could also reduce uncertainty among investors.

The administration could complete ongoing infrastructure projects, consolidate electricity reforms, expand domestic refining and improve agricultural production.

However, continuity should not mean automatic endorsement of every existing policy. A second term must demonstrate stronger commitment to poverty reduction, employment, security and accountability.

What are the possible risks or disadvantages for Nigerians if Tinubu wins another four years?

The principal risk is that continuity could become an excuse for retaining policies that have not delivered sufficient improvements in citizens’ welfare.

Failure to address the cost of living, unemployment, insecurity and inadequate electricity could prolong the frustrations already experienced by Nigerians.

A comfortable political mandate could also weaken accountability. Another four years must therefore be accompanied by improved delivery, transparency and responsiveness.

What should Nigerians demand from both Tinubu and the opposition before deciding who deserves their mandate in 2027?

Nigerians should demand measurable targets, clear timelines, credible financing plans and verifiable records.

Tinubu should explain what his administration has achieved, what it failed to achieve and what he intends to do differently if re-elected.

The opposition must equally explain how it intends to address the problems it criticises. Candidates promising cheaper fuel, a stronger naira and employment should explain the policies, costs and implementation strategies behind those promises.

Security, education, healthcare, electricity and infrastructure must also feature prominently. Nigerians deserve evidence-based alternatives rather than criticism without workable solutions.

Could an opposition government sustain the reforms while correcting what it considers Tinubu’s mistakes, or would a change of government necessarily mean a change in economic direction?

There is no reason a new administration must abandon every existing policy. Responsible governance requires continuity in programmes that serve the national interest, irrespective of the political party that introduced them.

An opposition government could retain exchange-rate reforms, improve revenue mobilisation, sustain domestic refining and continue worthwhile infrastructure projects while changing their implementation.

It could also address the social consequences of subsidy removal through better cash transfers, targeted transport support and improved public expenditure accountability.

Nigeria needs policy consistency, but consistency should not become resistance to necessary corrections.

The post Tinubu’s Reforms: Nigerians yet to feel impact of gains – Oshoniyi appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: NNPC, Renaissance seek fresh funding for pipeline infrastructure
description:
By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja



The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) and Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited have called for innovative financing mechanisms, stronger partnerships and improved security to attract investments into Nigeria’s pipeline infrastructure.



They said rel
content:
By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja

The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) and Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited have called for innovative financing mechanisms, stronger partnerships and improved security to attract investments into Nigeria’s pipeline infrastructure.

They said reliable pipeline networks were critical to strengthening the country’s energy security, maximising its hydrocarbon resources and driving industrial development.

The call was made at the 2026 Nigeria International Pipeline Technology and Security Conference (NIPITECS), organised by the Pipelines Professionals Association of Nigeria (PLAN) in Abuja.

Speaking on behalf of the NNPC Group Chief Executive Officer, Engr. Bayo Ojulari, the Managing Director of NNPC Gas Infrastructure Company (NGIC), Mr Audu Ibrahim, described pipelines as a critical link in the oil and gas value chain.

He warned that inadequate transportation infrastructure could undermine Nigeria’s efforts to harness its hydrocarbon resources, noting that the upstream, midstream and downstream segments of the industry were interconnected.

According to him, gas fields without pipelines to power plants, refineries without adequate feedstock and fertiliser plants without reliable gas supply could become stranded economic opportunities.

Ibrahim highlighted progress on major pipeline projects, including the 105-kilometre Oben-Ajaokuta-Obigbo (OB3) pipeline, the 640-kilometre Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano (AKK) pipeline and the West African Gas Pipeline.

He said the challenging River Niger crossing on the OB3 project was completed on February 26, 2026, while pre-commissioning activities were concluded in August, positioning the facility for first gas delivery.

On the AKK pipeline, designed to transport 2.2 billion standard cubic feet of gas daily, Ibrahim said mainline welding had been completed, with the pipeline reaching Abuja and undergoing commissioning.

He put the project’s completion level at approximately 95 per cent, adding that NNPC was targeting first gas delivery to Abuja before the end of 2026, followed by Kaduna and Kano.

The NGIC managing director disclosed that NNPC had raised about $1.5 billion against projected pipeline revenues, demonstrating the potential of properly structured pipeline infrastructure to attract financing independently of upstream and downstream projects.

He further disclosed that Nigeria’s gas production had reached 7.5 billion standard cubic feet per day, against a national target of 10 billion standard cubic feet daily, with the country holding more than 215 trillion cubic feet of gas reserves.

Ibrahim attributed improved pipeline performance to stronger collaboration among operators, host communities and security agencies, saying the country had achieved 100 per cent pipeline availability for the first time in two decades.

Also speaking, the Vice President, Projects and Engineering, Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited, Mr Abimbola Tijani, who represented the company’s Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Engr. Tony Attah, said pipelines should be regarded as strategic economic infrastructure rather than merely technical assets for transporting oil and gas.

He identified three priorities for attracting investments into the sector: recognising pipelines as critical national infrastructure, building investor confidence through integrity, security and partnerships, and developing a diversified financing ecosystem supported by predictable regulatory frameworks.

Tijani said Nigeria’s ambition to sustainably increase crude oil production to three million barrels per day and expand domestic gas utilisation would depend significantly on investments in reliable pipeline networks.

He reaffirmed Renaissance’s commitment to securing Africa’s energy future and supporting Nigeria’s industrialisation, expressing optimism that the country could develop an extensive gas network connecting communities and households to cleaner energy.

Earlier, PLAN President, Engr. Ngozi Adeleke, said the theme of the conference, “Financing the Future: Unlocking Capital for Resilient Pipeline Infrastructure in Nigeria,” reflected the urgent need to mobilise investments to support increased hydrocarbon production, domestic gas utilisation and industrial growth.

She noted that pipeline development required substantial capital, innovative financing solutions, regulatory support, advanced technology and effective security frameworks.

Adeleke said PLAN would continue to promote professionalism, operational excellence, safety, infrastructure integrity and capacity development.

She also called for stronger collaboration among industry operators, financiers, regulators, technology companies and host communities to strengthen Nigeria’s pipeline infrastructure and improve the sector’s capacity to support economic growth.

title: IMF-World Bank jobs agenda underscores relevance of FirstBank’s SME financing
description:
By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor







There is a growing global challenge of job creation, and the need to accelerate private-sector investment, particularly through micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), featured prominently at the just-concluded 2026 Annual Meetings of the World Bank G
content:
By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor

There is a growing global challenge of job creation, and the need to accelerate private-sector investment, particularly through micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), featured prominently at the just-concluded 2026 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok, Thailand.

Discussions at the august gathering of finance ministers and central bank governors, among other participants, underscored the importance of small businesses in expanding economic activity, creating employment and improving livelihoods, placing access to finance and business support at the centre of efforts to achieve sustainable growth.

The World Bank Group President, Ajay Banga, underscored the importance of small businesses to the global economy, describing them as “the engine of the economy”.

According to Banga, MSMEs represent 90 per cent of firms and employ 75 per cent of workers in developing countries.

“Job creation is not automatic. It comes from businesses that can start, that can grow, that can hire, that can trade, and that can compete,” he said at the Bank’s October 13 session on MSME financing and job creation.

The scale of the challenge was further highlighted by projections that about 1.2 billion young people in developing countries would reach working age over the next 10 to 15 years, while only about 420 million jobs were expected to be created.

The employment gap, according to the World Bank Group, makes it imperative for governments and development institutions to mobilise private investment and support businesses capable of expanding production and generating jobs.

The IMF Managing Director, Kristalina Georgieva, also called for improvements in the business environment, stronger competition and investment in digital and energy infrastructure as part of measures to strengthen economic performance.

“For governments it means improving the business environment, strengthening competition. Investing in digital and energy infrastructure and embracing active labor market policies,” Georgieva said at the IMF’s October 14 Global Policy Agenda briefing.

For Nigeria, where small businesses operate across trade, agriculture, manufacturing, professional services and other sectors, the discussions underscore the importance of financing viable enterprises and strengthening their capacity to grow.

The issue also brings into focus the role of commercial banks in providing the credit, payment infrastructure, digital services and business support required by small enterprises to expand their operations.

Financing the SME sector

FirstBank of Nigeria’s disbursement of more than N200 billion to small businesses in 2024 provides an example of the financing role commercial banks can play in supporting the sector.

The figure highlights the scale of the Bank’s SME financing activities at a time when access to capital remains a major concern for many small businesses.

The financing included about N100 billion disbursed to businesses across diverse markets and approximately N70 billion to petty traders, according to the report. The Bank also said it assessed businesses’ repayment capacity and provided some financing without collateral.

The approach is relevant to the wider debate over how financial institutions can extend credit to viable enterprises that may lack conventional collateral but have demonstrable business activity and repayment potential.

For many small businesses, access to finance determines whether they can purchase inventory in sufficient quantities, acquire equipment, meet operating expenses, fulfil customer orders or take advantage of new market opportunities.

However, expanding SME credit requires banks to balance access with prudent risk management. Reliable transaction records, sound cash-flow projections, proper business documentation and realistic repayment plans remain important in determining whether lending can be sustained.

FirstBank Group Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, Olusegun Alebiosu, has argued that expanding business financing requires more than the willingness or capacity of banks to lend. The wider legal and institutional environment also determines whether lenders can extend credit confidently.

Speaking on the challenges confronting business financing in September 2026, Alebiosu said: “When people say, ‘you are not financing enough,’ the issue goes beyond the banks. The law, the legal system, the judiciary and the government must invest in creating a trusted environment and making it safe for everyone to transact.”

He added: “If that trust is broken, you cannot have a viable financial system. It is not going to work.”

The comments highlight an important dimension of the SME financing challenge: banks must be able to assess borrowers’ capacity to repay and have confidence that contractual obligations and legitimate business interests will be protected.

Beyond lending

FirstBank’s SME strategy extends beyond the provision of credit to include business advisory services, training and information intended to help entrepreneurs improve their operations.

Through its SMEConnect initiative, the Bank provides business guidance, seminars and practical resources to help small and medium-sized enterprises navigate operational challenges and pursue sustainable growth.

The programme covers businesses in manufacturing, trading, professional services, agriculture and other eligible sectors. FirstBank says its SME services target businesses with annual debit turnover of between ₦5 million and ₦500 million.

Helen Willie, Head of SME Banking at FirstBank, said the Bank’s support for small businesses went beyond financial solutions.

“At FirstBank, our commitment to SMEs extends far beyond providing financial solutions,” Willie said during the Bank’s third-quarter SMEConnect webinar in September 2026.

The webinar, themed ‘The SME Growth Blueprint: Practical Sales Strategies to Win Customers and Boost Revenue,’ focused on helping entrepreneurs improve customer acquisition, sales conversion and retention.

Willie said sustained growth required deliberate strategy, a deep understanding of customers, effective sales processes, strong brand positioning and the ability to adapt to changing business conditions. She also urged entrepreneurs to apply the lessons from the session to their businesses.

The focus on business capability is significant in an environment where small businesses may struggle not only with access to finance but also with financial management, inventory control, customer retention, marketing and business continuity.

Without adequate management systems, additional borrowing may increase an enterprise’s obligations without necessarily improving its profitability or capacity to repay.

By combining lending with business education and advisory support, banks can help entrepreneurs improve their ability to deploy funds productively, strengthen their market positions and build more sustainable enterprises.

Digital platforms and SME growth

Digital technology is another area in which FirstBank is seeking to support business operations.

In April 2026, the Bank highlighted its digital platforms for business transactions, payments and lending, describing them as tools for improving operational efficiency and supporting SME growth.

Olufemi Odumuboni, Head of Online Banking and Digital Channels at FirstBank, said the platforms were designed to provide seamless digital operations and support business financing.

The development aligns with the World Bank Group’s emphasis on using digital records to improve access to finance for smaller enterprises.

At the Annual Meetings, Banga said the institution’s new MSME strategy was designed to make small businesses “more visible, connected, enabled, and funded”, using data and digital solutions to address constraints limiting their growth.

Under the strategy, digital payment records, electronic invoices and other transaction data can help lenders assess businesses’ repayment capacity, while digital platforms can connect smaller enterprises to buyers, suppliers and markets. The initiative also seeks to simplify regulations and expand financing options for MSMEs.

For Nigerian SMEs, digital payments and transaction records can provide a clearer picture of business activity and cash flow. They can also help entrepreneurs monitor receipts and expenditure, improve payment efficiency and manage relationships with customers and suppliers.

For banks, reliable business data can complement conventional credit-assessment methods, although it does not remove the need to evaluate repayment capacity and other lending risks.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to smaller enterprises seeking to establish formal financial histories and expand their relationships with banks, suppliers and larger corporate customers.

Women entrepreneurs and inclusive growth

FirstBank’s support for SMEs also includes initiatives aimed at women entrepreneurs.

The Bank’s FirstGem offering and Spark A Gem Challenge combine financial services with training, mentoring and opportunities for business development.

The maiden Spark A Gem Challenge attracted 356 applications, with eight finalists participating in training and capacity-building activities. The three winners shared grants totalling N10 million.

Chuma Ezirim, Group Executive, e-Business and Retail Products at FirstBank, said access to finance alone was not enough to ensure that women-led businesses succeeded.

He emphasised the importance of combining capital with business capabilities, networks and other forms of support.

Such initiatives broaden the discussion about SME financing beyond the volume of credit disbursed to consider whether entrepreneurs also have access to the knowledge, relationships and market opportunities needed to grow.

Supporting women-owned enterprises can also widen participation in entrepreneurship and help businesses that might otherwise struggle to access finance and professional support.

Translating the jobs agenda into growth

The discussions at the IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings underscored the importance of private-sector development in addressing the global employment challenge.

For Nigeria, achieving that objective will require a combination of economic reforms, reliable infrastructure, access to markets, affordable and sustainable financing, and improved business capabilities.

Commercial banks have a role to play in that process, not only by lending to viable enterprises but also by providing payment services, digital infrastructure and support that helps businesses become more competitive.

FirstBank’s reported SME lending, SMEConnect advisory programme, digital banking services and targeted initiatives for women entrepreneurs illustrate the different ways a bank can support the development of small businesses.

Ultimately, the contribution of SME financing will be measured not simply by the amount of money disbursed, but by the extent to which businesses survive, expand production, improve productivity and create sustainable jobs.

The challenge for banks and policymakers alike is to ensure that more viable Nigerian enterprises can access the capital and support required to turn business opportunities into growth and employment.

The post IMF-World Bank jobs agenda underscores relevance of FirstBank’s SME financing appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Reps invite power minister, TCN MD over vandalisation of transmission towers
description: The House of Representatives has resolved to investigate the recurrent vandalisation of electricity transmission towers across the country, summoning the Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe; the Managing Director of the Transmission Company of Nigeria, Sule Abdulaziz; and his counterpart at the Niger De
content:
The House of Representatives has resolved to investigate the recurrent vandalisation of electricity transmission towers across the country, summoning the Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe; the Managing Director of the Transmission Company of Nigeria, Sule Abdulaziz; and his counterpart at the Niger Delta Power Holding Company, Jennifer Adighije, to explain the measures being taken to safeguard critical national power infrastructure.

The House also directed its Committees on Public Assets and Power to investigate the destruction of 10 transmission towers along the Kano-Bauchi, Kano-Katsina and Kano-Kaduna 330kV transmission lines within a five-month period.

The resolution followed the adoption of a motion sponsored by the member representing Surulere II Federal Constituency of Lagos State, Lanre Okunlola, titled, “Need to investigate the recurrent vandalism of Transmission Company of Nigeria and Niger Delta Power Holding Company Transmission towers and protect the national electricity infrastructure.”

Moving the motion, the lawmaker drew attention to a report published by THISDAY newspaper on October 29, 2026, which disclosed that 10 transmission towers had been vandalised within five months along the three transmission corridors.

He warned that the destruction of transmission towers and the theft of their components posed “a serious threat to the stability of the national grid, disrupts electricity supply and exposes members of the public to safety hazards.”

The lawmaker further expressed concern that the incidents imposed substantial and unbudgeted repair costs on the Federal Government, while raising questions about the effectiveness of existing security arrangements around critical electricity infrastructure.

The House noted that TCN and NDPHC operate critical components of Nigeria’s national electricity transmission network, describing the facilities as “vital national assets essential to electricity supply, economic development and national security.”

It expressed concern that the recurrence of such attacks pointed to possible weaknesses in surveillance, security architecture, intelligence gathering, asset management and the enforcement of existing laws.

Following the adoption of the motion, the House mandated its Committees on Public Assets and Power to invite the Minister of Power, the Managing Director of TCN and the Managing Director of NDPHC to brief them on the circumstances surrounding the reported incidents.

They are expected to provide “details of the extent of damage, estimated financial losses, the status of repairs and preventive measures put in place to forestall further attacks.”

The committees are also to request both companies to submit comprehensive reports covering all recorded incidents of transmission infrastructure vandalism from January 2024 to date.

The reports are expected to identify affected locations, damaged assets, repair and replacement costs, emergency procurements and the status of remedial measures taken by the companies.

Beyond the immediate investigation, the House directed the committees to ascertain the total financial implications of the vandalism, including repair costs, replacement expenditure, emergency procurement and demonstrable economic losses resulting from disruptions to electricity transmission.

They are also to assess the adequacy of existing security arrangements, surveillance systems, maintenance procedures and risk assessments for transmission towers and associated facilities.

The House further called for the involvement of relevant security and law enforcement agencies “to provide updates on investigations, arrests and prosecutions connected with the reported incidents, subject to applicable laws and the independence of judicial proceedings.”

The agencies are also expected to examine the effectiveness of existing regulatory and enforcement controls against the purchase, sale and recycling of stolen transmission components, with a view to dismantling the illicit market for materials taken from public infrastructure.

To address the problem, the lawmakers recommended stronger surveillance, routine inspections, intelligence sharing, community engagement and improved coordination among TCN, NDPHC, security agencies and host communities.

The committees were given four weeks to conclude the investigation and report back to the House for further legislative action.

The investigation comes against the backdrop of persistent challenges confronting Nigeria’s electricity sector, where the transmission network remains a critical link between power generation companies and distribution companies.

Transmission towers carry high-voltage electricity across long distances, and damage to the structures can disrupt power supply to several communities and place additional pressure on other parts of the network.

Repeated attacks on transmission infrastructure also impose additional costs on the electricity industry, as damaged towers require specialised equipment, materials and technical personnel to restore them.

The House said the investigation would help establish accountability for public funds spent on repairs, identify weaknesses in the protection of electricity assets and develop measures to prevent further attacks.

title: FG moves to track suspicious trade transactions using AI
description:
The Federal Government is moving to deploy artificial intelligence, automated trade monitoring and financial intelligence systems to identify suspicious import and export transactions as part of efforts to tackle illicit financial flows and protect public revenue.
The Head of Anti-Graft and Law Enfo
content:
The Federal Government is moving to deploy artificial intelligence, automated trade monitoring and financial intelligence systems to identify suspicious import and export transactions as part of efforts to tackle illicit financial flows and protect public revenue.

The Head of Anti-Graft and Law Enforcement Liaison at the Nigeria Revenue Service, Idris Abdullahi, disclosed this during a training workshop for journalists on evidence-based reporting of illicit financial flows in Nigeria.

Speaking at the workshop in Abuja on Tuesday, Abdullahi explained that the government was developing technology-driven systems to detect irregular trade transactions, strengthen tax compliance and prevent illegal transfers of wealth.

He said, “Nigeria’s future response must increasingly rely on data integration, artificial intelligence, entity resolution, transaction linkage, predictive analytics and early-warning capabilities.

“The proposed National IFF Estimation Software and Early Warning System will support the progressive transition from predominantly manual analysis to a more integrated and technology-enabled national analytical framework.”

According to him, the government is pursuing improved customs valuation, global reference pricing, automated trade anomaly detection and stronger integration of customs risk management systems.

He identified the B’Odogwu Unified Customs Management System and the National Single Window as important components of the country’s transition towards automated trade monitoring.

Abdullahi disclosed that a joint NRS-Nigeria Customs Service-Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit Trade Analytics Task Force had also been proposed to improve information sharing and identify suspicious trading patterns.

He said preliminary analysis of Customs transaction-level import data covering 2020 to 2024, using the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development’s Price Filter Method+, identified significant potential illicit financial flow risks.

“In 2024 alone, the estimated trade-related IFF value at risk stood at approximately N53.9 trillion,” he disclosed.

However, Abdullahi cautioned that the figure represented statistical estimates of potential risks rather than confirmed fraud or actual government revenue losses.

“They are statistical estimates of potential value at risk, not confirmed cases of fraud, established criminal proceeds or verified government revenue losses,” he explained.

He noted that differences in product quality, contractual arrangements and measurement errors could account for some unusual transaction values.

The NRS official further disclosed plans to strengthen beneficial ownership monitoring through social network analytics, enabling authorities to identify individuals behind corporate structures and examine potentially suspicious relationships.

He added that the government was pursuing a National Transfer Pricing Intelligence Centre to strengthen oversight of multinational companies and address artificial profit shifting.

Other interventions include cryptocurrency taxation, enhanced monitoring of oil and mineral exports, electronic procurement and the development of a Centralised National Public Asset Register.

Abdullahi explained that the proposed National Action Plan for 2027–2030 would consolidate these measures and establish a framework for periodic assessment of illicit financial flows.

Speaking with journalists after the workshop, he identified inadequate access to reliable data as a major obstacle to combating illicit financial activities.

“First and foremost, the fight against illicit financial flows is data-driven. Therefore, the availability of data from the relevant agencies responsible for generating it has been one of the major challenges,” he said.

He added that the NRS-led Technical Working Group, comprising agencies including the EFCC, ICPC, NBS, NFIU and Bureau of Public Procurement, was working to improve data collection and institutional coordination.

The workshop also featured presentations by financial crime investigator and forensic expert Adedayo Kayode, the Managing Consultant of Aideasbanc Consulting Limited.

Kayode identified commercial activities, particularly those involving the extractive industry, as major channels of illicit financial flows.

He estimated that commercial activities accounted for about 65 per cent of illicit financial flows, criminal activities for less than 20 per cent and corruption for approximately 15 per cent.

He explained that trade misinvoicing, tax evasion, illegal mining and oil-related transactions were significant sources of illicit financial movements.

“Before now, we had been focusing largely on the corruption sector, illicit financial crime, which just accounts for 15 per cent,” he said.

Kayode called for stronger inter-agency cooperation, improved financial intelligence, effective prosecution and transparent management of recovered assets.

He also cautioned against treating allegations as established crimes, explaining that investigations must establish sufficient evidence before prosecution.

The post FG moves to track suspicious trade transactions using AI appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Fountain of Life board reaffirms Jimmy Odukoya’s removal, names Okpaise interim leader
description:
The Board of Trustees of Fountain of Life Church has reaffirmed its decision to remove Pastor Jimmy Odukoya as senior pastor, appointing Pastor Rotimi Okpaise to oversee the church’s interim spiritual and administrative leadership.







The board said the interim arrangement would remain in force
content:
The Board of Trustees of Fountain of Life Church has reaffirmed its decision to remove Pastor Jimmy Odukoya as senior pastor, appointing Pastor Rotimi Okpaise to oversee the church’s interim spiritual and administrative leadership.

The board said the interim arrangement would remain in force pending consultations and the completion of processes for appointing a substantive leadership structure in accordance with the church’s constitution and established procedures.

The latest decision comes amid an escalating leadership and succession dispute between the board and Jimmy, son of the church’s late founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, who had earlier rejected his removal.

In a statement on Tuesday, the trustees insisted that their November 16, 2026 resolution withdrawing recognition of Jimmy as senior pastor remained valid.

The board also alleged that individuals linked to Jimmy had taken control of the church’s social media platforms without its authorisation and were using them to publish what it described as inaccurate and misleading accounts of the dispute.

“The Board stands by its earlier statement in its entirety, and its resolution of 16 November 2026 remains in force,” it said.

The trustees explained that the decision followed a review of the church’s leadership and succession arrangements, as well as what they described as longstanding governance concerns and current doctrinal and moral controversies.

They said Jimmy had previously been asked to step down before the board resolved to withdraw its recognition of him as senior pastor with immediate effect.

“He is required to step down forthwith from the office and all functions of Senior Pastor,” the statement added.

The board said the decision was intended to create an atmosphere conducive to restoring peace, rebuilding trust and resolving the church’s leadership and governance challenges.

It stressed that the action was not motivated by vindictiveness, humiliation or personal condemnation but was considered necessary to protect the church’s spiritual heritage, institutional integrity and public reputation.

The trustees also warned that statements appearing on the church’s social media platforms should not be regarded as official positions of the board.

They said only statements issued and signed on behalf of the board should be recognised as official, adding that steps were being taken to restore the church’s communication channels to authorised control.

Background to succession dispute

Providing details of the succession disagreement, the board said Fountain of Life Church had built its reputation over three decades on biblical truth, sound doctrine, spiritual integrity and Christian leadership under its founding pastors.

It said responsibility for ensuring an orderly leadership transition rested with the board following the death of Taiwo Odukoya in 2023.

According to the trustees, Jimmy had informed them, and subsequently the congregation, that his late father had handed the leadership mantle to him.

The board said it relied on that representation when it appointed him senior pastor in accordance with the church’s constitution and the succession arrangements it understood to be in place.

However, it disclosed that a video recording made by Taiwo in December 2021, in which he expressly identified his preferred successor, was not presented to the board until late December 2025.

The recording, which the board said was witnessed by John Odukoya, Taiwo’s older son, did not identify Jimmy as the preferred successor.

It further claimed that the recording was not disclosed when it considered and approved Jimmy’s appointment as senior pastor.

“The fundamental issue, therefore, is not simply the identity of the person appointed, but whether the board’s decision was reached on the basis of full, accurate and transparent disclosure of all material information relevant to the succession process,” the trustees said.

The board maintained that it could not remain indifferent while, in its view, the church’s spiritual heritage, institutional integrity and public reputation faced continuing erosion.

The post Fountain of Life board reaffirms Jimmy Odukoya’s removal, names Okpaise interim leader appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: ECOWAS court president seeks improved justice delivery, harmonised judicial standards
description:
By Innocent Anaba



The President of the Community Court of Justice of the Economic Community of West African States, ECOWAS, Justice Charlyne Brumskine, has called for stronger institutional collaboration, harmonised judicial practices and improved justice delivery across the West African sub-regi
content:
By Innocent Anaba

The President of the Community Court of Justice of the Economic Community of West African States, ECOWAS, Justice Charlyne Brumskine, has called for stronger institutional collaboration, harmonised judicial practices and improved justice delivery across the West African sub-region.
Brumskine made the call while declaring open the Court’s 2026 Judicial Retreat in Niger State, Nigeria.
She described the five-day retreat as an important opportunity for judges and judicial support staff to review existing practices, address emerging institutional challenges and develop strategies for improving the administration of justice.
The ECOWAS Court president said the retreat was taking place at a critical stage in the institution’s development, following the adoption of a harmonised legal framework under Supplementary Act SA.1/12/25, the deployment of the Electronic Case Management System, ECMS, and the commencement of the implementation of the Court’s Strategic Plan 2026–2030.
She noted that the first strategic goal of the plan was to guarantee timely and impartial justice.
According to her, the developments require clear and harmonised institutional standards to ensure that the Court’s legal framework, technological infrastructure and judicial practices work together effectively.
“Our task this week is to build on that foundation, consolidate the best practices and experiences, and improve upon the standards where needed,” she said.
Brumskine stressed the importance of collaboration among the Judges’ Chambers, the Registry, the Research and Documentation Department and other support departments, noting that effective judicial administration depended on the collective efforts of all units.
“It is our collective responsibility to build a Court whose standards, systems and procedures consistently support judicial independence, efficiency, accountability and public confidence,” she added.
Earlier, the acting Deputy Chief Registrar of the Court, Mrs. Marie Saine, outlined the objectives and expected outcomes of the retreat.
She said the overall objective was to adopt harmonised standards, guidelines and working procedures to promote the effective and efficient administration of justice.
Saine identified the adoption of standardised judgment templates, a judgment-drafting style guide and quality-assurance procedures, as well as the establishment of an Editorial Committee, among the key objectives.
Others include strengthening legal research support and collaboration between the Judges’ Chambers and the Research and Documentation Department.
She said the retreat would also consider the 2027 judicial calendar, external court sessions, guidelines for virtual sittings and priorities for further development of the Electronic Case Management System.
The review and determination of Instructions to the Chief Registrar and Practice Directions are also expected to form part of the deliberations.
Saine added that participants would develop an implementation framework with clearly assigned responsibilities to ensure that recommendations from the retreat were effectively executed.
Expected outcomes include harmonised judgment templates and drafting standards, a quality-assurance framework, improved legal research support and stronger institutional collaboration.
The retreat is also expected to produce an agreed 2027 judicial calendar, guidelines for external and virtual court sessions, recommendations on procedural instruments and measures to improve the utilisation of the electronic case management system.
The 2026 Judicial Retreat is aligned with the ECOWAS Court’s Strategic Plan 2026–2030, which seeks to strengthen judicial efficiency, expand access to justice, promote regional integration and reinforce the rule of law and protection of human rights across West Africa.

The post ECOWAS court president seeks improved justice delivery, harmonised judicial standards appeared first on Vanguard News.
