title: US confirms probing Singapore-based firm over chip exports
description:
The US government confirmed Monday it was investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed over chip exports, following the scandal that has rocked tech giant Nvidia.
Data centre company Megaspeed is suspected of helping to shift Nvidia’s most powerful technology to China in circumvention of US rules.
T
content:
The US government confirmed Monday it was investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed over chip exports, following the scandal that has rocked tech giant Nvidia.

Data centre company Megaspeed is suspected of helping to shift Nvidia’s most powerful technology to China in circumvention of US rules.

Those concerns emerged publicly after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang revealed an extramarital affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a Chinese former executive from Megaspeed whom US authorities also suspect of spying for Beijing.

Huang, a pivotal figure in the AI boom, stepped down last week after at least two affairs were revealed, including the one with Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old.

The US Commerce and Justice departments said in a joint statement they were working together to “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

China is in a race for tech dominance against the United States, which restricts the export to China of cutting-edge silicon chips crucial for artificial intelligence.

Washington has announced tougher export control measures on AI chips in the wake of the scandal.

The Commerce Department began a probe into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations, the statement said.

The department requested records from Nvidia “concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed” in May 2025.

The following month, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on a “no sell” list, while US federal agents conducted an “on-site, in-person” check at the Singapore-based firm and interviewed Alice Huang.

“Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed,” the statement added.

The scandal has exposed a rift within the administration of US President Donald Trump, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accusing the Commerce Department of ignoring reports that Megaspeed was shifting Nvidia technology to China.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate on the matter.

Jensen Huang has agreed to testify behind closed doors in the House of Representatives before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26.

He has led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, acknowledged an extramarital affair in a letter to the firm’s employees that did not name the woman involved.

title: Stay away from tomorrow’s APC campaign rally, Itsekiri youths warn Oborevwori
description:
By Jimitota Onoyume



Some youths under the aegis of Itsekiri ethnic nationality have advised Itsekiri political leaders and governor of the state, Sheriff Oborevwori to stay away from the forthcoming campaign rally of the All Progressives Congress, APC, scheduled to hold at Nana College on Wednesd
content:
By Jimitota Onoyume

Some youths under the aegis of Itsekiri ethnic nationality have advised Itsekiri political leaders and governor of the state, Sheriff Oborevwori to stay away from the forthcoming campaign rally of the All Progressives Congress, APC, scheduled to hold at Nana College on Wednesday.


In a statement online by Appearance Efejuku and Joseph Okotie, the youths said their position was necessitated by the rejection of what they described as the alleged fraudulent ward structure delineation in Warri South Local Government Area, adding that Itsekiri political leaders who choose to attend the rally would be labeled enemies of the ethnic nation.
The statement further advised Governor Oborevwori and his political allies to stay away from the campaign until the legitimate concern raised by the Itsekiri people on the issues were addressed.
The statemtnt said: The general youths of Warri Kingdom and the Itsekiri people hereby advise all Itsekiri political leaders, elected and appointed office holders, and stakeholders to boycott the forthcoming APC campaign scheduled to hold at Nana College on Wednesday.
According to the statement, “This position is necessitated by the rejection of the fraudulent ward structure delineation in Warri South council.
“We further advise the state governor and his political allies to stay away from the said campaign until this legitimate concern is addressed.
“For the avoidance of doubt, any Itsekiri son or daughter who chooses to participate in the campaign against this collective position will be treated as an enemy of Itsekiri Nation. Our position is clear: No legitimate ward structure, no political participation.”

title: Ogun ASUP strike: NAPS renews 48-hour notice, appeals for urgent govt intervention
description:
The National Association of Polytechnic Students (NAPS), Ogun State Liaison Council, has renewed its 48-hour notice to the Ogun State Government to intervene in the ongoing strike by the Academic Staff Union of Polytechnics (ASUP) in state-owned polytechnics.
The Chairman of NAPS Ogun State Liaison
content:
The National Association of Polytechnic Students (NAPS), Ogun State Liaison Council, has renewed its 48-hour notice to the Ogun State Government to intervene in the ongoing strike by the Academic Staff Union of Polytechnics (ASUP) in state-owned polytechnics.

The Chairman of NAPS Ogun State Liaison Council, Comr. Boluwatife Joshua Opatunmibi, announced the renewed notice at a press conference on Monday.

He said the fresh 48-hour notice commences at 12:00 noon on Monday, November 16, and ends at 12:00 noon on Wednesday, November 18.

Opatunmibi said, “We hereby issue a fresh 48-hour notice, commencing at 12:00 noon on Monday, 16th November 2026, and ending at 12:00 noon on Wednesday, 18th November 2026.

“Within this period, we appeal to the Ogun State Government and all relevant stakeholders to demonstrate clear commitment towards resolving the ongoing dispute through meaningful engagement with ASUP.”

He disclosed that the council had on Thursday, November 12, 2026, issued an initial 48-hour notice calling for urgent intervention, but renewed it after the strike persisted.

He said academic activities across Ogun State-owned polytechnics have been disrupted, academic calendars affected, and students left uncertain about their academic future.

“As the representative body of polytechnic students in Ogun State, we consider it our responsibility to speak up.

“Let me state our position clearly: We stand for the interest of students. We are not here to fight ASUP. We are not here to fight the Ogun State Government. We are not here to create political tension or encourage violence. We are here to appeal for a solution,” he stated.

Lecturers deserve welfare, students deserve uninterrupted education

Opatunmibi said NAPS believes lecturers deserve their legitimate welfare and entitlements, institutions deserve adequate funding, and students deserve uninterrupted education.

“We believe lecturers deserve their legitimate welfare and entitlements. We believe our institutions deserve adequate funding. But we equally believe that students deserve uninterrupted education. These interests should not be in conflict. They should be protected together,” he said.

He lamented the rising cost of education, noting that many political leaders in authority today received education when it was free or considerably less expensive.

“Education has become increasingly expensive. Parents and guardians are paying more. Students are making greater sacrifices. Families are stretching their resources to ensure that their children receive an education. Yet, despite these increased costs, we are still struggling to enjoy uninterrupted academic activities,” he said.

He added that while ordinary students endure disruptions, some children of those in authority have access to private institutions where academic activities continue without interruption.

“Our concern is not where anybody’s children attend school. Our concern is that the ordinary Ogun State student should not receive less attention simply because their parents cannot afford private alternatives,” he said.

Understanding ASUP dispute

Opatunmibi said following engagement with ASUP representatives, NAPS understands the dispute involves outstanding welfare and funding concerns, including the implementation of applicable allowances under the renegotiated 2026 Federal Government-ASUP agreement, reportedly signed on April 8, 2026.

He listed ASUP’s concerns in Ogun State to include implementation of applicable allowances including CATA and EAA, improved funding of state-owned polytechnics, and outstanding pension deductions and contributions.

“Among the demands communicated by the union is an increase in monthly subvention from ₦5 million to ₦100 million per polytechnic,” he said.

He said NAPS acknowledged that state-owned institutions may operate under different financial and administrative arrangements from federal institutions, but expects government to engage the union and clearly communicate its position.

“Let us be clear: we are not asking lecturers to abandon their legitimate demands. We understand that the welfare of academic staff is essential to the quality of education. A poorly supported lecturer cannot be expected to deliver the best possible educational experience. But we also insist that the resolution of these concerns must not continually come at the expense of students,” Opatunmibi said.

Appeal to Governor Abiodun

Opatunmibi made a direct appeal to Governor Dapo Abiodun to personally ensure relevant authorities engage ASUP leadership with urgency.

“Your Excellency, we recognise the responsibilities that come with governing a state. We recognise that government must balance competing demands and financial obligations. However, education is too important to be left in prolonged uncertainty.

“We appeal to Your Excellency to personally ensure that the relevant authorities engage ASUP leadership with the urgency this situation deserves. We appeal for an open and constructive negotiation that will address the outstanding concerns of lecturers while protecting the academic interests of students,” he said.

He also appealed for a clear position on funding, outstanding staff entitlements, and a realistic timeline for resolving the dispute.

“We are not asking for promises that cannot be fulfilled. We are asking for sincere engagement, concrete commitments, and a lasting solution,” he said.

Not a protest notice

Opatunmibi clarified that the renewed notice is not a declaration of hostility, an invitation to violence, or an announcement of a protest.

He said, “Let nobody misunderstand the purpose of this notice. It is not a declaration of hostility. It is not an invitation to violence. It is not an announcement of a protest. It is an appeal backed by a renewed deadline because students cannot continue to wait indefinitely.

“Our preferred approach is peaceful negotiation. We want government and ASUP to reach an understanding. We want our institutions to function. We want our students back in their classrooms.”

He said NAPS does not celebrate protests and its first choice has always been dialogue, consultation and peaceful engagement.

“We would rather sit around a negotiation table and announce a successful resolution than stand before the press repeatedly explaining why students are still out of school,” he said.

“We want negotiations, not confrontation. We want solutions, not street battles. We want our education to continue.”

PVC is power

Opatunmibi also used the briefing to encourage eligible students to obtain their Permanent Voter’s Card (PVC).

“The PVC is not merely an identification card for elections. It is an instrument of democratic participation, accountability, and the ability to influence the direction of government,” he said.

“Our vote is our voice. We must become a generation that understands its rights, accepts its responsibilities, and participates actively in shaping the society it wants to live in. This is not a call for partisan politics. It is a call for civic awareness and responsible democratic participation.”

In his final appeal, Opatunmibi urged students to remain calm, united and law-abiding.

“To the Ogun State Government, we appeal once again: please act within this renewed 48-hour window. Let this matter be resolved through sincere negotiation before the situation becomes more difficult. To ASUP, we recognise your concerns and encourage continued constructive engagement,” he said.

title: Aiding our traders to embrace manufacturing
description: Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu’s call at the recent 19th China Commodities Expo and 40th Lagos International Trade Fair was timely. The governor urged traders to move beyond importing finished goods into local assembly, manufacturing, agro-processing and exports. He challenged Chinese inves
content:
Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu’s call at the recent 19th China Commodities Expo and 40th Lagos International Trade Fair was timely. The governor urged traders to move beyond importing finished goods into local assembly, manufacturing, agro-processing and exports. He challenged Chinese investors to establish factories, transfer technology and partner with Nigerian businesses. The message is sound. But it collides with a business environment that makes production punishingly difficult.

Nigeria remains heavily dependent on imported manufactured goods, while exporting too little value-added output. The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, MAN, recently noted that manufactured goods accounted for only N2.5 trillion, or 2.94 per cent, of the N85.13 trillion in total exports recorded in 2025. The NESG has warned that manufacturing’s contribution to GDP is declining, with energy costs, import competition, inadequate finance and weak industrial coordination suppressing productive capacity.

NESG’s October 2026 business monitor identified power outages, costly inputs, poor infrastructure, limited credit and raw-material shortages. Traders understandably gravitate towards importing. Chinese producers enjoy scale, technology, cheaper finance, reliable power and efficient logistics. A Nigerian entrepreneur contemplating a factory faces expensive electricity, high interest rates, volatile foreign exchange, costly machinery and inputs, multiple taxation, port delays, poor roads, smuggling and unpredictable regulations. Policy reversals and overlapping levies make long-term investment hazardous.

It is easier and often more profitable to import a container than build a factory whose costs may overwhelm its owner. That is why government must do the heavy lifting. The NESG, NACCIMA and MAN have demanded policy consistency, affordable energy, accessible long-term finance, efficient infrastructure, simpler taxation, predictable trade rules and protection against dumping and substandard imports. These are not special favours; they are foundations of competitive production.

President Bola Tinubu’s Nigeria First policy, directing public institutions to prioritise Nigerian-made goods, must become enforceable procurement practice, not a slogan. Government should publish compliance records, pay local suppliers promptly and enforce quality standards. It must expand industrial power through gas, embedded generation and renewables, lower financing costs through development banks, clear port bottlenecks, support research, skills and technology transfer, and provide stable incentives for investors who create local value and jobs, with transparent eligibility rules and measurable local-content targets.

Traders should respond through joint ventures, contract manufacturing and gradual local assembly, rather than wait to become industrial giants overnight. Chinese partnerships must build Nigerian capacity, not perpetuate dependency. Manufacturing will retain value at home, create skilled jobs, broaden exports, diversify revenue, strengthen the naira by reducing import demand and enlarge GDP through productivity.

But exhortation cannot overcome hostile economics. Sanwo-Olu is right to call traders into factories; Tinubu’s government must make factories viable. Nigeria needs fewer speeches about localising production and more dependable power, credit, infrastructure and fair regulatory environments.

The task is to make producing in Nigeria more rewarding than importing into it.

title: Why must the opposition campaign in fear while the ruling party campaigns freely? By Ejiro Ofoye
description: There is something fundamentally wrong with a democracy when political parties cannot freely organise meetings, hold rallies, address citizens or mobilise supporters without the fear of being attacked. Nigeria is supposed to be a constitutional democracy, not a country where political power determin
content:
There is something fundamentally wrong with a democracy when political parties cannot freely organise meetings, hold rallies, address citizens or mobilise supporters without the fear of being attacked. Nigeria is supposed to be a constitutional democracy, not a country where political power determines who enjoys the freedom to assemble and who must conduct political activities under the threat of violence.

The increasing reports of attacks against opposition political parties, particularly the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), in Delta State, Lagos, Enugu, Benue and other parts of the country should worry every Nigerian. What is unfolding is embarrassing, dangerous and completely unacceptable in a country preparing for another general election.

The situation is becoming so alarming that Nigerians must begin to ask whether the country is gradually approaching an election season in which political participation will be determined not by the strength of ideas, manifestoes and candidates, but by the capacity of political parties to deploy violence and intimidation.

On October 10, 2026, during activities surrounding the governorship campaign flag-off of the NDC in Enugu State, suspected political attackers reportedly invaded areas where party supporters had gathered, including the campaign office of the party’s governorship candidate, Sir Christian Chinyeaka Ohaa, in the Government Reserved Area of Enugu. The violence resulted in gunshot injuries, damaged vehicles and the eventual death of an NDC supporter, Ifeanyi Nwolie.

The Enugu State Government initially disputed reports of a fatality. However, subsequent reporting by Premium Times confirmed that Nwolie died from injuries sustained during the attack and was buried on October 22, 2026. The police had earlier announced an investigation into the shooting and directed its State Criminal Investigation Department to identify and apprehend the perpetrators.

This is no longer an ordinary political disagreement. A Nigerian citizen has lost his life in an incident connected with political activities. What could be more disturbing than a situation in which a citizen cannot safely welcome a political candidate or participate in a political gathering?

In Delta State, the experience has been equally disturbing.

On September 18, 2026, the NDC’s One Million March in Warri and Effurun was disrupted by suspected political thugs. The confrontation reportedly occurred at different locations, including Airport Road, Ogboroke and Jakpa Junction. Participants sustained injuries, and there were disturbing accounts of weapons being displayed during the confrontation.

What makes the incident particularly troubling is the allegation by participants that security personnel were present but failed to intervene promptly as the attackers confronted NDC members. A video of the incident circulated widely, raising questions about the conduct and effectiveness of the security personnel around the procession.

The Guardian and Channels Television reported on the incident, while the Delta State Government announced that Governor Sheriff Oborevwori had directed security agencies to investigate and ensure that anyone found culpable was prosecuted.

But the fundamental question remains: why should citizens have to defend themselves against political attackers while security personnel are expected to protect them?

The police must not become spectators when political thugs attack innocent citizens. Their responsibility is to prevent violence, protect lives and restore order. Watching an attack unfold and subsequently issuing a statement cannot be considered adequate policing.

The situation became even more disturbing on November 7, 2026, when the political consultation of Deacon Chris Iyovwaye, the NDC governorship candidate in Delta State, in Warri South Local Government Area was reportedly disrupted at Cinema Site, Okumagba Avenue. NDC supporters were allegedly attacked and beaten, disrupting the candidate’s engagement with party faithful.

The matter was reportedly taken to the B Divisional Police Headquarters in Warri. Yet, according to information available to the affected political organisation, there has been no satisfactory public account of the investigation or any meaningful information about arrests and prosecutions.

Why should a political candidate who has formally notified security authorities of his consultation activities be exposed to attacks? What exactly is the purpose of notifying the police if citizens cannot receive adequate protection when violence occurs?

A candidate’s consultation with party members is a legitimate political activity. It is not a declaration of war. It is not an invitation to political opponents to mobilise thugs. It is an exercise of constitutional freedom.

There was also the November 7 incident in Asaba, where an NDC political procession reportedly ended in violence, leaving one person dead and five others injured, according to the police. The Delta State Police Command confirmed the incident and announced an investigation. The Command also stated that it had received intelligence about possible violence before the event and advised the organisers against an open-road procession, recommending an alternative venue with appropriate security arrangements.

That explanation raises an important question: when security threats are identified, should the responsibility of the police end with issuing advice, or should it extend to ensuring that citizens can exercise their constitutional rights safely through reasonable security arrangements?

If the police possess intelligence about possible violence, that should be an even stronger reason to deploy adequate personnel, identify potential troublemakers and prevent an attack.

On November 12, another disturbing incident occurred in Oregun, Ikeja, Lagos, where suspected political thugs invaded an NDC town hall meeting venue. Participants were attacked, proceedings were disrupted and journalists were caught in the violence. The Cable reported that its journalist, Samuel Adebanjo, was assaulted, his wrist was reportedly struck with an axe, and his camera equipment was stolen.

The question Nigerians must ask is whether political thuggery is gradually becoming an acceptable instrument of political competition.

What makes this situation even more disturbing is the apparent contrast in the political atmosphere. The ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) continues to organise its political activities, mobilise supporters and conduct political engagements across the country, while opposition organisations are increasingly reporting intimidation, attacks and destruction of property.

The ruling party must understand that democracy is not measured by how freely the governing party can campaign. It is measured by whether every political party, including those seeking to remove the incumbent government, can exercise the same constitutional freedoms without intimidation.

Why should opposition supporters have to calculate the security risks of attending a political meeting? Why should a candidate worry about being attacked while consulting with citizens? Why should a political organisation require extraordinary courage simply to open an office or organise a procession?

There is another disturbing dimension to this problem. Following some of these incidents, political leaders and government officials have taken to social media to advance different narratives, sometimes attempting to explain away the violence before the appropriate investigations have been concluded.

Recently, the Chairman of Uvwie Local Government Area, in a recording reportedly aired by Arise TV, was alleged to have made a threatening statement directed at residents of the Alaka area of Effurun, Uvwie. The statement, delivered in the Urhobo language, was interpreted in English to mean that anyone who did not intend to vote for the APC should not come out, or risk being killed.

If the recording and its translation are accurate, this is an extremely serious matter that cannot be dismissed as ordinary political rhetoric.

A local government chairman is not a street political activist. He is a public officer entrusted with responsibilities that include protecting the interests and welfare of all residents, irrespective of their political affiliations.

How can a chairman elected to serve an entire local government threaten citizens because they may not support his political party? Who gave any public officeholder the authority to determine whether Nigerians are entitled to come out and exercise their democratic rights?

The police should investigate the recording, establish its authenticity and invite the chairman to explain the statement. If the words were accurately translated and the threat established, appropriate legal action should follow.

No Nigerian should be threatened with death for refusing to vote for the APC, the NDC or any other political party. The ballot is a secret constitutional choice, not an obligation imposed through threats.

I am not suggesting that every reported attack has been sponsored by the ruling party. Such allegations must be established through credible investigations, and nobody should be condemned without evidence. However, the frequency and geographical spread of these incidents demand answers. Government officials must not substitute social media narratives for credible investigations.

The law is not ambiguous on this matter. Section 91(1) of the Electoral Act, 2022, expressly places responsibility on the Commissioner of Police in every state and the Federal Capital Territory to provide adequate security for the proper and peaceful conduct of political rallies and processions.

Section 91(4) further provides that no registered political party, its aspirants or candidates shall be prevented from holding rallies, processions or meetings for constitutional political purposes. It also requires the police to resolve conflicts concerning time and venue through consultation.

Similarly, Section 4 of the Nigeria Police Act, 2020, establishes the responsibilities of the police in preventing crime, protecting lives and property, maintaining public order and protecting the rights and freedoms of citizens.

These are statutory responsibilities, not political favours to be extended at the discretion of whoever occupies government.

The Nigeria Police Force is a federal institution. Its loyalty must be to the Constitution and the Nigerian people, not to the political interests of any administration. A police officer cannot decide that an APC gathering deserves protection while an NDC, ADC, Labour Party or SDP gathering can be left exposed.

The Inspector-General of Police must therefore issue clear instructions to all state commands that opposition and ruling-party political activities must receive equal protection. He should demand comprehensive reports concerning the incidents in Delta, Enugu and Lagos, establish whether there were security failures, investigate allegations of police inaction and ensure that anyone found culpable faces appropriate disciplinary or criminal proceedings.

The police must also investigate reports that officers sometimes stand by while suspected political thugs attack NDC supporters. The allegation surrounding the One Million March in Warri deserves particular attention. Officers who abandon their statutory responsibilities or deliberately allow violence to continue must be held accountable.

The consequences of allowing this situation to continue could be far more serious than some political leaders imagine.

Nigeria must understand that an election is not merely an exercise in counting votes. It is the culmination of a democratic process in which citizens must be able to organise, mobilise, campaign, persuade and freely make political choices.

If the political space becomes so dangerous that opposition candidates cannot campaign, supporters cannot attend meetings and journalists cannot report political activities without being attacked, what exactly are Nigerians preparing to participate in during 2027?

I am particularly concerned that if this situation continues, Nigeria may eventually face a crisis in which the credibility and legitimacy of the entire electoral process become questionable.

A country cannot expect citizens to maintain confidence in elections when their democratic rights are constantly threatened. When people begin to believe that the security institutions exist to protect only those in government, frustration and public anger will inevitably grow.

If political violence is allowed to continue unchecked, the possibility of widespread public resistance, mass protests and even a popular revolt against a political order perceived as unjust cannot be dismissed. This is not a threat or an endorsement of violence. It is a warning about the consequences of institutional failure and the suppression of democratic freedoms.

There may come a point when citizens lose confidence not only in political parties but also in the institutions expected to guarantee their constitutional rights. At that point, the possibility of conducting credible, peaceful and widely accepted elections could be seriously undermined.

The police and government must prevent Nigeria from reaching that dangerous destination.

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the governors must also speak up. They are leaders of the entire country and their respective states, not merely political leaders of their parties. Their responsibility extends to Nigerians who support alternative political platforms.

A government confident in its achievements should have no reason to fear opposition campaigns. If the APC believes its policies and programmes are acceptable to Nigerians, it should allow the electorate to make that judgement freely. Democracy is about competition, persuasion and the freedom to choose. It is not about intimidating opponents into silence.

The ruling party must also understand that political power is not permanent. Those who enjoy the protection and privileges of government today may become opposition politicians tomorrow. The institutions they weaken or allow to be compromised today may be the same institutions they will need to protect their rights in the future.

Nigeria must not allow the 2027 general elections to become a season of political intimidation, organised thuggery and the suppression of opposition voices.

The police must act before lives are lost, not merely issue statements after blood has been spilled. The government must protect the political space, not preside over its destruction. The Inspector-General of Police must demonstrate that the Nigeria Police Force remains an institution for all Nigerians, irrespective of political affiliation.

No political party owns Nigeria. No governor owns a state. No president owns the democratic rights of citizens.

The opposition has the same constitutional right to campaign as the ruling party. Deacon Chris Iyovwaye has the same right to consult with Deltans as the APC governorship candidate. The NDC governorship candidate in Enugu has the same right to open a campaign office as any candidate of the ruling party. Peter Obi has the same right to address Nigerians as President Tinubu.

The right to seek political power must never become a death sentence for those who exercise it.

If Nigeria cannot guarantee the safety of citizens during political consultations and campaigns, how can it guarantee the safety and credibility of the elections themselves?

This is a question the Inspector-General of Police, the President, the governors and the National Security Adviser must answer without delay.

Nigeria must not become a country where the ruling party campaigns freely while the opposition campaigns in fear.

The police must protect all political campaigns, without fear or favour. That is what the law demands, that is what democracy requires, and that is what Nigerians deserve.

*Dr Ofoye writes from Lagos.

…National supply inadequate to meet demand – NALPGAM

..Falcon CEO advocates infrastructure-focused subsidies

By Udeme Akpan & Ediri Ejoh

The price of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG), popularly known as cooking gas, has risen by 14 per cent to N1,600 per kilogramme (kg) in November 2026, from N1,400 in October, amid growing supply shortages.


Checks by Vanguard yesterday showed that several suppliers had run out of commercial stocks in Lagos and other parts of the country, with Dangote Petroleum Refinery among the few suppliers with available products.


The development has sustained the upward movement in cooking gas prices over the past three months, raising concerns about the adequacy of domestic supply to meet growing demand.

National supply inadequate to meet demand — NALPGAM

Speaking with Energy Vanguard, National President of the Nigerian Association of Liquefied Petroleum Gas Marketers (NALPGAM), Mr. Inyang Edu, said the scarcity exposed the gap between national supply figures and the actual experience of consumers.


He said: “The national supply is still struggling to keep pace with actual consumption. Although domestic LPG supply has increased, demand has also grown.


“If this imbalance persists, the market must draw on existing inventories or secure additional supplies to maintain availability. A rise in supply is not sufficient to stabilise prices if consumption continues to exceed incoming volumes.”


Edu identified inadequate storage and transportation infrastructure as additional constraints, explaining that the availability of gas at production facilities or coastal terminals did not guarantee access in inland markets.


“The cost of transporting LPG over long distances, road conditions, haulage charges, loading and offloading, storage limitations and the availability of suitable LPG trucks can all contribute to regional price differences,” he said.


He warned that increased national production should not be mistaken for improved supply across all states, particularly those far from major supply points.


He added: “The appropriate policy is therefore not to eliminate imports indiscriminately, but to use domestic production as the foundation of supply while retaining sufficient flexibility to cover genuine shortfalls.”

Falcon CEO advocates infra structure-focused subsidies

Similarly, Chief Executive Officer of Falcon Corporation Limited, Audrey Joe-Ezigbo, has called for subsidies to target infrastructure that reduces LPG delivery costs rather than the price of the product.


Speaking during a panel session on government-led LPG interventions at the 16th NLCGA Conference and Exhibition in Abuja, she stressed the need for coordinated government and private-sector investment to sustain household adoption.


“We should subsidise access, not consumption. That means funding the infrastructure that lowers delivery costs, such as inland depots, bottling plants and better logistics, rather than the price. Some of these incentives already exist, and we need more of them,” she said.


Joe-Ezigbo noted that transportation costs significantly affect what consumers in northern Nigeria pay for cooking gas, adding that trucking, railways and pipelines would be critical to expanding nationwide distribution.


“We should avoid subsidising the molecule itself, because that discourages the investment needed to expand LPG use,” she said.
She also called for improved household purchasing power and greater awareness of LPG’s health benefits, particularly as an alternative to traditional cooking fuels.


On measuring the success of government interventions, she recommended tracking whether households benefiting from support programmes could independently afford cylinder refills at prevailing market prices 24 to 36 months after the assistance ended.


To attract private investment, she advocated guaranteed supply, predictable regulations and an enforceable domestic LPG supply obligation, backed by performance-based offtake contracts linked to verified refills.

title: Constant frustration of INEC Chairman, by Eric Teniola
description: Every chairman of the Federal Electoral Commission (FEDECO) or National Electoral Commission (NEC), now the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), has always been accused of partisanship. content:
Every chairman of the Federal Electoral Commission (FEDECO) or National Electoral Commission (NEC), now the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), has always been accused of partisanship. Some of them, if not all, left office in frustration. Some of them have been accused of compromising their office and of not being neutral. They have been accused of being agents, disciples or henchmen of the ruling party.

That has been part of our political history.

This was the reason why the former Ondo State Chief Judge and first Nigerian Director of the Law School, Honourable Justice Olakunle Orojo CFR (16 February, 1923 – 3 July, 2009), from Arigidi in Akoko North West Local Government Area of Ondo State, rejected the job after his appointment to replace Professor Humphrey Nwosu (2 October 1941 – 20 October 2024) was announced by General Ibrahim Babangida (85) GCFR in 1993.

One needs to read the 392-page book by Professor Humphrey Nwosu titled “LAYING THE FOUNDATION FOR NIGERIA’S DEMOCRACY: MY ACCOUNT OF JUNE 12, 1993 PRESIDENTIAL ELECTIONS AND ITS ANNULMENT”. His close friend, Mr. Fab Uche, who is equally close to me, is never tired of telling me about the humiliation Professor Nwosu faced as Chairman of the electoral body during and after his tenure till he died in the United States of America on October 24, 2024.

Professor Nwosu’s laudable efforts ended in the annulment of the election, the consequences of which we are still enduring till today.

The process for the selection of the INEC Chairman is wrong, and it gives room for suspicion.

In English, we have the saying that “He who pays the piper calls the tune,” which means that the person who pays for something decides on what happens to that something. In Hebrew, it says, “The man who controls the riches is the man who controls the judgement.” A French version says, “Celui qui tient les rênes tourne la tête.” He who holds the reins turns the head.

Salman Iqbal, an author, wrote, “He with the big stick has got to be the owner of the she-bufalo!”

Past Chairmen of INEC felt that they owed their appointments to the man who appointed them.

Section 50 of the 1963 Constitution says, “(1) There shall be an Electoral Commission for the Federation. (2) The members of the Electoral Commission of the Federation shall be—(a) a Chief Electoral Commissioner, who shall be chairman; and (b) a member representing each territory. (3) The members of the Electoral Commission of the Federation shall be appointed by the President, acting in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister. (4) Before tendering any advice for the purposes of this section in relation to the appointment of the member of the Electoral Commission of the Federation representing a Region, the Prime Minister shall consult the Premier of that Region. (5) A person shall not be qualified to hold office as a member of the Electoral Commission of the Federation if he is a member of either House of Parliament, a member of a legislative house of a Region, a Minister of the Government of the Federation, a Minister of the Government of a Region or a member of the public service of the Federation or the public service of a Region.”

Section C of the Third Schedule of the 1979 Constitution says, “The Federal Electoral Commission shall comprise the following members, namely—(a) a Chairman, who shall be appointed from among members specified in sub-paragraphs (b) and (c) of the paragraph; (b) one member from each of the States of the Federation; (c) not more than 5 additional members who shall be appointed on their merit.”

The Section gave the President the power to appoint members of the Commission, including the Chairman.

Section 153 of the 1999 Constitution equally gives the President the power to appoint the Chairman and members of INEC. Subsection 3 of Section 154 of the Constitution states, “In exercising his powers to appoint a person as Chairman or member of the Independent National Electoral Commission, National Judicial Council, the Federal Judicial Council Service Commission or the National Population Commission, the President must consult the Council of State.”

We have to devise means and ways to appoint the members of INEC in a way that does not make them suspects.

I want to limit myself to the fate of the four pioneers of the electoral body.

The chairmen of the electoral body have been Mr Roland Edward Wraith (1958–1963), Sir Kofoworola Adekunle Abayomi (1963–1964), Chief Eyo Esua (1964–1966), Chief Michael Ani (1976–1979), Justice Victor Ovie-Whiskey (1980–1983), Professor Eme Awa (1987–1989), Professor Humphrey Nwosu (1989–1993), Professor Okon Uya (1993, June–November), Chief Sumner Dagogo-Jack (1994–1998), Justice Ephraim Akpata (1998–2000), Sir Abel Guobadia (2000–2005), Professor Maurice Iwu (2005–2010), Professor Attahiru Jega (2010–2015), Professor Mahmood Yakubu (2015–2025) and Professor Joash Ojo Amupitan (SAN)—2025 till date.

Professor Joash Amupitan hails from Ayetoro Gbede in Ijumu Local Government Area of Kogi State.

If we are to judge Ayetoro Gbede by the likes of Senator Dino Melaye, what of notables like Major General (rtd) David Medayese Jemibewon (86), Shola Ameobi, who once played for Newcastle United football club in the English Premiership, John Obaro, founder of Systemspecs, and others?

I first visited Ayetoro Gbede in 1975 when it was part of Kwara State. I was there for the grand reception by the people of Ayetoro Gbede in honour of Colonel Jemibewon, who was appointed the Military Governor of Western State to replace Captain Akintunde Aduwo (86). I was then the Western State Editor of the Kwara State-owned THE NIGERIAN HERALD, reporting from Ibadan.

The people of Ijumu have a passion for education. They are intrepid and doughty. They are fearless. I have in mind the likes of Chief Bayo Ojo, SAN, CON; Senator Smart Adeyemi, Lt. General (rtd.) Rufus Modupe Kupolati, Lt. General (rtd.) Joseph Olorungbon Owonibi, Major General (rtd) Funso Samson Owonibi, Mrs Folashade Yemi-Esan, Dapo Olorunyomi, CON, Mr. Eniola Bello, Gbenga Ogunleye, Prince Olushola Akanmode, Mr. Tunde Ipinmisho, S. A. Ajayi, Professor Yemi Akinwumi, Professor Gbenga Ibileye, Honourable Abiodun James Faleke, Barrister Ayo Abraham Olorunfemi and so many others.

Coincidentally, an illustrious Ijumu Professor is to conduct our coming general elections. Those who love Nigeria must wish Professor Joash Ojo Amupitan the best of luck.

After the Constitutional conference in London, it was agreed that an electoral body be established for the 1959 elections and other elections. Mr. Roland Edward Wraith was therefore appointed to head the body. Other members of the commission were Alhaji Bello Dan Amar, Mr. Anthony Aniagolu, Mr. H. Orisejolomi Thomas, Mr. K.A. Bohu and Mr. M. A. Sho-Silva. Mr. Orisejolomi Thomas later resigned to go back to academics, which was his calling, and was replaced by Prince Peter Akenzua.

Mr. Ronald Edwards Wraith was born in 1908 in Derby, Derbyshire, England. He was a British scholar and public administrator specializing in colonial and post-colonial governance in Africa. Mr. Wraith authored influential studies on local government systems in West Africa, including examinations of structures in Nigeria, Ghana, and Sierra Leone, and co-wrote Corruption in Developing Countries (1963) with Edgar Simpkins, analyzing administrative challenges and graft in emerging nations. His works emphasized practical reforms to build effective institutions amid decolonization, drawing from direct experience in British colonial service.

His tenure, which extended until 1960, focused on establishing impartial mechanisms for voters’ registration and election conduct amid Nigeria’s diverse ethnic and regional divisions. Mr. Wraith, drawing from his prior administrative experience in colonial service, prioritized logistical preparations, including the compilation of electoral rolls across Nigeria’s expansive territory, where infrastructure limitations posed significant hurdles such as inadequate transportation and communication networks.

Under Mr. Wraith’s leadership, the ECN organized the 1958 regional elections, which served as a precursor to federal polls, achieving widespread voter registration despite challenges like low literacy rates and geographic isolation in rural areas. The subsequent 1959 federal elections, held on December 12, saw the Northern People’s Congress secure 134 seats in the 312-member House of Representatives, forming a coalition government with the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons.

Voter participation reached approximately 79.5%, reflecting effective mobilization efforts, though ethnic-based campaigning intensified regional rivalries. Wraith’s commission addressed logistical issues by deploying polling stations in remote locations and training local staff, enabling the process to proceed without widespread disruption despite predictions of potential violence. The outcomes of these elections contributed to short-term political stability, paving the way for Nigeria’s independence on October 1, 1960, with Alhaji Abubakar Tafawa Balewa appointed as Prime Minister.

Success metrics included the acceptance of results by major parties, minimal reported irregularities in vote counting, and the establishment of a precedent for federal oversight of polls. However, persistent ethnic tensions, evident in the uneven regional vote distributions—such as the Northern People’s Congress dominating the North while the Action Group prevailed in the West—foreshadowed future instability, including the 1964 election crises that undermined the nascent democratic framework. Wraith’s role emphasized procedural integrity over partisan influence, though critics later noted that structural ethnic imbalances limited long-term cohesion.

By 1963, there was agitation for a Nigerian to be appointed to head the body. Nigerianisation became the key word. So, Alhaji Tafawa Balewa’s friend, Dr. Moses Adekoyejo Majekodunmi (17 August 1916 – 11 April 2012), a pioneering Obstetrician, Gynaecologist, Administrator, and Politician who served as Federal Minister of Health from 1961 to 1966 and as Administrator of the Western Region in 1962, introduced his friend, Sir Kofo Abayomi, to replace Mr. Wraith, who resigned his appointment in frustration. Thereafter, Mr. Wraith went back to England and Sir Kofo Abayomi was appointed chairman of the electoral body.

Sir Kofo Adekunle Abayomi was a doctor and politician born on 10 July 1896 in Lagos. He attended the UNA School and then, from 1909, the Wesleyan College (now Methodist Boys’ High School) in Lagos, where he became a pupil teacher on completing his studies in 1912. He later transferred to a similar job at the Eko Boys’ School. He joined the civil service as a government dispenser in 1914, working first at the African Hospital in Lagos. A few months later, when the First World War broke out, he worked as a dispenser with the Nigerian Forces, which fought for the British in the Cameroons Campaign. He was decorated for this service.

In 1922, he went to Edinburgh University, where several other West African doctors had already qualified, to study medicine. He completed those studies at Moorfields Eye Hospital, London, and specialized as an Ophthalmologist. He won the M.B. and Ch.B. of Edinburgh in 1928, and the M.D. in 1936. From 1928 to 1930 he was a demonstrator in Physiological Methods at Edinburgh.

Returning to Nigeria in 1930, he combined private medical practice with politics. In 1938, he took over from the deceased Dr. J.C. Vaughn the presidency of the Nigeria Youth Movement (NYM), which he had joined on its foundation as the Lagos Youth Movement in 1933. Also, in 1938 he was elected to the Legislative Council as an NYM member for Lagos. He served for two years but resigned in 1940 to go to Britain for further studies.

In 1958, Sir Kofoworola Adekunle Abayomi was appointed Chairman of the Lagos Executive Development Board, which had authority to demolish unsanitary buildings and undertake town planning schemes. The board was also involved in freehold housing and estate development in Surulere, the North East and South West Ikoyi reclamation schemes and the reclamation of up to one thousand acres in Victoria Island.

Sir Abayomi became the first Nigerian Chairman of the Board of the University College Hospital, Ibadan, in 1958, a position he held until 1965. In 1959, he was chairman of the Board of Management of the Lagos University Teaching Hospital in Lagos. He served on the board or as chairman of several companies for the rest of his life.

By 1964, at the age of 68, it became clearer that Sir Abayomi was too old to function as the chairman of the electoral body. He spent less than a year in office, but conducted the Mid-West House of Assembly election in 1964. He too resigned in frustration.

Following his resignation as the Chairman of the Federal Electoral Commission (FEC), the electoral body at that time, the then Prime Minister, Alhaji Tafawa Balewa, replaced him with Chief Eyo Ita Esua (14 January 1901 – 6 December 1973).

Chief Esua was a school master and a founding member of the Nigeria Union of Teachers. He was the first full-time general secretary of the union from 1943 until his retirement in 1964. He was an Efik man from Calabar, renowned for his dedication to duty and uprightness.

The Esua-led commission organized the December 1964 elections, which were mired in controversy. Two members of the commission, Mr. Anthony Aniagolu from the Eastern Region and Prince Peter Akenzua from the Mid-Western Region, disagreed with the chairman and resigned from the commission. Prince Akenzua later served as Vice-President of the Legal Aid Council under Chief Timothy Chimezie Ikeazor SAN (1930–October 12, 2012), the Oboli Obosi from Anambra State. As for Mr. Anthony Nnaemezie Christopher Aniagolu (October 22, 1922–June 28, 2011), he later served as Chief Judge of Anambra State from 1976 to 1978 and was a justice of the Supreme Court from 1978 to 1987. In 1988, he chaired a Constituent Assembly to propose a draft constitution for the Third Republic.

Chief Esua also conducted the 1965 Western Region elections, which were violent and were disputed by the opposition United Party Grand Alliance. A few days before these elections, Chief Esua acknowledged that his organisation could not guarantee a free and fair poll. The widespread electoral abuses may have been a factor in the success of the military coup of January 1966 in which Major General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi came to power.

The major task Chief Esua faced as the chairman of the electoral commission was the delimitation of constituencies. By mid-July 1964, the Commission announced far-reaching changes in the numbers of Federal members representing each administrative division. These changes were presumably based on the figures of the 1963 population census, still to be published in detail. The main changes showed the North reduced from 1974 to 1967, the East reduced from 73 to 70, the Mid West from 15 to 14, the West increased from 47 to 57, and Lagos from 2 to 3. Among changes in the West, Osun division was increased from 9 to 12, and Ekiti from 3 to 8; in the East, Brass, Calabar and Degema were increased from 1 to 2 each, and Eket was increased from 2 to 4. In the North, Kano (31) and Sokoto (21) were increased by one.

In August, during the Northern Nigeria tour of the Commission, Mr. Esua, chairman and the leader of the delimitation committee, said that to divide Nigeria into 312 constituencies was an exclusive prerogative of the Federal Government, and that the figures of the recent census were the basis of delimitation. Each constituency was based on a population quota of 178,000.

In 1965, the Federal Electoral Commission under Chief Esua held a sham election in the Western Region. Chief Esua was forced to resign in frustration on December 15, 1965 and was replaced by Chief Michael Ani on December 16, 1965 by the then Prime Minister, Alhaji Tafawa Balewa. Chief Esua wrote in his memoirs, before he died, about his frustration. The memoirs are with his children and grandchildren in the ancient city of Calabar.

The military came in on January 16, 1966, so there was no election thereafter and no need for an electoral commission.

On November 15, 1976, the then Head of State, General Olusegun Obasanjo GCFR, inaugurated the Federal Electoral Commission at the Nigeria Institute of International Affairs, Victoria Island, Lagos. The Commission had twenty-four members, including four women, and was headed by Chief Michael Ani. The four women were Mrs Yetunde Gbadebo, Mrs Elizabeth Pam, Mrs Hassan Iro and Mrs Ethel Onwu. It was the second time Chief Ani would head that body.

Speaking on Chief Ani on Wednesday, July 26, 1989 at Calabar, the former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Chief Allison Akene Ayida (June 16, 1930–October 12, 2018), narrated the circumstances that led to Chief Ani being reappointed as the Chairman of the electoral body: “We are here to honour a man who spent the better part of his life defending the integrity of the public service as the Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Establishments and Service Matter (Personnel Management to the new generation), and Member of the Federal Public Service Commission. He is better known in Calabar as the Administrator for the Liberated Areas of South-Eastern State during the civil war, and the Founding Father of the South-Eastern State Civil Service as its first Secretary to the Military Government and Head of Service. He attained membership of the International Civil Service Commission in 1974, having previously served on the UN Panel of Experts on Public Administration for setting up the proposed Federal Service for Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania in 1963.

“When I was appointed to act as Permanent Secretary to the Federal Ministry of Economic Development, in 1963, I was the youngest permanent secretary in the Federation. It was part of an experiment to try out the then new breed in the civil services as PermSecs. I had to look up to senior colleagues such as the late Chief Ani for guidance and leadership. We received their full co-operation. If the experiment succeeded, it was due partly to Chief Ani’s fatherly guidance and support.

“It is not generally known that Chief Ani retired prematurely from the Federal Civil Service in 1965 to accept the challenge of the late Prime Minister, Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, for him to be appointed the Chairman of the Federal Electoral Commission. I was one of those people he consulted and I advised against the move. But Chief Ani decided to accept the appointment for two reasons: first, as a good civil servant he felt obliged to respect the Prime Minister’s wishes and, second, he was anxious to demonstrate that Nigerian elections could be conducted fairly and justly without fear or favour. Before he could demonstrate this, the Military seized power on 15 January 1966 and Chief Ani suddenly became an unemployed pensioner at the tender age of 49 years, judging by the standard of those days!

“By an act of providence, when the Obasanjo administration was, in 1976, conducting the search for a suitable person to head the Federal Electoral Commission to supervise the elections for the return to civil rule in 1979, I was the Secretary to the Federal Military Government and Head of Service. When consulted, I advised that the man the Prime Minister appointed in December 1965 had never functioned and was untainted. But I told General Obasanjo that the late Chief, as a good civil servant, might not be sufficiently independent of the Government to be seen to conduct the elections fairly and that

the FMG might be seen to have a preference for one of the Presidential candidates. The General, to my surprise, replied, ‘That is the man we want.’

“When Chief Ani was approached, he came to my house to seek my opinion once again as a trusted friend. I told him candidly what transpired between General Obasanjo and me and once again, I advised him against the reappointment as Chairman of FEDECO but he still saw it as a challenge and an opportunity to establish that Nigerians could conduct an impartial and fair democratic election. The rest of the story is better left to the verdict of history but I believe the Chief did his best in the difficult circumstances of the countervailing powers and conflicting instructions on the 1979 elections. No wonder all the honours followed—New Nigerians Newspaper’s ‘Man of the Year 1977’ and ‘Commander of the Federal Republic’ (CFR) in 1978.”

However, the two major issues which FEDECO under Chief Michael Ani faced were the tax issue of the Presidential candidates of the five parties before the 1979 elections and the issue of 12 2/3 of nineteen states.

On April 21, 1979, under the heading “Zik and Aminu Out: ‘Tax papers not in order’”, THE NEW NIGERIA published that Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe, Presidential candidate of the Nigerian People’s Party (NPP), was completely out of the presidential race.

Also out was Alhaji Aminu Kano, Presidential candidate of the People’s Redemption Party (PRP).

This was because the Federal Electoral Commission (FEDECO) confirmed in Lagos that the two presidential candidates did not pay their taxes as they were due. The same paper had earlier carried exclusively a story with a banner, “Zik, Aminu Out of Race.”

In the story it was said that both Dr. Azikiwe and Alhaji Aminu were virtually out of the race because the Federal Military Government was reluctant to grant them security cover because of their tax positions.

This story generated a lot of interest and controversy. Both NPP and PRP issued statements claiming that the tax positions of their presidential candidates were in order. But at a Press conference on April 20, the Chairman of FEDECO, Chief Michael Ani, said that the Commission could not recommend “additional security coverage for Dr. Azikiwe and Aminu because of their tax position.” He said that the Commission still had to carry out formal clearance or disqualification exercises in connection with the forthcoming elections.

Dr. Azikiwe disputed the allegations made by FEDECO, which he described as “absolutely false and without foundation.” He threatened to sue newspapers which published Chief Ani’s statement. He said he would continue electioneering “and expose the clown hoof of our detractors.”

In his statement to the Press Conference, Chief Ani said that in the letters FEDECO had sent to the two Presidential candidates announcing that it felt unable to recommend them for additional security coverage, it was stated:

“This letter does not in any way imply that the Federal Electoral Commission has, as of now, disqualified you as a presidential candidate, or has even yet given consideration to such a course. But it will have the duty to take full account of the tax documents submitted by you when nomination papers are received.”

Chief Ani went on to say that none of the five candidates was known to have been found guilty by a commission of inquiry and so all that was needed was evidence of payment of income tax as it became due for each of the three fiscal years preceding the date of the election (i.e. for 1976/77, 1977/78 and 1978/79). The Commission could not recommend two of the candidates for additional security cover because:

“One of them, Alhaji Aminu Kano, submitted evidence of payment of poll or community tax (not income tax): N4.00 on a tax ticket purported to be issued on April 1, 1976 in respect of 1976/77; N5.00 on a tax ticket purported to be issued on January 31, 1979 in respect of 1978/79. Upon a very careful examination of the relevant books of tax tickets, it was clear that, the dates shown on the first two tax tickets notwithstanding, the tax for those two years was all paid during 1978/79 along with the tax that actually became due in that fiscal year. There is no evidence whatsoever of payment of income tax by this candidate.

“The other candidate, Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe, paid no income tax at all during 1976/77; he paid a part of his tax for 1976/77 during 1977/78 and the remainder during 1978/79; he paid the whole of his 1977/78 tax in three separate instalments not during the fiscal year but all during 1978/79, in addition, of course, to the tax due for that year. Nearly all the payments made during 1978/79 were after the Commission’s letter dated February 6, 1979 calling on the leaders of the political parties to arrange for the respective presidential candidates to submit particulars of their tax payments as agreed at the meeting on December 28, 1978.”

On April 26, 1979, Chief Obafemi Awolowo (6 March 1909 – 9 May 1987), leader and Presidential candidate of the UPN, paid a total of N373,563.70k as income tax for the years 1976/77, 1977/78 and 1978/79. His income for the three years totalled N753,031.00k.

These details were issued by the Unity Party in Lagos, in apparent response to Dr. Azikiwe’s call on the Federal Electoral Commission to “let the nation know how much tax Chief Awolowo, Alhaji Shagari and Alhaji Waziri paid in the last three years and when and how they paid it”.

The party said categorically that while it never wanted to dabble in a problem that was squarely between Dr. Azikiwe and the FEDECO authorities, the Owelle’s statement had necessitated its publishing its Presidential candidate’s tax details.

“Our leader and Presidential candidate, Chief Obafemi Awolowo, has never defaulted in the payment of his tax and he has always discharged his civic duties as a responsible Nigerian citizen.”

The photocopy of a Lagos State Government income tax clearance certificate, issued by the Inland Revenue Division of the Ministry of Finance, showed that Chief Awolowo paid a tax of N44,505.50k on an income of N199,811.00k for the year 1976/77. He paid N102,327.70k tax on an income of N177,884 in 1977/78.

For 1978/79, Chief Awolowo paid N226,730.50k on a total income of N375,326.00k. Chief Awolowo’s receipts bore numbers 6807A and 2533 for 1976/77; 53904 for 1977/78 and 5850B for 1978/79.

The UPN torch-bearer paid the above tax on his income as a legal practitioner. The tax clearance certificate, No. 19315, was signed by B.O. Fasunloro, the statement said.

However, in the end all five Presidential candidates were finally cleared to contest the election, which ended in a dispute over FEDECO’s ruling of 12 2/3 of the nineteen states to mean thirteen. The issue was finally settled by the Supreme Court, which endorsed Alhaji Usman Aliyu Shagari GCFR as the winner of the 1979 elections. After the Supreme Court verdict, Chief Ani felt frustrated. It was as if he was abandoned. I am not sure he wrote a book or memoirs on his frustration.

There is an urgent need for us to re-examine the report of Justice Uwais on electoral reforms. Till then we are trapped with whatever Professor Amupitan will offer us.

In the conduct of the coming elections, we expect Professor Amupitan to be fair and ensure that our votes will count. That is our expectation. If he is not fair, like his predecessors, we shall feel frustrated too and that will be a tragedy.

Our fate is in the hands of Professor Joash Ojo Amupitan. All eyes are on him. He has a golden opportunity to write his name in the annals of history.

•Eric Teniola, a former director at the Presidency wrote from Lagos.

By Steve Oko



UMUAHIA — Abia State Government has secured approval for ₦1.041 billion in intervention funding for small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs), in a move aimed at expanding businesses, stimulating job creation and improving access to affordable c
content:
…₦382.9m disbursed to 31 businesses

By Steve Oko

UMUAHIA — Abia State Government has secured approval for ₦1.041 billion in intervention funding for small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs), in a move aimed at expanding businesses, stimulating job creation and improving access to affordable credit.

Of the amount, ₦382.9 million has already been disbursed to 29 micro-enterprises and two small and medium-scale businesses, while another ₦206.7 million in approved applications is undergoing documentation ahead of disbursement.

The state government also announced a review of the remuneration of ad-hoc workers engaged by the Abia State Environmental Protection Agency (ASEPA), with the new payment structure taking effect from November 2026.

Commissioner for Information, Prince Okey Kanu, who disclosed the developments during the weekly briefing on the State Executive Council meeting at Government House, Umuahia, said the SME intervention was being implemented through the Bank of Industry (BOI).

Kanu, represented by the Special Adviser to the Governor on Media and Publicity, Mr Fredinald Ekeoma, said the initiative was part of Governor Alex Otti’s administration’s efforts to strengthen the state’s productive sector and create sustainable employment opportunities.

Providing further details, Commissioner for Industries and SMEs, Mazi Mike Akpara, said the outstanding approved facilities would be released once beneficiaries fulfilled the necessary conditions, including documentation and provision of guarantors and collateral, where applicable.

He stressed that access to the intervention was not restricted by political affiliation, insisting that any genuine business operating in Abia was eligible.

“Whether you belong to the Labour Party, PDP or APC, we are not concerned about that. Once you are doing business in Abia and can provide evidence of your business operations, you are eligible to benefit.

“SMEs are the engine of the economy, and this initiative is intended to encourage and strengthen them,” Akpara said.

He said interested businesses could access the programme through the Ministry of Industries and SMEs at the Nnamdi Azikiwe Secretariat, Umuahia, or the BOI office in Aba.

Akpara described the facility as a major relief for local entrepreneurs, given its relatively low interest rates of 8.5 per cent for overdrafts and 7.5 per cent for other facilities, with a three-year repayment period.

He contrasted the rates with commercial bank lending rates, which he said could rise to between 28 and 30 per cent, arguing that the intervention would ease the financing burden on businesses and improve their capacity to expand.

In another development, Kanu said the Ministry of Industries and SMEs had verified and documented more than 110 workshops and 120 shops at the Ohiya-Umuogo-Nsukwe Industrial Cluster.

He said the exercise aligned with Goal Eight of the Sustainable Development Goals, which focuses on inclusive economic growth, productive employment and decent work.

On the forthcoming AfrICANDO 2026 conference, the Information Commissioner announced that Governor Otti would formally declare the global event open on Tuesday, November 17, at the International Conference Centre, Umuahia.

He said the conference would attract local and international participants, offering opportunities for investment partnerships, trade expansion and business development across different sectors.

Kanu urged the media to give the event adequate coverage, noting that Abia was open to investors seeking viable business opportunities.

The Commissioner also dismissed any suggestion that ongoing political activities ahead of the 2027 general elections had slowed down governance in the state.

He said the machinery of government remained fully operational despite the distractions associated with electioneering, adding that preparations for the 2027 fiscal year were nearing completion.

“In this connection, we affirm that the Abia State 2027 Budget is almost ready for presentation to the Abia State House of Assembly,” he said.

title: Dry season farming: Shettima directs swift release of 3m fertiliser bags nationwide
description: ‎—Orders ONSA to monitor declared stocks ahead of distribution‎‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru‎‎ABUJA — THE Vice President Senator Kashim Shettima has directed relevant government agencies and stakeholders in the fertiliser industry to expedite arrangements for the production and release of over three milli
content:
‎—Orders ONSA to monitor declared stocks ahead of distribution
‎
‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru
‎
‎ABUJA — THE Vice President Senator Kashim Shettima has directed relevant government agencies and stakeholders in the fertiliser industry to expedite arrangements for the production and release of over three million bags of fertiliser to farmers across the country ahead of the forthcoming dry-season farming.
‎
‎The directive followed President Bola Tinubu’s approval of funding under the Renewed Hope Agricultural Stabilisation and Productivity Initiative, aimed at making fertiliser more affordable, boosting food production and reviving Nigeria’s fertiliser blending industry.
‎
‎The Vice President gave the directive on Monday at the Presidential Villa during a meeting with stakeholders in the fertiliser sector in Abuja, where the Fertiliser Producers and Suppliers Association of Nigeria (FEPSAN) disclosed that available raw materials could support the production of approximately three million bags of NPK fertiliser within the next few weeks.
‎
‎He also directed the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) to verify and track fertiliser stocks declared by stakeholders to ensure transparency, accountability and a hitch-free distribution exercise.
‎
‎He further urged the NSA’s office to ensure that farming communities in states facing security challenges are not neglected in the distribution programme, stressing the need for the intervention to reach farmers in vulnerable and hard-to-access areas.
‎
‎Speaking on the broader economic importance of the presidential intervention, the Vice President said revitalising Nigeria’s fertiliser industry would strengthen agricultural productivity while creating jobs and supporting rural livelihoods.
‎
‎”A strong fertilizer value chain supports hundreds of thousands of direct and indirect jobs. Revitalizing this sector is therefore important not only for agriculture but also for employment, rural livelihoods and economic activities across the country,” he stated.
‎
‎Senator Shettima expressed concern that many of the country’s fertiliser blending plants were operating below capacity despite the growing demand for affordable agricultural inputs.
‎
‎”Today, many of our fertilizer blending plants are operating below capacity at the same time the high cost of fertilizer continues to increase the cost of production for our farmers,” he observed.
‎
‎According to him, President Tinubu’s intervention is designed to address these challenges by stimulating domestic production, restoring jobs and making fertiliser available to farmers at affordable prices.
‎
‎”The government wants to support the rehabilitation and full utilization of our fertilizer blending capacity. We want the factories producing, we want workers back to work. We want transporters, warehouse, and agro-dealers to be engaged again,” he said.
‎
‎The Vice President emphasised that farmers remained the principal beneficiaries of the initiative, noting that the Federal Government would purchase fertiliser produced by Nigerian blending companies and make it available at affordable prices.
‎
‎”But ultimately the Nigerian farmer is at the centre of this initiative. Under the Renewed Hope Agricultural Stabilisation and Productivity Initiative, government intends to purchase fertilizers produced by Nigerian blenders and make it available to our farmers at affordable prices,” he added.
‎
‎Senator Shettima thanked industry operators and other stakeholders for their willingness to partner with the government, stressing that the success of the intervention would depend on timely production, effective coordination and efficient distribution.
‎
‎”Every stakeholder is expected to prepare accordingly in ensuring the success of the Presidential mandate to deliver fertilizer to farmers for the fast approaching dry-season farming,” he charged.
‎
‎Earlier, the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Senator Abubakar Atiku Bagudu, said President Tinubu’s directive was aimed at making agricultural inputs more affordable while strengthening domestic production and food security.
‎
‎He disclosed that stakeholders had identified approximately 496,000 metric tonnes of fertiliser-related stocks, describing the quantity as a reasonable starting point for implementing the programme.
‎
‎”From what has been presented, we have about 496,000 metric tonnes of stock, and it is a good, reasonable starting point,” the minister said.
‎
‎Bagudu assured that the government would work with relevant stakeholders to identify additional funding opportunities through existing programmes to sustain the intervention beyond the immediate presidential directive.
‎
‎”We will work with every other stakeholder to identify other government programmes that will have funding that can be used to support this initiative even beyond the duration of the President’s directive,” he stated.
‎
‎Also speaking, the President of FEPSAN, Alhaji Abubakar Sadiq Kassim, commended President Tinubu for personally intervening to revive the country’s fertiliser industry.
‎
‎”I want to thank the President for taking a personal interest in reviving the Nigerian fertiliser industry. We are extremely encouraged by this intervention because this is about food security, jobs, rural livelihoods and economic and social stability of our country,” he said.
‎
‎Kassim noted that Nigeria had already made substantial investments in fertiliser blending plants, warehouses, distribution infrastructure and agro-dealer networks, but many of these facilities were operating below their installed capacity.
‎
‎He explained that reviving the industry would not only increase fertiliser availability but also restore economic activities across production, transportation, storage and distribution networks.
‎
‎According to him, FEPSAN members had completed an assessment of available NPK fertiliser stocks, raw materials and the industry’s capacity to produce additional quantities within the implementation period.
‎
‎”Based on information received from our members, the raw materials currently available can support the production of about 148,000 metric tonnes of NPK 20-10-10 within the next few weeks as targeted. This will give about three million bags of fertiliser,” he disclosed.
‎
‎The FEPSAN president further revealed that members were holding approximately 29,000 metric tonnes of finished NPK fertiliser that could be immediately purchased and released for distribution.
‎
‎He expressed confidence that the industry had the capacity to make approximately 3.5 million bags of fertiliser available within the stipulated period, noting that existing stocks and blending facilities were spread across different parts of the country.
‎
‎Kassim added that the geographical distribution of the facilities would support faster delivery and reduce the logistical burden of reaching farmers.
‎
‎As part of the implementation framework, President Tinubu also approved the Bank of Agriculture (BOA) and the Bank of Industry (BOI) to serve as fund administrators and financial intermediaries for the initiative.
‎
‎In a related presentation, a representative of the Ministry of Finance Incorporated (MOFI) disclosed that the organisation had approximately 90,000 metric tonnes of materials on the ground, with additional goods in transit bringing the combined quantity to about 248,000 metric tonnes.

title: Wike to opposition: Stop creating chaos to blame Tinubu
description:
Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Mr Nyesom Wike, yesterday, accused opposition political parties of deliberately fomenting trouble to make it appear that President Bola Tinubu is responsible for political violence ahead of the 2027 elections.



Wike made the allegation during the ina
content:
Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Mr Nyesom Wike, yesterday, accused opposition political parties of deliberately fomenting trouble to make it appear that President Bola Tinubu is responsible for political violence ahead of the 2027 elections.


Wike made the allegation during the inauguration of the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council (APC-PCC) in the FCT at the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre in Abuja.


The minister, who expressed confidence in the APC’s chances in the upcoming elections, claimed that opposition parties knew they had already lost and were creating political tension to discredit the ruling party.


Wike said: “You have what it takes to win this election. The other parties know. Let me just tell you the simple truth. The other parties know they have lost the election.


“What are they doing now? What they are doing now is to foment crisis—foment problems to make it look as if it is the government; it is the presidential candidate of the APC party who is fomenting trouble.


“They (opposition) are the ones causing trouble. You (APC PCC) don’t need to cause trouble because you have already won the election.


“They (opposition parties) foment trouble and report as if they are not the ones that have created that problem. So, we must be on alert.”


Wike also told members of the Rainbow Coalition to make sure the African Democratic Congress, ADC, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, do not get 25 per cent of the votes in the FCT in the January 16, 2027 general elections.


He warned the members against assuming the contest was already won, saying the election was a chance for the APC to show its political strength in the territory.


On how to sell the president’s record, he said: “You don’t need to go and see a prophet. You don’t need to go and see any doctor or anybody to tell you what to do. It is obvious; it is factual. Look at what Mr President has done for the people of the FCT. These are the tools you need to campaign.”


Wike also dared opposition politicians to set projects built before 2023 beside those delivered since Tinubu took office, arguing that the work going on in the city centre and the satellite towns spoke for itself.
