title: Justice Lifu’s judgment, Atiku’s fate and the road to 2027
description:
By Tunde Rahman



Some judgments settle a dispute. Some judgments can reorder a nation’s politics. The judgment delivered on November 5, 2026, by Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, in Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025 – Nafiu Bala Gombe versus African Democratic Congress and Others –
content:
By Tunde Rahman

Some judgments settle a dispute. Some judgments can reorder a nation’s politics. The judgment delivered on November 5, 2026, by Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, in Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025 – Nafiu Bala Gombe versus African Democratic Congress and Others – belongs to the second category.

That judgment did not just decide who leads a party. It has placed former Vice President Atiku Abubakar’s presidential ambition and the future of the ADC in suspense, and perhaps created a crisis of perception for the 2027 general election.

What did the court actually decide? Let me state from the get-go that neither the All Progressives Congress nor President Bola Tinubu filed the case. A member of the ADC itself– Nafiu Bala Gombe, the former Deputy National Chairman (North-East), – filed it.

Gombe argued that after the former National Chairman, Ralph Nwosu, resigned, leadership should have devolved to him under the party’s constitution. Instead, he argued, a caretaker leadership led by former Senate President David Mark and former Osun Governor Rauf Aregbesola was imposed at the 99th National Executive Committee meeting on July 27, 2025, without a democratic election.

Justice Lifu agreed with him. Among other things, the judge held that David Mark’s emergence as National Chairman and Rauf Aregbesola’s emergence as National Secretary were unlawful. He also stated that Nafiu Bala Gombe’s purported resignation letter was fictitious. After comparing the signatures on the letter with Gombe’s sworn witness statements, the judge found material differences and held that the document could not be relied upon.

Justice Lifu then ordered that all actions, decisions, and steps taken by the David Mark-led National Working Committee from July 27, 2025, are null, void, and without effect, and that the Independent National Electoral Commission should not recognise the Mark-led leadership.

The legal anchor was Section 82 (3) of the Electoral Act 2022, which requires political parties to elect their officers democratically. According to Justice Lifu, neither a NEC resolution nor INEC’s administrative recognition could substitute for that statutory requirement.

This is how the judgment affects former Vice President Atiku Abubakar. Admittedly, Atiku was not a party to the suit, and his name, according to his lawyers, was not expressly mentioned in the operative orders after the Certified True Copy was finally released on Wednesday, November 11.

But this logic is consequential. If the leadership that conducted the ADC presidential primary was essentially invalid, then the primary it conducted is also called into question. That is why news media reports from the judgment concluded that the process that produced Atiku as the ADC presidential candidate for the January 16, 2027 election has been invalidated.

Expectedly, the ADC disagrees. Its lawyer, Kalu Kalu, SAN, argued on national television thus: “The judgment of Honourable Justice Peter Lifu does not in any way void the candidacy of Atiku Abubakar… No portion of that judgment voids the candidacy of Atiku Abubakar and other candidates of the party.”

That is now the central legal argument that will be tested at the Court of Appeal. The ADC filed its notice of appeal on November 6, alongside an application for stay of execution, and has urged INEC not to act until the appeal is determined.

INEC, for its part, has taken a cautious approach. Its National Commissioner, Mohammed Haruna, said the Commission would not act until it receives and studies the Certified True Copy. That delay – five days before the CTC was released – itself became a controversy, with ADC candidates protesting at the Federal High Court and petitioning the Chief Judge, Justice John Tsoho.

Two Conflicting Judgments, One Party

The crisis is also deepened by another fact: the ADC says it already had a judgment in its favour.

An earlier judgment by Justice Musa Liman of the same Federal High Court had, according to the party, affirmed the legitimacy of the Mark-led leadership. The ADC says it relied on that judgment.

The country now faces a familiar problem: two judgments from courts of coordinate jurisdiction, pointing in different directions, on the same party leadership tussle. Can a party or the electoral commission choose which of the two judgments to respect? Only the Court of Appeal – and ultimately the Supreme Court – can resolve which one stands.

This development is not new in Nigerian politics. From PDP to APC to Labour Party, internal leadership disputes have repeatedly been a deciding factor regarding who is on the ballot, not the voters, or who the voters actually voted for among warring candidates.

The law has apparently become the new primary election.

What does all of this mean on the road to the 2027 governorship election?

For President Bola Tinubu and the APC, the judgment is politically convenient, but it may also be legally delicate.

It removes – at least temporarily – APC’s most experienced challenger from the ballot. Atiku, contesting for the seventh and perhaps last time, was the anchor for some opposition figures who adopted the ADC as their platform. Without him, the coalition loses its centre of gravity.

That is why the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, through its spokesman Kola Ologbondiyan, has accused the APC of working towards a “coronation, not an election”, and seeking to ensure no strong opposition candidate stands against President Tinubu.

The APC rejects that charge. Its position is simple: the crisis is self-inflicted. The ADC broke its own constitution; a member went to court, and the court ruled.

President Tinubu and the APC cannot be blamed for a party’s internal failure to follow the Electoral Act.

Nonetheless, both parties’ narratives will dominate the campaign.

But a larger question goes beyond Atiku and President Tinubu, and is now being discussed in some circles: can a democracy be healthy if a court removes its main opposition rather than the ballot box?

Supporters of the judgment argue that the rule of law must apply to parties too. If a party does not elect its leaders democratically, it cannot claim to be democratic. Atiku and company failed to carry out sufficient due diligence in their quest to “privatise” another party. So, who should be blamed for that? Couldn’t they have formed their own new party?

For Atiku, though, there is something that seems just so poetic – or increasingly like the hand of Karma, in the conundrum he finds himself. It could indeed be described as a comeuppance of sorts for the former vice president who is busy moving from one court in Nigeria and the United States to another, seeking President Tinubu’s disqualification.

However, critics argue that the timing of the Justice Lifu judgment – barely two months to the election – and the consequential effect on all ADC candidates, from President to State Assembly, risks disenfranchising millions of voters who have already aligned with the party.

Rotimi Amaechi, Atiku’s running mate, warned that the judgment “could cause a civil war if not properly managed”. This statement seems unguarded and could be self-indicting even for the ADC, because the law is what it is: the law.

In the 2019 general elections, the Supreme Court ruled that Rivers APC had no candidate for the governorship and House of Assembly elections. The situation in Zamfara was even more dramatic. The APC had won every political contest in the state: governorship, the three Senatorial seats, the seven House of Representatives seats and the 24 seats in the State House of Assembly.

But when the matter got to the court, the Supreme Court thought otherwise. Even though the electorate had voted for the APC, the court ruled that since the party didn’t conduct primaries, it had no candidates in the election. The court awarded the victory to the PDP, which came second in the election. Yet, the heavens did not fall.

As it stands today, Atiku has three possible futures. One, victory at the Court of Appeal: if the Court of Appeal sets aside Justice Lifu’s judgment or grants a stay, Atiku returns to the ballot, and the ADC contest proceeds. The ADC and Atiku are banking on this scenario.

Two, a defeat at the Court of Appeal: if the judgment stands, Atiku would need a new platform – but with INEC’s timetable almost closed, defecting to another party and conducting a fresh primary would seem legally and logistically impossible.

Three, political settlement: Nigerian politics has a long history of out-of-court settlements in party crises. Nafiu Gombe could withdraw, or a fresh, court-supervised convention could be ordered. This is the least talked-about outcome.

None of these is certain. And that uncertainty is itself the story.

In the final analysis, in my view, Justice Lifu’s judgment is a test of two principles that must co-exist if our democracy is to have a firm root: party discipline and democratic competition.

The court was right to insist that parties must obey the Electoral Act. A party that cannot conduct a democratic election for its own chairman cannot be trusted to conduct a democratic election for Nigeria.

But the courts must also be mindful that judgments delivered on the eve of an election have consequences far beyond the parties in the suit. They affect voters and candidates, and carry a heavy burden of legitimacy for the outcome.

For Atiku, this is perhaps the most consequential legal battle of his long political career. For President Tinubu, who is the odds-on favourite to win a second term, the absence of a major political party on the ballot, especially of a major opposition figure like Atiku Abubakar, could cast unnecessary controversy on the outcome of the election.

*•Rahman, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Media and Special Duties, is a Fellow of the Nigerian Guild of Editors.

The post Justice Lifu’s judgment, Atiku’s fate and the road to 2027 appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: 2027: APC rallies deepening Nigerians’ anger, Kawu warns party leaders
description:
…Senator decries disconnect between northern masses and political elite, urges grassroots mobilisation



By Henry Umoru



ABUJA — Chairman of the Senate Committee on Petroleum (Downstream), Senator Kawu Sumaila Suleiman (APC, Kano South), has warned the leadership of the All Progressives Congress
content:
…Senator decries disconnect between northern masses and political elite, urges grassroots mobilisation

By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — Chairman of the Senate Committee on Petroleum (Downstream), Senator Kawu Sumaila Suleiman (APC, Kano South), has warned the leadership of the All Progressives Congress (APC) that displays of opulence, celebrations and merrymaking at presidential campaign rallies are deepening the pains and anger of Nigerians.

The senator, who is the APC senatorial candidate for the January 16, 2027 election, said there was a growing disconnect and misunderstanding between ordinary people in the North and the political elite.

In a statement addressed to party leaders and members on Monday, his second intervention on the matter, Suleiman called for a change in the party’s approach and strategy ahead of the 2027 general elections.

He urged the APC leadership and Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) to prioritise effective communication of President Bola Tinubu’s policies and ongoing reforms to Nigerians at the grassroots.

The lawmaker also called on the party to identify and empower credible individuals and stakeholders with genuine grassroots influence in their respective constituencies rather than relying on what he described as “Abuja politicians” and entitled individuals disconnected from the people.

In the statement titled, “A Clarion Call for Self-Reflection, Humility, and Grassroots Reconnection”, Suleiman said the party’s message was still not reaching ordinary Nigerians.

He said: “Following my earlier message, we must once again be completely honest with ourselves: our message is still not reaching the grassroots. We need to acknowledge and accept that there is a growing disconnect and misunderstanding between the common people in the North and the political elites. We must change our approach and strategy.

“There is an urgent need to effectively communicate our government’s policies and the ongoing reforms of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu directly to the grassroots.”

The senator warned that the celebratory atmosphere at campaign rallies was insensitive to the hardship and insecurity confronting many Nigerians, particularly in the North.

He urged party leaders to remember victims of terrorism, thousands of Nigerians displaced from their communities and those forced to flee across the border into the Niger Republic.

“The current displays of celebration, opulence, and pomp-dancing and merrymaking during presidential campaign rallies are only deepening the pains and anger of the citizens.

“We must remember the countless people currently trapped in the hands of terrorists, the thousands suffering in internally displaced persons (IDP) camps, and those who have been forced to flee across the border into the Niger Republic,” he said.

Suleiman called for deep reflection among APC leaders, reminding them of the responsibility entrusted to them by Tinubu.

“It is time for deep self-reflection. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has entrusted us with a sacred responsibility (Amana), and we must protect and honour it,” he said.

Acknowledging that his message might offend some party leaders, the senator said genuine loyalty required speaking honestly about issues affecting the party’s collective interest.

He also cautioned against sycophancy and selfish political ambitions, urging party members to place the country’s stability and the party’s success above personal interests.

Suleiman prayed for Tinubu’s continued success, victory for APC candidates in the forthcoming elections and lasting peace and security across Nigeria.

The post 2027: APC rallies deepening Nigerians’ anger, Kawu warns party leaders appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Why growing communities deserve fair electoral structure
description:
By Christopher Nwayalani



In a democracy, political representation should reflect the realities of the people. As a community expands in population, geography and economic importance, its electoral structures deserve periodic examination to ensure that the citizenry enjoys fair, equitable and mean
content:
By Christopher Nwayalani

In a democracy, political representation should reflect the realities of the people. As a community expands in population, geography and economic importance, its electoral structures deserve periodic examination to ensure that the citizenry enjoys fair, equitable and meaningful representation.

Where existing arrangements appear inadequate to reflect changing circumstances, the responsible response should be a lawful, evidence-based review.

This is the central issue behind the growing call for equitable political representation for Okpanam Kingdom, a rapidly developing community in Oshimili North Local Government Area of Delta State.

On Saturday, November 7, 2026, the people of Okpanam took a strategic and significant step in articulating this aspiration when traditional rulers, community leaders, political stakeholders, professionals, youths, women and members of the diaspora gathered at the Ugo Ani Palace Hall for the Okpanam Political Summit 2026.

Organised with the theme, “Equitable Political Representation for a Growing Okpanam: The Imperative of INEC Electoral Delineation and the Creation of Additional Wards,” the summit provided a platform for constructive engagement over the relationship between the community’s meteoric growth and expansion as well as its current electoral arrangement.

The gathering was more than a discussion about political boundaries. It was a call for responsible community advocacy, democratic fairness and a development process driven by credible evidence rather than sentiment.

A growing urban community

Okpanam has witnessed remarkable transformation over the last two decades and a half. Its growth is reflected in expanding residential estates, emerging neighbourhoods, economic and commercial activities and increasing population.

Areas such as Obodogba, Ogbeozoma, Amachai and Ogbogwugwu, alongside several new estates and residential layouts, illustrate the wholesome evolving character of the community. What was once largely regarded as a traditional settlement on the outskirts of Asaba has increasingly become part of the expanding urban landscape of the Delta State capital territory.

The transformation did not only bring opportunities, but also created new demands on infrastructure, public services, planning and democratic representation.

The fundamental question is whether the existing electoral arrangement adequately reflects the community’s present realities. For the people of Okpanam, this question deserves serious consideration by the relevant government authorities and agencies.

Political representation is not merely about occupying elective positions. It determines how effectively communities participate in decision-making, articulate their needs and engage with government and government institutions.

The figures behind the call for review

A major consideration at the summit was the electoral composition of Ward 9 in Oshimili North LGA, which comprises Okpanam and Ugbolu. Available 2023 voter registration figures indicate that Ward 9 had a total of 29,832 registered voters. Of this number, Okpanam accounted for 23,721, representing approximately 79.51 per cent, while Ugbolu accounted for 6,111, representing 20.49 per cent.

With the total registered electorate of Oshimili North standing at 103,657, Ward 9 represents approximately 28.78 per cent of the local government’s registered voters.

The increase in polling units within Ward 9, from 11 in 2019 to 38 in 2023, also presents an important development that deserves examination. Although this increase must be understood in the context of INEC’s polling-unit expansion and decongestion exercise, it reinforces the need to examine the distribution of electoral facilities alongside population, geography and other relevant factors.

These figures do not, by themselves, automatically establish an entitlement to additional wards. Rather, they provide a basis for a serious and objective assessment of whether the existing arrangement remains appropriate.

The responsibility for such an assessment rests with the relevant electoral authorities, guided by the law and reliable technical information.

Why INEC must listen

One of the principal resolutions of the Okpanam Political Summit is to formally approach INEC for an objective review of the existing electoral structure involving Okpanam and Ugbolu.

The intention is to seek consideration for additional electoral wards for Okpanam, justified by extant laws and established criteria. This is a legitimate democratic request. It is neither a demand for political favour nor an attempt to diminish the interest of Ugbolu or any neighbouring sister-community.

Indeed, the summit deliberately emphasised the need to preserve the historical, cultural and social relationship between Okpanam and Ugbolu. The two sister-communities have enjoyed close fraternity that should not be undermined by political discussions about electoral representation.

The issue must, therefore, be approached with maturity, mutual respect and a clear understanding that the quest for fairness by one community does not require hostility towards another.

INEC’s statutory responsibility is to ensure that electoral arrangements are consistent with constitutional provisions, electoral laws and relevant administrative considerations.

Okpanam’s request is that its present realities be examined objectively within that framework.

Electoral mapping: Building a case on facts

Perhaps, one of the most significant outcomes of the summit was the decision to strengthen the ongoing Okpanam Electoral Mapping Project and develop it into a comprehensive technical document.

The initiative involves research collaboration between Dr Christopher Chiedu Nwayalani, Researcher, Electoral Representation, Community Development and Public Policy Analyst, and Surveyor Bright Iruoghene Idike, Geotechnical Engineer, GIS and Data Analyst.

The proposed document will cover the community’s settlements, residential estates, polling units, geographical expansion and electoral history. It is intended to provide a reliable foundation for the proposed engagement with INEC.

This approach is important because electoral delineation should not be reduced to emotional arguments or political pressure. It requires credible data, professional mapping, geographical analysis and proper documentation.

A well-prepared technical submission will enable the community to present its concerns more effectively and allow the relevant authorities to evaluate them on their merits.

The objective is not to predetermine the outcome of INEC’s review, but to ensure that Okpanam’s case is properly documented and receives the attention it deserves.

Funding the advocacy: A collective responsibility

The summit also recognised that research, technical documentation and sustained engagement with public institutions require resources.

Consequently, it resolved to establish the Okpanam Electoral Delineation and Advocacy Fund.

The fund is intended to support research, professional services, technical documentation, stakeholder consultations, public enlightenment and official engagements with INEC and other relevant authorities.

The Okpanam Community Development Union is expected to provide the institutional framework for its management, while a fundraising and financial management committee will be constituted to coordinate contributions and ensure accountability.

The initiative is open to voluntary contributions from individuals, families, organisations, corporate bodies, friends of Okpanam and sons and daughters of the kingdom in the diaspora.

However, the success of this initiative will depend not only on the willingness of people to contribute but also on the transparency with which the resources are managed. Proper records, an approved dedicated account or payment channel, and regular financial reports must remain central to the process.

Community confidence is essential to the sustainability of any collective project.

The diaspora: A vital development partner

Okpanam’s development cannot be an exclusive responsibility of the residents. Across Nigeria and different parts of the world are sons and daughters of the kingdom, whose professional experience, financial capacity, networks and exposure can contribute significantly to the community’s progress.

The summit, therefore, called for stronger diaspora participation through professional contributions, financial support, virtual engagement and sustained collaboration with stakeholders at home.

The participation of community members through digital platforms and other communication channels demonstrates that physical distance need not be a barrier to involvement in community affairs.

The diaspora should see the electoral delineation initiative as an opportunity to contribute knowledge, expertise and resources to a legitimate community aspiration.

Beyond wards: The long-term vision for Okpanam

The summit also acknowledged the long-standing aspiration for Okpanam to attain local government area status.

However, it wisely recognised that the creation of a new local government area is a separate constitutional process involving distinct legal, administrative and political requirements.

It is, therefore, important not to confuse this long-term aspiration with the immediate objective of securing equitable electoral representation.

For now, the priority is to build a credible case for an objective review of the existing electoral arrangement and the consideration of additional wards where justified by law.

Clear priorities and a step-by-step approach will make the community’s advocacy more focused and productive.

Keeping the struggle non-partisan

Another important resolution of the summit was the insistence that the campaign must remain non-partisan.

The quest for equitable representation is a struggle by the entire Okpanam community and does not belong to any political party, individual or political interest group. Traditional institutions, OCDU, political leaders, youths, women, professionals, civil society stakeholders and the diaspora must work together in advancing the cause.

This is particularly important in a politically diverse community. Differences in political affiliation should not prevent people from supporting a common community-based development objective.

The advocacy must also recognise and respect the interest of neighbouring sister-communities and be firmly rooted in peaceful engagement, dialogue and the rule of law.

From resolution to action

The communiqué issued at the end of the summit provides a roadmap for the next phase of the initiative.

OCDU is expected to provide institutional leadership and support. The Technical/Planning Committee will continue the electoral mapping and research work, while a delegation will be constituted to engage INEC and other relevant authorities. The Advocacy Fund is also expected to become operational, with regular progress and financial reports presented to the community.

These are important steps, but resolutions alone cannot achieve the desired result. Their success will depend on consistent implementation, responsible leadership, transparency and the willingness of all stakeholders to work together.

The Okpanam Political Summit 2026 has, therefore, opened a new chapter in the community’s democratic engagement. It has moved the conversation from general expressions of concern towards a structured process supported by research, institutional collaboration and collective responsibility.

Ultimately, the demand is simple: a growing community deserves an electoral structure that fairly reflects its realities, subject always to the law and the established criteria for electoral delineation.

Okpanam is not asking for preferential treatment. It is asking for an objective hearing, a transparent assessment and a fair opportunity to have its democratic representation reviewed.

As the community pushes forward, unity must remain its greatest strength, facts its strongest argument, and peaceful, lawful engagement its guiding principle.

The journey has convincingly and confidently begun. The task now is to stoically sustain it with unity, facts, commitment, collective responsibility and determination.

•Dr Nwayalani is the Secretary, Technical/Planning Committee, Okpanam Political Summit 2026/National Publicity Secretary, Okpanam Community Development Union.

title: Don’t turn churches into campaign arena, Soludo cautions politicians
description:
By Vincent Ujumadu



Governor Charles Soludo of Anambra State, on Sunday, cautioned politicians against turning churches and other places of worship into a political arena, stating that sacred spaces must remain neutral grounds for people of all political persuasions.



Soludo made the remark duri
content:
By Vincent Ujumadu

Governor Charles Soludo of Anambra State, on Sunday, cautioned politicians against turning churches and other places of worship into a political arena, stating that sacred spaces must remain neutral grounds for people of all political persuasions.


Soludo made the remark during the 30th anniversary celebration of the Mountain of Holy Ghost Intervention and Deliverance Ministry founded by Prophet Chukwuemeka Ohanaemere, popularly known as Odumeje.


Addressing the congregation, the governor stressed the need for the men of God to clearly separate politics from worship.
According to Soludo, the place of worship should be a holy place where people of all political persuasion should come and worship God in peace.


“It should not be a place for politics. There is a venue for politics. If you want to worship God, you have to go to the house of God. We must separate the two things clearly,” Soludo said.


He recalled that six months before his election, he took a deliberate decision never to go to any church to cup a microphone to ask them to vote for him or to campaign.
“It was a deliberate decision. I worshipped in the government house chapel until the election day and afterwards,” the governor stated.
“We must never politicise the church. We must never politicise the place of worship. Politicians, keep off churches. Keep off places of worship. That’s a deliberate message, and it is my kind of consistency of character”, he further said.

title: Tinubu pardons 78 convoy attack suspects, police arrest 8 over Kwankwaso assault
description:
From Desmond Mgboh, Kano and Molly Kilete, Abuja
President Bola Tinubu has ordered the release of 78 suspects arrested over Friday’s attack on his motorcade in Abuja, granting them presidential clemency, while police in Kano have arrested eight suspects over a separate attack on the campaign convoy
content:
From Desmond Mgboh, Kano and Molly Kilete, Abuja

President Bola Tinubu has ordered the release of 78 suspects arrested over Friday’s attack on his motorcade in Abuja, granting them presidential clemency, while police in Kano have arrested eight suspects over a separate attack on the campaign convoy of Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) vice-presidential candidate, Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, and the party’s governorship candidate, Aminu Abdussalam Gwarzo.

The Abuja attack occurred on Friday, November 13, after Tinubu attended Jumu’ah prayers at a mosque in Garki District, while the Kano violence erupted on Sunday, November 15, during the NDC campaign team’s visit to Bichi Local Government Area.

The Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Police Command announced the presidential directive yesterday, saying the 78 suspects were undergoing release procedures. The Kano Police Command, on its part, confirmed that 13 vehicles were vandalised and five persons injured in the attack on the opposition campaign entourage.

FCT Police Public Relations Officer, Josephine Adeh, who announced the presidential intervention in a statement, said the suspects were arrested after some individuals attacked Tinubu’s departing motorcade with stones and other dangerous objects, damaging several vehicles and injuring some security operatives.

She explained that a joint security team, led by the police, responded to the incident, while subsequent intelligence-led raids in the area resulted in further arrests, bringing the total number of suspects apprehended to 78.

“Following the extension of presidential clemency to the individuals involved in the attack, the Presidency directed that the suspects arrested in connection with the incident be warned and released.

“In compliance with the directive, the Command wishes to inform the public that the suspects are currently undergoing the necessary release processes,” Adeh stated.

The police did not disclose whether any of the suspects had been formally charged before the presidential intervention or whether their release would be subject to conditions beyond the warning issued by the Presidency.

FCT Commissioner of Police, Ahmed Mohammed Sanusi, condemned the attack and directed Area Commanders, Divisional Police Officers and tactical units to intensify security operations across the territory as preparations for the January 16, 2027 presidential election gather momentum.

He also urged political parties and their supporters to shun violence, intimidation and inflammatory statements capable of threatening public peace.

In the separate Kano incident, police arrested eight suspects following Sunday’s attack on the campaign convoy of Kwankwaso and Gwarzo in Bichi Local Government Area.

The incident occurred as the NDC campaign team was returning from a political tour of Tofa, Rimin Gado, Kabo, Gwarzo, Shanono and Bagwai local government areas.

Spokesperson for the NDC governorship candidate, Ibrahim Garba Shuaibu, alleged that suspected opposition political thugs had blocked sections of the road leading into Bichi to prevent the party from holding a campaign rally in the town.

Shuaibu said the campaign team had received intelligence reports about the planned disruption while approaching Bichi but subsequently encountered hostile youths who began throwing stones at the convoy.

According to him, shortly after the entourage passed the local government secretariat, another group of youths, allegedly armed with dangerous weapons, emerged and attacked vehicles conveying party leaders and supporters.

He said several supporters sustained injuries, while a number of vehicles were damaged during the disturbance.

Shuaibu disclosed that he personally counted about seven vehicles with smashed windscreens at the scene, adding that Kwankwaso and Gwarzo escaped unhurt.

Confirming the incident, the Kano State Police Command said it received a report at about 4:45 p.m. on Sunday, November 15, concerning a violent clash within Bichi township, which resulted in injuries and the destruction of campaign materials and vehicles.

In a statement issued by its spokesperson, Abdullahi Kiyawa, the command disclosed that 13 vehicles were vandalised, while five persons sustained injuries and were taken to hospital for treatment.

The police also recovered one gariyo, two cutlasses, two hard sticks, a bottle of solution and a substance locally referred to as “Suck and Die”.

Kiyawa said the eight suspects had been transferred to the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID), Bompai, for further investigation and would be charged in court upon completion of the investigation if sufficient evidence was established against them.

The Kano Commissioner of Police condemned the violence and destruction of campaign materials, warning that attacks on political gatherings and other acts capable of breaching public peace would not be tolerated.

Although the NDC alleged that opposition political thugs carried out the Bichi attack, the police have yet to establish the political affiliations of those arrested or identify the individuals who allegedly organised the violence.

The post Tinubu pardons 78 convoy attack suspects, police arrest 8 over Kwankwaso assault appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Appeal Court declares war on corruption, manipulation of election petitions
description:
From Godwin Tsa, Abuja
Ahead of the 2027 general elections, the Court of Appeal has declared zero tolerance for corruption, manipulation of court records, backdating of processes and other fraudulent practices capable of undermining the credibility of election petition tribunals, warning that offici
content:
From Godwin Tsa, Abuja

Ahead of the 2027 general elections, the Court of Appeal has declared zero tolerance for corruption, manipulation of court records, backdating of processes and other fraudulent practices capable of undermining the credibility of election petition tribunals, warning that officials found compromising the administration of electoral justice would face severe sanctions.

President of the Court of Appeal, Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem, who issued the warning in Abuja yesterday, said the judiciary would not hesitate to deal with tribunal secretaries and registry officials who allow themselves to be compromised by politicians, litigants or their lawyers in the course of handling election petitions.

Speaking at the opening of a two-day capacity-building workshop for Election Petition Tribunal registry staff at the Body of Benchers, Dongban-Mensem cautioned that the approaching elections would place the judiciary under intense public scrutiny, making integrity, transparency and strict adherence to legal procedures indispensable.

The workshop, themed: “Modern Registry Practices for Effective Election Petition Tribunal Administration,” was organised to prepare tribunal officials for the challenges of managing election petitions arising from the presidential, National Assembly, governorship and state Houses of Assembly elections.

Dongban-Mensem warned participants against regarding their appointments as opportunities for personal enrichment, stressing that their conduct could either strengthen public confidence in the judiciary or undermine the credibility of the electoral dispute resolution process.

“Your integrity and that of the Tribunal and its members are in the public searchlight,” she declared, urging the officials not to allow themselves to be used “as weapons to truncate the process.”

She reminded them that the responsibility entrusted to tribunal secretaries and registry personnel went beyond routine administrative duties, as their actions could have far-reaching consequences for the determination of election petitions and the protection of democratic institutions.

The Court of Appeal president advised them to place professional integrity above financial inducements, noting that a good name was better than silver and gold.

She explained that Section 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, empowered her to constitute election petition tribunals across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, while Section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act 2026 required the tribunals to be constituted at least 30 days before an election and their registries opened seven days before polling.

Describing the registry as a vital organ of the tribunal system, Dongban-Mensem said its responsibilities included receiving petitions, serving court processes, issuing hearing notices, preparing proceedings and safeguarding judicial records.

She stressed that modern registry administration demanded efficient electronic filing, reliable case management systems, accurate documentation, proper archiving and prompt service of processes, particularly because election petitions were governed by strict constitutional and statutory timelines.

In a separate warning, Chief Registrar of the Court of Appeal, Umar Bangari, said tribunal officials who engaged in backdating of court documents, collusion with litigants, tampering with case files or unauthorised disclosure of confidential information would face severe consequences.

Bangari specifically warned against giving litigants or their counsel advance copies of court processes, manipulating filing dates to accommodate petitions submitted outside statutory deadlines and leaking draft rulings, panel deliberations or other privileged judicial information.

He identified integrity, strict adherence to timelines, proactive communication and professionalism as essential requirements for the effective administration of election petition tribunals.

“A single administrative lapse, delayed endorsement, or misplaced process can occasion a damaging miscarriage of justice,” he warned.

According to him, the credibility of election petition tribunals rests heavily on the conduct of their registry officials, whose handling of documents, processes and records could determine whether justice is properly administered.

He cautioned that any secretary found conniving with a political party, candidate or legal practitioner to manipulate tribunal proceedings would be sanctioned, adding that officials who demonstrated outstanding diligence and professionalism would be rewarded.

Bangari noted that the presidential and National Assembly elections were scheduled for January 16, 2027, while the governorship and state Houses of Assembly elections would take place on February 6, stressing that the judiciary must be adequately prepared for the petitions that could arise from the contests.

He said the spotlight of the entire nation would turn on the judiciary as candidates and political parties challenged election outcomes, making it imperative for tribunal officials to maintain the highest standards of professional conduct.

The chief registrar disclosed that the Chief Justice of Nigeria had, the previous week, inaugurated 375 judicial officers drawn from trial courts across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory to serve on election petition tribunals.

He explained that the workshop was a continuation of preparations for the tribunals, with seven sessions covering the Electoral Act, the Judicial Electoral Manual 2026, electronic case management, record-keeping and statutory deadlines for filing and serving court processes.

Also speaking, Acting Deputy Chief Registrar in charge of the Election Petition Tribunal Unit, Maitumbi D.A., disclosed that the Court of Appeal was strengthening its case management system to address recurring concerns over conflicting judgments by election petition tribunals.

She said a committee had reviewed the 2022 edition of the Judicial Electoral Manual and produced an updated 2026 edition, which would soon be made available to tribunal officials.

According to her, the Election Petition Tribunal Case Management System was being upgraded to ensure that tribunal decisions were scanned and uploaded to a central database, providing judicial officers with access to previous decisions for reference and guidance.

She explained that the initiative was intended to improve consistency in tribunal decisions, strengthen record management and enhance the efficiency of election petition adjudication.

Maitumbi also outlined a code of conduct requiring tribunal secretaries to submit regular reports to the Election Petition Tribunal Unit and provide weekly updates through the electronic reporting platform.

She warned that tribunal officials were prohibited from granting media interviews without express authorisation, soliciting gratification from lawyers, litigants or members of the public, or releasing official documents and confidential information without approval.

The warnings come as the judiciary intensifies administrative and judicial preparations for the 2027 general elections, with particular attention to the integrity of tribunal proceedings, compliance with statutory timelines and the proper handling of election petitions.

The post Appeal Court declares war on corruption, manipulation of election petitions appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: Sunbeth completes acquisition of controlling stake in Livestock Feeds Plc
description:
Sunbeth Treenuts and Sesame Limited, a subsidiary of Sunbeth Agro HoldCo, announces the completion of its acquisition of UAC of Nigeria Plc’s 73.29% shareholding in Livestock Feeds Plc, following approval from Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission.
The completion establishes Sunbeth as the ma
content:
Sunbeth Treenuts and Sesame Limited, a subsidiary of Sunbeth Agro HoldCo, announces the completion of its acquisition of UAC of Nigeria Plc’s 73.29% shareholding in Livestock Feeds Plc, following approval from Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission.

The completion establishes Sunbeth as the majority shareholder of Livestock Feeds Plc and marks the beginning of a new phase focused on preserving the company’s heritage, strengthening its operations and supporting its long-term growth.

Sunbeth’s immediate priority is to support business continuity, working closely with the Board, management and employees to strengthen operations and maintain dependable service to customers and partners.

Commenting on the completion, Peeyush Karnani, Chief Strategy Officer of Sunbeth Agro HoldCo, said: “Livestock Feeds is an established business with a proud heritage, trusted brands and longstanding relationships across Nigeria’s livestock industry. We recognise the responsibility that comes with becoming its majority shareholder.

“Our approach is to build on these foundations. Our immediate focus is continuity, operational stability and supporting the people and partnerships behind the business. We intend to combine Sunbeth’s strength in sourcing soya and other key feed ingredients with Livestock Feeds’ manufacturing expertise and established distribution network to improve supply reliability, strengthen competitiveness and create sustainable value for all shareholders.

“This acquisition also provides an important foundation for Sunbeth’s long-term strategy to build an integrated protein business spanning animal nutrition, poultry and cattle production, and meat processing. We will pursue this strategy through disciplined, phased investment, with a clear focus on strengthening Livestock Feeds and supporting the growth of Nigeria’s livestock industry.”

Sunbeth has also announced the appointment of five new directors to the Board of Livestock Feeds Plc, effective 17 November 2026.

The newly appointed directors are Mr Sam Okuwlehi, Mr Seyi Ebenezer, Professor Franklin Nnaemeka Ngwu, PhD, Mrs Mary Mulili, and Mr Farrukh Siddiqui. They will join three existing directors who will continue to serve on the Board: Mr Joseph I.D. Dada, Mr Adegboyega Adedeji, and Mr Abayomi Adeyemi.

Employees remain central to the company’s future. Sunbeth intends to work collaboratively with the Livestock Feeds team, drawing on its experience and knowledge as the business enters its next phase.

For customers, distributors and suppliers, the priority is to sustain trusted relationships, maintain product quality and strengthen supply reliability. Future improvements will be introduced through a structured and carefully managed process.

As majority shareholder, Sunbeth is committed to supporting sound governance, operational resilience and disciplined investment to build lasting value for Livestock Feeds Plc and all its shareholders.

The post Sunbeth completes acquisition of controlling stake in Livestock Feeds Plc appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

title: 6 opposition parties move to seal unity pact, explore joint presidential candidate
description:
• Coalition seeks common platform to challenge APC
From Ndubuisi Orji, Abuja
The African Democratic Congress (ADC), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Social Democratic Party (SDP), Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and Allied Peoples Movement (APM) have intensified move
content:
• Coalition seeks common platform to challenge APC

From Ndubuisi Orji, Abuja

The African Democratic Congress (ADC), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Social Democratic Party (SDP), Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and Allied Peoples Movement (APM) have intensified moves to forge a united front against the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) in the 2027 general election, with plans to sign a binding political pact on November 23 as discussions continue over the possibility of presenting a single presidential candidate.

The six parties are expected to endorse three documents aimed at strengthening opposition cooperation and establishing a common political agenda.

The agreement, to be signed at the Second Summit of Nigeria’s Opposition Political Parties in Abuja, will include the National Covenant for Democratic Renewal, Framework for Opposition Unity and National Reform Programme.

A statement by Salihu Lukman, on behalf of the Coalition for Democracy, said the summit would mark a new phase in efforts to build a formidable opposition capable of defending democratic institutions, restoring public confidence and offering Nigerians an alternative to the APC administration.

The initiative comes amid growing pressure on opposition leaders to close ranks ahead of the presidential election, with former Vice President Atiku Abubakar of the ADC, Peter Obi of the NDC, Seyi Makinde of the APM, Donald Duke of the PRP and Adewole Adebayo of the SDP among the major opposition presidential candidates.

The G-100, a group of opposition politicians advocating a single presidential candidate, had earlier convened a summit to explore the prospects of cooperation among the parties.

According to Lukman, the November 23 meeting will build on the First Summit of Opposition Leaders, organised by the G-100 in collaboration with the House of Representatives Minority Caucus at the Yar’Adua Centre, Abuja, on August 31, 2026.

He said working groups drawn from the participating parties had since developed the three documents to translate their shared political objectives into formal commitments.

“Since then, Working Groups drawn from the participating political parties have worked diligently to translate our shared convictions into three foundational documents: the National Covenant for Democratic Renewal, the Framework for Opposition Unity, and the National Reform Programme.

“On November 23, the parties will formally receive these documents, adopt them and append their signatures to them. What began as a shared recognition of the challenges confronting our democracy will become a collective commitment to addressing them,” the statement said.

The coalition maintained that the initiative was necessary to strengthen opposition parties and safeguard democratic competition, alleging that the ruling party was taking steps capable of undermining the independence of political organisations.

“The Summit comes at a defining moment for Nigeria’s democracy, when the gains of electoral transparency are increasingly under threat and the democratic space continues to narrow under the deliberate actions of the ruling party.

“Democracy cannot thrive where the ruling party seeks to determine not only the outcome of elections, but also the character and composition of the opposition. Nigeria needs a strong, independent and competitive opposition, not as a concession from those in power, but as a fundamental requirement of constitutional democracy,” it stated.

The coalition explained that previous attempts at opposition cooperation had often collapsed because they depended largely on personal agreements among political leaders rather than enduring institutional arrangements.

It said the proposed covenant would establish principles and commitments capable of sustaining cooperation beyond individual political interests and electoral calculations.

“In the past, opposition cooperation has too often rested on personal understandings that did not survive the political circumstances that brought them about. This time, we have chosen to build on a different foundation.

“Opposition parties are putting their commitments in writing, institutionalising our cooperation, and establishing principles that must outlive both the moment and the personalities.

“Our objective is not simply to unite against a ruling party. It is to unite around a vision of the country we want to build and the democratic principles by which we intend to govern,” the coalition stated.

It added that the participating parties would jointly sign the National Covenant for Democratic Renewal and Framework for Opposition Unity as a demonstration of their commitment to Nigerians.

Although the coalition is exploring the possibility of fielding a single presidential candidate, the statement did not indicate that the parties had reached an agreement on a joint ticket or the process for selecting a consensus candidate.

The November 23 summit is expected to provide further direction on the proposed opposition alliance as preparations intensify for the January 16, 2027 presidential election.

title: Obi defends record as Anambra gov, promises to transform Nigeria
description: Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has defended his eight-year record as governor of Anambra State, challenging Nigerians to scrutinise his achievements and insisting that the governance model he introduced could transform the country if replicated at the fed
content:
Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has defended his eight-year record as governor of Anambra State, challenging Nigerians to scrutinise his achievements and insisting that the governance model he introduced could transform the country if replicated at the federal level.

His defence comes amid renewed attacks on his leadership credentials by President Bola Tinubu, who recently accused him of failing to tackle the erosion crisis in Anambra while contrasting the former governor’s record with his own efforts to address coastal challenges in Lagos.

In a statement posted on his X account yesterday, Obi launched a series titled “Nigerians, Go and Verify,” detailing the policies, institutional reforms and development initiatives undertaken by his administration between 2006 and 2014.

He maintained that his record demonstrated what could be achieved through competent leadership, prudent management of public resources, effective planning and accountability.

The former governor said his administration inherited serious institutional and developmental challenges, including the absence of a coordinated framework for setting government priorities and allocating resources.

According to him, the situation informed the establishment of the Ministry of Economic Planning and the introduction of the Anambra Integrated Development Strategy (ANIDS), which provided a framework for interventions across critical sectors.

He explained that the strategy was aligned with the Millennium Development Goals and designed to address education, healthcare, poverty reduction, infrastructure, agriculture, environmental sustainability and institutional development.

Obi said his administration deliberately avoided concentrating resources on a single sector, arguing that sustainable development required simultaneous investment in essential public services and infrastructure.

He maintained that his government strengthened public institutions and introduced measures aimed at improving accountability and ensuring that government expenditure produced measurable benefits for residents.

“Our aim was to create a state where public resources produced tangible public benefits, institutions existed to serve the people and development was assessed by the lives transformed rather than by the promises made.”

He also recalled changing Anambra’s slogan from “Home for All” to “The Light of the Nation,” describing the decision as part of efforts to strengthen the state’s identity and restore confidence in government.

He said his administration was guided by four principles: character, competence, capacity and compassion, which he described as essential requirements for effective leadership.

The NDC candidate rejected suggestions that his achievements in Anambra were peculiar to the state or could not be reproduced nationally, insisting that the same principles could guide Nigeria’s development.

“I assure Nigerians that the progress demonstrated in Anambra State was neither a one-time occurrence nor an experiment that cannot be repeated.

“It reflected a proven model of governance that we are ready to extend to the national level. What we accomplished in Anambra can also be accomplished in Nigeria.

“With capable leadership, effective planning, responsible management and accountable institutions, Nigeria, too, can work for all its citizens,” he declared.

The latest defence follows Tinubu’s criticism of Obi during an All Progressives Congress (APC) rally in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, on November 6, where the President questioned his handling of erosion in Anambra.

“In Anambra State, he could not confront erosion. I, Bola Ahmed Tinubu, confronted the Atlantic Ocean,” Tinubu had said, while comparing their records as former state governors.

The President also questioned Obi’s leadership credentials and his ability to manage political challenges ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

Obi subsequently rejected the erosion allegation during a radio interview in Jos, Plateau State, maintaining that he worked with the Federal Government under former President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua to develop an intervention programme for Anambra.

He said he had approached Yar’Adua with proposals to address the erosion problem and that the former President directed the then Minister of Environment to work on the initiative.

The exchange has placed the respective governance records of Tinubu and Obi at the centre of their political disagreement ahead of the January 2027 presidential election.

Obi maintained that his administration’s policies and achievements were open to public scrutiny, insisting that his experience in Anambra provided the foundation for his proposed approach to national governance.

title: State police: Done deal as 36 assemblies endorse bill
description:
From  Adesuwa Tsanenyi, Abuja
Barely hours before the expiration of the National Assembly’s November 17 deadline, all 36 State Houses of Assembly have endorsed the constitutional amendment bill seeking to establish state police in Nigeria, bringing the country’s decades-long campaign to decentralise
content:
From Adesuwa Tsanenyi, Abuja

Barely hours before the expiration of the National Assembly’s November 17 deadline, all 36 State Houses of Assembly have endorsed the constitutional amendment bill seeking to establish state police in Nigeria, bringing the country’s decades-long campaign to decentralise its policing system closer to fruition.

The unanimous endorsement, announced yesterday, followed last-minute legislative consultations that saw Cross River and Niger states, earlier identified as the two outstanding states, join the other 34 assemblies in approving the proposed alteration to the 1999 Constitution.

The development represents a major milestone in the constitutional amendment process, which had already secured the mandatory approval of at least 24 state legislatures but was deliberately delayed by the National Assembly leadership to build a broader national consensus on the contentious issue of state policing.

It also comes amid growing concerns over insecurity across the country, with terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, communal violence and other violent crimes intensifying demands for a policing structure that would enable state governments to respond more effectively to security threats within their territories.

Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, who announced the development in Abuja yesterday, disclosed that his office had completed the verification of resolutions transmitted by the 36 State Houses of Assembly, confirming that the bill had secured 100 per cent endorsement, far exceeding the two-thirds requirement stipulated under Section 9(2) of the Constitution.

“The Clerk to the National Assembly wishes to announce that all the thirty-six (36) State Houses of Assembly have approved ‘A Bill for an Act to Alter the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 to Provide for the Establishment of State Police Services and for related Matters.

“This represents one hundred per cent endorsement by the State Houses of Assembly, which exceeds the threshold of twenty-four (24), provided under Section 9(2) of the Constitution (as amended),” he said.

The announcement came a day after Senate Leader, Opeyemi Bamidele, disclosed that 32 state assemblies had formally endorsed the proposal, while four others were expected to communicate their decisions before the National Assembly resumed plenary today.

Subsequent reports indicated that the number of approvals had risen to 34, leaving Cross River and Niger as the last two states yet to complete the process.

Bamidele had maintained that the National Assembly would proceed with the constitutional amendment process once the deadline elapsed, regardless of whether the outstanding states submitted their resolutions, since the bill had already met the constitutional threshold for approval.

However, Ogunlana’s announcement effectively removed the uncertainty surrounding the outstanding resolutions and gave the proposed amendment the backing of every state legislature in the federation.

The clerk explained that although the bill had earlier satisfied the constitutional and administrative requirements for transmission, the leadership of the National Assembly deliberately withheld the process to allow wider consultations and ensure that all states were carried along.

“It is important to note that the Bill had long satisfied all the constitutional and administrative requirements for transmission as prescribed by the Constitution and the Acts Authentication Act Cap. A2, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004, but the Leadership of the National Assembly directed a brief delay of transmission to allow for broader national consensus and engagement of all the States of the Federation.”

Ogunlana described the unanimous approval as an unprecedented demonstration of cooperation between the federal and state legislatures, as well as the executive arms of government at both levels, stressing that the achievement underscored the importance of consensus-building in constitutional reforms.

“The unanimous endorsement of the Bill is an unprecedented demonstration of synergy between the National Assembly and the State Houses of Assembly, as well as constructive cooperation between Executive Arms of government at both Federal and State levels.”

He added that the successful conclusion of the process would provide fresh momentum for other proposed alterations to the Constitution being pursued under the Sixth Constitution Alteration exercise.

“This achievement serves as a foundation for the National Assembly to complete and transmit the other Sixth Constitution Alteration Bills to the State Houses of Assembly for their consideration as soon as possible.”

The clerk commended the 36 state governors, Speakers and members of the State Houses of Assembly, as well as other stakeholders, for their cooperation and commitment to the constitutional amendment process.

The state police bill had earlier passed through the National Assembly before being transmitted to the state legislatures for concurrence, as required under the constitutional amendment procedure.

The Senate approved the proposal on June 24, 2026, while the House of Representatives followed on July 23, with the bill subsequently transmitted to the 36 state legislatures on September 16. Although the assemblies were initially expected to communicate their resolutions within 30 days, the consultation period was extended as the National Assembly sought to secure broader support for the reform.

By early November, the bill had already crossed the constitutional threshold of 24 states, with the number of approvals rising steadily until the final unanimous endorsement announced on Monday. The development marks a significant milestone in the campaign for state police, which has remained one of the most contentious issues in Nigeria’s constitutional and security reform discourse since the return to democratic rule in 1999.

Under the existing constitutional arrangement, policing is principally a federal responsibility, with Section 214 of the 1999 Constitution establishing the Nigeria Police Force and prohibiting the creation of another police force for the federation or any part of it, except as otherwise provided by the Constitution.

The centralised arrangement has long generated controversy, particularly because state governors, although commonly described as chief security officers of their states, exercise limited operational control over police formations deployed within their jurisdictions.

Successive governors have complained that the arrangement undermines their ability to respond promptly to security emergencies, especially in rural communities where police presence is inadequate and reinforcements often depend on decisions taken through federal command structures.

Advocates of state policing have consequently argued that Nigeria’s size, population, diversity and increasingly complex security challenges make a centrally controlled policing system insufficient to meet the country’s internal security needs.

They maintain that state police would strengthen intelligence gathering, improve community participation in crime prevention and enable law enforcement personnel familiar with local languages, geography and social conditions to respond more effectively to threats.

The agitation gathered greater momentum as insecurity spread across the country, with insurgency in the North-East, banditry and mass kidnappings in the North-West, farmer-herder conflicts in the North-Central region and violent attacks in several southern states exposing gaps in existing security arrangements.

The security challenges prompted some state governments to establish complementary security organisations, including the Western Nigeria Security Network, popularly known as Amotekun, and other state-backed vigilante and neighbourhood security outfits.

However, these organisations operate within legal limits that distinguish them from fully constituted police services, reinforcing demands for a constitutional framework that would give states clearly defined policing powers.

The clamour for state police has also featured prominently in successive national conferences, constitutional review exercises and debates over restructuring, devolution of powers and the proper operation of Nigeria’s federal system.

Despite growing support, the proposal has encountered sustained opposition from stakeholders concerned that state governors could deploy police formations under their control to intimidate political opponents, suppress dissent, manipulate elections or pursue partisan interests.

Others have questioned the financial capacity of some states to maintain professional police services, particularly where governments struggle to meet existing salary, pension and other recurrent obligations.

Concerns have also been raised over recruitment standards, training, funding, command structures, jurisdictional boundaries, disciplinary procedures and the relationship between federal and state police institutions.

These reservations have informed demands for strong constitutional safeguards, independent oversight mechanisms, transparent recruitment processes and clear provisions to prevent political interference in police operations.

President Bola Tinubu has previously expressed support for the establishment of state police as part of broader efforts to strengthen Nigeria’s internal security architecture and improve the protection of lives and property.

The Federal Government has also been working on complementary legislation intended to provide the institutional and operational framework for the proposed policing arrangement.

A Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, chaired by Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, had submitted a draft National Policing Bill, 2026, alongside consequential amendment proposals for further legislative consideration.

The proposed framework is expected to address critical issues relating to the powers, responsibilities, funding, supervision, accountability and coordination of federal and state police services.

With all 36 state legislatures now endorsing the constitutional amendment, attention has shifted to the National Assembly, which is expected to conclude the remaining legislative formalities and advance the bill towards completion.

The unanimous approval has given the proposed reform an unusually broad political consensus, reflecting growing recognition among federal and state authorities of the need to reconsider the country’s policing structure in the face of persistent security challenges.

For proponents of decentralised policing, the development represents the culmination of years of advocacy and constitutional debate over the distribution of security responsibilities in a federal system.

However, the ultimate test of the reform will lie in the safeguards established to prevent abuse, the capacity of states to fund and manage professional police institutions and the effectiveness of arrangements for cooperation between federal and state security agencies.

If successfully concluded and implemented, the constitutional amendment would fundamentally alter Nigeria’s policing architecture, ending the existing constitutional restriction on state-established police services and creating a new framework for shared responsibility in the maintenance of law and order.

title: Protests rock UniAbuja over FCTA land cuts
description: The University of Abuja land dispute escalated on Monday as five university unions staged a protest against the alleged reallocation of portions of the institution’s land by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, while the FCT Administration defended the decision, citing recomme
content:
The University of Abuja land dispute escalated on Monday as five university unions staged a protest against the alleged reallocation of portions of the institution’s land by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, while the FCT Administration defended the decision, citing recommendations by a committee set up in 2016.

The protesters, comprising academic and non-academic staff, students and alumni, urged President Bola Tinubu to intervene and reverse the land reduction, accusing the FCTA of disregarding the rule of law.

However, the administration maintained that Wike merely implemented a decision approved by his predecessor, former FCT Minister Mohammed Bello, following a review of the university’s landholding.

Earlier on Monday, the university community staged a protest, with members of the Academic Staff Union of Universities, Senior Staff Association of Nigerian Universities, Non-Academic Staff Union of Educational and Associated Institutions, Students’ Union Government and the university’s alumni association demanding an immediate reversal of the alleged land reallocation.

The unions accused the FCT minister of disregarding the rule of law by allegedly transferring portions of land allocated to the university to private individuals.

Speaking during the protest in Abuja, ASUU chairman, University of Abuja branch, Sylvanus Ugoh, said the land was allocated to the institution when it was established in 1988, insisting that it should not be taken away for private interests.

Ugoh described the alleged action as an attack on public education and called on the President to intervene by directing Wike to reverse the decision.

He said, “University is a public good; university is public interest. There is nowhere in the world where you take public interest for individual interest.

“We say no to the issue of the honourable minister taking the land that belongs to the university.”

The ASUU chairman warned that the dispute could undermine the Federal Government’s assurances that universities would not experience industrial action under the current administration.

According to him, the university community would not remain passive while land reserved for the development of future generations was allegedly transferred to private individuals.

“We cannot allow what is for unborn generations to be given to individuals. University development is for everyone,” he said.

Also speaking, SSANU branch chairman, Nurudeen Yusuf, said the unions would resist any attempt to take over the institution’s land, stressing that adequate land was critical to the growth of universities and their academic programmes.

Yusuf cited the university’s Departments of Nuclear Engineering and Aeronautical Engineering as examples of programmes requiring substantial space for research, practical training and other specialised activities.

He explained that nuclear engineering research, in particular, required buffer zones, arguing that the land was deliberately provided to accommodate the institution’s specialised academic and research needs.

The unions’ protest followed an earlier warning by the UniAbuja ASUU branch that it could embark on industrial action if the minister failed to rescind the alleged decision.

The union had also threatened legal action to prevent the disputed land from being taken over and reallocated.

The protesters urged the Federal Government to resolve the matter before it degenerated into a broader crisis capable of disrupting academic activities at the institution.

The PUNCH reports that the dispute dates back to June 2025, when Wike announced plans to reclaim about 7,000 hectares of land originally allocated to the university, reducing its landholding from 11,824 hectares to approximately 4,000 hectares.

The minister had accused the institution of occupying and fencing off extensive portions of land without adequate documentation, directing the FCT Administration to reallocate the reclaimed portion for other developments in the Giri District.

Defending the decision, the FCTA said the action was based on recommendations made by a joint committee established in 2016 by the administration of former FCT Minister Bello.

It said the committee, comprising representatives of the administration and the university, had recommended that the institution’s landholding of over 11,000 hectares be reduced to 100 hectares in line with the National Universities Commission’s recommended size for universities.

In a statement issued on Monday by the minister’s Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media, Lere Olayinka, the FCTA described the protest as misplaced, insisting that Wike merely implemented a decision taken by his predecessor.

According to the statement, the joint committee was inaugurated on November 10, 2016, to examine the university’s land size, encroachment by indigenous settlers, illegal developments around its Gwagwalada mini-campus and the issuance of title documents for the institution’s two campuses.

Olayinka disclosed that five of the committee’s 12 members were representatives of the university, namely Prof. Otaki Alanana, Prof. A. Mallam, Mohamed Kassim, A.E. Ripite and Sadiq O. Shuaibu.

He said the committee subsequently recommended that the university’s landholding of over 11,000 hectares was far beyond the size recommended by the NUC, adding that the 100-hectare recommendation was approved by Bello.

“It is on record that on November 10, 2016, the then FCT Minister inaugurated a Joint Committee of FCTA and UNIABUJA on Land and Sundry Issues.

“The committee was to look into the UNIABUJA land size vis-à-vis encroachment by indigenous settlers, encroachment on the Gwagwalada Mini Campus land by illegal developers and issuance of titles for the two campuses of the university with their actual land size.

“The committee recommended, amongst others, that the land area of over 11,000 hectares of the main campus was far beyond the recommended size by the National Universities Commission (NUC), and that the recommended size of 100 hectares by the NUC be given to the university.

“The report of the committee was approved by the immediate past FCT Minister, Mohammed Musa Bello, and going by the committee’s recommendation, only 100 hectares of land ought to be given to UNIABUJA,” the statement read.

Olayinka, however, said Wike approved 4,519.80 hectares for the university, rather than the 100 hectares recommended by the committee.

It added that the retained land could accommodate more than 80,000 buildings, using a plot size of 500 square metres.

The FCTA also accused the university of allocating portions of its land to individuals and corporate organisations without consulting the administration, citing the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission as one of the beneficiaries.

The statement questioned the rationale behind the university’s insistence on retaining more than 11,000 hectares, asking what significant expansion the institution had undertaken in its 38 years of existence to justify such a land requirement.

He asked: “Where in the civilised world is a university built on over 11,000 hectares of land, on which over 220,000 houses can be built at 500 square meters per plot?

“If the government that owns a university chooses to reduce the size of its land on which no structure has been built in the school’s 38 years of existence, what effect will that have on ASUU, SSANU and NASU? Will that affect the payment of their salaries? Will it affect the students in terms of their studies?”

The media aide urged the academic unions to be honest and clarify their interest in a land dispute between the administration and the management.

The controversy dates back to June 2025, when Wike announced that the administration had reclaimed about 7,000 hectares of land from the university, accusing the institution of laying claim to an extensive portion of government land without adequate documentation.

At the inauguration of access roads in Giri District, the minister directed relevant agencies to carve out about 4,000 hectares for the university, while the remaining portions would be made available for other developments.

Wike had argued that the university could not retain such an extensive landholding without developing it, particularly as the FCTA sought to open up the district for infrastructure and institutional development.

However, the university’s management and ASUU have maintained that the original land allocation was legitimate and necessary for the institution’s long-term development, including academic expansion, agricultural research and other infrastructure.

The university’s Pro-Chancellor, Olanrewaju Tejuoso, had also argued that much of the land left for the institution comprised rocky hills, raising questions about the actual amount of land available for development.

The dispute has also taken a legal dimension, with the university instituting Suit No. FCT/HC/CV/3500/2026 before the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory, Maitama.

In the suit, Justice F.E. Messiri, on August 18, 2026, reportedly ordered the parties to maintain the status quo ante bellum concerning Plot No. 1, Giri District, pending the determination of the substantive matter.

ASUU has subsequently accused the FCTA of violating the court order through alleged allocations of portions of the disputed land to private individuals and companies on September 26, 2026.

The post Protests rock UniAbuja over FCTA land cuts appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
