title: A’Ibom gov seeks 80,000 LG votes for Tinubu, APC
description:
Akwa Ibom State Governor, Umo Eno, has tasked voters in Mkpat Enin Local Government Area with delivering 80,000 votes for President Bola Tinubu and other All Progressives Congress candidates in the 2027 general elections.
Eno, who is seeking re-election on the APC platform, made the demand on Monday
content:
Akwa Ibom State Governor, Umo Eno, has tasked voters in Mkpat Enin Local Government Area with delivering 80,000 votes for President Bola Tinubu and other All Progressives Congress candidates in the 2027 general elections.

Eno, who is seeking re-election on the APC platform, made the demand on Monday at the kick-off of the party’s campaign tour of the local government, where he urged residents to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards and mobilise support for the party.

The governor’s vote target came alongside promises of fresh development projects, including the reconstruction of the abandoned Ikot Akata Technical College and Ukam Market, for which he said he had directed the constitution of an emergency implementation committee.

According to a statement issued by the Akwa Ibom APC Campaign Council’s Media Directorate on Monday, Eno said his administration had undertaken several infrastructure and empowerment projects in Mkpat Enin and would consolidate the interventions if returned to office.

He listed about 94 kilometres of roads, bridges, a model primary school at Ikot Ebak, a model primary healthcare centre at Ikot Ekpe, renovated and newly constructed classroom blocks, and a solar-powered water facility at Ukpom Minya among projects executed in the area.

The governor also cited the ARISE Youth Friendly Centre, which is nearing completion, 13 ARISE Compassionate Homes and empowerment programmes for farmers, traders and small business owners.

He said beneficiaries of the administration’s empowerment schemes included recipients of ₦5m grants, while 210 residents had benefited from the mega empowerment programme. Two minibuses and a car had also been distributed.

Eno further announced plans to distribute 50 bags of rice to every village in the local government for Christmas, amounting to more than 5,000 bags.

He urged residents to support Tinubu and APC candidates in the National Assembly elections scheduled for January 16 and the governorship and state House of Assembly elections on February 6.

The Deputy Governor, Akon Eyakenyi, described the state as united under Eno and urged the people to sustain their engagement with the administration.

The Coordinator of the Office of the First Lady, Helen Obareki, said the governor had fulfilled commitments to his late wife’s community.

Also, the wife of the Senate President, Ekaette-Unoama Akpabio, who represented her husband, Godswill Akpabio, urged voters to identify with the APC during the elections.

The Director-General of the campaign council, Assam Assam, said Mkpat Enin had an estimated 80,000 registered voters and called on them to support APC candidates at all levels.

The rally marked the beginning of the APC campaign council’s tour of the state’s 31 local government areas.

The post A’Ibom gov seeks 80,000 LG votes for Tinubu, APC appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: NDC loses Bauchi gov candidate, Kano executives to APC
description:
The Nigeria Democratic Congress governorship candidate in Bauchi State, Ibrahim Kashim, has dumped the party for the All Progressives Congress, ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Also, the vice-chairman of the NDC in Bichi Local Government Area of Kano State, Haladu Sa’adu, and five ward chairmen
content:
The Nigeria Democratic Congress governorship candidate in Bauchi State, Ibrahim Kashim, has dumped the party for the All Progressives Congress, ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Also, the vice-chairman of the NDC in Bichi Local Government Area of Kano State, Haladu Sa’adu, and five ward chairmen have defected to the APC.

The defections are coming also three months to the February 6, 2027 governorship election, with the list of candidates, including that of Kashim, already released by the Independent National Electoral Commission.

Kashim, a former Secretary to the State Government, announced his defection on Monday at a ceremony held at the Explaining his decision, the ex-SSG said he joined the APC because it offered Bauchi a stronger opportunity to participate in national governance and attract development.

He described the APC as the governing party at the federal level, with an overwhelming presence across Northern Nigeria, as well as the political structure and institutional capacity to advance the state’s interests.

Kashim said, “The APC is currently the governing party at the federal level and has an overwhelming presence across Northern Nigeria.

“It is also the party with the political structure, national reach and institutional capacity to provide a viable platform for the political and developmental aspirations we seek for Bauchi.

“I believe that Bauchi must be strategically positioned within this political reality.

“We cannot afford to gamble with the future of our state by placing our developmental aspirations on a platform that lacks comparable national reach and institutional influence.

“Our decision must be guided by the interests of Bauchi, not sentiment, political nostalgia or the convenience of individuals.”

The former SSG added, “The question is not simply which party can put forward a candidate. The question is which party has the organisational strength, national reach, political influence and institutional capacity to advance Bauchi’s interests. I am convinced that the APC offers the stronger platform.”

Kashim said his decision to leave the NDC followed his resignation from the party on October 16, 2026, adding that his commitment to the political struggle for a better Bauchi remained unchanged.

He appealed to his supporters, political associates and other stakeholders to join him in the APC, insisting that his political ambition was driven by the desire to improve governance and development in the state.

“Our ultimate objective is not the triumph of one political party over another. It is the triumph of good governance over poor governance, development over stagnation, opportunity over deprivation and hope over despair.

“I have chosen strategic engagement over political isolation. I have chosen a broader national platform over limited political reach.

“Above all, I have chosen what I sincerely believe offers Bauchi State a better opportunity for development and prosperity,” he said.

In Kano, the NDC vice-chairman in Bichi Local Government Area, Sa’adu, and five ward chairmen, including the party’s treasurer, Mannir Umar, ward secretaries, women and youth leaders and other members of the Kwankwasiyya movement, announced their decision to dump the party on Monday during a visit to the member representing Bichi Federal Constituency, Kabir Abubakar, at his office in Kano.

The PUNCH gathered that the five ward chairmen are from Waire, Danzabuwa, Kaukau, Muntsira and Bichi wards of the local government area.

Speaking on behalf of the defectors, the Danzabuwa Ward Chairman, Abdulkadir Lawan, said the lawmaker’s developmental projects and commitment to the people influenced their decision to join the APC.

“I want to inform you that we are all from Bichi, and we have decided to announce our defection from the NDC to the APC because we have recognised your dedication and the developmental projects you have executed in the Bichi Local Government,” Abdulkadir said.

He also commended the lawmaker for providing educational opportunities, saying he benefited from a scholarship programme facilitated by the Abubakar Kabir Foundation.

“I was previously a member of the opposition, but I benefited from your scholarship programme, which enabled me to pursue my master’s degree.

“Through your foundation, the Abubakar Kabir Foundation, I am now pursuing my PhD without any form of harassment or intimidation,” he said.

Abdulkadir also cited what he described as a lack of proper coordination and respect for members by the NDC leadership in Kano State, including issues surrounding the party’s leadership under Rabiu Kwankwaso, as reasons for their defection.

Speaking while receiving the defectors, the lawmaker welcomed them into the APC.

“I heartily welcome you all into the All Progressives Congress. Your decision to join us will further strengthen our grassroots structure in Bichi and the entire federal constituency,” he said.

He highlighted some of his interventions in Danzabuwa Ward, including the construction of a primary school, ongoing road projects and the provision of boreholes.

“We have continued to deliver projects that directly touch the lives of our people, and we will not relent. I urge you to work hard towards strengthening party unity and grassroots mobilisation ahead of the forthcoming elections,” Abubakar stated.

He also called for support for President Bola Tinubu, Governor Abba Yusuf and other APC candidates in the next elections.

“I urge all of you to continue to support President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf and all our candidates. Together, we will consolidate the gains of this administration,” he added.

The event was attended by the APC member representing Bichi Constituency in the Kano State House of Assembly, Lawan Bichi; the Director-General of the campaign council, Sani Bichi; the Vice-Chairman of Bichi Local Government, Babangida Danzabuwa; the APC State Secretary, Yusuf Sabo; and the Special Adviser on Publicity, Ahmad Aruwa, among other party leaders.

The post NDC loses Bauchi gov candidate, Kano executives to APC appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: A’Court vows sanctions for corrupt election tribunal
description:
The President of the Court of Appeal, Monica Dongban-Mensem, has warned secretaries and registry staff of election petition tribunals against accepting bribes or compromising judicial processes ahead of the 2027 general elections.
She warned that any staff found engaging in corrupt practices would b
content:
The President of the Court of Appeal, Monica Dongban-Mensem, has warned secretaries and registry staff of election petition tribunals against accepting bribes or compromising judicial processes ahead of the 2027 general elections.

She warned that any staff found engaging in corrupt practices would be sanctioned, stressing that the assignment was a call to national service and not an opportunity for personal enrichment.

Dongban-Mensem gave the warning on Monday at the opening of a two-day capacity-building workshop on the theme: “Modern Registry Practices for Effective Election Petition Tribunal Administration”, in Abuja.

The PCA said the exercise was designed to prepare tribunal staff for the administrative demands of handling electoral disputes, particularly as the presidential and National Assembly elections approach on January 16, 2027.

She described the registry as the engine room of every tribunal, noting that its efficiency, integrity and transparency were critical to the timely administration of electoral justice.

According to her, the responsibilities of registry staff include receiving and filing petitions, serving processes on parties, issuing hearing notices, preparing records of proceedings and orders, preserving tribunal documents and compiling records.

She said the performance of the registry directly affected the efficiency of tribunals and public confidence in the judicial process.

Citing Sections 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, Dongban-Mensem said the PCA was empowered to constitute election petition tribunals in every state of the federation and the Federal Capital Territory.

She also cited Section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act 2026, which provides that the tribunals must be constituted not later than 30 days before an election and open their registries for business not later than seven days before the poll.

The PCA stressed the need for confidentiality, professionalism and strict adherence to the timelines governing election petitions.

Dongban-Mensem charged the tribunal secretaries to familiarise themselves with the Electoral Act 2026 and the Election Petition Tribunal Proceedings Practice Direction 2026, warning that ignorance of the relevant provisions could expose them to manipulation and costly administrative errors.

“As tribunal secretaries, as prescribed by the Electoral Act 2026 and the Election Petition Tribunal Proceedings Practice Direction 2026, you must know the Practice Directions and have them at your fingertips. If you do not know them, you will be intimidated, you will be misled, and you will permit serious errors, and that will fetch serious consequences,” she said.

“There is no room for that now. You have been given a good chance to equip yourselves now, and we are giving you materials, so there will be no excuses. And we shall be constantly monitoring every aspect of your conduct,” she added.

Addressing the issue of integrity among tribunal staff, the PCA warned against allowing financial inducements to influence their conduct, saying their activities would be subjected to intense public scrutiny.

“Let me be clear that you must discharge your duties with utmost good faith and not be swayed by pecuniary inducements. Your conduct, and indeed that of the tribunal, will be under intense public scrutiny.

“You must not allow yourselves to be used as instruments to truncate the judicial process. You must live above board and protect the reputation of the judiciary,” she said.

Describing the assignment as an opportunity to serve the country, she said the court would not hesitate to sanction erring officials.

“This assignment is not an opportunity for self-enrichment, but a call to national service, which is also an opportunity to build a good name. It is said that a good name is better than silver and gold. We will not hesitate to sanction any staff found wanting,” she added.

She further urged the secretaries to ensure prompt service of processes and maintain regular communication with the Election Petition Tribunal Unit at the Court of Appeal headquarters.

She said the presiding justice of each tribunal was the immediate supervisor of its administrative staff and should be approached whenever they encountered difficulties.

The PCA described the participants’ selection as a demonstration of the confidence reposed in them by the court, urging them not to betray the trust.

Also speaking, the Chief Registrar of the Court of Appeal, Umar Bangari, said the integrity of Nigeria’s democratic process depended on the efficient, transparent and timely resolution of electoral disputes.

He recalled that the Chief Justice of Nigeria, Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, inaugurated 375 judicial officers from different jurisdictions across the country last week to serve on election petition tribunals ahead of the 2027 general elections.

He described Monday’s workshop as an administrative continuation of the training, designed to equip tribunal staff with the technical knowledge required for the assignment.

The Chief Registrar said the presidential and National Assembly elections would be held on January 16, 2027, while the governorship and state Houses of Assembly elections were scheduled for February 6, 2027.

He warned that the success of the tribunals rested significantly on registry staff, who were responsible for managing court processes, statutory timelines and administrative communication between the bench and litigants.

He identified integrity, timeliness, communication and professionalism as the key pillars of their assignment.

On corruption, the Chief Registrar warned that the court would not tolerate misconduct, compromise or dereliction of duty, noting that election petitions were high-stakes matters that could expose staff to financial inducements.

“Election petitions are high-stakes matters, and you will, inevitably, face pressure and temptations. I urge you to live strictly above board.

“Remember that your personal integrity, and of course, your career, and the institutional reputation of the court, as well as the Nigerian judiciary in general, are permanently in the public searchlight.

“Let me therefore reiterate the stern warning of the Honourable President that the court will show zero tolerance for any form of corruption, misconduct, compromise or dereliction of duty on your part, and advise that you take this warning very seriously,” he said.

The Chief Registrar further warned that the court would sanction staff found colluding with parties or lawyers, manipulating court processes, altering records for personal or political advantage, or leaking confidential internal communications.

However, he said the court had also resolved to reward secretaries and registry officials who demonstrated “outstanding commitment and diligence in the exercise of this assignment.”

He urged the participants to take advantage of the two-day workshop, which would cover the Electoral Act, the Judicial Electoral Manual, the 2026 Electoral Case Management System, record-keeping and compliance with filing and service deadlines.

Earlier, the acting Deputy Chief Registrar of the Election Petition Tribunal, Maitumbi Altine, disclosed that 655 staff and chief registrars were attending the workshop.

She said 223 of the participants had previously served in election petition tribunals, while 432 were first-timers.

Altine also disclosed that the Court of Appeal was working to update its Case Management System to “forestall the incidence of conflicting judgments which the tribunals had experienced in times past.”

She added that the court would upload judgments delivered by election petition tribunals since 1999 into the system to serve as judicial precedents on legal issues that might arise during the proceedings.

The Acting Deputy Chief Registrar also warned participants against granting interviews without express authorisation, cautioning them against any activity capable of undermining the neutrality of the tribunals and the Court of Appeal.

The post A’Court vows sanctions for corrupt election tribunal appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: FG pushes regional deal to prevent internet disruptions
description:
The Federal Government is seeking a regional agreement among West African countries to protect submarine telecommunications cables, coordinate repairs, and prevent prolonged internet disruptions that could affect businesses and digital services.
The proposed agreement would establish common procedur
content:
The Federal Government is seeking a regional agreement among West African countries to protect submarine telecommunications cables, coordinate repairs, and prevent prolonged internet disruptions that could affect businesses and digital services.

The proposed agreement would establish common procedures for rerouting internet traffic during cable failures, strengthen cross-border telecommunications infrastructure and reduce dependence on limited international connectivity routes.

The Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Bosun Tijani, advanced the proposal during engagements with member states of the International Telecommunication Union at its 2026 Plenipotentiary Conference in Doha, Qatar.

According to a statement issued by the ministry on Monday, Tijani “advocated for a shared regional protocol for digital infrastructure resilience, including mechanisms for rerouting network traffic and coordinating repairs when subsea cables fail.”

The ministry said the initiative formed part of Nigeria’s efforts to strengthen regional digital infrastructure and improve the reliability and affordability of internet services across West Africa.

It disclosed that Nigeria was collaborating with Chad, Burkina Faso and the Republic of Benin to improve cross-border connectivity, with plans to extend the cooperation to Cameroon.

Nigeria is also working with Togo on plans to establish a regional data park to expand access to computing capacity for researchers and businesses across West Africa.

The ministry said the initiatives would strengthen regional economic integration and reduce vulnerabilities arising from dependence on limited international telecommunications infrastructure.

It noted that submarine cables carry more than 99 per cent of international data traffic, making their protection essential to the functioning of the global digital economy.

Nigeria’s involvement in submarine cable protection gained prominence in 2024 when Tijani was appointed Co-Chair of the ITU International Advisory Body for Submarine Cable Resilience, established in partnership with the International Cable Protection Committee.

The country subsequently hosted the International Submarine Cable Resilience Summit in Abuja in February 2025, bringing together government officials, industry leaders and technical experts to address vulnerabilities affecting critical subsea infrastructure.

The advisory body’s work culminated in the adoption of recommendations in July 2026, following further international engagements, including a summit in Porto, Portugal.

The recommendations addressed cable protection, risk mitigation, infrastructure redundancy, timely deployment and repairs, and diversification of submarine cable routes.

Meanwhile, the ministry announced that Nigeria had secured re-election to the ITU Council for the 2027–2030 term.

Nigeria emerged among 13 African countries elected to the 48-member council, extending its participation in international telecommunications governance, which dates back to 1973.

The statement read, “The Federal Republic of Nigeria has secured re-election to the Council of the International Telecommunication Union for the 2027–2030 term, reaffirming the country’s growing influence in global telecommunications governance and its commitment to advancing inclusive digital development.

“The re-election was secured at the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference 2026 (PP-26), holding in Doha, Qatar, where Nigeria emerged among the 13 African countries elected to serve on the 48-member Council.

“The victory represents another important milestone in Nigeria’s longstanding engagement with the ITU and strengthens its voice in shaping international policies and decisions that will influence the future of global connectivity and digital development.”

Reacting to the development, Tijani said, “Nigeria’s re-election to the ITU Council is a strong affirmation of the confidence the international community has in our country’s leadership and contribution to the global digital agenda.”

He added, “Under the visionary leadership of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, we are positioning Nigeria to play an increasingly influential role in shaping the policies, partnerships and innovations that will define the future of telecommunications.”

“We will use this renewed mandate to advance meaningful connectivity, strengthen Africa’s voice and ensure that emerging technologies create opportunities for our people.”

The minister was elected Vice-Chair of the ITU Council in June 2025 and subsequently chaired its 2026 session in Geneva. During his chairmanship, the council considered emerging technologies, stakeholder engagement, sustainable funding arrangements and institutional reforms.

It also endorsed a revised draft strategic plan for consideration at the Doha conference and approved the union’s operational plan for 2027. Beyond telecommunications infrastructure, the ministry highlighted Nigeria’s participation in international efforts to strengthen child online protection.

It disclosed that Stella Chubiyo Erebor served as the African regional Vice-Chair of the ITU Council Working Group on Child Online Protection, contributing to discussions on online safety policies and regulatory practices.

The ministry linked these efforts to domestic initiatives, including the Nigerian Communications Commission’s establishment of a multi-stakeholder technical working group and the development of the Nigerian Child Online Protection Policy in 2014.

Tijani also called for inclusive access to artificial intelligence, arguing that people across different countries and communities should be able to develop technologies that reflect their languages and address local challenges.

The ministry credited the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, led by Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, and Nigerian diplomatic representatives in Qatar and Geneva with supporting the country’s re-election campaign.

Other participating institutions included the Nigerian Communications Commission, Nigerian Communications Satellite Limited, National Space Research and Development Agency, Defence Space Administration and National Emergency Management Agency.

The Federal Government said Nigeria would use its renewed ITU mandate to strengthen international cooperation on affordable connectivity, cybersecurity, digital skills, technology transfer and responsible innovation.

The post FG pushes regional deal to prevent internet disruptions appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: ’Public sector reforms need citizens’ trust’
description:
A former permanent secretary and Nigerian businesswoman, Dr Dere Awosika, has said public sector reforms must reflect the needs and realities of citizens to achieve their intended objectives.
Awosika said governments should consult affected communities and public servants before implementing reforms
content:
A former permanent secretary and Nigerian businesswoman, Dr Dere Awosika, has said public sector reforms must reflect the needs and realities of citizens to achieve their intended objectives.

Awosika said governments should consult affected communities and public servants before implementing reforms rather than impose policies without understanding the challenges they face.

She spoke recently on the Aig-Imoukhuede Foundation podcast, Reform Is Not a Guessing Game.

According to her, consultation would help reformers identify institutional weaknesses, understand stakeholders’ interests and develop implementation strategies suited to local realities.

“Reforms are not supposed to be a pass down of instructions. It’s supposed to be a discussion on the weaknesses, identify them, and see that the goals that you set to meet are not being met,” she said.

The Chief Executive Officer of Josephine Consulting Ltd said her experience leading polio eradication efforts in Nigeria demonstrated the importance of engaging communities in public programmes.

She explained that working with traditional and religious leaders helped address concerns and build acceptance of vaccination. “We need to build trust with the citizenry. They cannot believe us unless we trust them,” she said.

Also speaking, an economist and policy strategist, Dr Akin Olusoji-Akinyele, said governments must obtain feedback from beneficiaries throughout the reform process to determine whether policies were meeting their needs.

“The reform itself is not complete until the beneficiary has given you some form of feedback as to whether this is working,” he said.

The discussion was moderated by Ofovwe Aig-Imoukhuede, Executive Vice Chair of the Foundation, ahead of the launch of its Public Sector Reform Playbook in Abuja on November 19.

The post ’Public sector reforms need citizens’ trust’ appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Dangote, Sinotruk unveil electric truck
description:
Dangote Group, in partnership with Chinese commercial vehicle manufacturer Sinotruk, has unveiled what it described as Africa’s first locally assembled electric heavy-duty truck, marking a new phase in Nigeria’s commercial vehicle manufacturing industry.
The electric vehicle, equipped with a 600-kil
content:
Dangote Group, in partnership with Chinese commercial vehicle manufacturer Sinotruk, has unveiled what it described as Africa’s first locally assembled electric heavy-duty truck, marking a new phase in Nigeria’s commercial vehicle manufacturing industry.

The electric vehicle, equipped with a 600-kilowatt-hour large-capacity battery and a 375kW high-power motor, has a driving range of 350 kilometres, making it suitable for heavy-duty long-haul transportation.

The truck was built locally at the Dangote Sinotruk joint venture factory in Nigeria, according to the company.

Speaking at the unveiling in Lagos on Sunday, the Group Managing Director of Dangote Industries Limited, Devakumar Edwin, said the introduction of electric commercial vehicles was part of the company’s efforts to embrace emerging technologies and provide customers with more transportation options.

According to Edwin, the partnership between Dangote Group and Sinotruk was established to develop a world-class commercial vehicle business in Nigeria, strengthen local assembly capacity, create jobs and promote technology transfer.

“The whole objective of the JV was to establish a world-class commercial vehicle business in Nigeria and to bring the best of the technology from the world to Nigeria, strengthen the local assembly capabilities, create employment, and contribute to the economy and the development of the country,“ Edwin said.

He explained that the company had expanded its product range over the years to include heavy-duty trucks, tippers, light trucks, pickups and buses before venturing into compressed natural gas-powered vehicles and now electric vehicles.

According to him, the shift towards electric mobility reflects the company’s determination to keep pace with changes in the global automotive industry and adopt technologies that offer environmental and economic benefits.

“And as you know, globally today, the Chinese technology for electric vehicles is number one. They have overtaken Germany; they have overtaken the United States. So, we are bringing in the best of the technology, which will also be highly protective of the Nigerian environment,” Edwin noted.

He added that electric commercial vehicles could help operators reduce running costs and emissions, depending on the cost of electricity and the availability of charging infrastructure.

“The electric commercial vehicle offers the potential for lowering the operating cost and reducing the tailpipe emissions, and depending on their application, the electricity and the electricity cost in the charging infrastructure is going to be highly beneficial to the people,” he said.

Edwin, however, acknowledged that the successful adoption of electric vehicles would depend on the availability of reliable charging facilities, technical expertise, spare parts and after-sales support.

He disclosed that the company is preparing to provide the necessary technical and customer support to encourage the adoption of the new vehicles.

“We recognise that this successful adoption will also require reliable charging facilities, technical expertise, spare parts and strong after-sales support. So, we are already getting ready with strong after-sales support. We are setting up our team. We are also going to support in terms of charging facilities and other technical expertise, whatever is required,” he said.

The Dangote executive stated that the company planned to develop its automotive business into one of West Africa’s leading vehicle assembly and manufacturing operations, noting that Nigeria has the market size and industrial capacity to become a regional hub.

He said the partnership would also support the development of Nigerian technical personnel through training programmes, including opportunities for local workers to receive practical training in China.

Also speaking at the event, the President of Sinotruk Group, Liu Wei, described the unveiling as a significant milestone in the company’s 16-year partnership with Dangote Group and a step towards developing electric commercial vehicle manufacturing in Africa.

He mentioned that the electric heavy-duty truck was the first new-energy truck assembled on the continent, describing the development as a historic moment for Nigeria and West Africa.

“Most importantly, this is the very first new energy truck ever assembled on the African continent. This is truly a historic moment,” Liu said.

He emphasised that the partnership, which began in 2010, was formalised into a joint venture in 2014, leading to the establishment of local manufacturing operations.

According to him, the joint venture’s first heavy-duty truck rolled off the assembly line in 2017, while its commercial vehicle welding and e-coating paint line commenced operations in 2024, marking a transition from basic assembly to more extensive local manufacturing.

Wei disclosed that the partnership had assembled more than 8,000 vehicles locally over the past decade. He said Sinotruk would continue to invest in upgrading production lines, expanding its product range and training Nigerian engineers and technicians to strengthen the country’s automotive manufacturing capacity.

He added that the company planned to expand its product offerings to include heavy-duty trucks, light trucks, pickups, trailers and vehicle body-building. Wei said the partnership would remain aligned with Dangote Group’s industrialisation ambitions and its target of generating $100bn in revenue by 2030.

He added that the collaboration between the two companies demonstrates how Chinese and Nigerian businesses can work together to advance industrial development and support the transition to cleaner transportation technologies.

The post Dangote, Sinotruk unveil electric truck appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Obi, Kwankwaso have God’s grace to dislodge Tinubu — Babachir Lawal
description:
A chieftain of Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Babachir Lawal, has said Peter Obi, the party’s presidential candidate, and Rabiu Kwankwaso, his running mate, have God’s backing to defeat President Bola Tinubu in 2027.



Lawal, a former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, who made
content:
A chieftain of Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Babachir Lawal, has said Peter Obi, the party’s presidential candidate, and Rabiu Kwankwaso, his running mate, have God’s backing to defeat President Bola Tinubu in 2027.


Lawal, a former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, who made the declaration during an appearance on Arise Television late Sunday, cited the “widespread support” Obi and Kwankwaso enjoyed as a pointer to God’s grace upon their lives.
He said: “I have told everybody that talks to me that both Peter Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso have the grace of God upon their lives, which makes people like them.


“The population likes them. They just show up in the market. They don’t hire people to come to their rallies. People just turn out at their own expense.”


He said his experience in politics had enabled him to recognise signs that could favour the opposition alliance, adding that he previously occupied a similar position during the Muhammadu Buhari administration.


“It’s not the first time I am in the position I am in now in politics. I have been in this position during Buhari’s time. Even this your president, I drove his system up to the primaries.
“So I am a very skilled and experienced person in the game. I can see the signs and we know the loopholes. And we are working on the loopholes,’’ he said.
Lawal expressed confidence that the NDC would defeat the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC.
, saying the party had established structures and systems to achieve its objective.
“We have an inside chance of toppling this government. We are inside and we know we will beat this government.
“We know they are gone. We have put up structures and systems. I am 100 per cent confident,’’ he said.
Lawal added that the responsibility of the party’s technical team was to convert the popularity of its presidential candidates into electoral success by ensuring that votes were protected and counted.
“This grace that God has bestowed upon them, it’s our duty, the technical people, to harmonise and crystallise this thing into delivering it at the polling station and protecting the votes and ensuring it’s counted,” he said.
Lawal dismissed concerns over recent departure of Yunusa Tanko, former national coordinator of the Obidient Movement; Nana Kazaure, Doyin Okupe, and the former NDC’s deputy national publicity secretary, from Obi’s camp, saying politicians were free to leave parties when their expectations were not met.
He compared the development with the exit of some politicians from Tinubu’s inner circle, including Kashim Imam and Rauf Aregbesola.
“I was with Bola Tinubu, but I left. I can remember Kashim Imam; he has also left. I remember Rauf Aregbesola, who was also with Bola Tinubu. But he has left. These are big politicians. But they left Bola Tinubu.
“Leaving a political party is only natural. Nigeria is like a big company with many political parties. And people come in there with their own different ideas about what they can get out of it and what they can put into it,’’ the former SGF said.
He said while the majority of Nigerians joined politics to get something out of it, others participate to contribute to the system.
Lawal stated: “If you are the getting-out type and you go but don’t get anything, it’s only fair you move. That is life. You cannot be static.
“Moreover, the Obidient system is not about money. And people have families to feed, bills to pay. And if they join the Obidient Movement hoping to get the resources to settle these, they will be disappointed. So, it’s only fair. They have their reasons for leaving,”
Recounting his experience while serving as SGF, Lawal said some politicians tended to exaggerate their contributions to political campaigns.

The post Obi, Kwankwaso have God’s grace to dislodge Tinubu — Babachir Lawal appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: IBD urges African entrepreneurs to remove country boundary barriers
description:
Chairman of IBD Group, Ibrahim Egungbohun, has urged African entrepreneurs to look beyond national borders and build businesses that connect markets, boost regional trade and unlock the continent’s economic potential.
Egungbohun made the call following his recognition at the Nigeria Business Leaders
content:
Chairman of IBD Group, Ibrahim Egungbohun, has urged African entrepreneurs to look beyond national borders and build businesses that connect markets, boost regional trade and unlock the continent’s economic potential.

Egungbohun made the call following his recognition at the Nigeria Business Leadership Awards 2026, organised by BusinessDay Newspaper in acknowledgement of his entrepreneurial achievements and IBD Group’s contributions to enterprise development across multiple sectors.

The ceremony, held over the weekend, in Lagos, also marked the newspaper’s 25th anniversary with the theme, ‘25 Years of Shaping Impactful Decisions.’

Egungbohun was represented at the event by his wife, Mrs Omolara Egungbohun, Chief Executive Officer of IBD Hotels International, who led other senior officials of the IBD Group.

In his nomination letter, BusinessDay Publisher and Chief Executive Officer, Mr Frank Aigbogun, commended IBD Group’s transformation from an agriculture-focused business into a diversified enterprise with interests in logistics, construction materials, hospitality and energy.

Aigbogun noted that enterprise development went beyond setting up businesses to building operational capacity, developing markets, sustaining commercial activities and establishing institutions capable of outliving individual transactions.

In her remarks at the event, Mrs Egungbohun said Africa could only achieve its economic potential by connecting markets, strengthening commercial relationships and building businesses that operate beyond national boundaries.

Wife of the business Czar stated that, “Africa cannot unlock its full economic potential through isolated national markets. We must build enterprises that connect production, distribution, investment and trade across geographical boundaries.

“At IBD Group, we see agriculture, logistics, hospitality, construction materials and energy as interconnected parts of a wider economic ecosystem. Their integration creates value chains, facilitates trade, attracts investment and generates employment.

“Our ambition is to build businesses that contribute not only to national development but also to a more integrated African economy where entrepreneurs can compete, collaborate and create lasting value.”

She also dedicated the recognition to the group’s employees, management, partners and stakeholders, acknowledging their collective contributions to its growth.

The post IBD urges African entrepreneurs to remove country boundary barriers appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Energy firms struggle as unpaid debts threaten investments – NICA
description:
Nigeria’s oil, gas and wider energy sector is facing growing financial pressure as prolonged payment cycles, mounting receivables and poor credit management threaten investments, project execution and business operations, the National Institute of Credit Administration has warned.
The institute said
content:
Nigeria’s oil, gas and wider energy sector is facing growing financial pressure as prolonged payment cycles, mounting receivables and poor credit management threaten investments, project execution and business operations, the National Institute of Credit Administration has warned.

The institute said contractors, service providers, vendors and petroleum product marketers are struggling with delayed payments and increasing dependence on credit facilities, weakening liquidity across the energy value chain.

The Founding Registrar and Chief Executive Officer of NICA, Prof. Chris Onalo, raised the concern on Monday during a press conference with energy journalists in Lagos to unveil the objectives of the forthcoming National Credit Managers Conference 2026.

Onalo said Nigeria’s energy industry is not only battling infrastructure and production challenges but also a serious credit and receivables management crisis that requires urgent intervention.

He explained that contractors often finance their operations and waited for months to receive payments, while service providers and vendors operated under extended payment arrangements that sometimes lasted up to 180 days.

He added that petroleum product marketers depend heavily on credit facilities to finance product purchases and distribution, while gas off-takers rely on long-term commercial agreements that require all parties to meet their financial obligations.

According to him, unreliable credit relationships are affecting the entire industry, leading to delayed projects, constrained working capital, declining investor confidence and substantial receivables trapped in corporate balance sheets.

The NICA chief executive maintained that the inability of businesses to convert receivables into cash is weakening their capacity to sustain operations, meet contractual obligations and undertake new investments.

He stressed that Nigeria’s vast oil and gas reserves would not automatically translate into economic prosperity without adequate financing, investment, infrastructure and reliable commercial relationships.

“What is the value of oil in the ground if the credit required to develop, process, transport and commercialise it cannot flow?” he queried.

Onalo maintained that the country’s energy future would not be unlocked by megawatts alone but through the effective mobilisation of cash, credit and confidence.

He noted that the concerns informed the decision to dedicate a major session of the 2026 National Credit Managers Conference to the theme, ‘The Energy, Oil & Gas Credit Revolution: Unlocking the Cash, Credit and Confidence to Power Nigeria’s Energy Future’.

The conference, which is expected to bring together government officials, regulators, financial institutions, energy operators, investors and credit management professionals, will also examine the broader theme, ‘The Five Pillars of a Creditworthy Nation’.

Onalo stated that the event would provide a platform for developing practical solutions to financing and credit challenges confronting Nigeria’s productive sectors, particularly the energy industry.

The post Energy firms struggle as unpaid debts threaten investments – NICA appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: NLNG, NCDMB invest $9m in research at six varsities
description:
Nigeria LNG Limited and the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board have committed $9m to establish professorial chairs at six Nigerian universities to boost oil and gas research and innovation.
The event, which took place at the NLNG Corporate Headquarters in Port Harcourt on Tuesday, 10
content:
Nigeria LNG Limited and the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board have committed $9m to establish professorial chairs at six Nigerian universities to boost oil and gas research and innovation.

The event, which took place at the NLNG Corporate Headquarters in Port Harcourt on Tuesday, 10 November, 2026, was aimed at developing commercially viable solutions to industry challenges, strengthening local research capacity and advancing technological innovation.

Under the arrangement, each university would receive $1.5m to establish a specialised professorial chair focused on agreed industry research priorities.

In his keynote address titled ‘Reshaping Nigeria’s Future Through Innovation, Research and Capacity Development’, Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of NLNG, Engr. Adeleye Falade, described the programme as an investment in Nigeria’s capacity to translate academic knowledge into practical solutions.

Falade listed the beneficiary institutions and their focus areas as University of Ibadan: Natural Gas Processing, Pollution Control, and Environmental Management; Rivers State University: Digital Education, Intelligent Energy Systems, Automation, and Asset Integrity; Modibbo Adama University: Adamawa State, Energy Transition and Environment.

Others are Aliko Dangote University of Science and Technology (formerly Kano State University): Sustainable Energy Innovation and Climate-Resilient Food System; University of Nigeria, Nsukka, Enugu State: Green Energy Production and Geo-Environmental Engineering; and University of Abuja (now Yakubu Gowon University): Geoscience and Satellite Intelligence for Resilient Gas Infrastructures.

The institutions were selected across the country. NLNG’s General Manager, External Relations and Sustainable Development, Dr Sophia Horsfall, said: “As advised by NCDMB, we have ensured a pan-Nigerian approach by ensuring each geo-political zone of the federation is represented. NLNG will establish and endow professorial chairs in six universities across the zones, with each university bringing its own academic strength, experience and diversity just to enrich the programme.”

Falade explained that these universities will focus on their identified research areas based on earlier agreed critical research targets and commercialisation pathways to measure progress.

“They will also collectively host an information management hub for exchange programmes and knowledge sharing. Inclusive as part of the funding will be minor civil works and upgraded infrastructure to transform identified spaces into future-ready pieces of proposed research centres,” he stated.

Falade relished NLNG’s partnership with NCDMB, which birthed the initiative, describing the synergy as “very strong, and the foremost at this scale in Nigeria.”

The e-programme, he added, would support research into challenges central to the energy industry’s future, including improving operational efficiency, managing emissions, strengthening safety, maintaining critical infrastructure and making industrial processes more sustainable.

Beyond the research endowments, Falade outlined opportunities for a “triple helix” approach that brings government, which the NCDMB represents, the industry and academia together through specialised programmes, sabbaticals, exchange opportunities, practical testing of research assumptions and the joint development of postgraduate curricula.

According to the NLNG MD/CEO, continually reviewing how the initiative can translate research findings into practical industrial solutions will meet its objectives.

“What we’re looking forward to is to have people who come out from academia that will be able to solve today’s problem. They will be able to solve tomorrow’s problem, and academic institutions can continue to thrive on research, having people who are qualified but funded in partnership between NCDMB and NLNG.”

Falade stressed that research and development drive institutional progress, noting that organisations making significant breakthroughs invest heavily in research.

The Executive Secretary of the NCDMB, Engr. Felix Ogbe, represented by his Senior Technical Adviser, Engr. Austin Uzoka, shared Falade’s views, saying the $9m endowment programme represents a strategic investment in the future of Nigeria’s research and innovation ecosystem.

Ogbe added that these interventions demonstrate the Nigerian oil and gas industry’s commitment to creating an integrated research ecosystem that connects academic expertise, modern research infrastructure, industry requirements, and commercialisation opportunities.

By supporting specialised professorial chairs in critical areas of industry operations, he said NLNG and NCDMB are creating opportunities to bridge the longstanding gap between academic research and industrial application.

The NCDMB boss charged the institutions to “deliberately transition from research for publication to research for application, and from innovation as an academic pursuit to innovation as a driver of industrial transformation.”

“The beneficiary universities must see this endowment as both an opportunity and a responsibility, and they would be expected to deliver clearly defined research objectives, measurable outcomes, prudent resource utilisation, effective stakeholder engagement, and sustained collaboration with industry partners,” he added.

Responding, Vice-Chancellor of the Rivers State University, Prof. Isaac Zeb-Obipi, described the initiative as an investment in the intellectual sovereignty of Nigeria.

“For many years, we in the university have talked about industry-academia collaboration. Today, you have moved us from Memorandum of Understanding to Memorandum of Action.”

Meanwhile, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Abuja, Prof. Hakim Fawehinmi, said the area assigned to his institution helps protect Nigeria’s critical infrastructure such as gas pipelines.

The post NLNG, NCDMB invest $9m in research at six varsities appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Afreximbank loans to Dangote Group hit $18bn – Report
description:
The African Export-Import Bank has disclosed that it has disbursed more than $18bn to the Dangote Group since 2015, making it one of the conglomerate’s largest financiers and a major backer of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery in Lagos.
The financing covers different businesses within the Dangote Group
content:
The African Export-Import Bank has disclosed that it has disbursed more than $18bn to the Dangote Group since 2015, making it one of the conglomerate’s largest financiers and a major backer of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery in Lagos.

The financing covers different businesses within the Dangote Group, including support for the refinery’s construction, commencement of operations, crude oil procurement and debt refinancing.

According to documents obtained by The PUNCH from sources within Afreximbank, the institution has maintained a financing relationship with the conglomerate for more than a decade, providing funding across different stages of its industrial expansion.

One of the documents read, “Afreximbank is one of the largest providers of financing to the Dangote Group and has disbursed in excess of $18bn in the Group since 2015.”

The bank clarified that the $18bn represented financing disbursed to the entire Dangote Group rather than the petroleum refinery alone.

The documents showed that Afreximbank’s involvement in the refinery began during construction and subsequently expanded to working capital, crude oil procurement, financial advisory services and debt restructuring.

In 2018 and 2019, the bank provided $900m in construction financing, comprising a seven-year $650m term loan to Dangote Industries Limited and an additional $250m facility.

It subsequently extended other forms of financial support, including a $675m five-year corporate finance term loan to Dangote Cement Plc in 2024 and a $650m currency swap facility.

The document explained that the additional facilities were provided to support the wider conglomerate and accelerate the completion of the refinery.

Following the commencement of refining operations in February 2024, Afreximbank provided a $1bn working-capital facility to finance crude oil purchases, refined petroleum product offtake and operational continuity.

The bank also disclosed that it had issued letters of credit exceeding $6.8bn for crude oil procurement, demonstrating the substantial financing requirements associated with maintaining refinery operations.

The document read, “Following the commencement of refining operations, Afreximbank provided a $1bn working-capital facility to support crude-oil procurement, refined-product offtake and continuity of operations.”

Afreximbank also served as financial adviser on Nigeria’s naira-for-crude initiative, which was designed to facilitate crude oil purchases and refined petroleum product transactions in local currency.

The arrangement was intended to reduce dependence on foreign exchange in domestic petroleum transactions.

In March 2026, the bank further strengthened its financial involvement by underwriting $2.5bn of a $4bn five-year senior syndicated term loan for the refinery.

Afreximbank and Access Bank acted as co-mandated lead arrangers, with the continental trade finance institution accounting for the largest underwriting participation.

According to the documents, the refinancing arrangement was designed to consolidate existing obligations, improve the refinery’s capital structure and align its financing with operational requirements and expansion plans.

The bank explained that the transaction “consolidated existing financing, optimised the refinery’s capital structure and aligned its funding with its operational status and long-term growth plans.”

Beyond financing construction and operations, Afreximbank has developed trade finance arrangements to help African petroleum traders and buyers purchase refined products from the Dangote Refinery and other African producers.

The institution considers the refinery a strategic investment capable of reducing Africa’s dependence on imported petroleum products while promoting industrialisation and regional energy security.

The documents also disclosed that the refinery, originally designed to process 650,000 barrels of crude oil daily, had increased its operating capacity to approximately 700,000 barrels per day following operational improvements.

This expansion has strengthened its ability to supply Nigeria’s domestic market while exporting refined products to other countries.

Another document obtained from sources within the bank revealed that the refinery supplied more than 400,000 tonnes of aviation fuel to Europe in July 2026, representing approximately 20 per cent of the region’s jet fuel imports that month, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.

The shipments occurred amid disruptions to international petroleum supply routes associated with geopolitical tensions, particularly conflicts affecting Russia, Ukraine and the Middle East.

The bank noted that the refinery’s Atlantic location and ability to process predominantly Nigerian crude, alongside other Atlantic Basin supplies, provided an alternative source of refined products for international buyers.

It added that the refinery had helped Nigeria move beyond exporting crude oil and importing finished petroleum products towards domestic processing and exports of higher-value products.

The document explained, “The refinery has transformed Nigeria from a predominantly crude-exporting and refined-product-importing economy into a producer capable of exporting higher-value refined petroleum products.”

However, Afreximbank identified African markets as an important long-term commercial opportunity for the refinery, particularly countries that continue to import substantial quantities of petroleum products from Europe, Asia and the Middle East.

The post Afreximbank loans to Dangote Group hit $18bn – Report appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Weak data, uncollected royalties threaten Africa’s music boom — Experts
description: Weak metadata management, broken royalty collection infrastructure, and lopsided intellectual property agreements are preventing Africa’s booming music and creative industries from converting global cultural dominance into sustainable local wealth, industry executives and legal experts have warned.
content:
Weak metadata management, broken royalty collection infrastructure, and lopsided intellectual property agreements are preventing Africa’s booming music and creative industries from converting global cultural dominance into sustainable local wealth, industry executives and legal experts have warned.

Speaking at the Creative Africa Nexus Weekend, which concluded on 8 November at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Cultural and Creative Arts, Lagos, stakeholders noted that while African sounds continue to top international charts, systemic failures across the value chain leave creators and rights holders with a fraction of the revenues their works generate.

The scale of the revenue leakage was underscored by research presented at the summit by the Music Economy Development Initiative, which estimated that Nigeria and Kenya alone could collectively generate about $285m annually if copyright administration and royalty collection systems were strengthened.

Referencing the MEDI findings, Nigerian singer and founder of the CREAM Platform, Oladapo Oyebanjo, popularly known as D’Banj, captured the disconnect between international listenership and domestic financial returns.

“African music is a global business now, but the business still isn’t African enough,” he was quoted as saying.

At the CANEX IP Rights Summit’s roundtable on rights, royalties, and revenue, Executive Vice President of Chocolate City Music, Ibukun Abidoye, identified fragmented music data management as a primary bottleneck crippling revenue capture across the continent.

“While African music continues to attract substantial audiences, weak data infrastructure and gaps in collection management prevent the industry from fully realising its commercial potential,” Abidoye said, stressing that global visibility must be matched by coordinated, accountable systems capable of tracking usage and distributing royalties accurately.

Beyond collection infrastructure, Chief Executive Officer of Chocolate City Group, Abuchi Ugwu, warned that over-reliance on viral moments without underlying corporate structure leaves many emerging artists financially vulnerable.

Leading a masterclass at the CANEX Music Business Lab, Ugwu argued that talent alone cannot sustain a career unless songs are treated from inception as bankable intellectual property.

“Building a successful music career extends beyond producing a hit record; it requires creating the structures that allow artists, their teams, and the wider industry to benefit sustainably from the value of their work,” Ugwu stated, advising creators to properly document songwriting splits, understand master and publishing rights, and negotiate distribution deals from a position of leverage.

Legal blind spots in cross-border deals also came under scrutiny during a joint masterclass hosted by Chocolate City Group and commercial law firm, G. Elias, where experts examined how creators often sign away long-term value in pursuit of short-term visibility.

Vice President and Head of Businesses and Legal Affairs at Chocolate City Group, Ifeyinwa Anyadiegwu, cautioned creatives against entering brand partnerships, licensing deals, or film adaptations without scrutinising clauses governing exclusivity, territory, duration, and derivative works.

The post Weak data, uncollected royalties threaten Africa’s music boom — Experts appeared first on Punch Newspapers.

title: Africa needs own payment system to escape Western control – PAPSS CEO
description: In this interview with WALE AKINSELURE, the Chief Executive Officer of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, Mike Ogbalu, speaks on the platform’s expansion across Africa, efforts to boost intra-African trade through local currencies, reduce dependence on the dollar and make cross-border pa
content:
In this interview with WALE AKINSELURE, the Chief Executive Officer of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, Mike Ogbalu, speaks on the platform’s expansion across Africa, efforts to boost intra-African trade through local currencies, reduce dependence on the dollar and make cross-border payments faster and cheaper

PAPSS was launched in 2022 to facilitate cross-border payments across Africa. Four years on, how much progress has it made towards achieving this objective?

Over the past four years, we have built a payment network that spans 31 countries. We initially started in West Africa with six countries, but today, we have 31 countries across Africa. We are in partnership with 25 central banks, and we expect that number to grow to 26, while our countries of presence will increase to 39 before the end of the year. We currently have about 120 commercial banks connected to our network, and we have about 17 switches. Switches are technology banks that connect multiple banks within a market or across multiple markets.

In terms of our growth, we have recorded about 1,000 per cent growth in our transactions compared with last year, and clearly, we are now beginning to see a lot of this impact trickle down to our users. It is important to talk about the Nigerian market, where we have at least 95 per cent adoption by commercial banks. We are beginning to see many of them open up PAPSS within their digital channels and make it available to their consumers. We have also started engaging with many fintech companies, and some Nigerian fintech companies have begun integrating with PAPSS, enabling them to interact with all the countries where we are present.

What tangible benefits are users gaining from PAPSS?

PAPSS is an instant payment system. So, one of the things PAPSS does is save time. In the past, many payment systems could take two to five days for transactions to settle. But with PAPSS, settlement is instant. The transaction originates in one currency and terminates in another local currency in not more than 120 seconds. In fact, 120 seconds is the maximum; today, we are processing those transactions in an average of about seven seconds.

To put it in context, within those seven seconds, a transaction would have originated from the originating market – it may be through a mobile channel or across the counter in a bank branch – and would have gone through our system and all our compliance checks. It would pass through our anti-money laundering checks, fraud checks and other screenings before being delivered to the recipient’s account in the other market. The recipient would also have received an alert, with all these happening within seven seconds.

So, instead of spending three days making calls to confirm the alert, that extra time can be used by people to turn around their inventory and make more money from their businesses. They enjoy the benefit of the speed of the transaction.

Secondly, in terms of cost, PAPSS averages about 0.1 per cent of the transaction value in charges to users, compared with between three and five per cent charged through alternative payment channels, or even up to 10 per cent, as we see in intra-African remittances. This 0.1 per cent is PAPSS’s fee. Sometimes, commercial banks are designed to make money. So, we need to plead with them not to mark up the charges excessively so that some of those benefits can get to the consumers themselves.

We have seen significant progress. You can now have small shoemakers in Aba selling across Africa without worrying about how payments from those African countries will be settled into their accounts or wallets in Nigeria.

Why has PAPSS yet to connect all 54 African countries, particularly South Africa, one of the continent’s largest economies?

People sometimes look at PAPSS as a fintech company, but we are very far from that. A typical fintech company may start in one market, succeed in that market and then scale across other markets. We are carrying along many countries at the same time and trying to get all of them to scale.

The biggest challenge we have faced is standardisation. We are talking about 54 different countries with 54 different standards, payment systems and regulators. So, trying to harmonise all these countries into one coherent way of doing business across Africa is a challenge.

Secondly, there are issues of a few countries thinking that joining PAPSS means we will cannibalise some of their regional payment systems. For example, we tell them that if they like their regional payment system, they should keep it and use PAPSS for transactions that move from one region to another. So, the more we evangelise and show them that PAPSS does not cannibalise but only enhances the offerings of whatever payment system they have in place, the more acceptance we receive.

This year alone, we welcomed over 10 countries, and next year, we expect to welcome at least 10 more countries. So, the growth has been slow but steady.

But if you also look at some of the successes we have accomplished, this is the largest cross-border payment system within any of the regions. If you look at Europe, you are talking about 27 countries, but here, we are talking about 31. Some of these 31 countries are among the most complex to bring together because they do not have a single standard that cuts across all of them.

So, it has been a journey. The more voices speak about the benefits of integration, the more some of the challenges we have faced begin to disappear. Also, the more countries join, the more value they create for themselves and others. Some of these challenges existed in the past, but they are gradually disappearing, and I believe that, in no distant time, we will be able to have South Africa on board.

South Africa is the only major country that is not currently on PAPSS. All the other major countries have joined PAPSS, and I believe South Africa will join soon.

What proportion of Africa’s cross-border payment transactions currently goes through PAPSS?

We are still gathering our data, and we will make our PAPSS impact report available in the second quarter of next year. However, compared with last year, we have recorded growth of over 1,000 per cent in the transactions we have processed this year.

We expect that in the next five years, 80 per cent of all African countries will be transacting through our platform, and we expect to see 80 per cent of commercial payments on the continent routed through PAPSS.

Our focus in previous years was connecting as many African countries as possible, and I believe we have achieved significant success in that regard. Our next level of focus is driving adoption and usage, and that is what you will see in the next few years.

How close is PAPSS to achieving its goal of enabling African countries to trade in their local currencies without relying on the dollar?

We are already achieving that ambition. However, the success we are recording needs to be scaled up significantly.

For example, in a transaction between two countries, if one is sending $10bn worth of naira to Kenya and Kenya is sending about $11bn worth of Kenyan shillings to Nigeria, our system makes it possible for what would ordinarily have been a $21bn transaction to become just a $1bn transaction because only the net difference will be settled in a third-party currency.

Beyond that, 95 per cent of the value of those transactions is conducted in local currencies. So, what you are seeing is that Africa is beginning to reduce its dependence on foreign currencies. We are not chasing dollarisation because Africa still needs to trade with the rest of the world. But we are saying that when Africa trades with itself, let us use PAPSS to reduce the amount of foreign currencies required for trade among African countries.

We have modelled it such that you can actually reduce that requirement to as low as five per cent in some markets and 20 per cent in others. At 20 per cent, it represents significant progress towards strengthening African currencies. The 80 per cent you have saved represents 80 per cent more demand for African currencies compared with what we see today.

But we can scale it up so that there are multiple folds of the benefits we are recording today. In terms of benefits, all our member countries are beginning to see them; we just need to scale those benefits.

When a Nigerian exporter receives payment in Ghanaian cedis, how is the money converted into naira, and who determines the exchange rate?

Our system is pre-funded, so all our participants within the ecosystem provide some pre-funding to guarantee their transactions.

When transactions originate from Ghana, the exchange rate is supplied by the participant within that Ghanaian market, and our system supports multilateral settlement. You can set your rate for your market against one single currency. It also supports bilateral arrangements, in which you can set the rate from naira to cedis and from cedis to naira.

So, our system supports multiple rate settings. But, to be clear, the rate settings are guided by the central bank of each of the various markets and the commercial banks that are participants on our network. PAPSS, in itself, does not determine or set any country’s exchange rate. The participants on our system provide those rates.

So, once a transaction comes from one market onto our platform, it sees the rate that has been set from one currency to another, and the transaction is able to proceed. Some participants can also set their rates in a third-party currency, but the fact remains that only the net position will require foreign exchange to settle.

Can PAPSS reduce Africa’s dependence on the dollar despite the weakness and volatility of many African currencies?

Currencies operate according to the laws of demand and supply. So, the more people conduct a large part of their transactions in their local currencies, the greater the demand for those currencies, and we will begin to see local currencies strengthen against third-party global currencies.

PAPSS is keen on ensuring that, as more countries adopt the system, they significantly reduce their dependence on third-party global currencies and strengthen African currencies through increased utilisation of PAPSS.

How does PAPSS support the African Continental Free Trade Area in creating a single African market?

What you find is that the AfCFTA is a silver bullet for the continent. But it requires other silver bullets to succeed.

Everything around prosperity and human life is about creating value. The AfCFTA has done a fantastic job of bringing the rules for conducting trade together and harmonising them into a consistent set of rules for the continent.

The second critical component is that, before now, Africa’s payment system depended on third-party entities outside the continent for transactions to go through. The challenge with payment systems is that, as good as they are as tools of exchange, they are also instruments of control. A payment service provider can decide that your payment will not go through, and this is the instrument of Western sanctions across the world.

So, they can wake up, instruct certain people and say, ‘We do not want payments from this market to pass through to this other market.’

PAPSS is a critical instrument of the AfCFTA. I do not have any issue with people wanting to sanction a country, but essentially, let that decision be made by people sitting around the table on the continent, not by some people sitting somewhere around the world and making decisions that affect the economic destiny of Africans.

PAPSS is a critical pillar in enabling the AfCFTA, and the AfCFTA is one of the three promoters of PAPSS. The others are Afreximbank and the African Union Commission. This is why PAPSS enjoys the full endorsement of African heads of state.

How can small businesses and ordinary entrepreneurs benefit from PAPSS, beyond the involvement of central banks and governments?

We started with the regulators because we recognised that the payment system laws of each country across Africa give powers to the central banks of those countries. In the absence of a continent-wide payment framework, we got the central banks to sit in a room to draft a set of by-laws.

Essentially, each country joining is saying, ‘I agree to be bound by the provisions of these by-laws for transactions that relate to PAPSS.’

So, it was important for confidence, trust and regulatory oversight that we carried the central banks along and got them to be part of the creation of this system.

What the regulators have done is provide a covering. At the core, we built an instant payment system, and around that system, we created an anti-money laundering system, a sanctions screening system, a fraud management system and a dispute management mechanism. We then created governance organs. There is the PAPSS Governing Council, which has the power of regulation and oversight over PAPSS.

It is made up of 15 central bank governors and four other institutions, which are the representatives of Afreximbank, the African Development Bank, the AfCFTA and the African Union Commission. All these institutions provide oversight over PAPSS.

We have taken this technology and these governance organs and started connecting them with commercial banks through switches.

What this means is that an SME in Aba, Nigeria, who already has a wallet or an account with OPay or Moniepoint, or an account with a commercial bank, can initiate a payment to anybody in Africa without having to worry about all the things that come together in this ecosystem to ensure that the transaction goes through.

The SME can also receive payments from any part of Africa without knowing the intricacies of what happened or what was put together.

What PAPSS has done is take upon itself the headache of bringing all the participants together so that people can innovate and offer value to those SMEs.

For example, if you bank with First Bank, you can go to a UBA ATM and insert your card. You do not care about all the things that have been done behind the scenes to ensure that the ATM processes your transaction and gives you cash.

It is that same type of system we have put together so that payment service providers can now offer the service we have created to SMEs, enabling them to make and receive payments across Africa.

Once they are able to receive payments from across Africa, an SME that was previously selling to 200,000 or 220 million customers can suddenly sell to 1.4 billion people. That SME should also be able to increase its production capacity because it is producing for a larger market.

It is a value chain, and what we have done is take on the most difficult part, which is bringing together all the regulations and stakeholders, and now enable them to create value for SMEs to sell across the continent.

How can a small business owner access PAPSS, and what are the requirements?

You access it through your commercial bank or payment service providers. If my PSP has provided a wallet service, PAPSS has integrated with the PSP, and the PSP is able to extend that service to the SME.

If the person banks with Zenith Bank, the service is already embedded within the bank that the person is comfortable with.

PAPSS does not handle the last mile. PAPSS does not own those customers. We will not compete with the banks, but we expect that the banks will be able to take the value we have integrated into their systems and offer it as a service to those SMEs.

So, they access it through their existing commercial banks, PSPs or anybody that offers credit payment services in Nigeria.

Would the adoption of a single African currency strengthen or undermine PAPSS’s relevance?

It would make life easy for me if we had a single currency across the continent. But we also know that it is a long journey because anything that has to do with currency also has to do with the sovereignty of a country and control.

If you look at the euro, each country’s control over the currency has diminished significantly. It is something good to have, but whether the continent has the political will to make it happen is a different matter.

You need to have a set of criteria that must be met by all member countries, which has been very difficult.

I think the future will be technology-driven and that a single currency will emerge from available continental data rather than from the more traditional approaches adopted by countries.

I think the more we see data on our system showing the exchanges or payments from one country to another, the more we can establish the exchange relationships among African countries over time. This will make some of the challenges they face today gradually disappear because there will be enough data to support that.

The post Africa needs own payment system to escape Western control – PAPSS CEO appeared first on Punch Newspapers.
author: Wale Akinselure

title: Access Holdings records N129.5m insider share sale
description:
